title: STRUCTSURVEY: Structured Agentic Retrieval for Automated Survey Paper Generation
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, appendices, SurgeLLM, RAG4Reports, ACL
summary: The rapid growth of scientific publications makes it increasingly difficult to track and synthesize research progress. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can support automated survey generation, existing methods retrieve unstructured data and require models to infer conceptual, methodological, and taxonomic relations from raw text at generation time. We introduce STRUCTSURVEY, a hierarchical multi-agent framework that shifts structural reasoning from generation to retrieval by dynamically constructing graph-based representations of entities, relations, and topical taxonomies. We evaluate STRUCTSURVEY on a new reference-grounded benchmark of ACL survey papers for reproducible long-form scientific summarization. Compared with embedding-only retrieval baselines, STRUCTSURVEY improves ROUGE-1 recall by +2.9 and ROUGE-2 recall by +1.0 on average, without reducing precision. It also improves LLM-as-a-Judge ratings for logical structure, depth, and synthesis, showing that explicit structural retrieval yields surveys closer to human-written organization and reasoning.

AI.tldr: STRUCTSURVEY is a hierarchical multi-agent framework for automated literature survey generation that shifts structural reasoning from generation to retrieval by dynamically constructing graph-based representations of entities, relations, and topic taxonomies. It outperforms embedding-only retrieval baselines on ROUGE metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations.
AI.motivation: The explosion of scientific publications makes manual literature surveying increasingly untenable. Current LLM-based survey generation methods retrieve unstructured data and rely on the model to infer conceptual, methodological, and taxonomic relations at generation time, which is inefficient and produces poorly organized surveys.
AI.method: STRUCTSURVEY is a hierarchical multi-agent framework that pre-computes structural knowledge during retrieval rather than at generation time. It dynamically constructs graph-based representations capturing entities, relations, and topical taxonomies from the literature. The system is evaluated on a new reference-grounded benchmark of ACL survey papers for reproducible long-form scientific summarization.
AI.result: Compared to embedding-only retrieval baselines, STRUCTSURVEY improves ROUGE-1 recall by +2.9 and ROUGE-2 recall by +1.0 on average without reducing precision. It also achieves higher LLM-as-a-Judge ratings for logical structure, depth, and synthesis.
AI.conclusion: Explicit structural retrieval — organizing entities, relations, and taxonomies into graph structures — yields surveys that more closely match human-written organization and reasoning, demonstrating the value of shifting structural reasoning into the retrieval phase rather than deferring it to generation.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation to Support Railways Engineering Tasks: A Case Study
summary: The growing number and complexity of technical regulations represent an important challenge for all professionals in regulated industries. This paper describes a case study, from design to deployment, of building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system for the consultation of complex technical regulations in the railway domain. Although developed for the railway sector, this testimony of an industrial experience is of particular value for technical domains where regulatory compliance and accurate information retrieval from complex documentation are essential requirements. It also constitutes a human-centered approach for implementing LLM-powered technical documentation consultation across various regulated industries, balancing technological capabilities with domain expertise.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an industrial case study on designing and deploying a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system for consulting complex railway technical regulations, offering a human-centered blueprint applicable across regulated industries.
AI.motivation: The growing volume and complexity of technical regulations pose a significant challenge for professionals in regulated industries, who need efficient, accurate access to dense regulatory documentation. Existing consultation methods are insufficient for handling this complexity at scale.
AI.method: The authors document a full lifecycle case study — from design through deployment — of building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system. The approach is human-centered, integrating LLM capabilities with domain expertise to enable accurate retrieval and consultation of complex railway technical regulations.
AI.result: The deployed RAG system successfully enables consultation of complex railway regulations, demonstrating that a human-centered implementation can balance technological capabilities (LLM-powered retrieval and generation) with the precision demanded by domain experts in regulated industries.
AI.conclusion: The case study provides a transferable, human-centered methodology for implementing LLM-powered technical documentation consultation systems in regulated industries, where regulatory compliance and retrieval accuracy are critical. The railway-sector experience offers valuable lessons for other technical domains facing similar challenges.

title: Bi-NAS: Towards Effective and Personalized Explanation for Recommender Systems via Bi-Level Neural Architecture Search
summary: Recommender systems are vital in helping users navigate vast amounts of information, offering personalized suggestions and effective explanations for these recommendations. While previous efforts have attempted to provide such explanations, evaluating their effectiveness across various scenarios remains a challenge. Enhancing these explanations is essential for improving user engagement, trust, and decision-making. To facilitate effective explanations within the recommender system, we propose a Bi-level Neural Architecture Search (Bi-NAS) framework to optimize explanations. This approach simultaneously refines cross-attention mechanisms and feature interaction functions by exploring both intra-layer and inter-layer design spaces. Furthermore, we integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance explanation generation, leveraging zero-shot prompting to produce more effective and personalized justifications. By aligning user feature preferences with item quality scores, our approach ensures that explanations reflect both user intent and item attributes, improving transparency and reasoning depth. Extensive evaluations on four real-world datasets demonstrate that Bi-NAS not only boosts recommendation accuracy but also significantly improves the effectiveness of explanations for recommender systems, providing users with clear and reliable insights into the suggestions they receive.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Bi-NAS, a bi-level neural architecture search framework that jointly optimizes cross-attention mechanisms and feature interaction functions, augmented with LLM-generated explanations via zero-shot prompting, to improve both recommendation accuracy and explanation quality.
AI.motivation: Existing recommender systems struggle to evaluate explanation effectiveness across diverse scenarios, limiting user engagement, trust, and decision-making. There is a need for a principled framework that can automatically discover optimal architectures for generating transparent, personalized, and effective explanations.
AI.method: Bi-NAS employs a bi-level neural architecture search over both intra-layer (cross-attention mechanisms) and inter-layer (feature interaction functions) design spaces. LLMs are integrated via zero-shot prompting to generate personalized justifications. User feature preferences are aligned with item quality scores so that explanations reflect both user intent and item attributes.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on four real-world datasets show that Bi-NAS improves both recommendation accuracy and explanation effectiveness, delivering clear and reliable justifications.
AI.conclusion: Bi-NAS successfully bridges automated architecture optimization with LLM-driven explanation generation, offering a scalable solution for building transparent and trustworthy recommender systems.

title: Cache Merging as a Convergent Replicated State for Multi-Agent Latent Reasoning
summary: Multi-agent latent reasoning composes agents' KV-caches into one context for a final agent. Prior work (Agent Primitives) does this by concatenating caches along the sequence axis with RoPE re-encoding, which we call BagMerge. BagMerge is non-commutative, and the best input ordering is unpredictable, shifting with the regime, the latent-step budget, and the model scale. We make this exchange a convergent replicated state. First, CanonicalMerge fixes the layout by content: ordering caches by mean K-norm at a middle layer renders the merged cache byte-identical under any input permutation, verified algorithmically (arity N<=5) and bit-for-bit on real Qwen3-1.7B and 4B state. Second, we separate the replicated state from decode-time layout: the state is a set of content-addressed latent fragments whose merge is set union, a state-based CvRDT (commutative, associative, idempotent, absorbing), and CanonicalMerge is its deterministic render. Because the render is byte-equivalent, every N=2 accuracy number carries over unchanged and re-delivered duplicates are absorbed rather than re-concatenated. On a partitioned-reasoning benchmark, CanonicalMerge matches the best BagMerge ordering in every regime-by-budget-by-ordering cell without knowing which order is best, trading a small, statistically insignificant accuracy margin for an unconditional structural guarantee. The behaviour transfers to real multi-document QA (HotpotQA), while the closest training-free output-fusion baseline (PackLLM) loses by 45 points at matched budget, placing cache-level merging in a regime distinct from output-level fusion. Finally, at k>2 the approach transports and colocates latent traces but does not by itself compose them, which we characterize to motivate future work.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CanonicalMerge, a method for merging multiple agents' KV-caches that is permutation-invariant by ordering caches via mean K-norm, creating a byte-identical merged state regardless of input order. The method is formalized as a state-based CvRDT (commutative, associative, idempotent, absorbing). It matches the best BagMerge ordering across all regime-budget-scale combinations with negligible accuracy loss while providing unconditional structural guarantees, and significantly outperforms output-level fusion baselines like PackLLM on HotpotQA.
AI.motivation: Prior multi-agent latent reasoning methods (Agent Primitives) use BagMerge — concatenating KV-caches along the sequence axis with RoPE re-encoding — which is non-commutative and has unpredictable optimal ordering that varies with regime, latent-step budget, and model scale. This unpredictability demands costly search or heuristics. The authors aim to eliminate this ordering dependency by making the merge operation a convergent replicated state, providing a principled, deterministic alternative.
AI.method: Two components: (1) **CanonicalMerge** fixes layout by sorting caches according to mean K-norm at a middle layer, producing a byte-identical merged cache under any input permutation (verified up to arity N≤5 on Qwen3-1.7B and 4B). (2) **Formalization as a CvRDT**: the replicated state is a set of content-addressed latent fragments where merge is set union, satisfying commutativity, associativity, idempotence, and absorption. CanonicalMerge serves as the deterministic render of this state. The render's byte-equivalence means duplicate delivery results in absorption rather than re-concatenation, and all N=2 accuracy results transfer unchanged.
AI.result: On a partitioned-reasoning benchmark, CanonicalMerge matches the best BagMerge ordering in every regime-by-budget-by-ordering cell without requiring knowledge of the optimal order, with a small, statistically insignificant accuracy margin. On HotpotQA (multi-document QA), it retains performance while PackLLM (training-free output-fusion baseline) loses by 45 points at matched budget. At arity k>2, the approach successfully transports and colocates latent traces but does not compose them, characterized as a limitation motivating future work.
AI.conclusion: CanonicalMerge provides a principled, permutation-invariant cache merging method that eliminates ordering dependency in multi-agent latent reasoning, matching the best-case BagMerge performance with unconditional structural guarantees. The approach places cache-level merging in a regime distinct from and superior to output-level fusion. However, for k>2 agents, colocation alone is insufficient for composition, identifying a clear direction for future research.

title: CoPersona: Collaborative Persona Graphs for Robust LLM Personalization
comment: Accepted at KDD '26. 12 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables
summary: Real-world LLM personalization is often constrained by sparse and skewed user histories: most users provide only a handful of interactions, while even frequent users' logs capture an incomplete and biased view of their preferences. As a result, weakly observed user attributes are difficult to infer, leading to brittle personalization when test-time requests shift toward under-supported facets. Motivated by this limitation, we present CoPersona, a graph-based collaborative personalization framework that completes sparse user profiles by borrowing signals from behaviorally similar peers. However, directly transferring signals is difficult because uneven facet coverage introduces bias into interaction histories, obscuring user similarity in the unstructured global space. To address this issue, CoPersona decomposes interaction histories into multiple facet-level representations and explicitly models peer-to-peer, facet-level alignment through a multiplex persona graph. To effectively leverage peer information at inference time, we employ a dual-branch architecture that combines non-parametric peer retrieval with parametric graph reasoning. Experiments across multiple domains and model scales demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, validating CoPersona as an effective approach for robust LLM personalization.

AI.tldr: CoPersona is a graph-based collaborative personalization framework that addresses sparse and biased user histories in LLM personalization by decomposing interactions into facet-level representations and leveraging peer signals through a multiplex persona graph with dual-branch inference.
AI.motivation: Real-world LLM personalization suffers from sparse (few interactions per user) and skewed (incomplete, biased coverage) user histories, making it difficult to infer weakly observed user attributes and causing brittle personalization when test requests shift toward under-supported facets.
AI.method: CoPersona decomposes interaction histories into multiple facet-level representations and constructs a multiplex persona graph to model peer-to-peer, facet-level alignment. It employs a dual-branch architecture at inference that combines non-parametric peer retrieval with parametric graph reasoning to effectively leverage peer information.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple domains and model scales demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: CoPersona is validated as an effective approach for robust LLM personalization under real-world data sparsity and skewness constraints.

title: Simulation Based Reward Function Validation for Multi-Agent On Orbit Inspection
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures. This submission integrates a published correction made to the original manuscript. The DOIs for both the original manuscript as well as the correction are provided
summary: A proposed method for the control of groups of inspection spacecraft is Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). While MARL has already been employed for this purpose in previous work, the reward functions used focus on reaching a finite set of predetermined inspection points around the target. In this work, we study and develop a generalized reward function for the MARL inspection task informed by the analysis of 3D reconstructions of inspected objects in orbit. Because the reward function is generalized such that any number of images at arbitrary locations may evaluated, we also allow trained agents to have complete control over when images are collected. With this approach, we gather insights into best practices for not only the specific MARL inspection task, but also gain key takeaways informative to the broader inspection task outside of a MARL context.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a generalized reward function for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) based spacecraft inspection, informed by 3D reconstruction analysis, enabling agents to autonomously decide when and where to collect images rather than relying on predetermined inspection points.
AI.motivation: Previous MARL approaches for spacecraft inspection rely on reward functions tied to reaching a finite set of predetermined inspection points, which limits flexibility. The authors aim to create a more generalized reward function that evaluates arbitrary image collections, giving agents full control over imaging decisions and yielding broader insights for inspection tasks.
AI.method: The authors design a generalized reward function for MARL-based inspection that evaluates image collections at arbitrary locations. This reward function is informed by the analysis of 3D reconstructions of inspected objects in orbit, allowing any number of images taken at any positions to be assessed for reconstruction quality.
AI.result: The generalized reward function enables trained agents to autonomously determine optimal imaging positions and timing. The approach yields best practices for the MARL inspection task and provides key takeaways applicable to broader inspection scenarios beyond the MARL context.
AI.conclusion: A generalized reward function informed by 3D reconstruction analysis improves MARL-based spacecraft inspection by removing the constraint of predetermined inspection points, offering both task-specific improvements and transferable insights for general inspection problems.

title: ExPerT: Personalizing LLM Responses to Users' Domain Expertise via Query-Wise Semantic and Keystroke Behavioral Cues
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by end users, yet existing personalization methods relying on static profiles or text-only signals fail to capture query-specific expertise variation. We present ExPerT, a query-wise personalization framework that adapts LLM responses to users' query domain expertise by combining semantic and behavioral cues. ExPerT consists of two key components: (i) a semantic-behavioral expertise inference module that jointly interprets query text and keystroke dynamics via in-context LLM prompting, and (ii) an expertise-conditioned response generation that adapts the level of detail, terminology, and conceptual complexity. Our user study with 40 participants and 1270 queries demonstrated that ExPerT reduced expertise inference error by 65.7% compared to the strongest baseline (MAE = 0.398 vs. 1.162) and improved response satisfaction by 17.52% (from 3.71 to 4.36) on a 5-point Likert scale.

AI.tldr: ExPerT is a query-wise personalization framework that adapts LLM responses to users' domain expertise by combining semantic (query text) and behavioral (keystroke dynamics) cues, achieving a 65.7% reduction in expertise inference error and 17.52% improvement in response satisfaction over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM personalization methods rely on static profiles or text-only signals, which fail to capture how a user's expertise varies from query to query. A user may be an expert in one domain but a novice in another, yet current systems cannot dynamically adapt to this query-specific expertise variation.
AI.method: ExPerT has two components: (1) a semantic-behavioral expertise inference module that jointly interprets query text and keystroke dynamics through in-context LLM prompting, and (2) an expertise-conditioned response generation module that adapts detail level, terminology, and conceptual complexity based on inferred expertise. Evaluated via user study with 40 participants and 1270 queries.
AI.result: ExPerT reduced expertise inference error by 65.7% compared to the strongest baseline (MAE = 0.398 vs. 1.162) and improved response satisfaction by 17.52% (from 3.71 to 4.36 on a 5-point Likert scale).
AI.conclusion: Integrating behavioral signals (keystroke dynamics) with semantic signals via in-context prompting enables highly accurate query-level expertise inference, which in turn allows LLMs to generate responses better tailored to individual users' domain knowledge, significantly outperforming static profile and text-only approaches.

title: Embedding Inference Attack
summary: Embedding models are essential components of modern Information Retrieval (IR) systems, yet they are typically hidden behind APIs. Recent works have shown that dense IR system can lead to security vulnerabilities such as embedding inversion attacks. However, such attacks usually require that the attacker knows the embedding model for the attack to be applicable. In this paper, we study IR systems under a black-box setting in which the adversary observes only the unordered set of retrieved documents, without ranking or similarity scores. We demonstrate that in such contexts, tailored queries allow an adversary to identify which embedding model is in use from a set of known model candidate, which we coin as an embedding inference attack (EIA). We also show that certain queries remain discriminative even when the system includes a reranker as a potential defense mechanism. We further validate our method on a real Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system, in which the tailored queries bypass the LLM's tendency to reject inputs it does not recognize as well-formed questions. Finally, we propose and evaluate other mitigation strategies such as similarity thresholds.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Embedding Inference Attack (EIA), a black-box method that identifies which embedding model an IR system uses by observing only the unordered set of retrieved documents, bypassing defenses like rerankers and LLM-based RAG systems.
AI.motivation: Embedding models in IR systems are typically hidden behind APIs and treated as black boxes. While embedding inversion attacks exist, they require knowing the target model. The authors aim to demonstrate that even under a strict black-box setting—where only unordered retrieved document sets are visible—an adversary can infer the underlying embedding model, exposing a previously unrecognized vulnerability.
AI.method: The authors design tailored discriminative queries that produce distinct retrieval patterns across different candidate embedding models. By observing which documents are retrieved (without ranking or similarity scores), the adversary matches the observed retrieval set against known model behaviors to infer the embedding model. The attack is validated against systems with rerankers and tested on a real RAG system where crafted queries bypass the LLM's input rejection mechanisms. Mitigation strategies including similarity thresholds are also proposed and evaluated.
AI.result: Tailored queries successfully discriminate between candidate embedding models under black-box conditions. The attack remains effective even when a reranker is deployed as a defense. On a real RAG system, the crafted queries evade the LLM's tendency to reject non-well-formed inputs. Proposed mitigation strategies like similarity thresholds offer partial but incomplete protection.
AI.conclusion: Embedding model identity can be reliably inferred in black-box IR settings through carefully constructed queries, exposing a new class of security vulnerability. Existing defenses (rerankers, LLM input filters) are insufficient, and while similarity thresholds provide some mitigation, further research into robust defenses is needed.

title: Benchmarking Code Improvement with Progressive, Adaptive, and Interactive Feedback
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on code generation and program repair using binary functional correctness: a generated program or patch either passes or fails a test suite. This protocol is simple but coarse, as it ignores partial progress, feedback use, regressions, and the refinement trajectory through which models often improve code. We introduce PAIR-Bench, a progressive and adaptive benchmark for evaluating code improvement: transforming an incorrect or incomplete program into a more correct one through feedback-guided refinement. PAIR-Bench uses progressive hinting, a structured feedback protocol with two controls. Failure-region control determines what the feedback targets by grouping hidden failing tests into failure scenarios, while hint-depth control determines how much repair-relevant information is revealed, from coarse symptoms to implementation-level guidance. This design enables PAIR-Bench to measure whether a model repairs targeted failures, generalizes beyond the hint, preserves already-correct behavior, and how much assistance it requires. By evaluating repair trajectories progressive metrics rather than only final pass/fail outcomes, PAIR-Bench provides a finer-grained assessment of LLM code-improvement capability.

AI.tldr: PAIR-Bench introduces a progressive, adaptive benchmark that evaluates how LLMs iteratively refine incorrect code through structured feedback, using failure-region and hint-depth controls to measure repair trajectories rather than just binary pass/fail outcomes.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluation on code generation and program repair relies on binary functional correctness (pass/fail on test suites), which is too coarse. It fails to capture partial progress, how models use feedback, whether they introduce regressions, and the iterative refinement trajectories through which models improve code.
AI.method: PAIR-Bench employs progressive hinting with two control dimensions: (1) Failure-region control, which groups hidden failing tests into failure scenarios to target feedback; and (2) hint-depth control, which modulates how much repair-relevant information is revealed — ranging from coarse symptoms to implementation-level guidance. The benchmark evaluates repair trajectories using progressive metrics that track whether a model repairs targeted failures, generalizes beyond the hint, preserves already-correct behavior, and how much assistance it requires.
AI.result: PAIR-Bench enables finer-grained assessment of LLM code-improvement capability by measuring progressive repair trajectories rather than only final pass/fail outcomes, revealing how models respond to structured feedback at varying levels of specificity and across different failure scenarios.
AI.conclusion: PAIR-Bench provides a more nuanced evaluation framework for LLM code-improvement capabilities, moving beyond binary correctness to capture the dynamics of feedback-guided refinement, generalization, regression avoidance, and assistance dependence.

title: PACE: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Plausible and Actionable Counterfactual Explanations
summary: Counterfactual explanations explain machine learning predictions by identifying minimal input changes that would alter a model's decision. Although many existing methods successfully generate prediction-changing alternatives, they often produce unrealistic or infeasible recommendations due to a lack of explicit mechanisms for incorporating domain knowledge and intervention constraints. Neuro-symbolic AI offers a promising direction by combining data-driven predictive models with symbolic reasoning capable of representing human-understandable rules and feasible actions. This paper presents PACE, a modular neuro-symbolic framework for generating feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations. The framework separates prediction and reasoning into two components: a neural predictive model for classification and a symbolic reasoning layer that enforces domain-specific constraints during counterfactual generation. By explicitly modeling feasible interventions, the framework produces explanations consistent with domain knowledge while remaining interpretable and actionable. The approach is model-agnostic and adaptable to domains requiring realistic decision support. A case study is conducted on the Adult Income dataset, combining a multilayer perceptron classifier with Answer Set Programming (ASP) rules encoding feasible modifications to education, occupation, and working hours while preserving immutable attributes. Results highlight the trade-off between counterfactual validity and plausibility and show that symbolic constraints yield explanations that better satisfy domain-specific feasibility requirements, illustrating the potential of neuro-symbolic methods for transparent, feasibility-aware counterfactual explanation in explainable AI.

AI.tldr: PACE is a modular neuro-symbolic framework that combines neural classifiers with symbolic reasoning (Answer Set Programming) to generate counterfactual explanations respecting domain constraints, demonstrated on the Adult Income dataset with improved feasibility over unconstrained methods.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods often produce unrealistic or infeasible recommendations because they lack explicit mechanisms for incorporating domain knowledge and intervention constraints. There is a need for explanations that are not only prediction-altering but also actionable within real-world constraints.
AI.method: PACE is a modular neuro-symbolic framework with two components: (1) a neural predictive model (multilayer perceptron) for classification, and (2) a symbolic reasoning layer using Answer Set Programming (ASP) to encode domain-specific constraints on feasible interventions (e.g., allowable changes to education, occupation, working hours) while preserving immutable attributes. The approach is model-agnostic.
AI.result: On the Adult Income dataset, the framework reveals a trade-off between counterfactual validity and plausibility. Symbolic constraints yield explanations that better satisfy domain-specific feasibility requirements compared to unconstrained methods, demonstrating the value of neuro-symbolic integration for actionable explanations.
AI.conclusion: Neuro-symbolic methods like PACE offer a promising direction for transparent, feasibility-aware counterfactual explanation in XAI. By explicitly separating prediction from constrained symbolic reasoning, the framework produces interpretable, actionable, and domain-consistent explanations suitable for realistic decision support across various domains.

title: TokenScope: Token-Level Explainability and Interpretability for Code-Oriented Tasks in Large Language Models
summary: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) make token-level decisions during code generation remains a major challenge for both researchers and practitioners. While recent tools provide insights into model internals or generation outcomes, they often lack decoding-time signals, fine-grained uncertainty measures, and interactive mechanisms for exploring alternative generation paths. We present TokenScope, an interactive interpretability and analysis tool for decoder-based LLMs that exposes token-level metrics, attention patterns, and structural information during generation. TokenScope supports interactive token replacement, counterfactual branching, and code-aware aggregation via abstract syntax trees. By unifying decoding-time signals with structural program analysis, TokenScope enables systematic investigation of LLM behaviour during code generation.

AI.tldr: TokenScope is an interactive tool for analyzing decoder-based LLMs during code generation, exposing token-level metrics, attention patterns, and structural information. It supports token replacement, counterfactual branching, and AST-based aggregation to enable systematic investigation of LLM behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM interpretability tools lack three key capabilities: (1) decoding-time signals to understand real-time decision-making, (2) fine-grained uncertainty measures at the token level, and (3) interactive mechanisms for exploring alternative generation paths. This gap hinders systematic understanding of how LLMs make token-level decisions during code generation.
AI.method: TokenScope unifies decoding-time signals (token-level metrics, attention patterns, structural information) with structural program analysis. It provides interactive features including token replacement, counterfactual branching for exploring alternative generation paths, and code-aware aggregation via abstract syntax trees (ASTs) to map model internals onto program structure.
AI.result: The paper presents the TokenScope tool itself as the primary artifact, demonstrating its capability to expose decoding-time signals and enable systematic investigation of LLM behavior during code generation through interactive exploration and structural analysis.
AI.conclusion: By bridging decoding-time interpretability with program structure analysis, TokenScope fills a critical gap in LLM code generation understanding, offering researchers and practitioners a unified platform for probing model decisions as they unfold token by token.

title: Multilayer Q-Matrix-Embedded Neural Network for Cognitive Diagnosis (M-QCDNet): Structure-Aware Deep Learning Architecture for Psychometric Interpretability
summary: The research proposes a multilayer Q-matrix-embedded neural network for cognitive diagnosis (M-QCDNet), which integrates the structural interpretability of cognitive diagnostic models (CDMs) with the deep learning neural network (NN). M-QCDNet structures the item-skill relationship using the Q-matrix as a structural prior, ensuring latent mastery profiles remain interpretable and consistent with cognitive theory, followed by the proposed loss function with an L2 penalty to penalize skills not aligned with the Q-matrix and to balance predictive performance and structural alignment. Corresponding evaluation matrices, the interpretable alignment-based metrics that quantify the degree to which predicted skill activations correspond to item-level skills, were further developed. M-QCDNet offers practical benefits for classroom practice, enabling early detection of learning difficulties and supporting mastery-based interventions. By embedding diagnostic validity into model design, M-QCDNet bridges psychometric transparency and neural flexibility, advancing interpretable, fair, and actionable AI for cognitive diagnostics.

AI.tldr: M-QCDNet is a neural cognitive diagnosis model that embeds the Q-matrix as a structural prior, ensuring interpretable skill mastery profiles. It uses an L2-penalized loss function to enforce Q-matrix alignment and introduces interpretable alignment-based evaluation metrics.
AI.motivation: Traditional cognitive diagnostic models offer strong interpretability through the Q-matrix but lack the flexibility and predictive power of deep neural networks. Conversely, neural approaches often sacrifice psychometric transparency. The authors aim to bridge this gap by embedding structural interpretability directly into a neural framework.
AI.method: M-QCDNet uses a multilayer neural network with the Q-matrix embedded as a structural prior to govern item-skill relationships. A custom loss function with an L2 regularization term penalizes skill activations inconsistent with the Q-matrix, balancing predictive accuracy and structural fidelity. Novel interpretable alignment-based evaluation metrics are introduced to quantify how well predicted skill activations match the Q-matrix-defined item-skill mapping.
AI.result: The paper develops evaluation metrics that quantify the alignment between predicted skill activations and the item-skill Q-matrix, though specific empirical results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: M-QCDNet successfully integrates psychometric transparency with neural network flexibility, yielding an interpretable and actionable AI system for cognitive diagnosis. It supports practical classroom applications such as early detection of learning difficulties and mastery-based interventions.

title: IntentTune: Using user demand and personalization to resolve "unknown" query intents for e-commerce search
summary: Understanding user intent is fundamental to delivering relevant search results in e-commerce. However, substantial fraction of real-world queries are under-specified (e.g., "watch" or "shirt"), lacking explicit attributes such as gender or age group. This ambiguity poses a significant challenge for query intent detection models in e-commerce search systems, which must accurately infer latent user intent (e.g., age, gender) to support effective downstream retrieval. We introduce IntentTune, a framework for resolving ambiguous or under-specified query intents by leveraging either (1) user-specific behavioral signals including search history, browsing activity, and profile attributes or (2) population-level demand patterns aggregated across all users. Through experiments on real-world e-commerce data, we first demonstrate that population-level demand patterns alone are insufficient to reliably infer intent in under-specified queries. We then demonstrate that user-specific behavioral signals -- particularly prior search queries -- outperform both population-level statistics and static profile information for inferring gender, age group, product category, and size intent from underspecified queries.

AI.tldr: IntentTune is a framework for disambiguating under-specified e-commerce queries (e.g., "watch" or "shirt") by inferring latent user intent (gender, age group, category, size) using either user-specific behavioral signals or population-level demand patterns. Experiments show user-specific signals—especially prior search queries—significantly outperform population-level statistics and static profile attributes.
AI.motivation: A substantial fraction of real-world e-commerce queries are under-specified, lacking explicit attributes like gender or age group. This ambiguity hinders query intent detection and downstream retrieval quality. Existing approaches relying solely on population-level demand patterns may be insufficient, motivating a systematic comparison with user-specific behavioral signals.
AI.method: IntentTune is a framework that resolves ambiguous query intents through two strategies: (1) leveraging user-specific behavioral signals—search history, browsing activity, and profile attributes; (2) leveraging population-level demand patterns aggregated across all users. The framework is evaluated on real-world e-commerce data, comparing the effectiveness of these signal types for inferring gender, age group, product category, and size intent.
AI.result: Population-level demand patterns alone are insufficient to reliably infer intent for under-specified queries. User-specific behavioral signals—particularly prior search queries—consistently outperform both population-level statistics and static profile information across all intent dimensions (gender, age group, product category, and size).
AI.conclusion: User-specific behavioral signals, especially prior search queries, are the most effective source for disambiguating under-specified e-commerce queries. Population-level demand patterns alone are unreliable for this task, highlighting the importance of personalization in query intent detection for e-commerce search systems.

title: Congestion-Based Slot Pricing in a Railway Auction Game
summary:
We present a multi-agent system for studying the allocation of discrete, congested resources among heterogeneous strategic agents, motivated by the problem of railway slot allocation under deregulation. Multiple operator-agents, differing in size and capacity, interact through a shared auction mechanism over repeated rounds under time-constrained decision-making. The mechanism combines a congestion-based base price that increases with aggregate demand with an asymmetric corrective adjustment that penalises the agent requesting the most slots and rewards the agent requesting the fewest, and is designed to mitigate strategic dominance by large agents while preserving transparency and congestion sensitivity. We formulate the interaction as a repeated game with incomplete information and implement the system as a real-time, web-based multi-agent environment in which human participants control individual agents and observe live marginal-cost and competitor feedback.
  We report exploratory observations from two structured sessions with domain experts acting as operator-agents. The congestion mechanism responds to aggregate demand as designed and the corrective incentives are actively triggered, but agents representing large operators persist with high-request strategies despite the penalty, suggesting that corrective pricing is necessary but not sufficient to neutralise strategic dominance in this multi-agent setting. A post-session debrief indicates that participants' decisions were driven by the assumed agent role rather than personal disposition, and provides qualitative support for strategic motives, such as preserving market presence and raising rivals' costs, operating alongside short-term profit maximisation. We discuss implications for multi-agent mechanism design under asymmetric budgets and outline directions for analytical validation and larger-scale multi-agent experiments.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent system simulates railway slot allocation via a congestion-based auction with corrective pricing. Experiments with domain experts reveal that large operators persist with high-request strategies despite penalties, indicating corrective pricing alone insufficiently curbs strategic dominance.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the real-world problem of allocating discrete, congested railway slots under deregulation, where heterogeneous strategic agents (train operating companies) compete for limited infrastructure capacity. The authors seek to design and evaluate a transparent auction mechanism that mitigates strategic dominance by large operators while remaining sensitive to congestion.
AI.method: The authors formulate the interaction as a repeated game with incomplete information and implement a real-time, web-based multi-agent environment. The mechanism features a congestion-based base price (increasing with aggregate demand) plus an asymmetric corrective adjustment that penalizes the highest-requesting agent and rewards the lowest-requesting agent. Two structured sessions were conducted with domain experts acting as operator-agents, who observe live marginal-cost and competitor feedback.
AI.result: The congestion mechanism responds to aggregate demand as designed, and corrective incentives are triggered. However, large-operator agents persist with high-request strategies despite penalties. Post-session debriefs reveal participants' decisions were role-driven rather than personality-driven, with qualitative evidence of strategic motives beyond short-term profit maximization, including preserving market presence and raising rivals' costs.
AI.conclusion: Corrective pricing is necessary but not sufficient to neutralize strategic dominance in this multi-agent setting. The findings highlight challenges for mechanism design under asymmetric budgets and call for analytical validation plus larger-scale multi-agent experiments.

title: Mitigating Confirmation Bias through Hand-Drawing Videos
comment: Accepted to IEEE VIS 2026 Short Papers. 4 pages plus references
summary: Understanding data visualizations is essential for informed decision-making, yet interpretation is often shaped and even distorted by prior beliefs. We investigate whether an embodied pedagogical approach, in which viewers observe the dynamic hand-drawing of a visualization, can mitigate confirmation bias and improve interpretation accuracy. We conducted a study comparing static bar charts to videos in which charts are constructed through hand-drawing, across contexts that either align with or challenge participants' prior beliefs. The results indicate that hand-drawn videos helped participants accurately interpret data, even when the data conflicted with their prior beliefs. This approach also reduced belief-consistent errors and increased belief-overriding responses. These findings suggest that exposing the construction process of a visualization supports more accurate reasoning and mitigates the influence of confirmation bias. Consequently, this work introduces a promising design space for bias-mitigating data interfaces.

AI.tldr: Hand-drawn animated visualizations reduce confirmation bias and improve data interpretation accuracy compared to static charts, especially when data conflicts with prior beliefs.
AI.motivation: Prior beliefs often distort the interpretation of data visualizations, leading to confirmation bias. The authors explore whether an embodied pedagogical approach — specifically, showing the hand-drawing process of a visualization — can counteract this bias and improve interpretive accuracy.
AI.method: A controlled experiment compared static bar charts against video recordings of bar charts being hand-drawn. Participants viewed visualizations in contexts that either aligned with or contradicted their pre-existing beliefs. Interpretation accuracy, belief-consistent errors, and belief-overriding responses were measured across conditions.
AI.result: Hand-drawn videos significantly improved participants' ability to accurately interpret data that conflicted with their prior beliefs. This condition also reduced belief-consistent errors and increased the rate of belief-overriding responses relative to static charts.
AI.conclusion: Exposing the construction process of a visualization via hand-drawing supports more objective reasoning and mitigates confirmation bias. The work opens a novel design space for bias-resistant data interfaces grounded in embodied cognition principles.

title: Cognitive Firewall: A Proactive, Zero-Trust, Multi-Gate Framework for LLM Safety
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can be induced to produce harmful content through multi turn strategies in which no single user message appears clearly unsafe. Existing runtime safeguards commonly evaluate prompts or responses as isolated messages, which limits their ability to recover ac-cumulated intent, verify asserted authority, or detect harmful objectives decomposed across a dialogue. This paper presents the Cognitive Firewall, a proactive runtime oversight framework that interposes an independent oversight model between a user and a protected target mod l. The framework decomposes safety assessment into four categorical gates: an intent gate that identi-fies the operational objective of a request, a zero trust context gate that treats claimed roles and permissions as unverified evidence, a consistency gate that detects escalation and decomposition across turns, and an output risk gate that inspects candidate responses before release. Gate decisions are combined through escalation rather than score averaging, allowing any confident danger signal to block an interaction while preserving an auditable rationale. Experiments on four jailbreak benchmarks and a benign safety test set show that the Cognitive Firewall substantially reduces attack success across single turn, multi turn, authority based, and human crafted attacks. It lowers attack success to 2 percent or below on three attack sets and to 14 percent on the most difficult human crafted set, while maintaining an 8 percent over refusal rate. These results indicate that decomposed, conversation level oversight can improve proactive containment and auditability for LLM safety.

AI.tldr: The Cognitive Firewall is a runtime oversight framework that inserts an independent model between users and protected LLMs, decomposing safety assessment into four categorical gates (intent, zero-trust context, consistency, output risk) that escalate confident danger signals across multi-turn dialogues, reducing jailbreak attack success to ≤2% on three benchmarks and 14% on the hardest set.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM safeguards evaluate prompts or responses in isolation, failing to detect harmful intent accumulated across multi-turn conversations, verify claimed authority, or identify decomposed harmful objectives. This creates a vulnerability where no single user message appears clearly unsafe but the dialogue as a whole is malicious.
AI.method: The Cognitive Firewall interposes an independent oversight model between user and target LLM. It uses four categorical safety gates: (1) Intent Gate — identifies the operational objective of a request; (2) Zero-Trust Context Gate — treats claimed roles/permissions as unverified evidence; (3) Consistency Gate — detects escalation and decomposition across turns; (4) Output Risk Gate — inspects candidate responses before release. Gate decisions are combined via escalation rather than score averaging, so any confident danger signal blocks the interaction while preserving an auditable rationale.
AI.result: Evaluated on four jailbreak benchmarks and a benign safety test set, the Cognitive Firewall reduced attack success to 2% or below on three attack sets and 14% on the hardest human-crafted set, while maintaining an 8% over-refusal rate on benign queries.
AI.conclusion: Decomposed, conversation-level oversight via the Cognitive Firewall improves proactive containment and auditability for LLM safety compared to isolated message-level safeguards.

title: A global predicted-fMRI drive signal from TRIBE does not predict YouTube replay heatmaps
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure. Code, video-ID manifest, and per-video results: https://github.com/mercurialsolo/tribe-replay-heatmaps
summary: Deep multimodal brain-encoding models now predict fMRI responses to naturalistic video with high accuracy. Whether their predicted neural signals also forecast behavioral engagement is unknown. We run TRIBE, the winning model of the 2025 Algonauts brain-encoding challenge (Llama-3.2 + V-JEPA2 + Wav2Vec-BERT), on 48 YouTube videos and reduce its predicted cortical response to a per-second engagement curve, the global field power. Correlated against each video's "most replayed" heatmap, a passively-collected proxy for which moments viewers return to, the curve shows no evidence of predicting re-watch behavior. The pooled position-controlled partial correlation is +0.058 (95% CI [-0.04, 0.15]; one-sample t(47)=1.21, p=0.23), indistinguishable from zero and not significantly above simple loudness and motion baselines (loudness +0.04, paired p=0.74). The raw correlation is also near zero; the moderate values reported for music videos reflect a genre-specific intro/onset-replay artifact rather than content prediction, and do not generalize. The null holds across six cortical-network readouts and under an autocorrelation-preserving permutation test. We release the code, the video-ID manifest, and an acquisition method that works despite YouTube's SABR-only streaming.

AI.tldr: A state-of-the-art multimodal brain-encoding model (TRIBE) fails to predict YouTube re-watch behavior from predicted cortical responses, with correlations indistinguishable from zero and not significantly exceeding simple loudness/motion baselines.
AI.motivation: While deep multimodal brain-encoding models achieve high accuracy in predicting fMRI responses to naturalistic video, it remains unknown whether these predicted neural signals can forecast real-world behavioral engagement — specifically, which moments viewers choose to re-watch.
AI.method: The authors deployed TRIBE (the 2025 Algonauts challenge winner, combining Llama-3.2, V-JEPA2, and Wav2Vec-BERT) on 48 YouTube videos, reduced predicted cortical responses to per-second global field power curves, and correlated these against YouTube's "most replayed" heatmaps using position-controlled partial correlation, raw correlation, six cortical-network readouts, and autocorrelation-preserving permutation tests.
AI.result: The pooled position-controlled partial correlation was +0.058 (95% CI [-0.04, 0.15]; t(47)=1.21, p=0.23), indistinguishable from zero and not significantly above loudness (+0.04, paired p=0.74) or motion baselines. Previously reported moderate correlations for music videos were found to reflect a genre-specific intro/onset-replay artifact rather than genuine content prediction. The null result held across all six cortical-network readouts and permutation testing.
AI.conclusion: Predicted brain responses from state-of-the-art encoding models do not forecast re-watch behavior, challenging the assumption that higherfidelity neural encoding translates to behavioral prediction and highlighting a critical gap between brain-encoding accuracy and ecological validity.

title: Auto-FL-Research: Agentic Search for Federated Learning Algorithms
summary: Federated learning (FL) research often depends on many small but consequential algorithmic choices: optimizer variants, server aggregation rules, local training schedules, normalization, regularization, and model architecture. These choices are expensive to explore manually and difficult to compare fairly when candidate changes can also alter the FL training or evaluation path. In this work, we present Auto-FL-Research (AFR), a constrained coding-agent workflow for FL algorithmic recipe search. Agents may propose and implement candidate training algorithms, including server aggregation rules, client update schedules, local objectives, and registered model variants, while task profiles fix the mutation surface, compute budget, communication contract, and final model evaluation. Each campaign records candidate scores, runtime, edited files, artifacts, and failure status. We evaluate AFR on five healthcare cross-silo FLamby tasks and on grouped-client profiles for the five fixed LEAF datasets plus the LEAF synthetic task. Five-seed repeat evaluations support gains on four FLamby tasks and five of six LEAF profiles, while also exposing seed-sensitive and search-selected failure cases. Same-budget controls show that several gains correspond to FL-recipe changes, whereas other improvements are recovered by fixed-surface scalar controls or fail under repeat or held-out evaluation. These mixed outcomes are part of the contribution: they show how agent-generated candidates can be separated into repeated FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning effects, and selected single-run artifacts.

AI.tldr: Auto-FL-Research (AFR) is a constrained coding-agent workflow that automatically searches for algorithmic recipes in federated learning, evaluated on healthcare and LEAF benchmarks, revealing that gains can stem from genuine FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning, or single-run artifacts.
AI.motivation: Federated learning research involves many small, consequential algorithmic choices (optimizers, aggregation rules, local schedules, normalization, regularization, architecture) that are expensive to explore manually and difficult to compare fairly when candidate changes alter the training or evaluation path.
AI.method: AFR uses a constrained coding-agent workflow where agents propose and implement candidate FL algorithms (server aggregation, client update schedules, local objectives, model variants) under task profiles that fix the mutation surface, compute budget, communication contract, and final evaluation. Each campaign records scores, runtime, edited files, artifacts, and failure status.
AI.result: Five-seed evaluations on five FLamby healthcare cross-silo tasks and six LEAF profiles (five fixed + synthetic) show gains on four FLamby tasks and five of six LEAF profiles. Same-budget controls reveal some gains are due to FL-recipe changes, while others are attributable to fixed-surface scalar tuning or are single-run artifacts that fail under repeat or held-out evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Agent-generated FL candidates can be systematically separated into repeated FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning effects, and selected single-run artifacts — a decomposition that constitutes a core contribution alongside AFR itself.

title: Safeguarding LLM Agents from Misalignment through Provenance Analysis
summary: As LLM agents gain increasing access to powerful tools, ensuring that their actions are aligned with the user's intent becomes critical. When an agent's proposed tool invocation deviates from the user's intent -- a phenomenon called misalignment -- it may lead to harmful consequences that are difficult to undo. Existing runtime guardrails rely on an LLM-as-a-judge paradigm that lacks a systematic framework for reasoning about alignment, often producing judgments that are inconsistent or difficult to audit. Motivated by provenance analysis, we propose a provenance-based conceptual framework that formalizes misalignment detection as determining whether a proposed tool call is supported by traceable evidence in the agent's context. Building on this framework, we propose ProvenanceGuard, a multi-stage pipeline that analyzes the agent's action for three types of misalignment before the selected tool is executed and only allows the action to take place when it is considered aligned with the user's input query. We evaluated our proposed approach on two different benchmarks, Agent-SafetyBench and WorkBench, across 10 backbone LLMs. Compared to the LLM-as-a-judge baseline, ProvenanceGuard reduces error rate on misaligned traces from 42.9% to 1.8% on Agent-SafetyBench and from 32.1% to 17.3% on WorkBench, while reducing intervention burden on task-successful traces from 30.5% to 12.8% and introducing no statistically significant increase in unnecessary interventions on aligned traces. These results demonstrate that structured, provenance-based reasoning provides an effective and practical foundation for safeguarding LLM agents from misalignment.

AI.tldr: ProvenanceGuard introduces a provenance-based framework for detecting misalignment in LLM agent tool invocations, achieving dramatic error rate reductions (42.9% → 1.8% on Agent-SafetyBench) compared to LLM-as-a-judge baselines while reducing unnecessary interventions.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents gain access to powerful tools, misalignment between agent actions and user intent can cause harmful, irreversible consequences. Existing LLM-as-a-judge guardrails lack systematic reasoning frameworks, producing inconsistent and hard-to-audit judgments. The work is motivated by provenance analysis to provide traceable, evidence-based alignment verification.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-part contribution: (1) a provenance-based conceptual framework that formalizes misalignment detection as determining whether a proposed tool call is supported by traceable evidence in the agent's context, and (2) ProvenanceGuard, a multi-stage pipeline that analyzes agent actions for three types of misalignment before tool execution, only permitting actions deemed aligned with the user's input query.
AI.result: Evaluated on Agent-SafetyBench and WorkBench across 10 backbone LLMs, ProvenanceGuard reduced misaligned trace error rates from 42.9% to 1.8% (Agent-SafetyBench) and 32.1% to 17.3% (WorkBench). Intervention burden on successful traces dropped from 30.5% to 12.8%, with no statistically significant increase in unnecessary interventions on aligned traces.
AI.conclusion: Structured, provenance-based reasoning provides an effective and practical foundation for safeguarding LLM agents against misalignment, offering substantial improvements in both detection accuracy and intervention efficiency over the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm.

title: I\textsuperscript{2}RiMA: Spectral Riemannian Representation with Temporal Attention for Mental Stress Detection based on EEG Signals
summary: Cross-subject EEG stress detection remains challenging because discriminative stress-related patterns are both subject-dependent and frequency-specific. Conventional Riemannian methods model spatial covariance mainly in the time domain, overlooking neural oscillations that are critical for high-level cognitive state decoding, while standard temporal tokenization often fragments inter-slice temporal coherence. To address these limitations, we propose \method{}, an Intra-Inter Riemannian Manifold Attention Network for EEG-based stress detection. \method{} constructs spatial covariance matrices independently at each frequency point and maps them to the SPD tangent space, preserving channel-wise geometry together with frequency-specific discriminative cues. It further introduces frequency cluster aggregation to select informative spectral components and reduce redundancy by forming compact, data-driven frequency clusters aligned with EEG rhythms. Finally, an intra-inter slice attention module adaptively integrates local slice-level spectral dynamics and global temporal context across EEG sequences. Experiments on three datasets show that \method{} consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 82.78\% balanced accuracy while remaining efficient with only 1.60M parameters and 31.95M FLOPs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Intra-Inter Riemannian Manifold Attention Network (IIRMA-Net), which models EEG spatial covariance matrices per frequency on the SPD tangent space, aggregates informative frequency clusters, and applies intra-inter slice attention to capture both local spectral dynamics and global temporal context for cross-subject stress detection.
AI.motivation: Cross-subject EEG stress detection suffers from two key issues: (1) conventional Riemannian methods model spatial covariance only in the time domain, ignoring frequency-specific neural oscillations critical for cognitive state decoding; (2) standard temporal tokenization disrupts inter-slice temporal coherence. Stress-related patterns are both subject-dependent and frequency-specific, necessitating a method that jointly preserves spatial geometry, spectral cues, and temporal continuity.
AI.method: IIRMA-Net operates in three stages: (1) Spatial covariance matrices are constructed independently at each frequency point and mapped to the SPD tangent space, preserving channel-wise Riemannian geometry and frequency-specific discriminative cues. (2) Frequency cluster aggregation selects informative spectral components and reduces redundancy by forming compact, data-driven frequency clusters aligned with EEG rhythms. (3) An intra-inter slice attention module adaptively integrates local slice-level spectral dynamics with global temporal context across EEG sequences.
AI.result: IIRMA-Net consistently outperformed five state-of-the-art baselines across three datasets, achieving up to 82.78% balanced accuracy, with only 1.60M parameters and 31.95M FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed IIRMA-Net effectively addresses cross-subject EEG stress detection by combining frequency-specific Riemannian manifold modeling with attention-based temporal integration, delivering strong performance with computational efficiency.

title: Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Academic Texts
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems use the question-answering capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to access information outside their parameters. We evaluate if cluster-based semantic chunking improves retrieval and answer quality compared to fixed-size and recursive chunking evaluating on long, structured academic theses using the Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment (RAGAs) framework. RAGAs based faithfulness shows limited reliability in this setup. Performance on fixed versus document specific questions varied substantially, likely related to the formatting of documents and preprocessing. Under the tested configuration, cluster-based chunking did not outperform simpler strategies.

AI.tldr: Evaluates cluster-based semantic chunking against fixed-size and recursive chunking in RAG systems using long academic theses. Cluster-based chunking did not outperform simpler strategies, and RAGAs faithfulness proved unreliable in this setup.
AI.motivation: To determine whether cluster-based semantic chunking improves retrieval and answer quality in RAG systems compared to simpler chunking strategies (fixed-size, recursive), particularly for long, structured academic documents.
AI.method: Evaluated three chunking strategies (fixed-size, recursive, cluster-based semantic) on long academic theses. Used the RAGAs framework to assess retrieval and answer quality. Compared performance on both fixed/generic questions and document-specific questions.
AI.result: 1) Cluster-based semantic chunking did not outperform fixed-size or recursive chunking under the tested configuration. 2) RAGAs faithfulness metric showed limited reliability for this document type. 3) Performance varied substantially between fixed and document-specific questions, likely due to document formatting and preprocessing artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Semantic chunking via clustering offers no clear advantage over simpler chunking methods for structured academic theses in RAG pipelines. Furthermore, the RAGAs faithfulness metric may not be dependable for evaluating such setups, and question type significantly influences evaluation outcomes.

title: CausalSteward: An Agentic Divide-Conquer-Combine Copilot for Causal Discovery
summary: Learning causal models from high-dimensional data is a significant challenge, particularly in real-world settings where violations of core assumptions lead to causal identifiability issues. Although massive amounts of prior knowledge are available, and contain valuable causal information, effectively integrating this knowledge into the causal discovery process remains an open problem. We introduce CausalSTeward (CAST), a novel human-in-the-loop framework for interactively assembling large causal models. CausalSteward is a multi-agent collaborative system that tackles high-dimensional causality through a divide-and-conquer approach where large clusters of variables are iteratively partitioned and then separately analyzed. Our framework fuses prior knowledge with a data-driven approach by using tailored tools such as retrieval augmented generation and conditional independence tests. Finally, we use this work to examine the capabilities and limitations of causal reasoning in multi-agent frameworks, and how the human-in-the-loop can contribute to accurate and trustworthy results.

AI.tldr: CAST is a human-in-the-loop, multi-agent framework that uses a divide-and-conquer strategy to learn large causal models from high-dimensional data by integrating prior knowledge (via retrieval augmented generation) with data-driven conditional independence tests.
AI.motivation: Learning causal models from high-dimensional real-world data is difficult due to violations of core causal assumptions leading to identifiability issues. Although abundant prior knowledge exists, effectively incorporating it into causal discovery remains an open challenge.
AI.method: CausalSteward (CAST) employs a multi-agent collaborative system with a divide-and-conquer approach: large variable clusters are iteratively partitioned and analyzed separately. It fuses prior knowledge with data-driven methods using retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and conditional independence tests within a human-in-the-loop framework.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates a working human-in-the-loop, multi-agent system for assembling large causal models and provides an examination of the capabilities and limitations of causal reasoning within such multi-agent architectures.
AI.conclusion: Human-in-the-loop integration contributes to more accurate and trustworthy causal discovery results, and multi-agent frameworks show promise for scaling causal reasoning to high-dimensional settings when augmented with prior knowledge and human oversight.

title: Mind the Trust Gap: Identifying (Mis)alignments in Teacher-Student Views Toward Control and Agency in K-12 Classroom AI
comment: To be published in Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, Volume 10, Issue 6, Article CSCW124 (October 2026)
summary: As Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based technologies have been integrated into school classrooms where multiple stakeholders (with different roles) interact with each other, it is critical to deeply understand stakeholder views in the classroom. In particular, prior work has not fully uncovered how teachers' and school students' views might or might not align well with each other, especially in K-12 classrooms. We conducted a speed-dating study using storyboards with 16 school students and 15 school teachers in Germany to investigate alignments and misalignments between their views on student-AI decision-making control in K-12 classroom. Through an explicit pair-matching analysis, we found that students and teachers had misaligned views on several key topics, including how much they trust AI and social and emotional aspects of student learning with AI. Findings also revealed the importance of teacher-student relationships outside of AI use that shape stakeholders' views and interactions. We discuss potential reasons for the observed misaligned views and strategies to fill the perspective gaps. This study illustrates the complexities of preferences in teacher-student-AI interactions that depend on the dynamic relations among the stakeholders.

AI.tldr: A speed-dating study with 16 students and 15 teachers in Germany revealed misalignments in how both groups view student-AI decision-making control in K-12 classrooms, particularly regarding trust in AI and social-emotional aspects of learning. Findings highlight the importance of teacher-student relationships in shaping these views.
AI.motivation: As AI technologies become integrated into K-12 classrooms involving multiple stakeholders, prior research has not adequately examined how teachers' and students' perspectives align or diverge, especially regarding decision-making control between students and AI systems.
AI.method: A speed-dating study using storyboards was conducted with 16 school students and 15 school teachers in Germany. An explicit pair-matching analysis was employed to systematically compare and identify alignments and misalignments between the two stakeholder groups' views on student-AI decision-making control.
AI.result: Students and teachers held misaligned views on several key topics: (1) trust in AI, (2) social and emotional aspects of student learning with AI. Additionally, teacher-student relationships beyond AI use emerged as a significant factor shaping both stakeholders' views and interactions.
AI.conclusion: The study illustrates the complexity of preferences in teacher-student-AI interactions, which are contingent on dynamic stakeholder relationships. The authors discuss reasons for perspective gaps and propose strategies to bridge these misalignments in classroom AI integration.

title: Generative AI and Federated Learning for Intrusion Detection Systems: A Survey
summary: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) are essential for monitoring network traffic and identifying malicious activities in modern cyber-physical, Internet of Things (IoT), enterprise, and distributed network environments. However, developing reliable IDS models remains challenging because attack behaviors evolve over time, realistic datasets are difficult to obtain, traffic records may be incomplete, attack classes are often imbalanced, and privacy constraints limit centralized data collection. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) and Federated Learning (FL) provide new opportunities to address these limitations. Generative models can support anomaly detection, synthetic traffic generation, data augmentation, data imputation, adversarial traffic generation, and IDS alert explanation. FL enables distributed IDS training without directly sharing local network traffic, making it suitable for privacy-sensitive and geographically distributed environments. This survey provides a structured review of generative AI and FL techniques for IDS. We first summarize representative IDS research directions, including adversarial machine learning, anomaly-based detection, IoT-oriented IDS, explainable IDS, and benchmark datasets. We then categorize generative AI applications in IDS according to model families and task objectives, covering autoencoder-based models, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), diffusion models, and Large Language Models (LLMs). Finally, we review emerging studies that integrate generative AI with FL-based IDS and discuss open challenges, including synthetic data quality, realistic traffic generation, dual-use adversarial risks, non-IID client distributions, communication-efficient model sharing, federated IDS benchmarking, and domain-specific LLMs for network security.

AI.tldr: This survey systematically reviews the intersection of generative AI and federated learning for intrusion detection systems, categorizing techniques by model family (autoencoders, GANs, diffusion models, LLMs) and task objectives, while identifying open challenges such as synthetic data quality, non-IID distributions, and adversarial risks.
AI.motivation: IDS development faces persistent challenges: evolving attack behaviors, scarce realistic datasets, incomplete traffic records, imbalanced attack classes, and privacy constraints hindering centralized data collection. Generative AI and FL offer complementary solutions to these limitations.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured literature survey organized into three parts: (1) summarizing representative IDS research directions (adversarial ML, anomaly detection, IoT-IDS, explainable IDS, benchmarks); (2) categorizing generative AI applications in IDS by model family (autoencoders, GANs, diffusion models, LLMs) and task (anomaly detection, synthetic data generation, data augmentation, imputation, adversarial generation, alert explanation); (3) reviewing FL-integrated generative IDS approaches and identifying open challenges.
AI.result: The survey maps the landscape of generative-AI-assisted IDS, showing that autoencoders and GANs dominate anomaly detection and data augmentation tasks, while diffusion models and LLMs are emerging for traffic generation and alert explanation respectively. FL enables privacy-preserving distributed training but introduces non-IID data and communication efficiency challenges.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI and FL substantially expand IDS capabilities, but key open problems remain: ensuring synthetic data realism and quality, mitigating dual-use adversarial risks, handling non-IID client distributions, reducing communication overhead, establishing federated IDS benchmarks, and developing domain-specific LLMs for network security.

title: GPUAlert: A Zero-Instrumentation Process-Boundary Monitor for Diagnosing GPU Training-Job Failures
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables,3 Listings. Submitted as an arXiv preprint. Source, corpus and evaluation harness available at https://github.com/Parv-01/gpualert and https://github.com/Parv-01/gpualert-eval
summary: GPU training jobs fail often, roughly two in five on large production clusters, yet the operator typically learns of a failure only by reconnecting hours later. Experiment trackers require editing the training script and maintaining a cloud connection; the scheduler's mail hook delivers a single status line with no cause and no logs. GPUAlert is a command-line wrapper that monitors any training command at the process boundary, and with no change to that command, emails a structured notification on completion carrying a classified failure cause, durable logs, and output artifacts. The tool is organized around three reliability primitives: a pre-launch log guarantee that establishes the durable destination before the child process can crash, notifier isolation that makes the wrapper's exit code a pure function of the child's status regardless of whether the email succeeds, and a non-silent artifact budget that bounds attachment size without ever dropping output silently. We release a labelled corpus of 474 GPU training logs across 15 failure classes and a reproducible evaluation harness. On the twelve hardware-reproduced classes, the ordered-rule classifier reaches 0.997 macro-F1, against 0.830 for unordered keyword matching and 0.133 for exit-code inspection. Wrapper overhead is a constant approximately 3ms per job; the pre-launch guarantee preserves a log where a shell redirect yields nothing; and across all 15 failure modes the wrapper returns the child's exit code unchanged even when the SMTP relay is unreachable.

AI.tldr: GPUAlert is a lightweight command-line wrapper that monitors GPU training jobs, providing structured failure notifications with classified causes, durable logs, and output artifacts — achieving 0.997 macro-F1 on failure classification with negligible (~3ms) overhead.
AI.motivation: GPU training jobs fail frequently (~40% on large production clusters), but operators often learn of failures hours later. Existing solutions require script modification and cloud connectivity (experiment trackers) or provide only a single-line status with no cause or logs (scheduler mail hooks). A reliable, low-friction failure notification system is needed.
AI.method: The authors build GPUAlert, a process-boundary wrapper organized around three reliability primitives: (1) a pre-launch log guarantee that establishes durable log storage before the child process can crash; (2) notifier isolation ensuring the wrapper's exit code is a pure function of the child's status, independent of email delivery success; and (3) a non-silent artifact budget that bounds attachment size without silently dropping output. Failure classification uses an ordered-rule classifier trained on a labelled corpus of 474 GPU training logs spanning 15 failure classes.
AI.result: The ordered-rule classifier achieves 0.997 macro-F1 on 12 hardware-reproduced failure classes, substantially outperforming unordered keyword matching (0.830) and exit-code inspection alone (0.133). The wrapper incurs a constant ~3ms overhead per job. The pre-launch guarantee preserves logs where a shell redirect captures nothing. Across all 15 failure modes, the wrapper faithfully returns the child's exit code even when the SMTP relay is unreachable.
AI.conclusion: GPUAlert demonstrates that a minimally invasive, process-level wrapper with carefully designed reliability primitives can provide robust, classified failure notifications for GPU training jobs without modifying training code, addressing a practical pain point in production ML infrastructure.

title: The Wiola Architecture for Efficient Small Language Models
summary: We present Wiola, a fully original Small Language Model (SLM) architecture built from first principles, sharing no structural lineage with any existing model family including GPT, LLaMA, Mistral, or Falcon.
