Wiola introduces five independently novel components: (i) Spiral Rotary Positional Encoding (SRPE), which embeds token positions on a three-dimensional helical manifold combining absolute, relative, and hierarchical positional signals; (ii) Gated Cross-Layer Attention (GCLA), providing each decoder layer with soft cross-attention access to compressed summaries of two preceding layers for inter-layer coherence; (iii) Adaptive Token Merging (ATM), which dynamically merges se mantically redundant adjacent tokens in middle network layers to reduce attention complexity without information loss; (iv) Dual Stream Feed-Forward (DSFF), replacing the conventional MLP with two parallel streams fused by a learned per-dimension gate; and (v) WiolaRMSNorm, a modified normalisation introducing a per-dimension learned offset vector that prevents representation collapse. We provide complete mathematical derivations, architectural block diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic comparisons against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral. Wiola is released in four sizes (120M, 360M, 700M, and 1.5B parameters) and is fully compatible with the HuggingFace Transformers ecosystem, with all 22 architectural unit tests passing.

AI.tldr: Wiola is a novel Small Language Model (SLM) architecture built from scratch with five original components: Spiral Rotary Positional Encoding, Gated Cross-Layer Attention, Adaptive Token Merging, Dual Stream Feed-Forward, and WiolaRMSNorm. It is released in four sizes (120M–1.5B params), fully compatible with HuggingFace Transformers, and benchmarked against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral.
AI.motivation: To design a fully original SLM architecture from first principles that shares no structural lineage with existing model families (GPT, LLaMA, Mistral, Falcon), introducing independent novel components that each address known limitations in transformer design — positional encoding expressiveness, inter-layer information flow, attention complexity, feed-forward capacity, and normalization stability.
AI.method: Wiola integrates five novel components: (1) SRPE embeds positions on a 3D helical manifold capturing absolute, relative, and hierarchical signals; (2) GCLA gives each decoder layer soft cross-attention to compressed summaries of two preceding layers; (3) ATM dynamically merges semantically redundant adjacent tokens in middle layers to reduce attention complexity; (4) DSFF replaces the standard MLP with two parallel feed-forward streams fused via a learned per-dimension gate; (5) WiolaRMSNorm adds a per-dimension learned offset vector to RMSNorm to prevent representation collapse. The paper provides full mathematical derivations, block diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic comparisons. Four model sizes are released with 22 architectural unit tests passing.
AI.result: The paper reports systematic comparisons against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral, with all 22 architectural unit tests passing. Wiola is fully compatible with the HuggingFace Transformers ecosystem across all four released model sizes (120M, 360M, 700M, and 1.5B parameters).
AI.conclusion: Wiola demonstrates that a fully original SLM architecture, designed from first principles without inheriting structural design choices from existing model families, can achieve functional completeness and ecosystem compatibility. The five independently novel components each provide targeted architectural improvements, and the full test suite compliance with HuggingFace Transformers confirms practical deployability.

title: Kara: Efficient Reasoning LLM Serving via Sliding-Window KV Cache Compression
summary: Reasoning language models often generate long chain-of-thought (CoT), which accumulates a massive KV cache during the decoding phase and incurs high decoding latency and limited throughput. To address these issues, KV cache compression has emerged as a promising technique for reducing memory overhead by selectively removing unimportant KV pairs while preserving useful ones for subsequent decoding. Nevertheless, we identify two key limitations in existing KV cache compression methods: 1) their threshold-triggered compression policy may provide limited throughput improvement or even reduce throughput, and may fully eliminate KV pairs from certain blocks of the sequence, potentially worsening information loss. 2) they typically retain either isolated KV pairs or fixed-size chunks with rigid boundaries, failing to preserve important flexible-sized chunks at arbitrary token positions. To overcome these limitations, we propose Kara, a sliding-window KV cache compression method that performs decoding-time compression by operating only on the recently generated context. Kara leverages bidirectional attention to score and select informative KV pairs in the window. To enable flexible preservation of important semantic information, we design a Token2Chunk module to expand a subset of selected KV pairs into chunks. Furthermore, we adapt Kara to PagedAttention and develop KvLLM, an inference framework built upon vLLM, which reduces KV cache memory usage and effectively improves output throughput. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements of proposed Kara and KvLLM.

AI.tldr: Kara introduces a sliding-window KV cache compression method that operates on recently generated context during decoding, using bidirectional attention for KV pair selection and a Token2Chunk module for flexible chunk preservation. Integrated into vLLM as KvLLM, it improves throughput while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Existing KV cache compression methods suffer from two limitations: (1) threshold-triggered compression policies can hurt throughput and risk eliminating entire blocks, causing information loss; (2) they preserve only isolated KV pairs or rigid fixed-size chunks, failing to retain flexible-sized semantic chunks at arbitrary positions.
AI.method: Kara employs a sliding-window approach that compresses only recently generated context during decoding. It uses bidirectional attention to score and select informative KV pairs within the window. A Token2Chunk module expands selected KV pairs into variable-sized chunks for flexible semantic preservation. The method is adapted to PagedAttention and implemented as KvLLM, an inference framework built on vLLM.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements of both Kara and the KvLLM inference framework, with reduced KV cache memory usage and effectively improved output throughput.
AI.conclusion: Kara addresses critical shortcomings of prior KV cache compression techniques by enabling decoding-time, sliding-window compression with flexible chunk preservation, and its integration into vLLM (KvLLM) delivers practical throughput gains without sacrificing model performance.

title: Fixed-Set Robustness in Programming by Example: Example Corruption and Semantic Partition Recovery
summary: Programming-by-example systems infer programs from a small set of input-output examples. Robust PBE work usually models wrong examples as samples from a stochastic noise process and then minimizes an expected or empirical loss. This paper studies a different failure mode: an adversary who sees the synthesizer and chooses the examples whose corruption most damages the returned program. We formalize fixed-set worst-case corruption for finite PBE version spaces, implement exact-within-bounded-pool and heuristic corruption searches for a string-transformation DSL, and introduce version-space partition aggregation (VPA), a defense that synthesizes on disjoint example groups and votes by semantic signatures. The central claim is deliberately bounded and partly negative: low-margin PBE tasks have an adversarial robustness dimension that random-typo and noisy-PBE evaluations miss, while semantic partition aggregation helps only when the clean semantics keep a partition vote margin, which often fails on realistic tasks. Evidence from curated/generated DSL tasks, accepted public SyGuS PBE_SLIA slices, SYNTRA Playgol v2, and noisy-PBE objective baselines supports that boundary. One curated edit flips all 8 spike tasks while 200-trial typo, DSL-pool, and distance-matched random controls succeed on 10.3%, 11.0%, and 16.7%; generated margin-1 rows flip under budget 1 yet VPA recovers them; on public SyGuS the vote margin is near one, so an adaptive attacker drives VPA accuracy to zero; accepted public SyGuS slices move across exact-within-pool budget boundaries; and Playgol shows positive paired-bootstrap gaps against typo and same-pool random controls on the 141 accepted rows. A small exact-output prompt harness over 20 controlled margin-1 tasks shows the same qualitative clean-to-attacked pattern across local and API models, while it is treated as a scope check, not a broad LLM benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes adversarial corruption in programming-by-example (PBE) systems, where an attacker strategically selects worst-case examples to corrupt, rather than relying on random noise. The authors propose version-space partition aggregation (VPA) as a defense, but find its effectiveness is limited to tasks with sufficient vote margins, revealing a fundamental adversarial robustness dimension that standard noisy-PBE evaluations miss.
AI.motivation: Existing PBE robustness research models wrong examples as stochastic noise and minimizes expected loss. The paper argues this misses a critical failure mode: an adaptive adversary who understands the synthesizer and deliberately chooses which examples to corrupt for maximum damage. This adversarial perspective on PBE had not been formalized or systematically studied.
AI.method: The authors (1) formalize fixed-set worst-case corruption for finite PBE version spaces, (2) implement exact-within-bounded-pool and heuristic corruption search algorithms for a string-transformation DSL, and (3) introduce version-space partition aggregation (VPA) — a defense that synthesizes programs on disjoint example groups and votes by semantic signatures. Evaluation spans curated/generated DSL tasks, SyGuS PBE_SLIA benchmarks, SYNTRA Playgol v2, and a small LLM prompt harness as a scope check.
AI.result: Adversarial corruption is devastating: one curated edit flips all 8 spike tasks, while random controls succeed far less (typo: 10.3%, DSL-pool: 11.0%, distance-matched: 16.7%). Generated margin-1 rows flip under budget 1, but VPA recovers them. However, on public SyGuS where vote margins are near one, adaptive attackers drive VPA accuracy to zero. Playgol shows positive paired-bootstrap gaps against typo and same-pool random controls on 141 accepted rows. LLM scope checks reproduce the same clean-to-attacked pattern on 20 controlled margin-1 tasks.
AI.conclusion: Low-margin PBE tasks exhibit an adversarial robustness dimension that random-noise evaluations cannot capture. VPA helps only when clean semantics retain a partition vote margin — a condition that often fails on realistic tasks. The central claim is deliberately bounded and partly negative: adversarial robustness in PBE is real but defenses remain fragile.

title: Planning over Matrix-Factorization MDPs for Candidate Generation
comment: Accepted to the 5th Workshop on End-to-End Customer Journey Optimization at KDD 2026. 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: For a recommender service, we view the customer journey as a chain of item recommendations: a useful item changes the user's state and therefore what should be retrieved next. Standard matrix-factorization retrieval ignores this -- it builds one user vector and returns the top-$K$ items by a static score, treating them as independent. We ask a narrow question: when is it worth planning over the user-state dynamics that fold-in induces? To answer it we propose casting top-$K$ retrieval as an MDP over the implicit-ALS posterior $(A^{-1},u)$, where an action is an item and the transition is a closed-form rank-one fold-in, and the trajectory reward combines a relevance similarity with a posterior-alignment term. Under the same fixed embeddings we compare static retrieval, one-step planning, and horizon-$K$ MCTS across five datasets and two protocols: a per-user leave-last-$n$ split and a stricter global time split. Dynamics-aware planning tends to overcome static retrieval on all datasets under leave-last-$n$, and the gains hold on MovieLens-1M and the VK-LSVD slices under the global time split. A single step of lookahead already captures most of the gain, so the lightweight planning layer turns static top-$K$ scoring into a short decision and improves retrieval over fixed collaborative-filtering embeddings, with no retraining and no change to the representation. These gains depend on measuring relevance with cosine rather than inner-product similarity, which is otherwise entangled with item popularity.

AI.tldr: The paper frames top-K recommendation retrieval as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) over the implicit-ALS posterior, where recommending an item transitions the user state via a rank-one fold-in. Using the same fixed embeddings, dynamics-aware planning (particularly one-step lookahead) outperforms static retrieval across multiple datasets, with cosine similarity proving crucial for disentangling relevance from item popularity.
AI.motivation: Standard matrix-factorization retrieval treats recommendations as independent by building a single static user vector and scoring items independently, ignoring that each recommended item changes the user's state and thus what should be retrieved next. The authors aim to determine when planning over these user-state dynamics is beneficial compared to static top-K retrieval.
AI.method: The method casts top-K retrieval as an MDP over the implicit-ALS posterior (A^{-1}, u), where actions are items selected for recommendation and state transitions are computed via a closed-form rank-one fold-in operation. The trajectory reward combines relevance similarity with a posterior-alignment term. Three strategies are compared under the same fixed embeddings: static retrieval, one-step planning (lookahead), and horizon-K Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Evaluation uses five datasets under two protocols: per-user leave-last-n split and a stricter global time split.
AI.result: Dynamics-aware planning surpasses static retrieval on all datasets under the leave-last-n split. Gains persist on MovieLens-1M and VK-LSVD slices under the stricter global time split. A single step of lookahead captures most of the improvement, making the approach lightweight. Critically, these gains require measuring relevance with cosine similarity rather than inner-product similarity, as inner-product is confounded with item popularity.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight planning layer that performs a short lookahead over user-state dynamics can improve retrieval over fixed collaborative-filtering embeddings without retraining or altering the representation. The approach is most effective when relevance is measured via cosine similarity, which avoids popularity bias inherent in inner-product scoring.

title: AgentsCAD: Automated Design for Manufacturing of FDM Parts via Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning and Geometric Feature Recognition
summary: Parts manufactured with Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) often require Design for Additive Manufacturing (DFAM) modifications to ensure printability, structural integrity, and reduced post-processing. Current slicers identify defects such as steep overhangs but are unable to modify the underlying geometry. This work presents AgentsCAD, a multi-agent system that bridges raw boundary-representation (B-Rep) geometry and Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning to automate targeted DFM. The workflow begins by parsing a STEP file. The agentic system detects overhangs above a 45°threshold, constructs a face-adjacency topology graph, and optionally injects semantic feature labels from a GraphSAGE model trained on MFCAD++ (59,665 parts), before dispatching a Claude Sonnet design-reasoning agent that recommends reorientations, fillets, chamfers, and similar modifications. A GPT-4o vision-language verifier inspects rendered views to confirm geometric integrity. Outputs include a modified STEP file and a human-readable report. A test case on a birdhouse model demonstrates that the system correctly diagnoses overhangs, selects appropriate defect mitigation strategies, and proposes physically valid corrections, partially solving the geometry-to-language translation problem central to LLM-driven CAD modification.

AI.tldr: AgentsCAD is a multi-agent LLM-driven system that automates Design for Additive Manufacturing (DFAM) for FDM parts by parsing STEP files, detecting overhangs via topology graphs, using a GraphSAGE model for semantic labeling, and leveraging Claude Sonnet and GPT-4o for modification recommendations and visual verification.
AI.motivation: Current FDM slicers can identify printability defects like steep overhangs but cannot modify the underlying geometry. There exists a "geometry-to-language translation problem" that hinders LLM-driven CAD modification. The authors aim to bridge B-Rep geometry with LLM reasoning to automate targeted DFAM corrections.
AI.method: A multi-agent pipeline: (1) STEP file parsing; (2) overhang detection using a 45° threshold and face-adjacency topology graph construction; (3) optional semantic feature labeling via a GraphSAGE model trained on MFCAD++ (59,665 parts); (4) a Claude Sonnet design-reasoning agent that recommends reorientations, fillets, chamfers, and similar modifications; (5) a GPT-4o vision-language verifier that inspects rendered views for geometric integrity; (6) output of a modified STEP file and human-readable report.
AI.result: A test case on a birdhouse model demonstrated that the system correctly diagnoses overhangs, selects appropriate defect mitigation strategies, and proposes physically valid corrections, partially solving the geometry-to-language translation problem.
AI.conclusion: AgentsCAD demonstrates a viable approach for LLM-driven DFAM automation, successfully bridging B-Rep geometry and natural language reasoning to perform targeted geometry modifications that slicers alone cannot achieve.

title: OrchestrXR: A Multi-Agent System for Idea-to-Prototype XR Study Authoring
summary: Extended Reality (XR) has become an important interaction paradigm in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI). XR studies are used to investigate interaction, perception, and user behavior in immersive environments, and typically involve experimental tasks, 3D scenes, and interactive logic. However, turning an initial XR study idea into a runnable prototype remains fragmented across study design, scene construction, and interaction implementation. We present OrchestrXR, a multi-agent human-AI workflow for early-stage idea-to-prototype XR study authoring. Rather than treating XR study creation as one-shot generation, OrchestrXR supports a controllable workflow across study design, scene generation, and interaction generation through structured schemas, multi-agent orchestration, and interactive human-agent interfaces, producing a Unity-based prototype from a researcher's idea. A user study with 12 XR researchers suggests that OrchestrXR provides effective support for early-stage XR study authoring with strong intent preservation across stages.

AI.tldr: OrchestrXR is a multi-agent human-AI workflow that helps XR researchers transform study ideas into Unity-based prototypes through structured, controllable stages: study design, scene generation, and interaction generation.
AI.motivation: Current XR study authoring is fragmented across disconnected stages—study design, 3D scene construction, and interaction implementation—lacking an integrated pipeline to move from initial idea to runnable prototype efficiently.
AI.method: OrchestrXR employs a multi-agent architecture with structured schemas and interactive human-agent interfaces across three stages: (1) study design generation from researcher ideas, (2) 3D scene generation, and (3) interaction logic generation, culminating in a Unity-based prototype. The workflow is controllable and iterative rather than one-shot.
AI.result: A user study with 12 XR researchers demonstrated that OrchestrXR effectively supports early-stage XR study authoring, with strong preservation of researcher intent across all three stages of the workflow.
AI.conclusion: OrchestrXR demonstrates that a structured, multi-agent human-AI workflow can bridge the gap between XR research ideas and functional prototypes, offering a promising direction for integrated XR study authoring tools.

title: An alternative approach towards attacks against fully-split PLWE instances
summary: In the present work we address some key questions regarding the generalization of root-based attacks presented in a recent work by the authors. In particular, we analyze potential root-based attacks extensions via the construction of explicit isomorphisms from vulnerable instances, and provide a formal proof that this approach will not yield any new vulnerabilities under a fully-split setting. To do so, we first construct an explicit isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings and polynomial rings where previous attacks apply and show that the application of such an isomorphism will always distort the samples in a way that the resulting samples cannot be used to distinguish. Then, we prove that any isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings must be of the form of the constructed isomorphism.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that extending root-based attacks on certain cryptographic schemes via explicit isomorphisms from fully-split polynomial rings to vulnerable instances will not yield new vulnerabilities, because any such isomorphism necessarily distorts samples in a way that prevents successful distinguishing attacks.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to rigorously determine whether root-based attacks from their prior work can be generalized by constructing explicit isomorphisms from vulnerable polynomial ring instances to fully-split settings, thereby potentially exposing new weaknesses in lattice-based cryptographic schemes.
AI.method: The authors first construct an explicit isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings and polynomial rings where prior root-based attacks are applicable. They then demonstrate that applying this isomorphism always distorts samples such that the resulting samples lose their distinguishing power. Finally, they prove that any isomorphism between fully-split polynomial rings must necessarily take this constructed form.
AI.result: The constructed isomorphism always distorts samples in a way that renders them useless for distinguishing. Furthermore, all isomorphisms between fully-split polynomial rings are of the same form, implying no alternative isomorphism can bypass this limitation.
AI.conclusion: Under the fully-split setting, no new vulnerabilities can be derived from root-based attacks via isomorphism-based extensions, formally closing off this avenue of attack generalization.

title: Adoption and Impact of Command-Line AI Coding Agents: A Study of Microsoft's Early 2026 Rollout of Claude Code and GitHub Copilot CLI
summary: Organizations rolling out agentic command line tools like Anthropic's Claude Code and GitHub's Copilot CLI need to know who will try them, who will keep using them, and whether the tools produce enough output to justify their cost. At organizational scale, token spend can run into millions of dollars annually, so misreading adoption, retention, or impact can make a rollout expensive without changing engineering velocity. Studying tens of thousands of engineers at Microsoft over its early-2026 rollout, we find that first use spread primarily through social networks, retention was associated more with engineers' coding activity than with demographics, and adopters merged roughly 24% more pull requests than they would have otherwise. We use merged pull requests as our proxy for output -- acknowledging that a merged PR is not the same as the value it delivers -- and the lift persists across our four-month window. These results suggest that CLI coding agents are neither uniformly adopted nor mere novelty effects and that organizations should treat visible peer use as central to rollout strategy.

AI.tldr: A study of Microsoft's 2026 rollout of CLI coding agents (Anthropic's Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI) across tens of thousands of engineers found that adoption spread via social networks, retention correlated with coding activity rather than demographics, and adopters merged ~24% more pull requests — with the lift persisting over four months.
AI.motivation: Organizations deploying agentic CLI tools at scale face high token costs (potentially millions annually). They need to understand who adopts, who persists, and whether these tools genuinely boost engineering output to justify the investment and avoid expensive rollouts that fail to improve velocity.
AI.method: Observational study of tens of thousands of Microsoft engineers during an early-2026 rollout. Adoption spread was analyzed through social network patterns, retention was correlated with coding activity and demographic variables, and output impact was measured using merged pull requests as a proxy, compared against a counterfactual baseline over a four-month window.
AI.result: First use spread primarily through social networks. Retention was more strongly associated with engineers' coding activity than with demographics. Adopters merged approximately 24% more pull requests than they otherwise would have, and this lift persisted across the entire four-month observation window.
AI.conclusion: CLI coding agents are neither uniformly adopted nor mere novelty effects. Organizations should treat visible peer use as a central component of rollout strategy to drive adoption and realize sustained productivity gains.

title: Agent4cs: A Multi-agent System for Code Summarization in Large Hierarchical Codebases
comment: Accepted to the main track of the 23rd European Conference on Multi-Agent Systems (EUMAS 2026)
summary: Understanding large, complex codebases, especially those with obfuscated structures and incomplete documentation, remains a significant challenge. Existing code summarization solutions often rely on a single language model or coding assistant like Claude Code, and treat source code as flat text, underutilizing the rich interdependencies and hierarchical information within a repository. To address these shortcomings, we propose Agent4cs - a multi-agent framework that summarizes large codebases in a bottom-up fashion, where a summarization agent focuses on producing robust summaries; a keyword-extraction agent proactively identifies critical information from subfolders; and a quality-assurance agent iteratively refines the outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness. Evaluated on 7 frontier models, Agent4cs improves semantic consistency across all folder levels by average 8% compared to two structured prompting baselines with code segments. Furthermore, extensive evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates up to 38% gains in normalized keyword coverage rate over the same baselines.

AI.tldr: Agent4cs is a multi-agent framework that summarizes large codebases bottom-up using three specialized agents (summarization, keyword-extraction, quality-assurance), achieving 8% better semantic consistency and up to 38% gains in keyword coverage over structured prompting baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing code summarization tools treat source code as flat text and rely on single models, failing to exploit repository-level interdependencies and hierarchical structure. This is especially problematic for large, obfuscated, or poorly documented codebases.
AI.method: A bottom-up multi-agent framework with three agents: a summarization agent for robust summaries, a keyword-extraction agent that identifies critical information from subfolders, and a quality-assurance agent that iteratively refines outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness.
AI.result: Agent4cs improved semantic consistency by an average of 8% across all folder levels compared to two structured prompting baselines. Normalized keyword coverage rate improved by up to 38% on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: A multi-agent, bottom-up approach that explicitly leverages repository hierarchy and inter-file dependencies significantly outperforms flat-text, single-model baselines for codebase summarization.

title: SPARCLE: SPeaker-aware Aligned Representations via Contrastive Language Embeddings
summary:
Recent advances in speech synthesis have shifted from phoneme representations to direct grapheme modeling. While phonemes address the one-to-many mapping between text and acoustics, they rely on grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) systems that fail to capture speaker-specific acoustic variation. Prior work demonstrates that grapheme-based models outperform phoneme-based systems at scale, but not in low-resource settings.
  In this paper, we propose SPARCLE, a speaker-aware grapheme representation model that enriches characters with their precise acoustic realizations. SPARCLE is trained with a contrastive objective to align graphemes with corresponding Wav2Vec2 acoustic representations while conditioned on speaker identity. The resulting model serves as a replacement to G2P systems for downstream text-to-speech (TTS) tasks. We demonstrate that SPARCLE improves generation quality, reducing word error rates by half in extreme low-resource settings compared to standard grapheme-based models.

AI.tldr: SPARCLE is a speaker-aware grapheme representation model that uses contrastive learning to align graphemes with Wav2Vec2 acoustic representations conditioned on speaker identity, replacing G2P in TTS and achieving substantial WER reductions in low-resource settings.
AI.motivation: Grapheme-based TTS models outperform phoneme-based ones at scale but underperform in low-resource settings. Phoneme-based systems depend on G2P systems that fail to capture speaker-specific acoustic variation. There is a need for grapheme representations that encode precise, speaker-conditioned acoustic realizations without relying on G2P.
AI.method: SPARCLE is trained with a contrastive objective that aligns grapheme (character) representations with corresponding acoustic representations from Wav2Vec2, conditioned on speaker identity. The resulting model serves as a drop-in replacement for G2P systems in downstream TTS pipelines.
AI.result: SPARCLE reduces word error rates (WER) by half in extreme low-resource settings compared to standard grapheme-based TTS models, significantly improving generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Speaker-conditioned grapheme representations learned via contrastive alignment with self-supervised acoustic features (Wav2Vec2) can effectively replace G2P in TTS, particularly benefiting low-resource scenarios where standard grapheme models struggle.

title: Domain Knowledge Based Temporal-Spatial Graph Convolution Network for ECG Recognition
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Presented at ICONIP 2024, Auckland, New Zealand. Published in LNCS 15290, Springer, 2025
summary: In light of strides in Arti cial Intelligence (AI) and its wide spread application, challenges persist in the interpretability of AI models, particularly within specialized domains like healthcare, such as electro cardiograph (ECG) recognition. Rather than relying solely on end-to-end convolutional neural networks, this paper introduces a novel approach using a domain knowledge-based graph convolution network for ECG recognition. Key landmarks points of PRQST, vital to ECG interpreta tion, are incorporated as domain knowledge. The double-stream directed graph is employed to model both intra and inter ECG cycles. Speci cally, spatial directed graphs capture the positional relationships among key points, while temporal directed graphs delineate temporal dependencies between adjacent cycles in extended ECG sequences. Experimental re sults on the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset, which speci cally classify ECG into nine categories, prove the e cacy of the proposed model. The overall average F1 score is 88.1%, the average F1 score of rare categories is 76.3%, both outperform the state-of-the-art models. The introduction of domain knowledge did enhance the detec tion performance, especially for rare categories.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a domain-knowledge-based graph convolutional network for ECG recognition that uses key PRQST landmarks and double-stream directed graphs to model intra-cycle spatial relationships and inter-cycle temporal dependencies, achieving state-of-the-art F1 scores on a nine-category ECG classification benchmark, particularly improving rare category detection.
AI.motivation: Despite advances in AI, interpretability remains a challenge in specialized domains like healthcare, particularly ECG recognition. The authors aim to move beyond end-to-end convolutional neural networks by explicitly incorporating clinical domain knowledge (PRQST landmarks) to improve both performance and interpretability.
AI.method: A double-stream directed graph convolutional network is proposed: (1) spatial directed graphs capture positional relationships among key PRQST landmark points within a single ECG cycle; (2) temporal directed graphs model dependencies between adjacent cycles in extended ECG sequences. Domain knowledge is encoded through these key landmarks rather than raw waveform input.
AI.result: On the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset (nine categories), the model achieves an overall average F1 score of 88.1% and an average F1 score of 76.3% on rare categories, outperforming state-of-the-art models. Domain knowledge incorporation notably enhanced detection of rare categories.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating domain-specific knowledge (PRQST landmarks) via graph convolutional networks significantly improves ECG classification performance, especially for underrepresented categories, demonstrating the value of hybridizing clinical expertise with deep learning architectures.

title: Bringing Agentic Search to Earth Observation Data Discovery
summary: NASA and its data centers hold thousands of geoscience datasets and tools like Worldview, Giovanni, the Science Discovery Engine, and Harmony. Finding the right one is hard even for domain experts. We present an agentic search system, deployed as a public service for the geoscience community, that takes a natural-language research query and returns the matching datasets and tools. We demonstrate that, in the era of large language models, the latent value of knowledge graphs (KGs) can be substantially amplified through agentic search. From the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph (NASA EO-KG) we derive NASA-EO-Bench, an open benchmark of 47k query-dataset pairs (21k task-based queries). A neural scorer fine-tuned on NASA-EO-Bench beats cosine and BM25 baselines. Further combining it with BM25 via score fusion raises both Recall@10 (R@10) and MRR by over 5x. On top of this supervised pipeline, we add a zero-shot agentic reranking stage that, without any additional training, lifts MRR by 28% on a stratified N=200 subset, showing that LLM reasoning is complementary to supervised retrieval.

AI.tldr: NASA developed an agentic search system that uses a fine-tuned neural scorer on a knowledge-graph-derived benchmark (NASA-EO-Bench, 47k pairs) combined with BM25 and a zero-shot LLM reranking stage, achieving over 5x improvement in Recall@10 and MRR over baselines for discovering geoscience datasets and tools via natural-language queries.
AI.motivation: NASA hosts thousands of geoscience datasets and tools, but discovering the right resource is difficult even for domain experts. The authors aim to leverage large language models and knowledge graphs to build an accessible, high-accuracy search system that accepts natural-language research queries and returns relevant datasets and tools.
AI.method: The authors derive NASA-EO-Bench, a benchmark of 47k query-dataset pairs (including 21k task-based queries), from the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. A neural scorer is fine-tuned on this benchmark, outperforming cosine and BM25 baselines. Score fusion combining the neural scorer with BM25 yields substantial gains. A zero-shot agentic reranking stage, using LLM reasoning without additional training, is added on top of the supervised pipeline to further improve ranking quality.
AI.result: The neural scorer beats cosine and BM25 baselines. Score fusion (neural + BM25) raises both Recall@10 and MRR by over 5x. The zero-shot agentic reranking stage lifts MRR by 28% on a stratified N=200 subset, demonstrating that LLM reasoning complements supervised retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge graphs, when combined with supervised neural retrieval and zero-shot LLM-based reranking in an agentic architecture, can substantially amplify latent value for domain-specific search. The system is deployed as a public service for the geoscience community.

title: Adoption and Ecosystem Health: A Longitudinal Analysis of Open-Source Multi-Agent Frameworks
summary: Since ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, open-source agentic frameworks have proliferated, making framework selection important for engineering teams while obscured by popularity signals such as GitHub stars. This paper analyzes 15 major open-source AI agent framework repositories from late 2022 to early 2026, using 808,042 stars, 73,997 pull requests, 86,241 commits, and 987,330 user profiles to assess ecosystem health across awareness, adoption, and retention. Three findings emerge. First, headline popularity is unreliable. Star counts reflect hype cycles and inorganic activity. AutoGPT gained 111,967 stars in one month but converted fewer than 9 contributors per 1,000 stars, defined as contributor density in this research, compared with LangChain's 41. Lower-profile frameworks such as Pydantic-AI show higher contributor density, indicating deeper adoption. Second, mapping awareness against adoption shows that visibility and engagement diverge. MetaGPT and LangFlow have contributor density ratios below 5 even with their high visibility. Openai-agents-python's limited contributor base suggests institutional backing alone does not ensure community depth. By analyzing cross-framework contribution, we discover that LangChain functions as a shared infrastructure, attracting 82.5% of cross-ecosystem contributors. Third, retention drops most steeply in the first 30 days of initial contribution and stabilizes near 90 days. Overall, ecosystem health is better measured by contributor density, cross-ecosystem engagement, and retention than by stars alone. These metrics offer teams a more robust basis for framework evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the health of 15 open-source AI agent frameworks using metrics beyond GitHub stars—namely contributor density, cross-ecosystem engagement, and contributor retention—revealing that star counts are unreliable proxies for genuine adoption and community depth.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of open-source AI agent frameworks since ChatGPT's launch has made framework selection difficult for engineering teams, who may be misled by popularity signals like GitHub stars. The study aims to provide more robust, evidence-based metrics for evaluating ecosystem health.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 15 major open-source AI agent framework repositories from late 2022 to early 2026, using a dataset comprising 808,042 stars, 73,997 pull requests, 86,241 commits, and 987,330 user profiles. They assessed ecosystem health across three dimensions: awareness (stars), adoption (contributor density — contributors per 1,000 stars), and retention (contributor longevity). Cross-framework contribution analysis was also conducted.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Star counts reflect hype cycles and are unreliable — AutoGPT gained ~112K stars in one month but had <9 contributors per 1K stars vs. LangChain's 41; lower-profile frameworks like Pydantic-AI showed higher contributor density. (2) Visibility and engagement diverge — MetaGPT and LangFlow had contributor density ratios below 5 despite high visibility; OpenAI's agent-python demonstrated institutional backing alone doesn't ensure community depth. LangChain functions as shared infrastructure, attracting 82.5% of cross-ecosystem contributors. (3) Contributor retention drops most sharply in the first 30 days and stabilizes near 90 days.
AI.conclusion: Ecosystem health is better measured by contributor density, cross-ecosystem engagement, and retention than by stars alone. These metrics offer engineering teams a more robust basis for framework evaluation and selection.

title: Made to Feel: How Designers Bring Emotions into Affective Visualization
summary: Affective visualization is increasingly studied in visualization research, yet how designers bring emotions into their visualization work remains unexplored. This paper addresses this gap through semi-structured interviews with 15 visualization practitioners. Using hybrid thematic analysis, we identify: (1) three functions that emotions can serve for viewers (entry, engagement, outcome); (2) three facets of how designers work with emotion (data, design, audience), along with design strategies; and (3) ethical considerations in the design process. We also observe that affective intent often emerges during the design process rather than being planned from the outset, and that emotional impact arises from accumulated design choices rather than isolated visual elements. Finally, we highlight evaluation as a key challenge identified by our participants.

AI.tldr: Through interviews with 15 visualization practitioners, this study uncovers how designers intentionally or emergently incorporate emotion into visualization work, identifying three viewer-facing functions of emotion, three practitioner-facing design facets, ethical considerations, and key challenges like evaluation.
AI.motivation: Despite growing interest in affective visualization, there is a gap in understanding how practitioners actually bring emotions into their visualization design process. This paper aims to fill that gap by investigating real-world design practices.
AI.method: Semi-structured interviews with 15 visualization practitioners, analyzed using hybrid thematic analysis (combining deductive and inductive coding).
AI.result: Three viewer-oriented emotion functions (entry, engagement, outcome); three designer-oriented facets of working with emotion (data, design, audience) with corresponding strategies; ethical considerations; findings that affective intent often emerges during design rather than being pre-planned, and emotional impact stems from cumulative design choices rather than isolated elements. Evaluation is identified as a primary challenge.
AI.conclusion: Emotion in visualization is a nuanced, emergent, and cumulative aspect of practice. The paper contributes a structured framework for understanding affective design work and calls for better evaluation methods to assess emotional impact.

title: Chameleon: Recovering Cyber-Physical Systems from Memory Corruption Attacks via ML Surrogates
summary:
Cyber-physical systems (CPSs) are increasingly deployed in every aspect of our lives and can be compromised through memory corruption vulnerabilities, allowing attackers to hijack the control flow and take over the system. Existing techniques mostly focus on detecting such attacks but respond by terminating or halting execution upon attack detection, which is not acceptable in CPSs used in safety-critical tasks, as interrupted tasks can have catastrophic consequences. Other techniques replace compromised CPS components with simplified defaults that degrade system behavior, or reboot the system upon attack detection.
  We propose Chameleon, a novel framework for automatically recovering CPSs from memory corruption attacks using machine learning (ML)-based surrogates trained at compartment granularity that nearly replicate their original compartments' behavior but do not have the same memory corruption vulnerabilities. Upon attack detection, Chameleon replaces the compromised compartment with its trained surrogate. We implemented Chameleon using the LLVM compiler and evaluated its efficiency and effectiveness on seven different robotic vehicles (RVs), including simulated and real ones. We found that Chameleon can generate surrogates that closely approximate the original compartments (with an average R$^2$=0.96), successfully recover the system despite real-world memory corruption attacks unlike prior approaches, and complete their tasks while incurring low performance and memory overhead.

AI.tldr: Chameleon proposes a framework for CPS recovery from memory corruption attacks by replacing compromised compartments with ML-based surrogates that replicate original behavior without the same vulnerabilities, enabling continued operation in safety-critical tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing attack responses (termination, halting, degraded defaults, reboot) are unacceptable for safety-critical CPSs where interrupted tasks can have catastrophic consequences. A recovery mechanism that maintains functionality post-attack is needed.
AI.method: Chameleon trains ML-based surrogates at compartment granularity that approximate original compartment behavior. Upon memory corruption attack detection, the compromised compartment is transparently replaced with its pre-trained surrogate. Implemented via LLVM compiler infrastructure and evaluated on seven robotic vehicles (simulated and real).
AI.result: Surrogates achieved average R²=0.96 in approximating original compartments. Chameleon successfully recovered systems from real-world memory corruption attacks where prior approaches failed, completing tasks with low performance and memory overhead.
AI.conclusion: ML-based compartment surrogates provide a viable, low-overhead recovery mechanism for CPSs under memory corruption attacks, enabling continued safe operation without system termination or degradation.

title: Risk Architecture for AI-Native Engineering Teams: An Organizational Framework for Agentic System Governance
summary: Engineering management research has produced mature frameworks for software risk: ownership by feature, escalation by severity, and assurance by test coverage. These frameworks implicitly assume deterministic behavior, discrete and auditable change events, and clear component-to-owner mappings. Teams that build and operate agentic AI systems violate all three assumptions at once: outputs are probabilistic, systems take autonomous multi-step actions, and the risk surface mutates silently between deployments. Existing AI risk literature addresses this from above (policy frameworks such as the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001) or below (threat taxonomies such as OWASP's agentic AI guidance), but not at the layer where an engineering manager (EM) operates: roles, decision rights, and escalation structures. This paper contributes (i) a seven-dimension profile distinguishing pure software-engineering, hybrid, and AI-native teams; (ii) a six-cluster failure-mode taxonomy including a previously unarticulated cluster, dependency-boundary determinism mismatch; and (iii) a synthetic framework-adequacy methodology scoring how well each profile's risk architecture detects, contains, and escalates a defined scenario set. Because the object of study is framework adequacy rather than human behavior, the evaluation yields derived rather than observed coverage claims. Coverage degrades as teams move from pure software engineering to AI-native operation, monotonically in the median and abruptly in the count of uncovered, high-consequence failures appearing only at the AI-native step. The degradation concentrates in specific failure-mode categories, and the most severe, least-covered failures arise not inside AI-native teams but at the organizational boundary where their probabilistic outputs are consumed by determinism-assuming dependencies.

AI.tldr: Traditional software risk frameworks (ownership, escalation, assurance) assume deterministic, auditable systems. Agentic AI systems violate these assumptions. This paper bridges the gap between high-level AI policy and low-level threat taxonomies by providing engineering managers with: (i) a team-profile typology, (ii) a failure-mode taxonomy including a novel "dependency-boundary determinism mismatch" cluster, and (iii) a framework-adequacy methodology showing risk coverage degrades sharply at AI-native stages, with the most severe failures occurring at organizational boundaries where probabilistic AI outputs meet deterministic dependencies.
AI.motivation: Existing software risk management frameworks implicitly assume deterministic behavior, discrete auditable changes, and clear component-to-owner mappings. Agentic AI systems violate all three: outputs are probabilistic, actions are autonomous and multi-step, and risk surfaces mutate silently. While AI risk literature exists at the policy level (NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001) and the threat-taxonomy level (OWASP agentic AI guidance), no framework addresses the operational layer where engineering managers must make decisions about roles, decision rights, and escalation structures.
AI.method: The paper develops three contributions: (1) a seven-dimension profile that distinguishes pure software-engineering teams from hybrid and AI-native teams; (2) a six-cluster failure-mode taxonomy derived from analysis of agentic AI failure patterns, including a newly identified cluster termed "dependency-boundary determinism mismatch"; and (3) a synthetic framework-adequacy methodology that scores how each team profile's risk architecture performs on detection, containment, and escalation against a defined scenario set. The evaluation produces derived (not observed) coverage claims, as the object of study is framework adequacy rather than human behavior.
AI.result: Coverage degrades monotonically in the median as teams transition from pure software engineering to hybrid to AI-native operation. An abrupt drop occurs in the count of uncovered, high-consequence failures that appear only at the AI-native step. Degradation is concentrated in specific failure-mode categories. Critically, the most severe and least-covered failures do not originate inside AI-native teams but at organizational boundaries where probabilistic AI outputs are consumed by downstream dependencies that assume determinism.
AI.conclusion: Engineering management frameworks for software risk are systematically inadequate for agentic AI systems. The highest-risk failures emerge not within AI-native teams but at the seams where their outputs meet deterministic subsystems. This implies that organizational boundary design — rather than purely internal team practices — is the critical leverage point for managing agentic AI risk.

title: When Should Service Agents Reconsider? Difficulty-Routed Control in Customer-Service Operations
summary: Autonomous customer-service agents are shifting from conversational interfaces toward operational execution roles: they retrieve firm records, apply service policies, and execute backend writes such as refunds, cancellations, exchanges, order modifications, and reservation changes. This shift creates a service-control problem: firms must keep routine service fast and low-friction while preventing operational errors on requests where customer instructions, policy constraints, firm records, and backend writes interact. We propose a difficulty-routed service-control architecture that asks when service agents should reconsider before acting. A lightweight router keeps routine sessions on a low-cost baseline path and routes operationally coupled sessions to an escalated workflow. The escalated path uses conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration to concentrate deliberation and safeguards before consequential backend writes, rather than applying additional control uniformly across all service sessions. We evaluate the architecture on human-verified retail and airline tasks from $τ^{2}$-bench. In retail, the method improves reliability consistently on service requests with operational conflict. Routing evidence shows that stronger control is directed toward conflicted requests rather than broadly applied to routine ones. Dialogue and tool-use profiles suggest that gains do not come from indiscriminate interaction expansion or broader tool chains; instead, added turns and tool calls support evidence gathering, write separation, and pre-write reconsideration. Case-level evidence shows that the escalated workflow preserves fallback plans, binds retrieved records to the correct action, sequences writes, and decomposes multi-entity requests. Airline results extend the same service-control logic to reservation operations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a difficulty-routed service-control architecture for autonomous customer-service agents. A lightweight router directs routine sessions to a low-cost baseline and escalates operationally complex sessions (involving policy, records, and backend writes) to a conflict-aware workflow with write-triggered reconsideration. Evaluated on retail and airline tasks, the method improves reliability specifically on conflicted requests without indiscriminately expanding interactions on routine cases.
AI.motivation: As customer-service agents move from conversation to operational execution (refunds, cancellations, order modifications, etc.), firms face a service-control problem: balancing fast, low-friction routine service against the risk of operational errors when customer instructions, policy constraints, firm records, and backend writes interact. The authors argue that applying uniform control across all sessions is inefficient—stronger safeguards are needed only where operational coupling creates risk.
AI.method: A difficulty-routed architecture with two components: (1) a lightweight router that classifies sessions as routine or operationally coupled, keeping routine sessions on a low-cost baseline path; (2) an escalated workflow featuring conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration, which concentrates deliberation and safeguards immediately before consequential backend writes. This avoids uniformly applying additional control across all sessions.
AI.result: Evaluated on human-verified retail and airline tasks from τ²-bench. In retail, reliability improved consistently on requests with operational conflict. Routing evidence confirmed stronger control is directed toward conflicted requests, not broadly applied. Dialogue and tool-use analysis showed gains stem from evidence gathering, write separation, and pre-write reconsideration—not indiscriminate expansion. Case-level analysis revealed the escalated workflow preserves fallback plans, binds records to correct actions, sequences writes, and decomposes multi-entity requests. Airline results extended the same logic to reservation operations.
AI.conclusion: Difficulty-based routing with write-triggered reconsideration effectively targets operational safeguards where they are needed most, improving reliability on complex service requests without sacrificing the speed and efficiency of routine interactions.

title: Breaking Safety at the Token Boundary: How BPE Tokenization Creates Exploitable Gaps in LLM Alignment
summary: Character-level perturbations bypass safety alignment in modern LLMs despite leaving prompts human-readable. We identify and test a central structural mechanism: BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words into sub-word pieces, and the three public alignment datasets we surveyed contain no intentionally fragmented inputs. The mechanism is a chain, tested end-to-end on five model families (Qwen-3-4B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B). An optimization targeting safety-token fragmentation flips the first-token refusal trigger on 80-100% of refused HarmBench prompts, with 48% of those flips producing genuinely harmful outputs (per-model 29-65%; gap-vs-behavior ROC-AUC 0.66-0.98, pooled 0.84). Activation patching localizes the disrupted signal to the last ${\sim}30\%$ of layers; an alignment-data scan finds zero fragmented prompts among 30,000 examples (positive-control recall $\geq 99\%$ at attack-relevant intensities); and targeted-mutation experiments isolate safety words as the disruption locus. On the defense side, a 68-cell grid (55 trained checkpoints) shows that no DPO configuration achieves seed- and pool-stable ASR closure on the three families with closed pool-size confounds. SFT trained on fragmented prompts closes ASR on 3/5 families but only via global collapse that raises refusal on benign prompts as well, indicating the missing distribution is necessary but not sufficient under the LoRA-16 recipe we tested. To distinguish selective repair from global collapse, we introduce Conv-Benign, a candidate paired diagnostic. All ASR claims are 3-judge-calibrated (cell rankings stable across judges; absolute levels $\pm$18pp; see App.~B.13).

AI.tldr: Character-level perturbations (e.g., symbol substitutions, spacing) fragment safety-critical words during BPE tokenization. Alignment datasets lack such fragmented inputs, causing models to fail to recognize perturbed harmful prompts. Optimization-based attacks achieve 80-100% refusal-flip rates; activation patching localizes the disruption to the last ~30% of layers. Defense experiments show DPO fails to close the attack surface, while SFT with fragmented prompts closes it only via global refusal collapse.
AI.motivation: Modern LLMs are vulnerable to character-level jailbreaking perturbations that leave prompts human-readable yet bypass safety alignment. The authors hypothesize a structural root cause: BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words into sub-word tokens, and alignment datasets contain no such fragmented inputs, creating a blind spot that attackers exploit.
AI.method: The paper tests a causal chain: (1) an optimization procedure targeting safety-token fragmentation to flip first-token refusal on HarmBench prompts; (2) activation patching to localize disrupted signals to the last ~30% of transformer layers; (3) a scan of ~30,000 alignment examples confirming zero fragmented prompts; (4) targeted-mutation experiments isolating safety words as the disruption locus. Defense evaluation uses a 68-cell grid of 55 DPO checkpoints and SFT with fragmented prompts, introducing Conv-Benign as a diagnostic to distinguish selective repair from global refusal collapse. All ASR claims use 3-judge calibration.
AI.result: The optimization flips refusal on 80-100% of refused HarmBench prompts, with 48% producing genuinely harmful outputs (per-model range: 29-65%). Gap-vs-behavior ROC-AUC ranges 0.66-0.98 (pooled 0.84). Activation patching localizes disruption to the last ~30% of layers. The alignment-data scan finds zero fragmented prompts among 30,000 examples (positive-control recall ≥99%). DPO achieves no seed- and pool-stable ASR closure across three model families. SFT with fragmented prompts closes ASR on 3/5 families but only via global collapse that also raises benign-prompt refusal. Conv-Benign successfully distinguishes selective repair from global collapse.
AI.conclusion: BPE tokenization fragmentation of safety-critical words is a central structural vulnerability in LLM safety alignment. The absence of fragmented inputs in alignment data is the root cause. Current defense methods (DPO, SFT) either fail or achieve closure only through global refusal collapse, suggesting that simply adding fragmented data is necessary but insufficient under standard fine-tuning recipes. Conv-Benign is proposed as a diagnostic to evaluate future defenses.

title: Scaling Laws for Grid-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in High Dimensions
summary: Grid-based approaches to approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search have been absent from modern scaling analyses. We present a systematic characterization of a multiprobe grid algorithm with respect to dataset size $N$ and dimensionality $d$. Our experiments reveal a previously unreported $d$-scaling crossover on the GloVe embedding family, in which multiprobe grid search maintains an approximately constant dimensional scaling exponent while other graph-, tree-, and partitioning-based methods exhibit degrading throughput. The advantage comes with near-linear query scaling in $N$, but also with lower indexing cost than competing ANN methods. Our results suggest that grid-based methods such as multiprobe grid may be competitive in rebuild-heavy or high-dimensional settings where indexing cost and dimensional robustness dictate performance. More broadly, recent work has formalized self-attention as an ANN operation. Thus, the $N$- and $d$-scaling properties of ANN algorithms may guide cost analysis of efficient transformer architectures. Code is available at: https://github.com/weiz345/MultiProbeANN.

AI.tldr: A systematic characterization of multiprobe grid search for ANN reveals a dimensional scaling crossover where it maintains constant exponent while other methods degrade, with near-linear query scaling and lower indexing cost—suggesting competitiveness in high-dimensional or rebuild-heavy settings, with implications for efficient transformer analysis.
AI.motivation: Grid-based ANN methods have been overlooked in modern scaling analyses despite their potential advantages. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically characterizing multiprobe grid performance across dataset size and dimensionality, and connecting findings to the formalization of self-attention as an ANN operation.
AI.method: Systematic empirical characterization of a multiprobe grid algorithm, measuring throughput and scaling behavior with respect to dataset size N and dimensionality d on the GloVe embedding family, with comparison against graph-based, tree-based, and partitioning-based ANN methods.
AI.result: A previously unreported d-scaling crossover was discovered: multiprobe grid maintains an approximately constant dimensional scaling exponent while competing methods show degrading throughput. Near-linear query scaling in N is achieved with lower indexing cost than alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Grid-based methods like multiprobe grid are competitive in rebuild-heavy or high-dimensional settings where indexing cost and dimensional robustness matter. The N- and d-scaling properties of ANN algorithms may also inform cost analysis of efficient transformer architectures given self-attention's formalization as ANN.

title: Hardware-Enforced Semantic Coordination for Safety-Critical Real-Time Autonomous Systems
summary:
Recent advances in agentic AI are producing increasingly complex autonomous systems that integrate large language models, world models, optimization engines, specialized neural architectures, autonomous platforms, and human operators. While much current research focuses on improving reasoning capabilities, safety-critical real-time deployment also requires bounded and verifiable coordination among heterogeneous components operating concurrently under uncertainty. Software-mediated coordination presents fundamental limitations in domains where bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees are essential.
  Hence, we propose a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture in which selected coordination semantics are implemented directly at the hardware level via field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). The approach builds on the Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) framework, which separates semantic reasoning from interaction management.
  In this approach, selected TB-CSPN coordination mechanisms are mapped onto FPGA primitives, creating a hardware-native semantic coordination layer. Focus is not on acceleration, but on enforcing temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware. Semantic reasoning remains adaptive and software-driven, while embedded coordination semantics become deterministic.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture using FPGAs to implement the TB-CSPN framework at the hardware level, separating adaptive semantic reasoning (software) from deterministic coordination semantics (hardware) to achieve bounded latency and verifiable safety guarantees for autonomous AI systems.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems integrating LLMs, world models, and autonomous platforms face fundamental limitations in software-mediated coordination—particularly in safety-critical real-time domains requiring bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees. Current research prioritizes reasoning capabilities but neglects verifiable coordination among heterogeneous concurrent components operating under uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors propose mapping selected coordination mechanisms from the Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) framework onto FPGA primitives, creating a hardware-native semantic coordination layer. This implements temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware, while keeping semantic reasoning adaptive and software-driven.
AI.result: The architecture achieves a clean separation of concerns: adaptive semantic reasoning remains software-driven, while embedded coordination semantics become deterministic and hardware-enforced. The focus is not on computational acceleration but on enforceable temporal and safety guarantees for real-time multi-agent coordination.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-enforced semantic coordination via FPGAs offers a viable path to bounded, verifiable coordination for safety-critical autonomous AI systems, addressing a gap left by purely software-mediated approaches.

title: Evaluating Glanceable Multi-Device Family Health Tracking with Smartwatches and Home Displays
comment: Accepted with minor revisions for IMWUT 2026
summary: While ubiquitous computing research has explored diverse devices for personal health tracking, we know less about multi-device designs for family informatics, where health management is inherently collaborative. To understand how families adopt and perceive ubiquitous access to shared health data across contexts, we evaluated smartwatch-only, home display-only, and combined designs for tracking moods and goals, domains central to family health behavior regulation. 44 people across 12 families alternated between these designs over nine weeks. Log analysis revealed that mood tracking and goal reporting were significantly more frequent with the home display present compared to smartwatch-only use, despite an overall decline in mood tracking over time. Tracking peaked in afternoons, dropped on weekends, and occurred 2.6X more at home, with children tracking more consistently than adults across all designs. From interview analysis, we learned how family data glanceability on smartwatches supported opportunistic tracking and awareness while apart, whereas displays reminded families to self-track and collaborate during home routines including members that avoided wearables (e.g., non-participants). Multi-device redundancy accommodated diversity in routines, mobility patterns, and device preferences among members in the same family. We discuss opportunities for multi-device family informatics that accommodates different preferences through inclusive, glanceable, and adaptable ubiquitous data sharing.

AI.tldr: A 9-week study with 12 families (44 participants) comparing smartwatch-only, home display-only, and combined designs for family mood and goal tracking. Results showed home displays significantly increased tracking frequency, children tracked more consistently than adults, and multi-device redundancy accommodated diverse family routines and preferences.
AI.motivation: Ubiquitous computing research has focused heavily on individual health tracking devices, but little is known about multi-device ecosystems for family informatics, where health management is inherently collaborative. The authors sought to understand how families adopt and perceive ubiquitous, cross-context access to shared health data.
AI.method: A within-subjects, 9-week field study with 44 participants across 12 families. Families alternated between three conditions: smartwatch-only, home display-only, and a combined smartwatch + home display design. The systems tracked moods and goals. Data collection included quantitative log analysis (tracking frequency, timing, location) and qualitative post-study interviews.
AI.result: Log analysis: (1) Mood tracking and goal reporting were significantly more frequent with the home display present vs. smartwatch-only, despite overall decline in mood tracking over time. (2) Tracking peaked in afternoons, dropped on weekends, and occurred 2.6× more at home. (3) Children tracked more consistently than adults across all conditions. Interview findings: Smartwatch glanceability enabled opportunistic tracking/awareness while apart; home displays served as reminders during shared routines and engaged non-wearable-using members. Multi-device redundancy accommodated diversity in routines, mobility, and device preferences within families.
AI.conclusion: Multi-device family informatics should be designed for inclusivity, glanceability, and adaptability in ubiquitous data sharing, accommodating heterogeneous preferences and routines among family members rather than adopting a one-device-fits-all approach.

title: From Forgeries to Foundation Models: A Systematic Survey of Identity Document Attack and Detection
summary: Identity document forgery has undergone a fundamental capability shift: generative AI tools now enable high-fidelity document synthesis and field-level manipulation with minimal technical expertise, while detection methods remain constrained by benchmarks that do not reflect this threat. The resulting attack surface spans physical presentation, digital injection, and fully generative synthesis, introducing distinct forensic failure modes that require a unified threat model and evaluation framework. This survey provides, to our knowledge, the first unified treatment of Presentation Attacks, Digital Injection Attacks, and GenAI-driven synthesis within a single identity verification threat model. We trace detection methodologies from rule-based heuristics through forensic localisation, injection-aware pipelines, foundation models, and few-shot frameworks. A systematic audit of public datasets from 2019--2025 exposes a persistent Reality Gap between benchmark conditions and operational deployment. We further analyse large multimodal models for identity document manipulation, identifying Script-Dependent Generative Instability (SDGI) as a recurring typographic failure mode in non-Latin script inpainting. Finally, zero-shot benchmarking on unseen synthesised ID cards shows that even the strongest publicly available models achieve APCER values above 25% under security-oriented operating conditions, highlighting substantial limits in cross-domain generalisation. We conclude by outlining future directions toward forensically grounded, privacy-preserving, and legally accountable identity verification systems.

AI.tldr: This survey unifies Presentation Attacks, Digital Injection Attacks, and GenAI-driven synthesis under a single identity verification threat model, audits 2019–2025 datasets to expose a persistent Reality Gap, identifies Script-Dependent Generative Instability (SDGI) as a typographic failure mode in non-Latin script inpainting, and demonstrates that top public models still exceed 25% APCER on unseen synthetic IDs, underscoring weak cross-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Generative AI has democratized high-fidelity ID document forgery—enabling full synthesis and field-level manipulation with minimal skill—while existing detection benchmarks fail to capture this evolved threat. The attack surface now spans physical presentation, digital injection, and generative synthesis, each introducing distinct forensic failure modes that no prior framework has addressed holistically.
AI.method: The authors propose a unified threat model encompassing Presentation Attacks, Digital Injection Attacks, and GenAI-driven synthesis. They trace the evolution of detection methods from rule-based heuristics through forensic localization, injection-aware pipelines, foundation models, and few-shot frameworks. A systematic audit of public datasets (2019–2025) quantifies the Reality Gap. They analyze large multimodal models for ID manipulation, characterizing SDGI as a typographic artifact. Zero-shot benchmarking under security-oriented operating conditions measures APCER (Attack Presentation Classification Error Rate) on unseen synthesized ID cards.
AI.result: The dataset audit reveals a persistent Reality Gap between benchmarks and operational deployments. SDGI emerges as a recurring typographic failure mode in non-Latin script inpainting by large multimodal models. Zero-shot evaluation shows that the strongest publicly available models achieve APCER values above 25% under security-oriented thresholds, indicating poor cross-domain generalization to unseen synthetic ID cards.
AI.conclusion: Current detection models are insufficient for operational deployment against GenAI-driven ID forgery, particularly under strict security thresholds. The authors call for future work toward forensically grounded, privacy-preserving, and legally accountable identity verification systems that bridge the Reality Gap and address cross-domain generalization failures.

title: From Anatomy to Smells: An Empirical Study of SKILL.md in Agent Skills
summary: Agent Skills provide on-demand domain knowledge to LLM agents without requiring model retraining. Each Agent Skill is defined by a mandatory SKILL.md file containing metadata and an unstructured Markdown body whose contents are left entirely to the skill author. Despite the rapid adoption of Agent Skills, little is known about how these files are authored or whether existing authoring guidelines are followed in practice. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of SKILL.md files as a software artifact. We qualitatively analyze 238 real-world skills and derive a taxonomy of 13 higher-level and 44 lower-level semantic components. We then conduct a multivocal literature review of 29 sources to identify best practices for authoring SKILL.md files and introduce skill smells as violations of these practices. Finally, we develop an automated detector and apply it to real-world skills, finding that over 99% of SKILL.md files contain at least one skill smell, and once introduced, skill smells rarely disappear as skills evolve. These findings reveal a substantial gap between recommended and actual authoring practices, motivating the development of automated techniques to remediate skill smells while increasing developer awareness of this emerging quality issue.

AI.tldr: First systematic study of SKILL.md files in Agent Skills, identifying a taxonomy of semantic components, defining "skill smells" as violations of best practices, and finding over 99% of real-world skills contain at least one smell — revealing a major gap between recommended and actual authoring practices.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid adoption of Agent Skills (on-demand domain knowledge for LLM agents via SKILL.md files), no prior research has systematically examined how these files are authored in practice or whether existing guidelines are followed.
AI.method: (1) Qualitative analysis of 238 real-world SKILL.md files to derive a taxonomy of 13 higher-level and 44 lower-level semantic components. (2) Multivocal literature review of 29 sources to identify best practices. (3) Introduction of "skill smells" as violations of these practices. (4) Development and application of an automated detector to real-world skills to measure smell prevalence and persistence across skill evolution.
AI.result: Over 99% of SKILL.md files contain at least one skill smell. Once introduced, skill smells rarely disappear as skills evolve, indicating a persistent quality gap between recommended and actual authoring practices.
AI.conclusion: The findings expose a substantial disconnect between authoring guidelines and real-world practice, motivating the need for automated remediation techniques and increased developer awareness around skill quality.

title: CreativityNeuro: Steering Language Model Weights to Improve Divergent Thinking and Reduce Mode Collapse
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 Workshop on Creativity & Generative AI
summary: Divergent thinking is a crucial aspect of creativity, yet large language models (LLMs) tend to consistently generate similar responses to open-ended questions, in what has been termed the artificial hivemind effect. Here, we introduce CreativityNeuro, a data-free method for enhancing divergent thinking in LLMs via contrastive weight steering. We evaluate our method across multiple creativity assessments and report several main findings. On the Divergent Association Task (DAT), a vocabulary-space creativity test, CreativityNeuro improves performance by up to 14 human percentile points. Next, in a large-scale human evaluation (N=720) on the Alternative Uses Test (AUT) and the Task Task, CreativityNeuro achieves significant improvements in originality, surprise, and creativity, transferring to longer-form and more open-ended tasks. Importantly, we find that across all three tasks, CreativityNeuro demonstrably reduces measures of mode collapse. Moreover, activation steering achieves comparable performance to CreativityNeuro on the DAT, but it does not transfer to the AUT and Task Task, demonstrating the effectiveness of weight-space steering in generalizing to unseen tasks. In conclusion, CreativityNeuro improves divergent thinking and reduces mode collapse without requiring behavioral data, re-training, or gradient-based fine-tuning, providing a straightforward way to enhance LLM performance in creative domains.

AI.tldr: CreativityNeuro is a data-free, contrastive weight-steering method that enhances divergent thinking in LLMs, improving creativity metrics by up to 14 percentile points on the DAT and significantly boosting originality, surprise, and creativity in human evaluations, while reducing mode collapse without retraining or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit the "artificial hivemind effect" — a tendency to produce homogeneous, repetitive responses to open-ended prompts. This mode collapse stifles divergent thinking, a core component of creativity. Existing solutions often require behavioral data or gradient-based fine-tuning, which are costly and may not generalize. A lightweight, data-free intervention is needed.
AI.method: CreativityNeuro applies contrastive weight steering directly in weight space. The method identifies and modifies model weights associated with convergent vs. divergent response patterns, steering the model toward more varied outputs. No behavioral data, retraining, or gradient-based fine-tuning is required. For comparison, activation-space steering is also evaluated.
AI.result: On the DAT, CreativityNeuro yields up to a 14-percentile-point gain. In a large-scale human evaluation (N=720) on the AUT and Task Task, it significantly improves ratings of originality, surprise, and creativity.
