AI.tldr: PMD converts cross-episode signals from RLVR rollouts into a three-level procedural memory scaffold (trajectories, strategies, behavioral patterns) that co-evolves with the policy via a memory-conditioned self-teacher, enabling the student policy to internalize procedural knowledge and outperform SDPO by 3.8–13.6% on reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: RLVR and self-distillation methods like SDPO use only episode-level verifier signals and discard rich procedural information within rollouts. Cross-episode patterns—successful strategies, recurring failure modes, persistent behaviors—are lost because episode-local updates cannot capture them. The authors aim to retain and reuse this procedural knowledge across episodes to improve policy learning.
AI.method: Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD) organizes memory at three levels: (1) raw trajectories, (2) self-reflected strategies and lessons, (3) higher-level behavioral patterns recurring across problems—all extracted online. A memory-conditioned self-teacher uses accumulated experience to supervise the student on its own rollouts. The core principle is co-evolution: policy rollouts update the memory, and memory shapes supervision that updates the policy. At inference, the model is memory-free.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8–5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9–13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH. Ablation shows co-evolution is critical: freezing either memory or policy trails full PMD by over 10% across SCIKNOWEVAL domains.
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving procedural memory with the policy effectively internalizes cross-episode procedural knowledge into model weights, yielding substantial gains over episode-local RLVR methods without requiring memory at inference time.

title: TurnNat: Automatic Evaluation of Turn-Taking Naturalness in Dyadic Spoken Dialogue
summary: Turn-taking naturalness is central to full-duplex spoken dialogue systems, yet its automatic evaluation remains limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments or behavior-specific timing metrics, making it difficult to compare heterogeneous timing failures within a unified framework. We propose TurnNat, a likelihood-based framework for automatic turn-taking naturalness evaluation in two-channel spoken dialogue. A causal turn-taking prediction model trained on natural conversations estimates future two-speaker voice-activity states, and the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the observed future activity measures timing atypicality. TurnNat pools frame-level NLLs over turn-taking boundary units (TBUs) extracted from utterance onsets and offsets, and aggregates mean and tail TBU scores into a dialogue-level naturalness score. We further construct a controlled perturbation benchmark of paired natural and perturbed dialogue clips, validated by human naturalness judgments. Experiments on this benchmark show that TurnNat successfully identifies unnatural turn-taking perturbations across heterogeneous timing failures.

AI.tldr: TurnNat is a likelihood-based framework for automatically evaluating turn-taking naturalness in two-channel spoken dialogue. It trains a causal prediction model on natural conversations to estimate future voice-activity states, then uses negative log-likelihood of observed future activity as an atypicality measure, aggregated over turn-taking boundary units into a dialogue-level score. A controlled perturbation benchmark validated by human judgments demonstrates its effectiveness across heterogeneous timing failures.
AI.motivation: Automatic evaluation of turn-taking naturalness in full-duplex spoken dialogue systems is underdeveloped. Current methods rely on subjective human judgments or narrow, behavior-specific timing metrics, which cannot compare diverse types of timing failures within a single, unified framework.
AI.method: The authors propose TurnNat: (1) A causal turn-taking prediction model is trained on natural conversations to estimate future two-speaker voice-activity states. (2) The negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the observed future activity given the model serves as a frame-level timing atypicality measure. (3) Frame-level NLLs are pooled over turn-taking boundary units (TBUs), defined from utterance onsets and offsets. (4) Mean and tail TBU scores are aggregated into a single dialogue-level naturalness score. (5) A controlled perturbation benchmark of paired natural and perturbed dialogue clips is constructed and validated with human naturalness judgments.
AI.result: Experiments on the constructed benchmark show that TurnNat successfully identifies unnatural turn-taking perturbations across a variety of heterogeneous timing failures, aligning with human judgments of naturalness.
AI.conclusion: TurnNat provides a principled, unified framework for automatic turn-taking naturalness evaluation, overcoming the limitations of prior human-dependent or metric-specific approaches and demonstrating robust performance on systematically perturbed spoken dialogue.

title: Multi-modal Rail Crossing Safety Analysis
summary: Given one or more images of a railway crossing, can we leverage visual cues that allow us to robustly estimate how safe it is? Can we improve our ability to do so by introducing structured data (such as official accident reports) about the accident history of that crossing into our models? In this work, we explore how to best answer those questions towards building an AI system that can ingest multi-modal data for railway crossings and provide safety assessment and scores that align with expert opinion and with safety scoring used by the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA). To that end, we propose a proof-of-concept pipeline that delivers on that goal, while at the same time exploring and tackling a number of critical research challenges that pertain to different parts of the pipeline, from data preparation to different learning paradigms that can allow us to realize such a system. Indicatively, our proposed system identifies HIGH-RISK and LOW-RISK crossings with a macro F1 score of 0.757 and estimates FRA-based safety scores with an RMSE of 0.078 and correlation of 0.492 using a routed fine-tuned compact VLM pipeline, while producing qualitative results that align with domain-expert assessment.

AI.tldr: A proof-of-concept AI pipeline using multi-modal data (images + structured accident reports) estimates railway crossing safety, achieving macro F1 of 0.757 for high/low-risk classification and 0.078 RMSE for FRA safety score prediction via a routed fine-tuned compact Vision-Language Model.
AI.motivation: To determine whether visual cues from railway crossing images, combined with structured accident history data, can robustly estimate crossing safety in alignment with Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) standards and domain-expert judgment.
AI.method: A proof-of-concept pipeline leveraging multi-modal learning that ingests both images of railway crossings and structured accident report data. The core model is a routed fine-tuned compact Vision-Language Model (VLM) trained to classify crossings as HIGH-RISK or LOW-RISK and to regress FRA-based safety scores.
AI.result: The system classifies HIGH-RISK vs LOW-RISK crossings with a macro F1 score of 0.757, estimates FRA safety scores with an RMSE of 0.078 and a correlation of 0.492, and produces qualitative results consistent with domain-expert assessments.
AI.conclusion: Multi-modal AI combining visual and structured data shows promise for automated railway crossing safety assessment, with the proposed routed fine-tuned compact VLM pipeline demonstrating meaningful alignment with both FRA scoring and expert evaluation.

title: Synthetic Contact with AI Reduces Cross-Partisan Animosity
summary: Americans' warmth toward members of the opposing political party has fallen sharply over the past three decades -- yet meaningful cross-partisan contact remains scarce, in part because people actively avoid it. Across five preregistered studies (total N = 3,960 U.S. partisans), we test whether brief conversations with AI chatbots representing the political outgroup can substitute for the contact people shun. Synthetic contact first lowers the barrier to entry: partisans would endure almost twice as long contemplating their own mortality to avoid a human outgroup partner as an AI one. These conversations then correct the misperceptions that fuel division. At baseline, Democrats placed Republicans more than a standard deviation past their actual position on environmental consumption attitudes -- enough to flip the average Republican from supportive to opposed -- and a single ten-minute conversation with an outgroup chatbot corrected those beliefs and warmed affect in a within-person study of both parties. A three-arm experiment ruled out pure engagement and sociality as drivers. Synthetic contact also moved behavior, in a sample of both parties and on a more affectively charged issue: participants who spoke with an outgroup bot about immigration were six percentage points more likely than controls to choose to have a real conversation with a partisan from the other side. A final study tested whether these gains last: the warmth effect replicated immediately in a new sample; most of it faded within a week, with a small residual concentrated among the most extreme partisans. Analyzing conversation content showed that information, more than friendliness, distinguishes outgroup bots from control chatbots. Together, these findings establish synthetic contact as a scalable, behaviorally consequential, and -- unlike face-to-face contact -- widely acceptable form of cross-partisan engagement.

AI.tldr: AI chatbots representing the political outgroup can reduce cross-partisan animosity: brief conversations correct misperceptions about the other side's views, warm affective attitudes, and increase willingness to engage with real outgroup members. Effects largely fade within a week, with a small residual among extreme partisans. Information delivery, not mere friendliness, drives the effect.
AI.motivation: Americans' warmth toward political opponents has declined sharply, yet meaningful cross-partisan contact is rare because people actively avoid it. The authors ask whether AI chatbots can substitute for the human-to-human contact that partisans shun, offering a scalable and acceptable alternative to traditional intergroup contact interventions.
AI.method: Five preregistered studies (total N = 3,960 U.S. partisans) using within-person and between-subjects designs. Key manipulations include: (1) comparing willingness to interact with AI vs. human outgroup partners; (2) measuring baseline and post-conversation partisan misperceptions and affective warmth; (3) a three-arm experiment ruling out pure engagement/sociality confounds; (4) a behavioral choice measure for real cross-partisan conversation; and (5) a longitudinal follow-up testing effect durability over one week. Conversation content was analyzed for information vs. friendliness.
AI.result: Partisans showed far less avoidance of AI outgroup partners than human ones. At baseline, Democrats misperceived Republicans' environmental consumption attitudes by more than one standard deviation. A single 10-minute chatbot conversation corrected these beliefs and increased warmth. The three-arm experiment confirmed effects are driven by information, not mere social engagement. Participants who chatted with an outgroup bot about immigration were 6 percentage points more likely to choose a real cross-partisan conversation. Warmth effects replicated immediately but mostly faded after one week, with a small residual among extreme partisans.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic contact via AI chatbots is a scalable, behaviorally consequential, and widely acceptable form of cross-partisan engagement that corrects misperceptions and reduces affective polarization, though durability remains a limitation requiring further intervention designs.

title: Beyond Gradient-Based Attacks: Adversarial Robustness and Explainability Stability in Cybersecurity Classifiers
summary: Adversarial attacks on cybersecurity classifiers pose a dual threat: degrading predictions and destabilising the SHAP-based explanations that security analysts rely on to understand and triage alerts. We extend our prior MLP conference study to Random Forest and XGBoost across four tabular security datasets (phishing URLs, UNSW-NB15, NF-ToN-IoT, HIKARI-2021), evaluating five attacks including three black-box methods applicable to non-differentiable tree models. We introduce the Explainability Stability Index (ESI), a scalar metric computed from TreeSHAP attribution drift under adversarial perturbation, reported on the same [0,1] scale as the Robustness Index (RI). A key finding is that gradient-based black-box attacks (ZOO) produce degenerate results against XGBoost (apparent RI ~0.98) due to piecewise-constant prediction surfaces, while score-based Square Attack reveals genuine vulnerability (RI ~0.36). These degenerate perturbations still drive substantial attribution drift: XGBoost ESI ~0.06-0.16 despite near-perfect ZOO robustness, versus 0.14-0.29 for RF, showing that prediction robustness and explanation stability are distinct axes requiring joint measurement. A two-axis framework (gradient dependence, query efficiency) explains the observed attack ranking and yields practical guidance for tree ensemble evaluation. A step-size ablation explains a counterintuitive PGD anomaly on z-score normalised tabular data.

AI.tldr: This paper extends prior work on adversarial attacks against cybersecurity classifiers to tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost), introducing the Explainability Stability Index (ESI) to measure SHAP attribution drift under adversarial perturbation. A key finding is that prediction robustness and explanation stability are independent dimensions requiring joint evaluation, with degenerate gradient-based attacks (ZOO) producing near-perfect robustness scores against XGBoost while still causing severe explanation instability.
AI.motivation: Adversarial attacks on ML-based cybersecurity classifiers threaten both prediction accuracy and the SHAP explanations that analysts depend on for alert triage. Prior work focused on neural networks, leaving a gap in understanding how tree-based models — widely used in security operations — behave under adversarial perturbation, particularly regarding the relationship between prediction robustness and explanation stability.
AI.method: The authors evaluate five adversarial attacks (including three black-box methods: ZOO, Square Attack, and HSJA) against Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers across four tabular security datasets (phishing URLs, UNSW-NB15, NF-ToN-IoT, HIKARI-2021). They introduce the Explainability Stability Index (ESI), a scalar metric on [0,1] computed from TreeSHAP attribution drift, paired with the Robustness Index (RI). A two-axis framework (gradient dependence vs. query efficiency) is proposed to systematize attack behavior on tree ensembles, complemented by a step-size ablation study explaining PGD anomalies on z-score normalized data.
AI.result: Gradient-based ZOO attacks produce degenerate results against XGBoost (RI ≈ 0.98) due to piecewise-constant prediction surfaces, while Square Attack reveals genuine vulnerability (RI ≈ 0.36). Critically, ZOO's near-perfect robustness masks severe explanation instability: XGBoost ESI ≈ 0.06–0.16 versus RF ESI ≈ 0.14–0.29, demonstrating that prediction robustness and explanation stability are distinct, decoupled properties. The two-axis framework explains the observed attack ranking, and the step-size ablation clarifies a counterintuitive PGD anomaly under z-score normalization.
AI.conclusion: Prediction robustness and explanation stability must be treated as orthogonal evaluation dimensions for tree-based cybersecurity classifiers. Relying solely on prediction robustness metrics can be misleading, as degenerate attacks may hide genuine explanation fragility. The ESI provides a practical complementary metric, and the gradient-dependence/query-efficiency framework offers actionable guidance for selecting appropriate adversarial evaluation strategies for tree ensembles.

title: AgentFlow: Building Agent Dependency Graphs for Static Analysis of Agent Programs
summary: LLM agents are increasingly developed as source-code applications built on agent frameworks. These agent programs combine conventional host-language code with framework-defined semantics for models, prompts, tools, memory, and multi-agent orchestration logic. As a result, their behavior depends not only on traditional control and data flows, but also on a new class of agent dependencies. Such dependencies are often expressed as framework-induced semantics, such as agent constructors, tool decorators, and agent handoff declarations, making them difficult to recover with existing static analysis or dependency tracking tools. In this paper, we present AgentFlow, the first static analysis framework for recovering and analyzing agent dependencies from agent programs. AgentFlow constructs an Agent Dependency Graph (ADG), a framework-agnostic graph representation that represents agents, prompts, models, capabilities, memory states, and control policies as typed nodes, and captures their component-dependency, control-flow, and data-flow dependencies as typed edges. Built on ADGs, AgentFlow supports a range of analyses for agent governance and security, including Agent Bill of Materials (BOM) generation and prompt-to-tool risk detection. We implement AgentFlow for five representative agent frameworks and evaluate it on AgentZoo, a corpus of 5,399 real-world agent programs. Our evaluation shows that AgentFlow recovers richer agent entities and dependencies than existing AST-based agent static analysis tools, generates more dependency-aware Agent BOMs, and uncovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks in real-world agent programs. These results show that ADG provides a practical foundation for understanding, governing, and securing emerging agent software.

AI.tldr: AgentFlow is a static analysis framework that constructs an Agent Dependency Graph (ADG) to recover and analyze agent-specific dependencies (models, prompts, tools, memory, multi-agent orchestration) from LLM agent programs. Evaluated on 5,399 real-world agent programs across five frameworks, it outperforms existing AST-based tools, generates richer Agent Bills of Materials, and detects 238 prompt-to-tool security risks.
AI.motivation: LLM agent programs blend conventional host-language code with framework-specific semantics (agent constructors, tool decorators, handoff declarations). Traditional static analysis and dependency tracking tools cannot recover these novel "agent dependencies," creating blind spots for governance, security, and supply-chain understanding of agent software.
AI.method: AgentFlow introduces the Agent Dependency Graph (ADG), a framework-agnostic typed graph capturing agents, prompts, models, capabilities, memory states, and control policies as nodes, with component-dependency, control-flow, and data-flow edges. Implemented for five agent frameworks, it supports downstream analyses including Agent Bill of Materials (BOM) generation and taint-style prompt-to-tool risk detection.
AI.result: On the AgentZoo corpus (5,399 programs), AgentFlow recovers richer agent entities and dependencies than existing AST-based tools, produces more dependency-aware Agent BOMs, and discovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks in real-world agent programs.
AI.conclusion: The ADG provides a practical foundation for understanding, governing, and securing emerging agent software. AgentFlow demonstrates that static analysis tailored to agent-specific semantics is both feasible and effective at scale across diverse frameworks.

title: The Agentic Garden of Forking Paths
summary: Empirical research rarely admits a unique analysis. Different analytical choices can lead to different conclusions from the same data, yet these hidden forking paths are difficult to observe. We show that AI agents capture much of the analytical variation among human researchers while making these paths explicit. Across four high-stakes domains, assigning different personas is sufficient for AI agents to report divergent, often opposing, conclusions from the same data and question, with findings systematically aligned with those beliefs. In a study in which 42 human research teams analyzed the same immigration dataset, AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effect estimates. Despite reaching opposing conclusions, it is difficult to identify clear issues in each analysis based on the final AI reports: 86% passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review. These findings suggest that the central challenge is often not flawed analyses, but selective exploration and reporting from a large space of methodologically defensible analyses. AI agents may amplify this longstanding problem by making such exploration inexpensive and scalable. To address this, we introduce the m-value (multiverse value), the probability that an analysis path would produce a claim at least as extreme as the reported one. We further introduce Agentic Bootstrap, which estimates the m-value by using AI agents to sample plausible analysis paths. Applied to the human immigration study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05). Scientific evidence should therefore be evaluated not only by a single reported analysis but also by its position within the distribution of analyses that could reasonably have been reported. Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable and turns it into a criterion for scientific credibility.

AI.tldr: AI agents can replicate the analytical variation seen among human researchers, producing divergent conclusions from the same data based on assigned personas. This reveals that the core scientific challenge is not flawed analyses but selective exploration of defensible analytical paths. The authors introduce the m-value and Agentic Bootstrap to quantify and make observable the multiverse of plausible analyses.
AI.motivation: Empirical research suffers from "forking paths" — different defensible analytical choices leading to different conclusions from the same data. These paths are typically hidden, making it difficult to assess whether a reported result reflects selective reporting from a large space of reasonable analyses. The authors aim to make this analytical multiverse explicit and quantifiable.
AI.method: The authors deploy AI agents assigned different researcher personas (e.g., ideological leanings) across four high-stakes domains. They compare AI-generated analyses against a benchmark where 42 human research teams analyzed the same immigration dataset. They also introduce two methodological innovations: (1) the m-value, the probability that an analysis path produces a claim at least as extreme as the reported one; and (2) Agentic Bootstrap, which estimates the m-value by using AI agents to sample plausible analysis paths from the multiverse of defensible analyses.
AI.result: AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effect estimates from the immigration dataset. Despite reaching opposing conclusions, 86% of AI reports passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review. Applied to the human immigration study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05).
AI.conclusion: The central challenge in empirical science is often not flawed analyses but selective exploration and reporting from a large space of methodologically defensible analyses. AI agents amplify this problem by making such exploration inexpensive and scalable. Scientific evidence should be evaluated by its position within the distribution of analyses that could reasonably have been reported. Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable, turning it into a criterion for scientific credibility.

title: RusFinChain: A Russian Benchmark for Verifiable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Finance with Fuzzy-Aligned Evaluation
summary: Multi-step symbolic reasoning is essential for robust financial analysis, yet most benchmarks neglect intermediate reasoning steps. FINCHAIN introduced verifiable Chain-of-Thought (CoT) evaluation but is limited to English. FINESSE-Bench includes a Russian block but relies on multiple-choice questions without step-level supervision. We present RusFinChain, the first Russian-language symbolic benchmark for verifiable CoT reasoning in finance. It spans 17 domains, 172 topics, and comprises 5,280 parameterized examples from executable Python templates, ensuring contamination-free evaluation. Each example includes a gold-standard reasoning chain with intermediate numeric values for automatic verification. We also introduce enhanced metrics: Fuzzy Numeric Alignment and Soft-Attention Alignment. We evaluate 8 open-weight LLMs on a stratified sample, generating 8,100 responses. Results reveal a substantial reasoning gap: models achieve Hard F1 of ~0.65 for step alignment, but only ~29% of final answers are correct. Our fuzzy and soft metrics show stronger correlation with final-answer correctness (Spearman rho approx 0.48) than the original ChainEval (rho approx 0.38-0.46), demonstrating superior diagnostic power. We release dataset, code, and evaluation framework to foster verifiable financial AI for the Russian-speaking community.

AI.tldr: RusFinChain introduces the first Russian-language benchmark for verifiable Chain-of-Thought reasoning in finance, spanning 17 domains with 5,280 template-generated examples. It features gold-standard reasoning chains with intermediate values and new fuzzy evaluation metrics, revealing that open-weight LLMs achieve only ~29% final-answer accuracy despite ~0.65 Hard F1 step alignment.
AI.motivation: Existing financial reasoning benchmarks either lack step-level supervision (FINESSE-Bench uses multiple-choice), operate only in English (FINCHAIN), or neglect intermediate reasoning verification entirely. There is a critical gap for verifiable multi-step symbolic reasoning in non-English financial contexts, particularly for the Russian-speaking community.
AI.method: The authors construct RusFinChain using executable Python templates to generate 5,280 parameterized examples across 17 financial domains and 172 topics, each with gold-standard reasoning chains containing intermediate numeric values. They introduce two new evaluation metrics — Fuzzy Numeric Alignment and Soft-Attention Alignment — alongside stratified sampling of 8 open-weight LLMs producing 8,100 responses for evaluation.
AI.result: Models achieve approximately 0.65 Hard F1 for step-level alignment but only ~29% final-answer correctness, exposing a substantial reasoning gap. The proposed fuzzy and soft metrics show stronger correlation with final-answer correctness (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.48) compared to the original ChainEval metric (ρ ≈ 0.38–0.46), confirming superior diagnostic power.
AI.conclusion: RusFinChain fills a critical void in verifiable financial CoT reasoning for Russian. The contamination-free, template-based design ensures robust benchmarking, while the novel fuzzy metrics provide more faithful diagnostics of reasoning quality than prior approaches. The authors release the dataset, code, and framework publicly.

title: How Should Transformers Encode Numeric Values in Electronic Health Records?
comment: 16 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables, accepted to ICML 2026, to be published in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
summary: How do we encode numeric values in transformer-based sequence processing, particularly in electronic health record (EHR) data? We systematically compare discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding strategies using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded within real-world EHR data, as well as real-world clinical prediction tasks. Our study reveals trade-offs between numeric precision, optimisation stability, and architectural flexibility. We find that approaches that explicitly model value-concept interactions perform best on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks when architectural constraints permit. Hybrid token-based approaches that retain numeric values but apply binning prior to projection provide a more robust and broadly applicable alternative, with the optimal number of bins following a simple empirically derived power-law in dataset size. Across tasks, models consistently exhibit reliable "good enough" numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic, while clinical gains from incorporating laboratory values are task-dependent. This suggests that robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based approaches as a practical default.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares discrete, continuous, and hybrid numeric encoding strategies for transformers in EHR data, finding that hybrid token-based approaches with binning offer the best balance of precision, robustness, and deployability, while clinical gains from lab values are task-dependent.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based models lack a principled, empirically validated approach for encoding numeric values (e.g., lab results) in EHR data. The authors aim to systematically evaluate the trade-offs among discrete, continuous, and hybrid encoding strategies to guide practical model design.
AI.method: Systematic comparison of numeric encoding strategies (discrete, continuous, hybrid) on synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded in real EHR data and real-world clinical prediction tasks. Hybrid approaches use binning prior to projection, and the optimal bin count is studied via an empirical power-law relative to dataset size.
AI.result: (1) Explicit value-concept interaction models perform best on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks when architecture permits. (2) Hybrid token-based binning methods provide more robust, broadly applicable alternatives. (3) Optimal bin count follows an empirical power-law in dataset size. (4) Models exhibit "good enough" numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic. (5) Clinical benefit from lab values is task-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based encoding approaches as a practical default for numeric values in clinical transformer models.

title: What Types of Human-AI Teams Exist?
summary: Human-AI teaming has received increasing attention in the literature. However, the range of studies conducted in multiple domains make it difficult to understand what types of teams are being studied, and in what ways are they similar/different from one another. In this study, we analyse 53 papers on human-AI teams and categorise them into five main clusters based on psychological taxonomies of teaming; AI Assistant, Ad-hoc Dependency, Ad-hoc Forced Dependency, Paired Equanimity, and Group Equanimity. Each cluster represents a unique combination of holistic team-level characteristics, indicating there are multiple disparate team types studied under the same definition. In turn, this raises the question of whether insights are truly transferable between papers. We conclude with guidance on how to identify the types of human-AI teams studied, a checklist for reporting a human-AI team in research work, and ways in which the field can be further synthesised.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 53 studies on human-AI teams, categorizing them into five distinct clusters based on psychological teaming taxonomies: AI Assistant, Ad-hoc Dependency, Ad-hoc Forced Dependency, Paired Equanimity, and Group Equanimity. The authors reveal that disparate team types are studied under the same "human-AI teaming" label, raising questions about cross-study transferability, and provide guidance for reporting and synthesis.
AI.motivation: The growing literature on human-AI teaming spans multiple domains, yet there is no systematic understanding of what types of teams are actually being studied, how they differ, and whether findings are truly comparable across studies. This fragmentation hinders cumulative knowledge building in the field.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic analysis of 53 papers on human-AI teams. They applied psychological taxonomies of teaming to categorize the studies into clusters, identifying holistic team-level characteristics that define each cluster type.
AI.result: Five distinct clusters of human-AI teams were identified: (1) AI Assistant, (2) Ad-hoc Dependency, (3) Ad-hoc Forced Dependency, (4) Paired Equanimity, and (5) Group Equanimity. Each cluster exhibits unique configurations of team-level properties, demonstrating that fundamentally different team types are conflated under a single definition.
AI.conclusion: The field lacks consistency in what constitutes a human-AI team, threatening the transferability of insights. The authors offer a framework for identifying team types, a reporting checklist for future research, and strategies for better synthesizing the field.

title: Pmeta-TLA: Backdoor Attacks for Speech Classification Models via Meta-Learning with Timbre Leakage Attack
summary: Recently, speech classification methods have gained widespread adoption in intelligent gadgets. Current study indicates that backdoor attacks provide a substantial security concern to these models, underscoring the pressing necessity to investigate additional potential attack techniques to expose and prevent such risks. This work discusses the vulnerability of current speech triggers to detection by deep neural network defenders and introduces the Timbre Leakage Attack (TLA). The suggested trigger disseminates timbre information at the frame level within the deep self-supervised features, producing poisoned samples that appear natural to human perception. Furthermore, we introduce Pmeta-TLA, an innovative training mechanism for embedding numerous backdoors one time. This method proposes a multi-backdoor injection training strategy using meta-learning and Projected Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) and introduces TLA as a multi-target attack tool within it. We performed tests on data-poisoning backdoor attacks in keyword spotting tasks utilizing some deep neural network models. Experimental results indicate that the proposed strategy attains superior Attack efficacy, enhanced stealthiness, robustness, and a reduced attack cost relative to baseline methods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Timbre Leakage Attack (TLA), a stealthy speech backdoor attack that embeds timbre information at the frame level in self-supervised features, and Pmeta-TLA, a meta-learning framework with PCGrad for injecting multiple backdoors simultaneously, achieving superior attack efficacy, stealthiness, and robustness on keyword spotting tasks.
AI.motivation: Current speech backdoor triggers are detectable by deep neural network defenders. There is a pressing need to explore more stealthy and robust backdoor attack techniques in speech classification models to expose security vulnerabilities before they can be exploited maliciously.
AI.method: The authors propose TLA, which embeds timbre leakage triggers at the frame level within deep self-supervised speech features, making poisoned samples perceptually natural. They further propose Pmeta-TLA, which uses meta-learning combined with Projected Conflicting Gradients (PCGrad) to inject multiple backdoors in a single training session, enabling TLA as a multi-target attack tool.
AI.result: Experimental results on keyword spotting tasks across multiple deep neural network models demonstrate that TLA and Pmeta-TLA achieve superior attack success rates, enhanced stealthiness, greater robustness against defenses, and reduced attack cost compared to baseline backdoor methods.
AI.conclusion: The vulnerability of speech classification models to timbre-based backdoor attacks is significant. TLA and Pmeta-TLA expose critical security weaknesses that current defenses fail to detect, underscoring the need for more robust defense mechanisms in speech intelligence systems.

title: When Agents Do Not Stop: Uncovering Infinite Agentic Loops in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on iterative execution to solve tasks through planning, tool use, state updates, and agent collaboration. While this design enables flexible automation, it also creates a new class of failures: an agent may repeatedly execute model calls, tools, workflow transitions, or agent handoffs when the feedback path is not effectively bounded. We call this problem Infinite Agentic Loops (IALs). IALs are not ordinary programming loops; they arise from the interaction between agent logic, framework semantics, runtime observations, and termination mechanisms. Such failures can amplify a single request into long running model and tool execution, causing cost exhaustion, model denial of service, context growth, and repeated external side effects. We propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool for detecting IAL failures in real-world LLM agent projects. IAL-Scan abstracts heterogeneous agent code into a framework independent Agent IR, builds an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover explicit and framework induced feedback paths, and checks whether these paths can repeatedly reach costly or state growing operations without an effective bound. We evaluate IAL-Scan on 6,549 LLM agent repositories. It reports 74 potential findings, among which manual review confirms 68 IAL failures across 47 projects, achieving 91.9% precision.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses "Infinite Agentic Loops" (IALs), a failure mode in LLM agents where unbounded feedback loops cause repeated execution of model calls/tools, leading to cost exhaustion and denial of service. The authors propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis tool that uses an Agent IR and Agentic Loop Dependence Graph to detect such loops, achieving 91.9% precision across 6,549 repositories.
AI.motivation: LLM agents use iterative execution (planning, tool use, state updates, collaboration) but lack effective bounded feedback paths, creating Infinite Agentic Loops. These loops are not standard programming errors but emerge from agent logic, framework semantics, runtime observations, and termination mechanisms. They cause severe consequences: cost exhaustion, model denial of service, context window overflow, and repeated external side effects. No existing tool systematically detects these failures in real-world agent code.
AI.method: The authors propose IAL-Scan, a static analysis framework with three components: (1) abstracting heterogeneous agent code into a framework-independent Agent IR; (2) constructing an Agentic Loop Dependence Graph (ALDG) to recover both explicit and framework-induced feedback paths; (3) checking whether these feedback paths can repeatedly reach costly or state-growing operations without an effective bound, flagging potential IALs.
AI.result: IAL-Scan was evaluated on 6,549 LLM agent repositories. It reported 74 potential findings; manual review confirmed 68 true IAL failures across 47 distinct projects, yielding a precision of 91.9%.
AI.conclusion: Infinite Agentic Loops are a real and prevalent failure class in production LLM agent systems. Static analysis with IAL-Scan effectively detects these loops across diverse frameworks and codebases, enabling developers to identify and fix unbounded feedback paths before deployment.

title: Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
comment: Code and data released on GitHub: https://github.com/GraceBrigham/Janus
summary: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains under explored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user input is critical and can significantly strengthen privacy and security, that AI augmentation of user decisions can help reduce cognitive load, and that realistic user behavior including permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.

AI.tldr: Janus is a playground system for designing and evaluating user-involved permission management in AI agents. It includes a modular agentic core and an automated evaluation harness. Six permission assistant designs were tested across scenarios, showing that user input strengthens privacy/security, AI augmentation reduces cognitive load, and no single design is universally optimal.
AI.motivation: AI agents increasingly execute tool calls autonomously, raising critical questions about permission management. The user's role in agentic permission management remains underexplored despite numerous proposed approaches, creating a gap in understanding how to optimally involve users in authorizing agent actions.
AI.method: The authors introduce Janus, comprising Janus-Core (a modular agentic system supporting diverse permission management designs) and Janus-Harness (an automated evaluation framework). Grounded in a conceptual model identifying key design axes for user involvement, they implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders.
AI.result: User input critically strengthens privacy and security. AI augmentation of user decisions reduces cognitive load. Realistic user behaviors, including permission fatigue, must be accounted for in system design. No single permission management design performs optimally across all contexts.
AI.conclusion: A more principled, context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems is needed. Janus is publicly available to support future research into user-involved permission management for AI agents.

title: Multi-Objective Exploration and Preference Optimization via Mutual Information
summary: Aligning large language models with diverse and heterogeneous human values requires multi-objective alignment methods to effectively trade off conflicting preference dimensions. Current methods achieve this trade-off by training policies conditioned on preference vectors and leveraging online direct preference optimization. However, exploration uncertainty can cause the reward distributions of responses generated under different preference vectors to overlap, and the generated responses may fail to effectively align with the corresponding preference vectors. In this paper, we propose Multi-Objective Exploration and Preference Optimization via Mutual Information (MI-EPO), an information-theoretic framework. It unifies multi-objective exploration and alignment by maximizing the joint conditional mutual information among generated responses, preference feedback, and preference vectors. By incorporating a probabilistic routing mechanism, MI-EPO naturally decomposes objective alignment and preference-aware exploration, encouraging the model to generate responses that are distinguishable and aligned with different preference conditions. Experiments on safe alignment and helpful assistant tasks show that MI-EPO significantly improves the alignment between generated responses and preference vectors, makes the outputs more controllable, and achieves stable trade-offs across multiple objectives.

AI.tldr: MI-EPO is an information-theoretic framework that unifies multi-objective exploration and alignment in LLMs by maximizing joint conditional mutual information among responses, preference feedback, and preference vectors, using a probabilistic routing mechanism to improve controllability and trade-off stability.
AI.motivation: Current multi-objective alignment methods suffer from exploration uncertainty, causing reward distribution overlap across different preference vectors and poor alignment between generated responses and their intended preference conditions. A principled framework is needed to ensure responses are both distinguishable and well-aligned with diverse preference vectors.
AI.method: MI-EPO maximizes joint conditional mutual information I(Response; Feedback; Preference Vector | Context). It incorporates a probabilistic routing mechanism that decomposes the objective into alignment and preference-aware exploration components, encouraging distinguishable and aligned responses under different preference conditions.
AI.result: Experiments on safe alignment and helpful assistant tasks demonstrate that MI-EPO significantly improves alignment between generated responses and preference vectors, enhances output controllability, and achieves stable trade-offs across multiple objectives.
AI.conclusion: MI-EPO provides a principled information-theoretic approach to multi-objective LLM alignment, effectively addressing exploration uncertainty and enabling more controllable, preference-consistent response generation across diverse and conflicting human values.

title: NeuroBridge: Bridging Multi-Task MRI Knowledge for Neurodegenerative Disease Diagnosis
summary: INTRODUCTION: Accurate MRI-based identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and related dementias remains challenging because disease-related structural changes are often subtle and heterogeneous. We developed NeuroBridge, a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis. METHODS: NeuroBridge integrates large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated across ADNI and OASIS cohorts, including cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening. RESULTS: NeuroBridge achieved the highest performance across evaluated classification tasks, reaching 88.17% accuracy for AD versus cognitively normal controls in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS. The largest gains occurred in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. The framework demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization, systematic associations between predicted-class probability and accuracy, and the feasibility of probability-based opportunistic screening. DISCUSSION: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning improves neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond conventional single-task approaches. NeuroBridge provides a robust and scalable framework for dementia assessment and MRI-based opportunistic screening.

AI.tldr: NeuroBridge is a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework that combines self-supervised pretraining with hippocampal-focused objectives and gated fusion fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy in diagnosing AD and MCI across ADNI and OASIS cohorts, with strong cross-cohort generalization and opportunistic screening potential.
AI.motivation: Accurate MRI-based diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, and related dementias is difficult because disease-related structural brain changes are often subtle and heterogeneous, limiting the effectiveness of conventional single-task approaches.
AI.method: NeuroBridge employs large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining combined with three auxiliary objectives: hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and image reconstruction. These are integrated via a gated fusion mechanism during fine-tuning for downstream classification tasks.
AI.result: NeuroBridge achieved 88.17% accuracy for AD vs. cognitively normal (CN) classification on ADNI and 82.78% on OASIS, with the largest performance gains observed in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. The framework showed strong cross-cohort generalization, systematic probability-accuracy associations, and feasible probability-based opportunistic screening.
AI.conclusion: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning, as implemented in NeuroBridge, significantly improves neurodegenerative disease diagnosis from MRI over conventional single-task methods, offering a robust, scalable solution for dementia assessment and opportunistic screening.

title: Personality Without Persons? A Psychometric Critique of Big Five Testing in Large Language Models
summary: Human personality inventories are increasingly used to characterize large language models (LLMs), compare systems, and inform downstream governance claims. Yet, these inventories were developed and validated for humans, and it remains unclear whether they apply to LLMs. We present a systematic psychometric evaluation of Big Five personality measurements in LLMs. We ask three research questions: Do Big Five inventories a) appropriately describe LLMs, b) capture inter-individual differences across models, and c) reflect internal factors consistent with human personality. We assess content validity of five candidate Big Five inventories and administer the winning inventory to N = 244 different models spanning 49 model families. First, we found that Big Five items adapted for LLMs can reach sufficient content validity, while original human-developed items did not. Second, Big Five inventories did not capture meaningful differences between LLMs: We found low variability between models, accounting for only 3% of total score variance. Third, LLMs responses did not recover the Big Five five-factor structure with four of the Big Five facets collapsing into one (r >= .92). Direct comparisons between base and instruction-tuned model variants suggested that alignment training systematically shifted Big Five scores toward socially desirable traits. These findings demonstrate that Big Five scores do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality in LLMs. Applying human personality frameworks to LLMs produces misleading characterizations used to benchmark, compare, and govern LLMs. We highlight the need for evaluation frameworks that are developed for LLMs, rather than adopting human constructs without validation.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically evaluates whether Big Five personality inventories validly measure personality in LLMs. Across 244 models, it finds that these inventories fail to capture meaningful inter-model differences (only 3% of variance), do not recover the five-factor structure (four facets collapse into one), and are systematically shifted by alignment training toward social desirability. The authors conclude that applying human personality frameworks to LLMs without validation yields misleading characterizations.
AI.motivation: Human personality inventories are increasingly used to benchmark, compare, and govern LLMs, yet these instruments were developed and validated exclusively for humans. No systematic psychometric evaluation had been conducted to determine whether they meaningfully apply to LLMs. This gap risks producing invalid characterizations that could misinform downstream decisions about model deployment and governance.
AI.method: A three-part psychometric evaluation: (1) Content validity assessment of five candidate Big Five inventories, selecting the best-performing one; (2) Administration of the winning inventory to N=244 models across 49 families, with variance decomposition to quantify between-model vs. within-model variability; (3) Factor analysis to test whether LLM responses recover the expected five-factor structure, supplemented by comparisons between base and instruction-tuned model variants to assess the effect of alignment training.
AI.result: (1) LLM-adapted Big Five items achieved sufficient content validity, but original human items did not. (2) Between-model variability was negligible at 3% of total variance, indicating inventories fail to capture meaningful inter-model differences. (3) Four of the five Big Five facets collapsed into one (r ≥ .92), meaning the five-factor structure was not recovered. Alignment training systematically shifted scores toward socially desirable traits, further undermining construct validity.
AI.conclusion: Big Five scores do not measure a construct equivalent to human personality in LLMs. Using human personality frameworks without validation produces misleading characterizations. The field needs evaluation frameworks purpose-built for LLMs rather than uncritically adopting human constructs.

title: Trust Boundary Semantic Gaps: A Multi-dimensional Analysis and Mitigation for Security-by-Design
summary: Modern systems use format-, protocol-, and signature-based mechanisms before accepting artifacts across trust boundaries. These mechanisms are necessary: they show that an artifact is well formed, protocol-compliant, or properly authenticated. They do not, however, show that the artifact satisfies the semantic security properties required by the receiving domain. A signed update or an authenticated token may therefore be accepted yet enable compromise. We call this condition a Trust Boundary Semantic Gap (TBSG): an artifact crosses a trust boundary and passes correctly implemented syntactic validation, but the assertions established by that pass are insufficient to satisfy the receiving domain's security requirements. TBSG concerns what remains unestablished after a syntactic pass, not absent checks or implementation bugs. Analyzing 75 publicly reported security incidents (2014-2025) at the boundary level, we organize semantic misalignment into a four-dimensional analysis model: Identity, Spatial, Temporal, and Interpretation (MDTBSG). Building on it, we develop Trust Boundary Semantic Analysis and Mitigation (TBSAM), a design-time framework that identifies TBSGs from design specifications, prioritizes them, traces propagated gaps to their originating boundary, and maps each to candidate architectural controls. We apply TBSAM to a retrospective reconstruction of the SolarWinds/SUNBURST supply-chain attack, showing how it makes receiving-domain assumptions explicit, separates locally originating from propagated gaps, and identifies controls that interrupt the path. These results suggest that syntactic validation, while necessary, is not sufficient at trust boundaries, and that making trust-boundary assumptions explicit can complement Security-by-Design.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the concept of a Trust Boundary Semantic Gap (TBSG), where syntactically valid artifacts cross trust boundaries but fail to satisfy the receiving domain's semantic security requirements. The authors analyze 75 security incidents (2014–2025), develop a four-dimensional analysis model (MDTBSG: Identity, Spatial, Temporal, Interpretation), and propose TBSAM, a design-time framework for identifying, prioritizing, and mitigating TBSGs. A case study on the SolarWinds/SUNBURST attack demonstrates its practical utility.
AI.motivation: Existing trust-boundary mechanisms (format, protocol, and signature validation) only verify syntactic correctness — not whether an artifact satisfies the semantic security properties that the receiving domain actually requires. Signed updates or authenticated tokens can pass all checks yet still enable compromise. This gap is widespread and under-analyzed, motivating a systematic framework to identify and mitigate such design-level semantic misalignments.
AI.method: The authors analyze 75 publicly reported security incidents (2014–2025) at the boundary level to identify patterns of semantic misalignment. From this empirical basis, they construct a four-dimensional analysis model: Identity, Spatial, Temporal, and Interpretation (MDTBSG). Building on this taxonomy, they develop TBSAM (Trust Boundary Semantic Analysis and Mitigation), a design-time framework that (1) identifies TBSGs from design specifications, (2) prioritizes them, (3) traces propagated gaps to their originating trust boundary, and (4) maps each gap to candidate architectural controls. The framework is validated via retrospective reconstruction of the SolarWinds/SUNBURST supply-chain attack.
AI.result: The MDTBSG model organizes semantic misalignment into four dimensions. Applied to SolarWinds/SUNBURST, TBSAM makes the receiving domain's implicit security assumptions explicit, distinguishes locally originating gaps from those propagated across boundaries, and identifies architectural controls that would have interrupted the attack path. The analysis demonstrates that syntactic validation alone is insufficient and that surfacing trust-boundary assumptions can complement Security-by-Design practices.
AI.conclusion: Syntactic validation at trust boundaries is necessary but not sufficient for security. The TBSG concept and the TBSAM framework provide a structured, design-time approach to surface semantic-level trust assumptions, trace propagated gaps, and select architectural mitigations. This complements Security-by-Design by making implicit boundary assumptions explicit and actionable.

title: Refploit: Facilitating Exploit Construction via Code-Agent Trajectory Repair
summary: Vulnerability exploits play a crucial role in assessing the downstream impact of Java library vulnerabilities. While some vulnerabilities are accompanied by disclosed exploit references, automatically reproducing such references into runnable exploits remains challenging because they are often incomplete, unstructured, or only describe partial reproduction steps. Recent code agents provide a promising way to automate this process, but our study shows that their generated exploits often appear successful without triggering the actual vulnerable logic, such as replacing vulnerable APIs with self-implemented functions. To address this, we propose Refploit, an LLM-based trajectory recovery framework for facilitating vulnerability reproduction from public exploit references. The key insight is that a failed agent trajectory is not entirely useless. It may have already completed some reproduction subtasks while also revealing misleading directions that should be avoided. Refploit first validates an agent-generated exploit through differential execution. When the exploit is ineffective, Refploit analyzes its reproduction progress, locates the trajectory segments associated with the reproduction progress, and derives constraints to guide focused recovery. We evaluate Refploit on three open-source Java vulnerability datasets, covering 172 exploit references for 143 vulnerabilities. Under DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Refploit successfully reproduces 138 exploits, achieving a reproduction rate of 80.2%. It achieves a 64.3% relative improvement over the initially generated trajectories and outperforms both the SOTA exploit-generation method PoCGen and advanced code agents such as Codex with GPT-5.4. We further adapt Refploit to another code agent and observe consistent improvements, demonstrating its generality.

AI.tldr: Refploit is an LLM-based trajectory recovery framework that improves automatic reproduction of Java vulnerability exploits from public references. It validates agent-generated exploits via differential execution, analyzes failed trajectories to locate progress, and derives constraints for focused recovery. Evaluated on 172 exploit references across 143 vulnerabilities, it achieves 80.2% reproduction rate (64.3% relative improvement) and outperforms existing methods like PoCGen and Codex with GPT-5.4.
AI.motivation: Automatically reproducing vulnerability exploits from publicly available references is challenging because these references are often incomplete, unstructured, or only partially describe reproduction steps. Existing code agents frequently generate exploits that appear successful but fail to trigger actual vulnerable logic — for instance, by replacing vulnerable APIs with self-implemented functions. This motivates the need for a more robust approach that can recover from failed generation attempts.
AI.method: Refploit is an LLM-based trajectory recovery framework. It first validates agent-generated exploits through differential execution to determine if the vulnerable logic is actually triggered. When an exploit is ineffective, Refploit analyzes the failed agent trajectory to assess reproduction progress, identifies trajectory segments associated with that progress, and derives constraints to guide focused recovery. The key insight is that failed trajectories are not useless — they contain partially completed subtasks and reveal misleading directions to avoid.
AI.result: Evaluated on three open-source Java vulnerability datasets (172 exploit references, 143 vulnerabilities) using DeepSeek-V4-Flash: Refploit successfully reproduces 138 exploits (80.2% reproduction rate), achieving a 64.3% relative improvement over initially generated trajectories. It outperforms the SOTA exploit-generation method PoCGen and advanced code agents such as Codex with GPT-5.4. The framework also demonstrates generality by achieving consistent improvements when adapted to another code agent.
AI.conclusion: Refploit demonstrates that analyzing and recovering from failed agent trajectories — rather than discarding them — is an effective strategy for vulnerability exploit reproduction. The framework's strong performance across multiple datasets and its transferability to different code agents suggest it provides a generalizable solution to the challenge of converting unstructured exploit references into runnable, behaviorally faithful exploits.

title: Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Reasoning under Limited Supervision: Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as an effective approach for activating latent reasoning capabilities in large language models. However, most existing CoT methods use reasoning chains mainly as inference-time prompts, while the generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals. In this report, we define \textbf{Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning} and propose \textbf{Semi-CoT}, a simple framework that uses unlabeled questions to construct pseudo reasoning supervision. Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations. This extends the self-training view of CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised pseudo-supervision. Pilot experiments on AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith show that the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs, with pseudo-answer precision ranging from $91.36\%$ to $100\%$. Semi-CoT also gives small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, while AQuA shows negative transfer and MultiArith reaches a ceiling. These results suggest that unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but their effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training.

AI.tldr: Semi-CoT explores reusing chain-of-thought reasoning traces as semi-supervised learning signals. It samples multiple pseudo-CoTs per unlabeled question, uses answer-level semantic entropy to filter high-quality reasoning chains, and treats them as pseudo-demonstrations for training. Pilot results show the entropy gate achieves 91–100% pseudo-answer precision, but downstream gains are mixed.
AI.motivation: Most CoT methods use reasoning chains only as inference-time prompts and discard them afterward. The authors argue these generated traces could serve as valuable semi-supervised signals, enabling a self-training paradigm that moves CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised pseudo-supervision.
AI.method: Semi-CoT operates in three stages: (1) sample multiple reasoning chains per unlabeled question via a teacher model, (2) estimate answer-level semantic entropy across chains to gauge consistency, (3) select low-entropy chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations for student training (supervised fine-tuning or few-shot prompting).
AI.result: On AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith, the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs achieving 91.36% to 100% pseudo-answer precision. Small gains are observed on SVAMP and GSM8K; AQuA exhibits negative transfer; MultiArith hits a performance ceiling.
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled questions can yield reliable pseudo reasoning signals via entropy-based filtering, but effectively leveraging them for student training remains challenging. Stronger demonstration selection or improved student training strategies are needed for robust downstream improvement.

title: MultAttnAttrib: Training-Free Multimodal Attribution in Long Document Question Answering
comment: 25 pages (8 main, 17 references + appendix), 15 figures, Submitted to EMNLP 2026 Conference (Long Paper)
summary: As grounded QA systems are increasingly deployed in AI assistants, accurately attributing generated answers to evidence is critical for user trust and model safety. While unimodal attributions have been explored in depth, the multimodal setting remains relatively under-researched. As a result, we introduce MultAttnAttrib, a training-free attribution-generation method that leverages a model's prefill pass, selected attention heads, and calibrated thresholds to locate source evidence within a document. To establish baseline results for the method, we introduce MultAttrEval, a complementary benchmark dataset annotated with fine-grained, ground-truth attributions for answer components grounded in multimodal source documents. To our knowledge, this is the first evaluation dataset designed specifically for multimodal attribution in long-form documents. Experimental results show that MultAttnAttrib consistently outperforms a variety of attribution-generation methods, including several strong prompting-based approaches and matches the latest frontier models such as GPT 5.4. Our method not only substantially improves attribution accuracy for both unimodal and multimodal attribution types, but also produces attributions at up to one-seventh of the direct inference latency compared to prompting on the same base model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MultAttnAttrib, a training-free method using attention heads to locate source evidence for grounded QA in multimodal documents, and MultAttrEval, the first benchmark for multimodal attribution. The method outperforms prompting-based approaches and matches GPT-5.4, with up to 7x faster inference.
AI.motivation: As grounded QA systems proliferate in AI assistants, accurate attribution of answers to source evidence is critical for trust and safety. However, while unimodal attribution is well-studied, multimodal attribution in long-form documents remains under-researched and lacks dedicated evaluation benchmarks.
AI.method: MultAttnAttrib is a training-free attribution-generation method that exploits the model's prefill pass, selected attention heads, and calibrated thresholds to pinpoint source evidence within multimodal documents. The companion benchmark, MultAttrEval, provides fine-grained ground-truth attributions for answer components grounded in multimodal sources.
AI.result: MultAttnAttrib consistently outperforms various attribution-generation methods, including strong prompting-based baselines, and matches frontier models like GPT-5.4. It improves attribution accuracy for both unimodal and multimodal types while achieving up to a 7x reduction in inference latency compared to prompting on the same base model.
AI.conclusion: Attention-based attribution is a highly effective and efficient alternative to prompting-based methods for multimodal grounded QA, offering substantial accuracy gains and latency reductions. The work also fills a key gap with the first dedicated multimodal attribution benchmark, MultAttrEval.

title: Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics Enable Complete and Scalable $\mathrm{E}(3)$-Equivariant Networks
summary: $\mathrm{E}(3)$-equivariant networks are promising for 3D atomistic system modeling, yet their scalability is limited by the $O(L^6)$ complexity of the Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP). The recently proposed Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) reduces the complexity but is unable to capture the antisymmetric paths, resulting in incomplete expressivity. In this work, we present SpinGTP, an approach to overcome the GTP incompleteness by generalizing from scalar functions to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH). By relying on the algebraic properties of SWSH, SpinGTP recovers the missing antisymmetric interactions while maintaining the asymptotic efficiency of GTP. It also allows for a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally accounts for the parity-odd components of tensor products. We evaluate SpinGTP across diverse benchmarks, including Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20. Our results show that SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP. Notably, by explicitly capturing antisymmetric paths, SpinGTP exhibits superior performance in tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries. This work provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous path toward high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic system simulations.

AI.tldr: SpinGTP generalizes the Gaunt Tensor Product to spin-weighted spherical harmonics, recovering missing antisymmetric interactions while maintaining O(L^5) efficiency, achieving CGTP-level accuracy with superior performance on chiral and non-centrosymmetric systems.
AI.motivation: E(3)-equivariant networks for 3D atomistic modeling face a scalability bottleneck from the O(L^6) Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP). The Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) reduces complexity but sacrifices expressivity by failing to capture antisymmetric paths, limiting performance on chiral and parity-sensitive tasks.
AI.method: The authors formulate SpinGTP by generalizing GTP from scalar spherical harmonics to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH). Using the algebraic properties of SWSH, SpinGTP recovers antisymmetric interaction paths missing in GTP while preserving O(L^5) asymptotic complexity. The method also yields a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally incorporates parity-odd tensor product components.
AI.result: SpinGTP achieves accuracy comparable to full CGTP across Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20 benchmarks. It demonstrates superior performance specifically on tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries, where antisymmetric interactions are critical.
AI.conclusion: SpinGTP provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous framework for high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic simulations, effectively bridging the gap between the expressivity of CGTP and the efficiency of GTP.

title: Data Comics for Education: Evaluating Effectiveness, Benefits, and the Ethics of AI-Assisted Creation
summary: In today's data-driven world, students often struggle with interpreting visualisations due to limited visualisation literacy. Data comics have emerged as a promising medium to enhance engagement and understanding, but their educational value has seen little empirical examination, partly due to the effort required to create them. Recent advances in Generative AI (GenAI) offer a scalable solution to this challenge. We conducted a within-subjects study with 60 university students, comparing conventional visualisations with data comics, created with assistance from GenAI tools, across information retrieval and comprehension tasks. Students consistently performed better with data comics, particularly in insight comprehension tasks, independent of prior visualisation literacy. Students also commented data comics as more engaging and easier to understand, though concerns were raised about GenAI-driven misinformation and ownership. Our findings highlight the potential of data comics as a potentially effective tool for data communication in education, while underscoring the need to address ethical concerns related to AI-assisted creation.

AI.tldr: A within-subjects study (n=60) found that GenAI-assisted data comics outperform conventional visualizations for student information retrieval and comprehension, especially insight comprehension, regardless of prior visualization literacy. Students found comics more engaging and easier to understand, though concerns about AI-driven misinformation and ownership persist.
AI.motivation: Students struggle with interpreting visualizations due to limited visualization literacy. Data comics show promise for improving engagement and understanding but lack empirical validation, partly because of the high effort required to create them. GenAI offers a scalable way to produce data comics, enabling rigorous study of their educational efficacy.
AI.method: A within-subjects experimental design with 60 university students, comparing performance on information retrieval and comprehension tasks using conventional visualizations versus GenAI-assisted data comics. Performance was analyzed across task types and controlled for participants' prior visualization literacy levels. Qualitative feedback on engagement, ease of understanding, and ethical concerns was also collected.
AI.result: Students consistently performed better with data comics than with conventional visualizations, with the most pronounced gains in insight comprehension tasks. This advantage held independent of prior visualization literacy. Qualitatively, students rated data comics as more engaging and easier to understand but raised concerns about GenAI-driven misinformation and intellectual ownership.
AI.conclusion: Data comics, especially when scaled with GenAI assistance, represent an effective tool for data communication in education. However, adoption must be accompanied by careful attention to ethical issues, notably misinformation risks and questions of content ownership in AI-assisted creation.

title: Resilient Liquid Democracy: Mitigating Voting Power Imbalances via Secure Delegation Networks
summary: Liquid democracy promises to improve collective decision-making by allowing voters to vote directly, delegate their voting power to trusted participants, or combine both approaches through fallback mechanisms. However, existing deployments typically rely on transparent delegation, which exposes voters to popularity-driven herding, makes coercion verifiable, and introduces systemic fragility when highly-backed delegates abstain. In this paper, we propose a secure liquid democracy mechanism that resolves the tension between informed expertise routing and systemic robustness. We introduce a sealed delegation regime using decentralized timed-release encryption, which cryptographically hides delegation choices during the formation phase to prevent herding and coercion, while restoring full public auditability for the final tally. To address delegate failures, we extend the protocol with ranked multi-delegation and personal fallback ballots. We formally prove pre-reveal secrecy and resubmission receipt-freeness for our protocol. Finally, we evaluate the mechanism on four real datasets, a municipal participatory-budgeting election with a calibration survey, twenty further participatory-budgeting elections, and 60,000 US voters with an objective competence measure. They show that whether delegation improves representational accuracy follows a recoverable-gap law; it helps only when abstention is large and systematically unrepresentative, and is otherwise neutral or harmful, with representative-style delegation safer than delegating to a competence elite. The benefit of sealed formation is primarily structural, sharply reducing power concentration rather than directly improving accuracy; and ranked multi-delegation with personal fallback ballots sharply reduces vote loss under realistic and targeted delegate failures, a result that replicates across all twenty elections.

AI.tldr: Proposes a cryptographically sealed liquid democracy protocol using timed-release encryption to conceal delegation choices during formation (preventing herding and coercion), augmented with ranked multi-delegation and personal fallback ballots to handle delegate abstention. Formal proofs of secrecy and receipt-freeness are provided, and empirical evaluation across participatory-budgeting and voter competence datasets reveals that delegation benefits accuracy only under large, unrepresentative abstention, while sealed formation reduces power concentration and ranked fallbacks sharply reduce vote loss.
AI.motivation: Existing liquid democracy implementations use transparent delegation, which enables popularity-driven herding, verifiable coercion, and systemic fragility when highly-backed delegates abstain. The tension between informed expertise routing and systemic robustness remains unresolved.
AI.method: Proposes a sealed delegation regime using decentralized timed-release encryption to hide delegation choices during a formation phase, with post-tally public auditability. Extends the protocol with ranked multi-delegation and personal fallback ballots. Provides formal cryptographic proofs of pre-reveal secrecy and resubmission receipt-freeness. Evaluates on four real datasets: a municipal participatory-budgeting election with calibration survey, twenty further participatory-budgeting elections, and 60,000 US voters with objective competence measures.
AI.result: Delegation improves representational accuracy only when abstention is large and systematically unrepresentative (recoverable-gap law); otherwise it is neutral or harmful. Representative-style delegation is safer than delegating to a competence elite. Sealed formation primarily reduces power concentration structurally rather than directly improving accuracy. Ranked multi-delegation with personal fallback ballots sharply reduces vote loss under realistic and targeted delegate failures, replicating across all twenty participatory-budgeting elections.
AI.conclusion: Sealed liquid democracy with ranked multi-delegation and fallback ballots resolves key vulnerabilities of transparent delegation. The recoverable-gap law provides a principled criterion for when delegation is beneficial. The structural benefit of sealed formation lies in reducing power concentration, and fallback mechanisms robustly mitigate delegate failure across diverse electoral contexts.

title: KRCA: An Efficient Root Cause Analysis System in Hyper-Scale Microservice Systems via Agentic AI
summary: Hyper-scale microservice systems have become the standard infrastructure for large-scale Internet companies. These systems consist of numerous loosely coupled microservices that evolve independently through continuous development and deployment. Such complexity makes failures unavoidable, necessitating efficient Root Cause Analysis (RCA) to help Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) quickly localize root cause services and classify failure types. However, existing RCA methods often struggle to adapt to the extreme dynamism and massive scale of these systems.
