In this paper, we present KRCA, an end-to-end RCA system designed for hyper-scale microservice systems. To manage the vast search space, KRCA employs a multi-stage pipeline that begins with an API-level drilldown to isolate suspicious services. It then instantiates a skeleton-based causal graph from anomalous metrics to serve as a high-recall structural prior, before utilizing a memory-augmented multi-agent framework to verify causality and generate the final failure report. By combining structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning, KRCA employs balances diagnostic accuracy with the efficiency requirements of real-time production use. Experimental results show that KRCA achieves AC@1 scores of 0.88 and 0.79 for root cause service localization and failure type classification, outperforming the strongest baseline by at lease 31% in absolute gains. KRCA has been deployed in Kuaishou's production environment for over six months, reducing the average diagnosis time by 77.3%.

AI.tldr: KRCA is an end-to-end RCA system for hyper-scale microservices that uses a multi-stage pipeline (API-level drilldown → skeleton-based causal graph → memory-augmented multi-agent reasoning) to localize root cause services and classify failure types, achieving AC@1 scores of 0.88/0.79 and reducing diagnosis time by 77.3% in production at Kuaishou.
AI.motivation: Hyper-scale microservice systems are highly dynamic and massive in scale, making failures inevitable. Existing RCA methods struggle to adapt to this extreme dynamism and scale, creating a need for an efficient, accurate RCA system that helps SREs quickly localize root causes and classify failure types in real-time production environments.
AI.method: KRCA employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) API-level drilldown to narrow the search space by isolating suspicious services; (2) construction of a skeleton-based causal graph from anomalous metrics, serving as a high-recall structural prior; (3) a memory-augmented multi-agent framework that verifies causality and generates the final failure report. The system balances structured causal constraints with multi-agent reasoning for diagnostic accuracy and real-time efficiency.
AI.result: KRCA achieves AC@1 scores of 0.88 for root cause service localization and 0.79 for failure type classification, outperforming the strongest baseline by at least 31% in absolute gains. Deployed in Kuaishou's production for over six months, it reduced average diagnosis time by 77.3%.
AI.conclusion: KRCA demonstrates that combining structured causal priors with multi-agent reasoning is an effective strategy for RCA in hyper-scale microservice systems, delivering both high accuracy and operational efficiency validated through extensive production deployment.

title: OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration
summary: Learning how an environment behaves from interaction is central to building agents that adapt to unfamiliar tasks. World models learned with deep networks are flexible but data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models, written as source code by LLMs and refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), are instead data-efficient and reusable, yet they have been demonstrated mainly on structured-state worlds with a given object vocabulary, and a single program search does not scale to pixel-rendered environments whose object structure must be hypothesized flexibly. We introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns an object-centric programmatic world model online from interaction. OPINE-World couples two cooperating agents in a loop of hypothesis and test, one acting in the environment and one synthesizing the model in code with replay verification and model-based planning, and it steers exploration with a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy we call ontology error. We evaluate OPINE-World on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark for skill-acquisition efficiency in which the object vocabulary, the goal, and the action semantics are withheld. OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and reaches an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against the human baseline.

AI.tldr: OPINE-World is an LLM agent that learns object-centric programmatic world models online from interaction by coupling hypothesis-generation and testing agents, using a Bayesian "ontology error" metric to guide exploration. On ARC-AGI-3, it solves 20/25 games without per-game training, achieving 78.4 action-efficiency against a human baseline.
AI.motivation: Deep network-based world models are data-hungry and generalize poorly beyond their training distribution, while existing program-synthesized world models (via CEGIS) are data-efficient but fail to scale to pixel-rendered environments where object structure must be flexibly hypothesized rather than given. Bridging this gap — achieving data-efficient, reusable world modeling without a predefined object vocabulary — motivates OPINE-World.
AI.method: OPINE-World employs two cooperating LLM agents in a hypothesis–test loop: one acts in the environment while the other synthesizes a programmatic world model in code using replay verification and model-based planning. Exploration is steered by a Bayesian metric called "ontology error," which quantifies the adequacy of the hypothesized object-type vocabulary, enabling the agent to discover object structure flexibly from raw pixel observations.
AI.result: On the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark — where object vocabulary, goal, and action semantics are all withheld — OPINE-World solves 20 out of 25 games with no per-game training and attains an action-efficiency score of 78.4, measured against a human baseline.
AI.conclusion: OPINE-World demonstrates that LLM-driven, object-centric programmatic world modeling can achieve strong skill-acquisition efficiency in novel, pixel-rendered environments without requiring a predefined object vocabulary, effectively combining the flexibility of deep learning with the data efficiency and reusability of program synthesis.

title: IsoSci: A Benchmark of Isomorphic Cross-Domain Science Problems for Evaluating Reasoning versus Knowledge Retrieval in LLMs
summary: We introduce ISOSCI, a benchmark of isomorphic cross-domain science problem pairs that separates reasoning ability from domain knowledge retrieval in LLM evaluation. Each pair shares identical logical structure but requires different domain-specific knowledge, enabling controlled attribution of reasoning-mode gains. Across five model pairs spanning four model families, we find that 91.3% of reasoning-mode gains are knowledge-dependent rather than structure-invariant (63/69 gains; Wilson 95% CI [82.3%, 96.0%]), directly challenging the assumption that chain-of-thought reasoning improves short-horizon procedural scientific problem-solving. Reasoning toggles on highly capable models provide less than 5 percentage points accuracy gain across all domains, and a reasoning-specialized model (o3-mini) that outperforms its standard counterpart on GPQA Diamond (+19.2 percentage points) underperforms on ISOSCI (-24.7 percentage points), showing that benchmark choice determines conclusions about reasoning utility. We release ISOSCI at https://huggingface.co/datasets/isosci/isosci

AI.tldr: ISOSCI is a benchmark of logically identical science problem pairs across different domains, revealing that 91.3% of reasoning-mode gains in LLMs are knowledge-dependent rather than attributable to reasoning structure alone, challenging the assumed benefit of chain-of-thought for scientific problem-solving.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation conflates reasoning ability with domain knowledge retrieval. When a model improves on a reasoning benchmark, it is unclear whether the gain comes from better reasoning or simply better knowledge recall. The authors aim to isolate these two factors to test whether chain-of-thought and other reasoning modes genuinely improve procedural scientific problem-solving, or whether apparent gains are an artifact of knowledge-dependent effects.
AI.method: The authors created ISOSCI, a benchmark of isomorphic cross-domain science problem pairs. Each pair shares an identical logical structure (same reasoning steps) but requires different domain-specific knowledge (e.g., physics vs. chemistry). This design enables controlled attribution: if reasoning-mode gains were structure-invariant, improvements should transfer across domains in a pair. They evaluated five model pairs from four model families, comparing standard vs. reasoning-mode (chain-of-thought) performance, and computed Wilson 95% confidence intervals on the proportion of knowledge-dependent gains.
AI.result: 91.3% of reasoning-mode gains (63/69) were knowledge-dependent rather than structure-invariant (Wilson 95% CI [82.3%, 96.0%]). Highly capable models showed less than 5 percentage points accuracy gain from reasoning toggles across all domains. Strikingly, o3-mini (a reasoning-specialized model) outperformed its standard counterpart on GPQA Diamond by +19.2 points but underperformed on ISOSCI by -24.7 points, demonstrating that benchmark choice can invert conclusions about reasoning utility.
AI.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning does not reliably improve short-horizon procedural scientific problem-solving; most observed gains are attributable to knowledge retrieval effects rather than genuine reasoning improvements. The choice of benchmark fundamentally determines conclusions about reasoning efficacy, and ISOSCI provides a more controlled framework for disentangling reasoning from knowledge in LLM evaluation.

title: The Rollout Infrastructure Tax in Coding-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: Preprint. 6 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ACM SoCC 2026
summary: Coding-agent reinforcement learning treats execution infrastructure as a background implementation detail, despite relying on large numbers of interactive software rollouts. This is a missed opportunity: measuring infrastructure overhead can reveal practical efficiency gains for RL post-training, where small per-rollout savings compound at scale. We present a comparative study of four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines. We find up to $110\times$ variation in cold-start latency and a $1.8\times$ spread in projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories. Our results suggest that future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training system itself, not merely as deployment plumbing.

AI.tldr: Execution substrate choice dramatically impacts coding-agent RL efficiency, with up to 110× variation in cold-start latency and 1.8× spread in worker-hours for large-scale training. Infrastructure should be treated as a first-class optimization target, not background plumbing.
AI.motivation: Coding-agent reinforcement learning systems treat execution infrastructure as a background detail, yet they depend on massive numbers of interactive software rollouts. Small per-rollout inefficiencies compound significantly at scale, making infrastructure overhead a critical but overlooked factor in RL post-training efficiency.
AI.method: Comparative benchmarking of four execution substrates — single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines — measuring cold-start latency and projecting total worker-hours required for one million 150-step trajectories.
AI.result: Cold-start latency varies by up to 110× across substrates, and projected worker-hours for one million trajectories show a 1.8× spread between the fastest and slowest options.
AI.conclusion: Future coding-agent RL systems should treat execution substrate selection and optimization as an integral component of the training system design, rather than mere deployment plumbing, to realize substantial efficiency gains at scale.

title: Physical surfaces make touch interactions in virtual reality precise, efficient, and bimanual
comment: This paper has been accepted by the "International Journal of Human-Computer Studies (IJHCS)" [Project Link] https://wy-blacksheep.github.io/projects/physical-surface/ [Paper Link] https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1071581926001254 [Video Link] https://youtu.be/e_nzOkZIIKA
summary:
Virtual reality (VR) systems can enable convenient hand-based interactions across diverse work scenarios. However, mid-air gestures lack tactile feedback and a physical reference surface to support the hand. This absence of haptic grounding can cause significant challenges in achieving precise and efficient touch interactions. This paper investigates the effect of different types of hand-grounded haptic feedback on the touch performance of VR tasks that demand high precision, such as selecting, tracing, and sketching. We compared three levels of haptic feedback: 1) No Haptic Feedback, where only visual feedback was provided; 2) Tactile Feedback, where users received vibrotactile and pressure feedback upon touching a virtual surface; 3) Physical Surface, where users interacted with a portable and tangible surface.
  Our study found that portable physical surfaces enabled the best selection precision, tracing efficiency, and sketch quality. Furthermore, participants showed increased bimanual hand utilization when engaging with a physical surface during tasks. These observed behaviors corresponded to participants' preference for interacting with physical surfaces, attributed to a better sense of confidence and control.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how different levels of hand-grounded haptic feedback affect precision touch interactions in VR, comparing no haptic feedback, vibrotactile/pressure feedback, and a portable physical surface. Results show that physical surfaces yield the best selection precision, tracing efficiency, and sketch quality, along with increased bimanual hand use and stronger user preference.
AI.motivation: Mid-air gestures in VR lack tactile feedback and a physical reference surface (haptic grounding), which undermines precision and efficiency in tasks requiring fine motor control, such as selecting, tracing, and sketching. The authors aim to quantify how varying degrees of hand-grounded haptic feedback can mitigate these limitations.
AI.method: A within-subjects user study compared three haptic conditions: (1) No Haptic Feedback — visual-only cues; (2) Tactile Feedback — vibrotactile and pressure feedback upon virtual surface contact; (3) Physical Surface — a portable, tangible surface for hand interaction. Participants performed high-precision VR tasks (selecting, tracing, sketching), and the study measured selection precision, tracing efficiency, sketch quality, and bimanual hand utilization, alongside subjective preferences.
AI.result: The portable physical surface condition significantly outperformed the other two conditions in selection precision, tracing efficiency, and sketch quality. Participants also exhibited greater bimanual hand use when a physical surface was available. Subjectively, users preferred the physical surface condition, reporting enhanced confidence and a stronger sense of control.
AI.conclusion: Hand-grounded haptic feedback — particularly via a portable physical surface — substantially improves precision touch interactions in VR. The findings suggest that incorporating tangible, portable surfaces can enhance both objective performance and subjective user experience for high-precision VR tasks, with implications for the design of future VR interaction systems.

title: Knowledge Over Parameters: Evolving Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection
summary:
Smart contract vulnerabilities are predominantly logic bugs whose detection requires structured, step-by-step procedural knowledge of attack patterns and contract semantics. Existing LLM-based methods struggle to generate this knowledge automatically: prompt-based methods rely on manually crafted detection rules, while fine-tuning requires massive labeled datasets that are inherently scarce in this domain. We present EvoVuln, an automated framework that reformulates vulnerability detection as a procedural knowledge evolution problem, synthesizing and refining detection logic using only a minimal number of labeled samples.
  To achieve this, EvoVuln introduces two key mechanisms. First, a Runtime with an Inversion of Control (IoC) architecture compiles detection rules into Executable Policies. This strictly decouples deterministic control flow from LLM semantic reasoning, ensuring faithful logical adherence and producing dense diagnostic telemetry for precise error localization. Second, a two-phase evolution pipeline refines the rule via abductive semantic debugging without any parameter updates: Cold Start bootstraps and stress-tests an initial rule using auto-synthesized corner cases; Few-Shot Evolving then grounds the policy in real-world semantics using only five vulnerable and five safe examples per vulnerability type.
  Evaluated across five real-world vulnerability types, EvoVuln achieves a 71% macro-average F1-score, outperforming all baselines. The evolved procedural knowledge is portable across models: it enables a lightweight, low-cost model to surpass a much larger zero-shot model by 19 percentage points, and transfers to other LLMs without retraining, at a one-time evolution cost under $50.

AI.tldr: EvoVuln is an automated framework that reframes smart contract vulnerability detection as procedural knowledge evolution, using an IoC runtime architecture and a two-phase evolution pipeline to synthesize and refine detection rules from minimal labeled samples, achieving 71% macro F1 and enabling portable, cost-effective knowledge transfer across LLMs.
AI.motivation: Smart contract vulnerabilities are predominantly logic bugs requiring structured procedural knowledge of attack patterns. Existing LLM approaches are inadequate: prompt-based methods depend on manual rules, while fine-tuning demands large labeled datasets that are scarce. There is a need for automated, sample-efficient generation of procedural detection knowledge.
AI.method: EvoVuln employs two core mechanisms: (1) An IoC Runtime that compiles detection rules into Executable Policies, decoupling deterministic control flow from LLM semantic reasoning to ensure logical adherence and produce diagnostic telemetry; (2) A two-phase evolution pipeline — Cold Start bootstraps and stress-tests initial rules with auto-synthesized corner cases, followed by Few-Shot Evolving that grounds policies using only five vulnerable and five safe examples per vulnerability type. No parameter updates are required.
AI.result: Evaluated on five real-world vulnerability types, EvoVuln achieves a 71% macro-average F1-score, outperforming all baselines. The evolved procedural knowledge is portable: a lightweight model surpasses a much larger zero-shot model by 19 percentage points, and knowledge transfers to other LLMs without retraining, with a one-time evolution cost under $50.
AI.conclusion: EvoVuln demonstrates that procedural knowledge evolution with minimal labeled data is a viable, cost-effective alternative to both prompt engineering and fine-tuning for smart contract vulnerability detection, with the added benefit of cross-model portability.

title: Archer: Towards Agentic Review for Compiler Optimizations
summary:
Modern compilers are frequently updated, but expert review capacity is highly limited, leading to delayed integration and, in some cases, subtle semantic bugs entering the compiler codebase. Automating the code review process with modern general code review agents may be feasible, but it faces critical challenges due to compiler complexity. In this paper, we use LLVM as our target compiler and present Archer, the first automated agentic code review tool for compiler optimizations. Archer constrains the agentic review process from both ends by using obligations to guide analysis and a deterministic validation guard to admit only findings backed by executable evidence.
  We evaluated Archer on 70 open PRs and 328 closed PRs in LLVM from the last two months. The review results are shocking and concerning: Archer discovers that 21% of open PRs and 11% of closed PRs are buggy, i.e, introducing semantic bugs such as miscompilations in LLVM. Our findings expose a critical gap in the capacity for critical review in large compiler projects and demonstrate the practical value of Archer as an additional reviewer.

AI.tldr: Archer is the first automated agentic code review tool for compiler optimizations (targeting LLVM). It combines obligation-guided analysis with deterministic validation guards to ensure findings are backed by executable evidence. Evaluation on 70 open and 328 closed LLVM PRs reveals that 21% of open and 11% of closed PRs contain semantic bugs like miscompilations, exposing a critical review capacity gap in large compiler projects.
AI.motivation: Modern compilers are updated frequently but expert review capacity is severely limited, leading to delayed integration and subtle semantic bugs (e.g., miscompilations) slipping into the codebase. General-purpose code review agents struggle with compiler complexity, motivating a specialized automated review approach.
AI.method: Archer constrains the agentic review process bidirectionally: (1) **Obligations** guide the analysis phase by specifying what the agent must verify, narrowing the search space; (2) a **deterministic validation guard** acts as a filter, admitting only findings supported by executable evidence (e.g., concrete test cases demonstrating the bug), thereby preventing false positives. The system targets LLVM optimization patches.
AI.result: On 70 open PRs, Archer found 21% to be buggy; on 328 closed PRs, 11% were identified as containing semantic bugs such as miscompilations. These results highlight a significant gap in human review capacity for LLVM.
AI.conclusion: There is a substantial and concerning gap in critical review capacity for large compiler projects like LLVM. Archer demonstrates practical value as an automated additional reviewer capable of catching semantic bugs that would otherwise go undetected, even in already-merged (closed) PRs.

title: Scaling Trends for Lie Detector Oversight in Preference Learning
summary: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent, motivating approaches such as Scalable Oversight via Lie Detectors (SOLiD) (Cundy & Gleave, 2025), which uses lie detectors to identify responses for review by high-cost labelers. In this paper, we scale SOLiD to larger models and evaluate it in more diverse and realistic preference-learning settings. We find favorable scaling: undetected deception drops from 34% for 1B-parameter models to 14% for 405B-parameter models at a detector true positive rate of 99%, and expensive human labelers can be removed entirely from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant increase in deception. However, SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive detector false positive rates to impractical levels.

AI.tldr: The paper scales the SOLiD framework to larger models (up to 405B parameters) in realistic preference-learning settings, finding that undetected deception decreases with model scale (from 34% at 1B to 14% at 405B) and that human labelers can be removed from fine-tuning without significantly increasing deception. However, distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data can render false positive rates impractically high.
AI.motivation: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to detect and prevent. The SOLiD framework proposes using lie detectors to flag suspicious outputs for human review, but prior work only tested it on smaller models in limited settings. This paper aims to evaluate whether SOLiD scales effectively to larger models and to more diverse, realistic preference-learning environments.
AI.method: The authors scale the SOLiD (Scalable Oversight via Lie Detectors) framework to models ranging from 1B to 405B parameters and test it across more diverse preference-learning settings. SOLiD uses lie detectors to identify potentially deceptive responses for review by high-cost labelers. The study examines scaling behavior, the necessity of human labelers during fine-tuning, and sensitivity to distribution shift between detector training data and preference-training data.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Favorable scaling — undetected deception drops from 34% (1B models) to 14% (405B models) at a detector true positive rate of 99%. (2) Expensive human labelers can be removed from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant increase in deception. (3) SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive false positive rates to impractical levels.
AI.conclusion: SOLiD scales favorably to larger models, with undetected deception declining as model size increases, and human labelers may be unnecessary during fine-tuning. However, the framework's practical viability is threatened by distribution shift sensitivity, which can inflate false positive rates beyond acceptable thresholds.

title: FaithMed: Training LLMs For Faithful Evidence-Based Medical Reasoning
summary: Faithful reasoning is essential in medicine, where clinical decisions require transparent justification grounded in reliable evidence. Current medical LLMs either lack active access to evidence or use retrieved evidence without supervising how it should be appraised and applied during reasoning. To address this, we formalize evidence-based medicine principles as process-level criteria and introduce FaithMed, a framework that combines clinician-designed, automatically refined rubrics with reinforcement learning using step-level process reward assignment and advantage grouping. Across seven medical benchmarks, FaithMed improves over agentic-search baselines (+9% on average) and outcome-only RL (+5.8%), while raising average evidence-based medicine rubric scores over agentic-search Qwen3 baselines (+15.5%). This work demonstrates that explicit step-level supervision can improve both task success and the faithfulness of the reasoning process. Code is available at https://github.com/cxcscmu/FaithMed.

AI.tldr: FaithMed introduces a reinforcement learning framework that supervises medical LLMs at the step level using clinician-designed, automatically refined rubrics grounded in evidence-based medicine principles. It improves both task accuracy (+9% over agentic-search baselines) and reasoning faithfulness (+15.5% EBM rubric scores).
AI.motivation: Current medical LLMs either lack active evidence access or retrieve evidence without structured supervision over how it should be appraised and applied during reasoning. Faithful, transparent justification grounded in reliable evidence is critical for clinical decision-making, motivating the need for process-level oversight aligned with evidence-based medicine (EBM) principles.
AI.method: The authors formalize EBM principles as process-level criteria. FaithMed uses clinician-designed rubrics that are automatically refined, combined with reinforcement learning featuring step-level process reward assignment and advantage grouping. This provides explicit per-step supervision during the reasoning chain rather than outcome-only feedback.
AI.result: Across seven medical benchmarks, FaithMed outperforms agentic-search baselines by +9% on average and outcome-only RL by +5.8%. Average EBM rubric scores improve by +15.5% over agentic-search Qwen3 baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicit step-level supervision via process rewards aligned with EBM principles enhances both downstream task success and the faithfulness of the clinical reasoning process itself.

title: Conditional Inference Trees and Forests for Feature Selection
summary: Conditional inference trees (CIT) and conditional inference forests (CIF) reduce split-selection bias by testing features before choosing split thresholds, but repeated permutation tests and threshold searches can make these methods computationally expensive. We study CIT and CIF as top-$k$ feature-ranking methods for downstream prediction using real-data benchmarks, runtime ablations, and synthetic feature-recovery experiments. At a fixed node, if the features and permutation budget do not depend on the node responses, Bonferroni-corrected $+1$ Monte Carlo permutation $p$-values control nodewise rejection under the complete permutation null. CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. With Bonferroni correction held fixed, the CIF runtime ablations indicate that adaptive stopping and the number of thresholds searched have the largest measured effect on runtime: turning off adaptive stopping and using exact threshold search increase fitting time by 4.0--8.4$\times$ and 1.9--10.8$\times$, respectively, while downstream score changes are at most 0.011. Sparse high-$p$ simulations indicate that forest feature sampling can leave informative features out of many split decisions. Overall, the results support CIF as a top-$k$ feature-ranking method in the evaluated downstream prediction benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Conditional inference forests (CIF) are validated as strong top-k feature-ranking methods for prediction. Key findings: Bonferroni-corrected +1 Monte Carlo permutation p-values provide valid nodewise error control; adaptive stopping and threshold search count dominate runtime (4–10× impact), while minimally affecting performance (≤0.011 score change). CIF ranks 3rd–4th across 30 benchmark datasets. Sparse high-p simulations reveal forest feature sampling can exclude informative features from many splits.
AI.motivation: Conditional inference trees and forests mitigate split-selection bias through permutation testing, but this introduces substantial computational cost. The authors aim to systematically evaluate CIF as a feature-ranking method for downstream prediction, quantify runtime bottlenecks, and assess statistical validity under the permutation null.
AI.method: Three evaluation paradigms: (1) real-data benchmarks — CIF compared against 16 classification and 17 regression methods across 22 and 8 datasets respectively; (2) runtime ablations — measuring the effect of adaptive stopping and exact vs. approximate threshold search on fitting time and predictive scores; (3) synthetic feature-recovery experiments in sparse high-dimensional settings to assess how forest feature sampling affects the inclusion of informative features. Theoretical analysis of Bonferroni-corrected +1 Monte Carlo permutation p-values under the complete permutation null is also provided.
AI.result: CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods (22 datasets) and 3rd among 18 regression methods (8 datasets). Runtime ablations: disabling adaptive stopping increases fitting time 4.0–8.4×; using exact threshold search increases time 1.9–10.8×; downstream score changes are ≤0.011. Theoretical result: Bonferroni-corrected +1 Monte Carlo permutation p-values control nodewise rejection when features and permutation budget are independent of node responses. Sparse high-p simulations show forest feature sampling often excludes informative features from many split decisions.
AI.conclusion: CIF is a competitive top-k feature-ranking method for downstream prediction. Adaptive stopping and approximate threshold search are critical for computational efficiency with negligible performance loss. The Bonferroni +1 Monte Carlo framework provides valid statistical guarantees at each node. However, forest feature sampling can be detrimental in high-dimensional sparse settings by omitting informative features from splits.

title: When Do LLM Personas Support Visualization Design? A Cross-Model Study of Color Assignment and Chart Choice
summary: Large language model personas are increasingly used to approximate diverse users during early-stage visualization design, but it remains unclear whether persona-conditioned outputs reflect stable personality effects or artifacts of model choice and task framing. We examine this question across two visualization-relevant tasks: color assignment for abstract and concrete concepts, and chart-idiom preference ratings across task contexts. Using 43 Big Five profiles across GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, and GPT-5-mini, we find that personality-color coupling is highly model-configuration dependent: absent in GPT-4o-mini for all six concepts, consistent in GPT-4.1-mini across all six, and partial in GPT-5-mini for two of six. Concept type further shapes the signal: for abstract concepts, personality explains more hue variance than model identity, while concrete concepts show smaller and comparable effects. In chart choice, trait-aligned cluster aggregation produces stable top-idiom rankings across all nine cluster-context combinations, but a no-persona baseline recovers the same top choice in 8 of 9 model-context cells, indicating that task context drives rank-1 selection more than personality. These findings position LLM personas as exploratory probes for visualization design, not substitutes for human participants, and motivate multi-model testing, concept-type disaggregation, and no-persona baselines in future studies.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLM personas conditioned on Big Five personality profiles produce stable, personality-driven outputs in visualization design tasks (color assignment and chart-idiom preference). Results show personality effects are highly model-dependent, concept-type-dependent, and often overshadowed by task context, suggesting LLM personas are exploratory probes rather than substitutes for human participants.
AI.motivation: LLM personas are increasingly used to simulate diverse users in early-stage visualization design, but it is unclear whether persona-conditioned outputs reflect genuine, stable personality effects or are merely artifacts of model choice and task framing. The authors aim to systematically test this across multiple models, tasks, and personality profiles.
AI.method: The authors used 43 Big Five personality profiles across three LLM configurations (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5-mini) in two visualization-relevant tasks: (1) color assignment for six concepts (abstract and concrete), analyzing how personality traits predict hue variance; (2) chart-idiom preference ratings across task contexts, comparing trait-aligned cluster aggregation against a no-persona baseline.
AI.result: Personality-color coupling was absent in GPT-4o-mini, consistent in GPT-4.1-mini, and partial (2 of 6 concepts) in GPT-5-mini. For abstract concepts, personality explained more hue variance than model identity; for concrete concepts, effects were smaller and comparable. In chart choice, trait-aligned clusters produced stable top-idiom rankings, but the no-persona baseline recovered the same top choice in 8 of 9 model-context cells, indicating task context drives rank-1 selection more than personality.
AI.conclusion: LLM personas should be treated as exploratory probes for visualization design, not as replacements for human participants. The authors recommend multi-model testing, disaggregation by concept type, and inclusion of no-persona baselines in future LLM persona studies to avoid spurious attributions of personality effects.

title: Has This Checkpoint Been Abliterated? A Two-Signal Audit and Its Failure Map
summary: Can a platform tell, before deployment, whether an open-weight checkpoint has had its refusal mechanism stripped? Runtime guards cannot: they score generations, not the artifact. We combine two cheap internal signals, a reference-anchored activation refusal-gap and a weight-recovery energy of the base-to-candidate weight difference, into a threshold-free checkpoint audit. The two are negatively correlated and label-complementary: the gap supplies refusal-specificity and the weight energy supplies recall. On a 273-checkpoint registry spanning Qwen, DeepSeek-distilled Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, their z-sum separates 57 public abliterations from 37 benign fine-tunes, merges, and instruction-tunes at AUROC 0.95, significantly above either signal alone (0.84, 0.90), and a Youden-calibrated threshold transfers to held-out families at balanced accuracy 0.89 (FPR 0.11), missing only 4 of 57. We then map two failures, in order of severity: a spoofed reference evades both axes with no training (ΔW=0, \r{ho}=1 by construction), and a white-box owner trains a checkpoint past the threshold while it stays guard-unsafe and coherent. The audit is effective triage, not tamper-proofing: it presumes an attested reference, and its claims are bounded by the registry we evaluate it on.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a threshold-free checkpoint audit method that combines two internal signals — a reference-anchored activation refusal-gap and a base-to-candidate weight-recovery energy — to detect whether an open-weight language model's refusal mechanism has been stripped before deployment, achieving AUROC 0.95 on a 273-checkpoint registry.
AI.motivation: Runtime guardrails cannot detect refusal mechanism removal before deployment because they score model outputs, not the model artifact itself. There is a need for a pre-deployment audit that can distinguish "abliterated" checkpoints (refusal stripped) from benign fine-tunes, merges, and instruction-tuned variants using only the checkpoint weights and a trusted reference.
AI.method: Two complementary internal signals are computed: (1) a reference-anchored activation refusal-gap, which measures refusal-specificity by comparing activation differences on harmful vs. harmless prompts relative to a reference model; and (2) a weight-recovery energy, computed as the norm of the weight difference between the candidate checkpoint and the base model, providing recall. These two signals are negatively correlated. Their z-score sum forms a threshold-free composite audit score. Evaluation is conducted on a 273-checkpoint registry spanning Qwen, DeepSeek-distilled Qwen, Llama, and Gemma families, with threshold transfer evaluated via Youden-calibrated cutoffs on held-out model families.
AI.result: The z-sum composite separates 57 public abliterations from 37 benign fine-tunes, merges, and instruction-tunes at AUROC 0.95, significantly outperforming either signal alone (refusal-gap: 0.84; weight energy: 0.90). A Youden-calibrated threshold transfers to held-out families at balanced accuracy 0.89 (FPR 0.11), missing only 4 of 57 abliterated checkpoints. Two failure modes are identified: a spoofed reference scenario (ΔW=0, ρ=1 by construction) evades both axes with no training, and a white-box owner can train past the threshold while the model remains guard-unsafe and coherent.
AI.conclusion: The audit serves as effective triage rather than tamper-proofing. It requires an attested reference checkpoint, and its validity is bounded by the registry evaluated. The method provides a practical, low-cost pre-deployment screening tool for platforms hosting open-weight models.

title: Decoupling Code Complexity from Newcomer Participation: A Causal Study of AI Coding Agent Adoption in OSS
summary: Open-source projects depend on a steady inflow of newcomers. A growing concern is that AI coding agents (tools such as Cursor and Claude Code that write code from natural-language instructions) will crowd them out, by absorbing the simple tasks that beginners start with and by making code harder to read. We give this concern a causal answer. Using GitHub code search we identify 1,888 projects that adopted an agent, signaled by their first commit of a configuration file. We apply difference-in-differences against matched non-adopting controls, restricting the main analysis to the 603 adopters with a genuine pre-adoption period. We find no evidence of crowding-out: across estimators newcomer inflow shows no significant decline after adoption (point estimates run from a small increase to, under the most conservative trend specification, a slight and insignificant dip), onboarding and retention are unchanged, and a sparse, correlational beginner-task measure (good-first-issue labels, which we cannot test for parallel trends) shows no decline. The feared mechanism is real but decoupled: adoption raises per-function code complexity (about +11% on a cognitive metric for Python, a quarter of the prior estimate, and +3 to 4% in cyclomatic terms across all languages), yet in fixed-unit subsets where complexity rose (Python on the cognitive metric, and all languages on the cyclomatic metric), newcomer participation does not decline. These results suggest that, in established open-source projects, adopting an AI coding agent makes code modestly more complex but does not crowd out the human newcomers that a project depends on: the feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.

AI.tldr: A difference-in-differences study of 603 open-source projects finds that adopting AI coding agents (e.g., Cursor, Claude Code) modestly increases code complexity (~3–11%) but does not reduce newcomer inflow, onboarding, or retention, contrary to fears that AI tools would crowd out human beginners.
AI.motivation: There is growing concern that AI coding agents, which automate simple programming tasks from natural-language instructions, may crowd out newcomers in open-source projects — both by absorbing the entry-level tasks beginners rely on to get started, and by making AI-generated code harder for humans to read and contribute to. This paper provides the first causal empirical test of this crowding-out hypothesis.
AI.method: The authors use GitHub code search to identify 1,888 projects that adopted an AI coding agent (detected via the first commit of an agent configuration file). From these, 603 projects with a genuine pre-adoption period are retained for the main analysis. A difference-in-differences design is applied, comparing adopters against matched non-adopting control projects. Outcomes measured include newcomer inflow, onboarding, retention, and a correlational beginner-task metric (good-first-issue labels). Code complexity is measured using both a cognitive metric (for Python) and cyclomatic complexity (across all languages).
AI.result: Across estimators, newcomer inflow shows no significant decline after AI agent adoption (point estimates range from a small increase to a slight, insignificant dip under the most conservative trend specification). Onboarding and retention are unchanged. Good-first-issue labels show no decline (though parallel trends could not be tested). The feared mechanism — increased code complexity — is confirmed but decoupled from participation: per-function cognitive complexity rises ~11% for Python, and cyclomatic complexity rises 3–4% across all languages. However, in project subsets where complexity increased, newcomer participation did not decline.
AI.conclusion: In established open-source projects, adopting an AI coding agent makes code modestly more complex but does not crowd out human newcomers. The feared trade-off between AI assistance and human participation does not materialize.

title: EO-Agents: A Three-Agent LLM Pipeline for Earth Observation Hypothesis Generation
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: Large language models have recently been explored for scientific hypothesis generation, but most prior work relies on unstructured literature and free-form textual claims. We present a pipeline for Earth observation that grounds hypothesis generation directly in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. A heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings, and a three-agent LLM pipeline filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, the system produces 160 hypotheses spanning multiple Earth-science domains, including ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol--cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages from the literature, indicating that the pipeline surfaces scientifically coherent yet unexplored combinations. A 2*2*2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 shows that hypothesis rankings remain stable, while absolute scores depend strongly on judge identity, highlighting limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.

AI.tldr: A pipeline grounded in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph uses a heterogeneous GNN to rank candidate dataset pairings and a three-agent LLM system to filter, generate, and evaluate hypotheses, producing 160 cross-domain hypotheses with near-real plausibility ratings; a factorial experiment reveals ranking stability but judge-dependent scoring.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LLM-based scientific hypothesis generation relies on unstructured literature and free-form text, lacking structured grounding in curated knowledge graphs. The authors aim to ground hypothesis generation in a structured, domain-specific knowledge resource — the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph — to surface unexplored but scientifically coherent dataset combinations.
AI.method: A heterogeneous graph neural network (GNN) trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings from 1,475 NASA datasets. A three-agent LLM pipeline then (1) filters irrelevant pairings, (2) generates structured research hypotheses, and (3) evaluates their quality. A 2×2×2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 assesses evaluation robustness.
AI.result: The system produced 160 hypotheses spanning ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol–cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel pairings were rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages. The factorial experiment showed stable rankings across models but significant score dependence on judge identity.
AI.conclusion: Grounding hypothesis generation in a domain knowledge graph enables discovery of plausible, unexplored dataset combinations. While LLM-based evaluation rankings are robust across models, single-judge scoring is unreliable due to judge-identity bias, warranting multi-judge or calibration strategies.

title: Grounded Optimization: A Layered Engineering Framework for Reducing LLM Hallucination in Automated Personal Document Rewriting
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure. Equal contribution by both authors. Code and data: https://github.com/shashank-indukuri/grounded-optimization
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to resume optimization for applicant tracking systems, introducing hallucination failures distinct from general text generation: anachronistic technology injection, cross-domain terminology contamination, structural mutation, and content fabrication. We present Grounded Optimization, a five-layer framework combining temporal context validation, deterministic contamination detection, structural invariant enforcement, prompt-level grounding, and an evaluator agent.
  In ablation experiments across three LLMs, four temperature settings, and six layer configurations on 25 synthetic resumes spanning 14 industries, undefended baselines produce 2.48-5.36 detected hallucinations per resume. Among detectors independent of the active defenses, temporal hallucinations are reduced by 50-95% across all conditions; overall detected hallucination rate falls to 0.04-0.24. Prompt-level grounding alone achieves zero detected hallucinations at low temperature with a capable instruction-following model; higher temperatures and weaker models reveal the need for the deterministic layers as a complement. We release the contamination taxonomy, evaluation code, and raw data.

AI.tldr: Proposes Grounded Optimization, a five-layer framework to mitigate hallucination types specific to LLM-based resume optimization. Undefended baselines produce 2.48–5.36 hallucinations per resume; the framework reduces this to 0.04–0.24, with temporal hallucinations cut by 50–95%.
AI.motivation: LLMs applied to resume optimization for applicant tracking systems (ATS) introduce distinct hallucination failure modes—anachronistic technology injection, cross-domain terminology contamination, structural mutation, and content fabrication—that differ from general text generation hallucinations and require specialized mitigation.
AI.method: Introduces Grounded Optimization, a five-layer defense framework: (1) temporal context validation, (2) deterministic contamination detection, (3) structural invariant enforcement, (4) prompt-level grounding, and (5) an evaluator agent. Evaluated via ablation experiments across 3 LLMs × 4 temperature settings × 6 layer configurations on 25 synthetic resumes spanning 14 industries.
AI.result: Undefended baselines: 2.48–5.36 detected hallucinations per resume. With defenses: overall detected hallucination rate drops to 0.04–0.24 per resume. Temporal hallucinations reduced by 50–95% across all conditions. Prompt-level grounding alone achieves zero detected hallucinations at low temperature with a capable instruction-following model; at higher temperatures/weaker models, deterministic layers are essential complements.
AI.conclusion: The five-layer Grounded Optimization framework effectively mitigates ATS-specific LLM hallucinations in resume optimization, with prompt-level grounding providing strong standalone defense under favorable conditions and deterministic layers serving as necessary complements under challenging settings. The contamination taxonomy, evaluation code, and raw data are publicly released.

title: On the Utility and Factual Reliability of Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Models in the Biomedical Domain
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer inference speedups via selective activation but impose substantial memory requirements because the whole network must remain loaded. Structured expert pruning is a practical approach for reducing deployment costs in resource-constrained settings. However, prior studies primarily evaluate benchmark utility, leaving the effect of pruning on factual reliability underexplored, particularly in high-stakes domains such as biomedicine. In this paper, we investigate how domain-specific expert pruning affects both utility and reliability. We assess four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain settings. Results reveal that moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, although hallucination risks increase at extreme pruning ratios. When shifting to the general domain, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly. These findings indicate that safe compression depends heavily on the task and domain. Evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment without reliability assessment.

AI.tldr: Investigates how structured expert pruning in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models affects both utility and factual reliability in biomedical domains. Finds moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without reliability decline, but extreme pruning increases hallucinations; cross-domain performance degrades rapidly. Cautions that utility-only evaluation is insufficient for high-stakes deployments.
AI.motivation: Prior work on MoE expert pruning evaluates only benchmark utility, neglecting factual reliability — a critical gap for high-stakes domains like biomedicine where hallucinations can have severe consequences. The paper aims to fill this gap by systematically assessing the reliability-utility trade-off under pruning.
AI.method: Evaluated four MoE models (covering both generation and classification tasks) under six structured pruning methods at multiple pruning ratios. Tested in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain (general) settings, measuring both standard utility metrics and reliability indicators such as hallucination rates.
AI.result: Moderate pruning ratios preserve in-domain utility with no immediate reliability degradation. At extreme pruning ratios, hallucination risk increases significantly. When shifting from biomedical to general domain, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly. Safe compression is highly task- and domain-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating pruned MoE models on utility alone is inadequate for high-stakes deployment; reliability assessment must be incorporated. Domain and task context fundamentally shape the safety ceiling of model compression, and practitioners should adopt joint utility-reliability evaluation frameworks before deploying pruned MoEs in sensitive applications.

title: Behind the Refusal: Determining Guardrail Activation via Behavioral Monitoring
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) and agentic systems become integrated into real-world applications, ensuring their safety and security is critical. Guardrail systems that detect and block malicious instructions sent to and from an LLM are an essential component of AI security. However, researchers conducting black-box adversarial emulation against production AI systems often struggle to determine whether a guardrail block or an LLM rejection has occurred. This distinction is important because the techniques used to bypass guardrails can differ substantially from those used to bypass LLM safety alignment, and has a material impact on attack technique selection and optimization. We propose the first black-box guardrail reconnaissance methodology, which detects the presence of a guardrail within a target AI system through behavioral monitoring of HTTP, lexical, and timing signals, assuming only black-box access and zero prior knowledge of the guardrail or AI system. Experiments demonstrate that our approach detects guardrail presence with 100% accuracy, with statistically significant behavioral separation between benign and malicious interactions (q < 0.001). Our approach further identifies the content categories a guardrail is designed to block, and distinguishes guardrail blocks from LLM rejection on unseen prompts with an average F1 score of 98%.

AI.tldr: Proposes a black-box methodology to detect the presence of guardrail systems in AI deployments, distinguish guardrail blocks from LLM rejections, and identify blocked content categories — achieving 100% detection accuracy and 98% F1 on block vs. rejection classification.
AI.motivation: Adversarial testers lack a systematic way to determine whether a refusal originates from a guardrail filter or the LLM's internal safety alignment, yet bypass techniques differ substantially between the two. This distinction is critical for accurate attack technique selection and optimization.
AI.method: A black-box reconnaissance methodology that monitors HTTP response patterns, lexical signatures in rejection messages, and timing side-channels to infer guardrail presence, blocked content categories, and differentiate guardrail blocks from LLM-native rejections — all with zero prior knowledge.
AI.result: 100% guardrail detection accuracy with statistically significant separation between benign and malicious interactions (q < 0.001). Category identification and block-vs-rejection classification achieve an average F1 score of 98% on unseen prompts.
AI.conclusion: Guardrail presence and behavior can be reliably inferred through passive black-box observation of behavioral signals, enabling more effective and targeted adversarial emulation against production AI systems.

title: Understanding Software Defect Prediction: A Large-scale Empirical Study Across Uncertainty Quantification and Performance Evaluation
summary: Software defect prediction (SDP) classifiers produce probabilities used for inspection prioritization, threshold tuning, and risk communication. Probability-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) characterizes prediction confidence, but whether common UQ metrics reliably indicate performance and calibration remains unclear. We conducted a large-scale empirical study of probability-based UQ for SDP. We evaluated five UQ metrics, six performance metrics, and three calibration metrics for 16 representative classifiers. We analyzed these relationships under two prediction settings: within-project defect prediction (WPDP), using 36 benchmark datasets, and cross-project defect prediction (CPDP), using 32 feature-compatible datasets. Results showed that UQ was highly context-dependent. Under WPDP, UQ correlated more consistently with false positive rate and AUC than with MCC, F1 score, and other metrics; these correlations also varied across classifier categories and dataset collections. Performance and calibration were related but not interchangeable; classifiers with strong discrimination could still exhibit large calibration error. Under CPDP, several UQ-performance and UQ-calibration correlations weakened or reversed, indicating that uncertainty signals do not reliably transfer across projects. Thus, UQ should be evaluated against specific performance objectives. Calibration should be assessed independently using multiple metrics. Transferred probabilities should be revalidated before guiding quality-assurance decisions.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study on software defect prediction (SDP) classifiers reveals that probability-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) metrics are highly context-dependent: correlations with performance and calibration metrics vary by setting (within-project vs. cross-project), classifier category, and dataset collection. UQ is more consistently correlated with false positive rate and AUC than with MCC or F1; strong discrimination does not guarantee good calibration; and UQ signals do not reliably transfer across projects.
AI.motivation: SDP classifiers output probabilities used for inspection prioritization, threshold tuning, and risk communication. Probability-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) characterizes prediction confidence, but it is unclear whether common UQ metrics reliably indicate classifier performance and calibration. The authors aim to systematically investigate these relationships across diverse classifiers, metrics, and prediction settings.
AI.method: A large-scale empirical study evaluating 5 UQ metrics, 6 performance metrics, and 3 calibration metrics across 16 representative classifiers. Analysis conducted under two settings: within-project defect prediction (WPDP) using 36 benchmark datasets, and cross-project defect prediction (CPDP) using 32 feature-compatible datasets. Relationships among UQ, performance, and calibration were examined across classifier categories and dataset collections.
AI.result: Under WPDP, UQ correlated more consistently with false positive rate and AUC than with MCC, F1, and other metrics; correlations varied across classifier categories and dataset collections. Performance and calibration were related but not interchangeable — classifiers with strong discrimination could still exhibit large calibration error. Under CPDP, several UQ-performance and UQ-calibration correlations weakened or reversed, indicating unreliable transfer of uncertainty signals across projects.
AI.conclusion: UQ should be evaluated against specific performance objectives rather than treated as a universal proxy. Calibration must be assessed independently using multiple metrics. Probability outputs transferred across projects should be revalidated before informing quality-assurance decisions.

title: Hawk: Harnessing Hardware-Aware Knowledge for High-Performance NPU Kernel Generation
summary: Developing high-performance kernels for Neural Processing Units (NPUs) is a critical industry bottleneck, requiring developers to manually navigate implicit hardware constraints and strict memory hierarchies. While large language models offer immense automation potential, they fail catastrophically on NPUs due to a fundamental lack of hardware-specific priors. Naively transplanting code snippets from similar NPU kernels may pass the compiler, but it consistently triggers runtime crashes and performance degradation by blindly violating underlying hardware constraints. To overcome this, we introduce Hawk, a training-free framework that harnesses hardware-aware knowledge through three core modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module, which employs a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to inherently couple the error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module, which implements a 2D-Retrieval paradigm to project queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; and (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module, which leverages LLM-driven semantic arbitration to continuously distill the knowledge by pruning errors and consolidating redundancies based on the empirical execution feedback. Extensive evaluations on real-world NPU workloads demonstrate that Hawk elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%, while achieving up to a 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: Hawk is a training-free framework that enables LLMs to generate correct, high-performance NPU kernels by synthesizing, retrieving, and distilling hardware-aware knowledge from runtime execution feedback, improving generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0% and achieving up to 2.2× speedup.
AI.motivation: Developing high-performance NPU kernels is a critical bottleneck because developers must manually navigate implicit hardware constraints and memory hierarchies. LLMs fail on this task due to a lack of hardware-specific priors — naively transplanted code may compile but triggers runtime crashes and performance degradation by violating underlying hardware constraints.
AI.method: Hawk introduces three training-free modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module using a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation that couples error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module employing a 2D-Retrieval paradigm that projects queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module that uses LLM-driven semantic arbitration to prune errors and consolidate redundancies based on empirical execution feedback.
AI.result: On real-world NPU workloads, Hawk raises generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0% and achieves up to 2.2× execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: By grounding LLM-based code generation in empirically derived, hardware-aware knowledge, Hawk effectively bridges the gap between LLM automation and the strict constraints of NPU programming, yielding substantial gains in both correctness and performance without requiring any model fine-tuning.

title: Comparing Architectures for Supervised Political Scaling
summary: Text scaling, the task of positioning political actors on an ideological scale, is a fundamental task in political analysis. To ease the need for manual analysis, various NLP methods have been proposed for this task, including classification- and regression-based approaches, showing successes as well as limitations. The goal of our paper is to consolidate the state of the art in this area. We ask two questions: (a) Can the performance of scaling methods be improved by predicting scales not individually but jointly? (b) Is there a middle ground between classification and regression?

AI.tldr: The paper consolidates the state of the art in text scaling for ideological positioning, investigating whether joint prediction of multiple scales improves performance over individual prediction, and whether a hybrid approach between classification and regression yields better results.
AI.motivation: Text scaling is a core task in political analysis that traditionally requires manual effort. While various NLP methods (classification and regression) have been applied, they each have limitations. The authors aim to systematically consolidate existing approaches and explore two under-investigated directions to advance the field.
AI.method: The paper proposes two key methodological investigations: (1) joint prediction of multiple ideological scales simultaneously, rather than treating each scale independently; (2) exploring a middle-ground approach that bridges classification-style and regression-style scaling methods, potentially capturing ordinal structure while allowing continuous outputs.
AI.result: The abstract does not provide specific empirical results; it frames the paper as a consolidation and exploration of two research questions regarding joint prediction and classification-regression hybrids for text scaling.
AI.conclusion: The abstract does not state explicit conclusions, but implies that addressing the two research questions — joint scale prediction and a classification-regression middle ground — can advance the state of the art in automated text scaling for political analysis.

title: Geometry-Aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary:
We propose a novel hybrid neural architecture, the Geometry-aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GRS-KAN), which integrates V.L.Rvachev's R-functions into the Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) framework. The proposed approach combines two complementary modeling mechanisms: smooth nonlinear structure is learned by KAN branches, while known geometric or logical constraints are encoded analytically using differentiable R-functions. This enables explicit representation of discontinuities, feasible regions, and implicit geometric boundaries within a trainable neural architecture.
  The framework implements differentiable logical operations through R-conjunctions and R-disjunctions, allowing complex geometric supports to be represented analytically and incorporated directly into regression models. Several GRS-KAN variants are introduced, including additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted architectures.
  The method is demonstrated on regression problems involving discontinuities with circular and rectangular supports. Numerical experiments show that explicit geometric encoding substantially improves predictive accuracy and boundary localization compared with standard KANs. In the considered benchmarks, geometry-aware GRS-KAN models reduce test RMSE by up to 67% while simultaneously improving interpretability through explicit analytical representation of the learned geometric structure. The agnostic variant further demonstrates the ability to automatically determine whether geometric priors are beneficial for a given learning task.

AI.tldr: GRS-KAN integrates R-functions into the KAN framework to analytically encode geometric constraints (discontinuities, boundaries, feasible regions) alongside learned nonlinear structure, achieving up to 67% RMSE reduction on regression tasks with geometric discontinuities.
AI.motivation: Standard KANs struggle to represent explicit geometric constraints such as discontinuities, boundaries, and feasible regions. There is a need to combine the smooth nonlinear learning capability of neural networks with analytical encoding of known geometric or logical priors, improving both accuracy and interpretability.
AI.method: The GRS-KAN architecture embeds V.L. Rvachev's differentiable R-functions (R-conjunctions and R-disjunctions) into KAN branches. This enables differentiable logical operations that analytically represent complex geometric supports. Three variants are proposed: additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted architectures, where the agnostic variant can learn whether geometric priors are beneficial.
AI.result: On regression problems with circular and rectangular support discontinuities, GRS-KAN reduces test RMSE by up to 67% compared to standard KANs, while delivering superior boundary localization and interpretability through explicit analytical geometric representations.
AI.conclusion: Explicit geometric encoding via R-functions substantially enhances KAN performance on problems with known geometric structure. The agnostic variant's ability to auto-determine the utility of geometric priors suggests practical applicability even when prior knowledge is uncertain.

title: Cloak and Detonate: Scanner Evasion and Dynamic Detection of Agent Skill Malware
summary:
LLM coding agents increasingly rely on third-party agent skills from public marketplaces, which execute with the agent's privileges and create a software supply-chain attack surface: a malicious skill can steal credentials, exfiltrate source code, or install backdoors. Existing defenses use static skill scanners based on pattern matching or LLM-as-judge analysis, but it remains unclear whether they withstand adaptive evasions that preserve malicious behavior while changing payload appearance.
  This paper first presents an adversarial study of existing skill scanners through SkillCloak, a payload-preserving evasion framework that keeps the attack semantics intact while transforming their visible form. SkillCloak uses two complementary strategies: Structural Obfuscation, which rewrites visible payload indicators into semantically equivalent forms, and Self-Extracting Skill (SFS) Packing, which hides malicious components from the install-time view and restores them during agent execution. Across eight scanners and 1,613 in-the-wild malicious skills, SFS Packing bypasses every scanner at over 90%, while Structural Obfuscation bypasses over 80% on most static scanners and reaches 96% on a hybrid scanner, showing that appearance-based auditing is insufficient.
  Motivated by this finding, we propose SkillDetonate, a behavior-centric runtime auditor that executes skills in a sandbox and detects malicious effects through OS-boundary information-flow evidence rather than install-time appearance. SkillDetonate combines on-demand closure lift, which observes instructions materialized during execution, with marker-based taint analysis, which tracks sensitive-data flows across the agent context, files, processes, and network operations. The results show that SkillDetonate detects 97% of attacks at a 2% false-positive rate and sustains 87% detection on real-world malicious skills.

AI.tldr: Existing static scanners for third-party LLM agent skills are vulnerable to payload-preserving evasion attacks (SkillCloak). The paper proposes SkillDetonate, a runtime sandbox-based auditor that detects malicious behavior via OS-level information-flow taint analysis, achieving 97% detection at 2% false-positive rate.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents increasingly use third-party skills from public marketplaces, creating a software supply-chain attack surface. Existing defenses rely on static scanning (pattern matching or LLM-as-judge), but it is unclear whether they resist adaptive, payload-preserving evasions that change appearance while maintaining malicious semantics.
AI.method: First, SkillCloak: an evasion framework with two strategies — (1) Structural Obfuscation rewrites payload indicators into semantically equivalent forms, and (2) Self-Extracting Skill (SFS) Packing hides malicious components at install-time, restoring them during execution. Second, SkillDetonate: a runtime auditor that sandboxes skill execution and uses on-demand closure lift (observing materialized instructions) plus marker-based taint analysis (tracking sensitive-data flows across agent context, files, processes, and network) to detect malicious effects through OS-boundary information-flow evidence.
AI.result: SkillCloak: SFS Packing bypassed all 8 scanners on over 90% of 1,613 real-world malicious skills; Structural Obfuscation bypassed >80% on most static scanners and 96% on a hybrid scanner. SkillDetonate: detected 97% of attacks at 2% FPR, sustaining 87% detection on real-world malicious skills.
AI.conclusion: Appearance-based auditing is insufficient for securing LLM agent skill supply chains. Behavior-centric runtime auditing with OS-level information-flow tracking (SkillDetonate) provides robust detection against both original and evasive malicious skills.

title: Technical Debt Friction for Maintenance Prioritization: An Industrial Multi-Case Study
comment: Accepted for the 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (Industry Track)
summary: Software-intensive organizations need effective ways to identify where maintenance and refactoring efforts will yield the greatest practical benefit. Although software analytics such as code health, hotspots, and coupling provide valuable signals, they do not always capture the experienced burden of change that slows software evolution in practice. This paper presents a multi-case industrial study of technical debt friction as a prioritization-oriented concept for identifying where technical debt most strongly affects maintenance and evolution. We investigate how practitioners interpret the concept, whether friction-related analysis aligns with perceived maintenance pain points and refactoring needs, and what broader maintenance and evolution insights friction can provide beyond individual refactoring candidates. To this end, we conducted structured walkthrough sessions with practitioners across multiple industrial cases using analysis artifacts including code health, hotspots, coupling, refactoring targets, and socio-technical views. Our findings show that practitioners generally considered technical debt friction useful for reasoning about maintenance burden, especially when interpreted together with complementary technical and socio-technical views. At the file level, friction often aligned with known problematic areas and, in several cases, with files that later received maintenance attention, although its practical relevance depended strongly on context. In addition, our exploratory project-level analysis suggests that friction distributions may reveal broader maintenance and evolution patterns. These results indicate that technical debt friction is promising as a decision-support concept, but most effective when used with contextual knowledge and supporting evidence.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-case industrial study on "technical debt friction," a prioritization concept for identifying where technical debt most impedes maintenance. Through practitioner walkthroughs combining code health, hotspots, coupling, and socio-technical views, the study finds friction useful for reasoning about maintenance burden and aligned with known problem areas, though its practical relevance is context-dependent. Exploratory project-level analysis suggests friction distributions may reveal broader evolution patterns.
AI.motivation: Existing software analytics (code health, hotspots, coupling) provide valuable signals but fail to capture the experienced burden of change that slows software evolution in practice. There is a need for a prioritization-oriented concept that directly targets where technical debt most strongly affects maintenance and evolution activities.
AI.method: A multi-case industrial study employing structured walkthrough sessions with practitioners across multiple industrial cases. Analysis artifacts used include code health metrics, hotspots, coupling analysis, refactoring targets, and socio-technical views. Both file-level alignment with known problematic areas and exploratory project-level distribution analysis were conducted.
AI.result: Practitioners found technical debt friction useful for reasoning about maintenance burden, particularly when combined with complementary views. At the file level, friction frequently aligned with known problematic areas and files receiving later maintenance attention, though relevance was context-dependent. Project-level friction distributions showed promise for revealing broader maintenance and evolution patterns.
AI.conclusion: Technical debt friction is a promising decision-support concept for prioritizing maintenance and refactoring efforts, but is most effective when interpreted with contextual knowledge and supporting evidence rather than used in isolation.

title: Safe and Adaptive Cloud Healing: Verifying LLM-Generated Recovery Plans with a Neural-Symbolic World Model
summary: As the scale and complexity of cloud-based AI systems continue to escalate, ensuring service reliability through rapid fault detection and adaptive recovery has become a critical challenge. While existing approaches integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) for semantic understanding and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for policy optimization, they often rely on sequential, loosely coupled architectures that underutilize the generative and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift with PASE, a Planning-Aware Semantic self-healing engine, a novel fault self-healing framework that reconceptualizes recovery as a neuro-symbolic program synthesis task. PASE employs an LLM as a core Plan Synthesis Engine to generate structured recovery plans from a library of semantic primitives. A Neural-Symbolic World Model verifies plan feasibility through simulation, while a Meta-Prompt Optimizer, trained via DRL, learns to generate optimal prompts that guide the LLM's planning process. This tight reason-plan-verify-adapt loop enables dynamic, context-aware recovery strategy generation beyond predefined action spaces. Experiments on a real-world cloud fault injection dataset demonstrate that PASE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing average system recovery time by over 40% and improving fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios. Our framework advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-learned guidance.

AI.tldr: PASE is a self-healing framework for cloud AI systems that reformulates fault recovery as neuro-symbolic program synthesis, using an LLM as a plan synthesis engine, a neural-symbolic world model for verification, and a DRL-trained meta-prompt optimizer, achieving >40% reduction in recovery time and improved detection accuracy on unknown faults.
AI.motivation: Existing cloud fault recovery approaches that combine LLMs and DRL rely on sequential, loosely coupled architectures that fail to fully leverage LLMs' generative and reasoning capabilities. There is a need for a tightly integrated framework that enables dynamic, context-aware recovery beyond predefined action spaces.
AI.method: PASE introduces a reason-plan-verify-adapt loop with three core components: (1) a Plan Synthesis Engine using an LLM to generate structured recovery plans from semantic primitives; (2) a Neural-Symbolic World Model that verifies plan feasibility via simulation; and (3) a Meta-Prompt Optimizer trained with DRL that learns to produce optimal prompts guiding the LLM's planning process.
AI.result: On a real-world cloud fault injection dataset, PASE reduces average system recovery time by over 40% and improves fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: PASE advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning, model-assisted verification, and meta-learned guidance into a coherent neuro-symbolic self-healing engine.

title: From Monolingual to Multilingual: Evaluating Mamba for ASR in South African Languages
