summary: Recent advances in automatic speech recognition (ASR) have explored different sequence models, including Conformer-based models and newer state space models such as Mamba. Although prior work has evaluated these architectures in multiple languages, their effectiveness in African languages remains underexplored. In this work, we evaluate Mamba for ASR on seven South African languages. In monolingual experiments, each model is trained on 50 hours of speech per language, and we compare Mamba to a Conformer baseline of similar parameter scale. Mamba achieves similar recognition accuracy to Conformer while using fewer computational resources and training faster. We further evaluate generalization in this setting and find that both models struggle to generalize to speech that is much longer than what they were trained on. We then study multilingual ASR using Mamba models, where the baseline is pooling all languages together. On top of this, we tested three extensions: training with language-family information by adding both language and language-family embeddings as biases to the downsampled acoustic representations, and multitask learning with a CTC ASR objective and a language identification (LID) head. We find that multilingual training consistently improves performance over monolingual training. However, adding explicit language information does not improve in-domain performance but does improve cross-corpus robustness. We conducted ablation studies in low-resource multilingual settings using 5-hour and 10-hour per-language training data, where we observed gains from using language embeddings and further demonstrated that removing or altering them hurt model performance. Lastly, we analysed these embeddings and find that they do not capture linguistic similarity in a typological sense, but instead act as task-specific control vectors.

AI.tldr: Evaluates Mamba vs. Conformer for ASR on seven South African languages. Mamba matches Conformer accuracy with fewer resources and faster training. Multilingual training improves performance; explicit language embeddings help cross-corpus robustness but not in-domain performance. Embeddings act as task-specific control vectors, not typological similarity encoders.
AI.motivation: State space models like Mamba have shown promise for ASR but remain underexplored for African languages. The authors aim to benchmark Mamba against Conformer for monolingual and multilingual ASR in low-resource South African language settings, and to investigate whether explicit language information improves performance.
AI.method: Monolingual: Train Mamba and Conformer models of comparable parameter count on 50 hours per language for seven South African languages. Compare accuracy, compute, and training speed; evaluate generalization to longer utterances. Multilingual: Pool all languages for a baseline Mamba model. Three extensions tested: (1) language + language-family embeddings added as biases to downsampled acoustic representations; (2) multitask learning with CTC ASR + language identification head; (3) low-resource ablations at 5h and 10h per language. Embeddings analyzed post hoc.
AI.result: Mamba achieves comparable WER to Conformer monolingually with lower compute and faster training. Both models struggle to generalize to utterances longer than training samples. Multilingual training consistently outperforms monolingual. Explicit language information does not improve in-domain WER but enhances cross-corpus robustness. In 5h/10h low-resource settings, language embeddings provide gains; removing or altering them degrades performance. Embedding analysis reveals they function as task-specific control vectors rather than encoding typological linguistic similarity.
AI.conclusion: Mamba is a viable, efficient alternative to Conformer for ASR in low-resource African languages. Multilingual training is beneficial, and while explicit language embeddings aid robustness and low-resource performance, they operate as learned control signals rather than capturing inherent linguistic relatedness.

title: Token Geometry
summary: Language models learn continuous programs over discrete symbols, with the embedding table and LM-head acting as the read/write interface between them. We show that this interface has gradient geometry distinct from dense hidden weights which can be exploited to improve the Pareto frontier across supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining, while only utilizing kilobytes of optimizer state. We introduce Ember, a lightweight optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that utilizes O(V + D) VRAM, instead of Adam's O(2VD), and forgoes the need to shard both token table optimizer states. We provide empirical evidence that Ember scales effectively across batch size and parameter count. We show that the optimization trajectory of tokens can be well described by a simple 1D ray, counter to the popular belief that neural net parameters navigate a heavily nonconvex landscape. We provide a principled view on the surprisingly narrow space of optimizers that suffice for Transformer training. Finally, we open-source our distributed Ember implementation that merges cleanly with existing ZeRO/FSDP setups to support further research at https://github.com/katop1234/ember

AI.tldr: Ember is a lightweight optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that uses O(V+D) VRAM instead of Adam's O(2VD), exploiting the distinct gradient geometry of the discrete/continuous interface to improve the Pareto frontier across training regimes.
AI.motivation: The embedding table and LM-head act as read/write interfaces between discrete symbols and continuous representations. Standard optimizers like Adam allocate O(2VD) VRAM for these matrices, creating a significant memory bottleneck. The authors hypothesize that this interface has distinct gradient geometry from dense hidden weights, enabling memory-efficient optimization without performance degradation.
AI.method: Ember leverages the observation that token optimization trajectories follow a simple 1D ray (linear path), rather than navigating a highly nonconvex landscape. This enables the optimizer to maintain only O(V + D) optimizer state — tracking per-token (vocabulary) and per-dimension statistics separately — instead of the full O(2VD) per-parameter state used by Adam. The method integrates cleanly with distributed training via ZeRO/FSDP.
AI.result: Ember scales effectively across batch size and parameter count, improving the Pareto frontier for supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining while using only kilobytes of optimizer state. The findings also provide a principled view that a surprisingly narrow space of optimizers suffices for Transformer training.
AI.conclusion: The embedding/LM-head interface exhibits gradient geometry that permits drastically lighter optimization. Ember demonstrates that O(V+D) state is sufficient, challenging the necessity of full Adam-style optimizers for these layers and opening avenues for memory-efficient large-scale training.

title: Copewell: A Multi-Agent Swarm Architecture for Equitable Mental Wellness Support
summary: Mental health disorders affect nearly one billion people globally, yet 75% of individuals in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost barriers, and stigma. Current AI-powered wellness solutions predominantly rely on single-mode conversational interfaces that suffer high abandonment rates and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief calibrated to users' dynamic emotional states. This paper presents Copewell, a novel multi-agent swarm system designed to expand access to mental wellness support through human-centered AI principles. Our architecture introduces three technical innovations: (1) a multi-source assessment framework integrating self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to mitigate algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model of Affect to route users to specialized AI agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. We examine the sociotechnical design considerations underlying Copewell's development, including a privacy-first architecture, embedded ethical oversight through a dedicated Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design informed by mental health practitioners. Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment inform design decisions and identify directions for future empirical evaluation. This work contributes to responsible AI discourse by demonstrating how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception.

AI.tldr: Copewell is a multi-agent AI swarm system for mental wellness that combines self-reported, physiological, and contextual data with Russell's Circumplex Model to route users to specialized agents, delivering both conversational and sensory-based interventions with embedded ethical oversight.
AI.motivation: Nearly one billion people suffer from mental health disorders, with 75% untreated in low- and middle-income countries due to workforce shortages, cost, and stigma. Existing AI wellness tools rely on single-mode conversational interfaces with high abandonment rates and lack measurable, immediate, emotion-calibrated relief.
AI.method: Copewell employs a multi-agent swarm architecture with three innovations: (1) multi-source assessment fusing self-report, physiological, and contextual data to reduce algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping via Russell's Circumplex Model to route users to specialized agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. The system includes a privacy-first design, a dedicated Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory input from mental health practitioners.
AI.result: Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment have informed design decisions and identified directions for future empirical evaluation. No quantitative efficacy results are reported at this stage.
AI.conclusion: Copewell demonstrates how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception, contributing to responsible AI discourse in mental health. Future empirical evaluation is planned based on early deployment insights.

title: SoK: A Taxonomy for Cybersecurity Incident Response Influence Factors
comment: To be published in Proceedings of EuroS&P 2026
summary: Cybersecurity incident response has emerged as a critical area of interest for both researchers and practitioners. The corpus of literature on cybersecurity incident response is expanding, yet a unified framework for systematically organizing the accumulated knowledge remains absent. The aspects of incident response span multiple domains, including technology, human-computer interaction, organizational theory, and human factors. A comprehensive, integrative perspective on these factors can enable researchers to identify underexplored areas and more effectively target their empirical and theoretical investigations. Our study systematizes the factors that influence organizational preparedness for and response to cybersecurity incidents. Through a systematic review of academic literature (n = 417) and non-scientific publications (n = 40), we derived the "Cybersecurity Incident Response Influencing Factor Taxonomy" (\textit{CIR-IF Taxonomy}). Existing empirical findings were classified within this taxonomy, providing a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of knowledge from the period 1999 to mid-2024. The taxonomy categories were systematically compared with seven established scientific frameworks and with the \textit{NIST Cyber Security Framework} elements referenced in the \textit{NIST Special Publication 800-61r3} incident response profile. The results of this comparison show that the \textit{CIR-IF Taxonomy} delivers a richer, more rigorous, and more systematically organized view of the factors that drive and shape incident response.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the CIR-IF Taxonomy, a comprehensive framework for organizing factors influencing organizational cybersecurity incident response, derived from a systematic review of 417 academic and 40 non-scientific publications (1999–mid-2024). The taxonomy outperforms seven established frameworks and the NIST CSF incident response profile in richness, rigor, and systematic organization.
AI.motivation: Despite growing literature on cybersecurity incident response spanning technology, HCI, organizational theory, and human factors, no unified framework exists to systematically organize accumulated knowledge. A comprehensive integrative perspective is needed to help researchers identify underexplored areas and better target empirical and theoretical investigations.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic review of academic literature (n=417) and non-scientific publications (n=40) spanning 1999 to mid-2024. From this, they derived the "Cybersecurity Incident Response Influencing Factor Taxonomy" (CIR-IF Taxonomy). Existing empirical findings were classified within the taxonomy, and its categories were systematically compared against seven established scientific frameworks and the NIST Special Publication 800-61r3 incident response profile elements.
AI.result: The CIR-IF Taxonomy provides a comprehensive, up-to-date synthesis of factors influencing incident response preparedness and response. Comparative analysis demonstrated that the CIR-IF Taxonomy offers a richer, more rigorous, and more systematically organized view of the factors driving and shaping incident response than existing frameworks.
AI.conclusion: The paper highlights the need for a unified organizing framework in cybersecurity incident response research. The CIR-IF Taxonomy fills this gap, providing a rigorous structure for synthesizing knowledge across multiple domains. It serves as a foundation for future empirical and theoretical work by identifying underexplored research areas and offering a more comprehensive lens than existing frameworks.

title: Regression Accumulation in Multi-Turn LLM Programming Conversations
summary:
In LLM-assisted software development, coding is often iterative. We study regression accumulation in multi-turn LLM programming conversations, where later code suggestions may break requirements introduced in earlier turns. Reliability therefore depends not only on satisfying the current request, but also on preserving previously satisfied behavior.
  We construct 542 tasks from HumanEval+ and MBPP+ and extend each task into an 8-turn requirement-evolution chain. We evaluate six LLMs on 26,016 turn instances (542 x 6 x 8). At each turn, we test whether the current code still passes earlier benchmark tests. We also analyze 384 failure cases from the failure population and build a taxonomy of multi-turn regression bugs through independent four-annotator labeling.
  Our results show that regression accumulation appears across all six models: 40% to 73% of tasks lose previously correct behavior over the full conversation. Final-turn quality is lower than initial-turn quality across models, especially when later turns add input validation or broader input types. Manual analysis shows that Cross-Turn Conflict, where later code conflicts with earlier requirements, is the main failure class. We further find that Verification Gate, which checks new code against prior tests and triggers rollback and retry, is the only strategy that consistently improves all models, raising final-turn quality from 75.8% to 87.9% on DeepSeek-V3 and from 31.6% to 47.3% on Llama-3.1-8B.
  These findings suggest that strong single-turn performance can overestimate reliability in multi-turn coding conversations. Future evaluation and tool design should test whether later code suggestions preserve earlier requirements and should include Verification Gate mechanisms.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates "regression accumulation" in multi-turn LLM-assisted coding, where later code suggestions break previously satisfied requirements. Evaluating six LLMs across 26,016 turn instances (542 tasks × 8 turns), they find 40–73% of tasks lose previously correct behavior. A Verification Gate strategy—checking new code against prior tests and triggering rollback/retry—consistently improves all models, raising final-turn quality significantly. The work shows single-turn performance overestimates multi-turn reliability.
AI.motivation: Real-world LLM-assisted software development is iterative and conversational, yet existing benchmarks evaluate only single-turn correctness. Later code suggestions in a multi-turn conversation may silently break requirements introduced earlier — a phenomenon the authors term "regression accumulation." There is a gap in understanding how well LLMs preserve previously satisfied behavior across conversational turns.
AI.method: The authors construct 542 tasks from HumanEval+ and MBPP+, extending each into an 8-turn requirement-evolution chain (e.g., adding input validation, broader types, new features, refactoring). Six LLMs are evaluated on 26,016 total turn instances. At each turn, prior benchmark tests are re-run to detect regressions. Additionally, 384 failure cases undergo independent four-annotator manual labeling to build a taxonomy of multi-turn regression bugs. The Verification Gate mitigation strategy is tested: after each code generation, prior tests are run, and on failure the model rolls back and retries.
AI.result: Regression accumulation is pervasive: 40–73% of tasks lose previously correct behavior across all six models. Final-turn quality is consistently lower than initial-turn quality, especially when later turns add input validation or broader input types. The dominant failure class is Cross-Turn Conflict, where later code contradicts earlier requirements. Verification Gate consistently improves all models (e.g., DeepSeek-V3: 75.8% → 87.9%; Llama-3.1-8B: 31.6% → 47.3%).
AI.conclusion: Strong single-turn performance overestimates reliability in multi-turn coding. Future LLM coding benchmarks and tools should explicitly test whether later suggestions preserve earlier requirements, and should incorporate Verification Gate mechanisms to mitigate regression accumulation.

title: SemHash-LLM: A Multi-Granularity Semantic Hashing Framework for Document Deduplication
summary: Large scale document deduplication must preserve semantic equivalence while remaining efficient over massive corpora. We present SemHash LLM, a multi granularity framework that unifies semantic projection hashing, attention weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM based adjudication. The method combines character, token, and document level signals through gated fusion, then applies a cascaded filtering pipeline for efficient candidate reduction. Semantic projection hashing learns compact binary codes in distilled LLM embedding space, while attention weighted Min- Hash suppresses boilerplate and emphasizes informative content. Adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation further improve robustness across template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments. Experiments show that SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality with less than one percent neural verification cost.

AI.tldr: SemHash LLM is a multi-granularity document deduplication framework that combines semantic projection hashing, attention-weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM adjudication to achieve high-quality duplicate detection with under 1% neural verification cost.
AI.motivation: Large-scale document deduplication faces a fundamental trade-off: it must preserve semantic equivalence (detecting paraphrases and semantic duplicates, not just exact matches) while remaining computationally efficient over massive corpora. Existing methods typically lean toward one extreme — either cheap but superficial hash-based approaches or accurate but prohibitively expensive neural methods.
AI.method: SemHash LLM operates at character, token, and document levels fused via a gated mechanism. The pipeline includes: (1) Semantic projection hashing that learns compact binary codes in a distilled LLM embedding space; (2) Attention-weighted MinHash that down-weights boilerplate and emphasizes informative content; (3) Contrastive boundary learning with adaptive decision boundaries for robust similarity thresholds; (4) Uncertainty estimation to identify borderline cases; and (5) A cascaded filtering pipeline where only uncertain candidates are escalated to selective LLM-based adjudication.
AI.result: SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality while requiring neural (LLM) verification on less than 1% of candidate pairs, demonstrating that the cascaded filtering and uncertainty estimation effectively isolate only the most ambiguous cases for expensive adjudication.
AI.conclusion: The multi-granularity, hybrid approach successfully balances the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in large-scale semantic deduplication. By reserving LLM adjudication for only the hardest, most uncertain cases, SemHash LLM delivers near-neural quality at near-hash efficiency, and the framework proves robust across diverse challenge patterns including template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments.

title: Parameter Golf: What Really Works?
summary: How far can a language model improve under a strict artifact budget? Parameter Golf posed this question as an open community challenge in which participants trained the best language model, with the complete artifact (training code + compressed weights) required to fit within 16 MB and be trained in under ten minutes on 8xH100 SXM GPUs. Quality was measured in bits-per-byte (BPB), the average number of bits required to encode each byte of unseen text. We analyze 2,037 pull requests and 1,430 clean scored submissions from the contest, build a taxonomy of 84 optimization techniques, and measure each technique's contribution to BPB. The verified leaderboard score dropped from 1.2244 to 1.058 BPB across three phases -- a 13.6% reduction, despite individual techniques rarely improving BPB by more than 1%. We show that most gains in techniques shrink across competitive submissions, isolating the few methods that improve performance across stacks.

AI.tldr: Analysis of the Parameter Golf challenge, where participants trained language models under strict constraints (16 MB artifact, <10 min on 8×H100). Across 2,037 pull requests and 1,430 scored submissions, the leaderboard improved 13.6% in BPB (1.2244 → 1.058). A taxonomy of 84 techniques was built, revealing that most individual techniques yield <1% gain and that gains shrink in competitive settings, with only a few methods consistently improving performance across stacks.
AI.motivation: To systematically understand how far language models can be improved under a strict artifact budget, and to identify which optimization techniques genuinely contribute to performance when combined competitively, rather than in isolation.
AI.method: The authors orchestrated a community challenge (Parameter Golf) with fixed constraints: full training artifact ≤ 16 MB, training time ≤ 10 minutes on 8×H100 SXM GPUs, evaluated by bits-per-byte (BPB) on unseen text. They collected and analyzed 2,037 pull requests and 1,430 clean scored submissions across three contest phases, built a taxonomy of 84 distinct optimization techniques, and measured each technique's marginal contribution to BPB improvement in both isolated and competitive (stacked) settings.
AI.result: The verified leaderboard BPB dropped from 1.2244 to 1.058 (13.6% reduction). Most individual techniques improved BPB by less than 1%. Crucially, gains from techniques shrank when combined in competitive submissions — only a small subset of methods proved robust and transferred improvements across different optimization stacks.
AI.conclusion: Under strict compute and storage constraints, language models can be significantly improved through compounding many small optimizations, but the marginal value of most techniques diminishes in competitive settings. The few techniques that robustly improve performance across stacks represent the most principled advances, while many seemingly effective isolated techniques fail to generalize when combined.

title: Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum and Faster Hyperparameter Exploration to Tackle Class Imbalance in Federated Learning
summary: Class imbalance poses a critical challenge in federated learning (FL), where underrepresented classes suffer from poor predictive performance yet cannot be addressed by standard centralized techniques due to privacy and heterogeneity constraints. We propose FedCGNM (Federated Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum), a client-side optimizer in FL that partitions classes into a small number of groups based on minimum within-group variance, maintains a momentum per group, normalizes each group momentum to unit length, and uses the summation of the normalized group momentums as an update direction. This design both equalizes gradient magnitude across majority and minority groups and mitigates the noise inherent in rare-class gradients. We further provide a theoretical convergence analysis explicitly accounting for time-varying resampling-rates. Additionally, to efficiently optimize these rates in small-client regimes, we introduce FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit (XAB) based algorithm that exploits federated parallelism that evaluates many combinations of two candidate rates per client at linear cost. Empirical evaluation on four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset demonstrates that FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines, with FedHOO yielding further gains in small-scale federations.

AI.tldr: FedCGNM addresses class imbalance in federated learning by partitioning classes into groups with minimal within-group variance, maintaining normalized per-group momentum to equalize gradient magnitudes and reduce noise. The companion FedHOO algorithm uses an X-armed-bandit approach to efficiently optimize resampling rates in small-client settings.
AI.motivation: Class imbalance in federated learning leads to poor performance on underrepresented classes. Standard centralized techniques (e.g., resampling, re-weighting) cannot be directly applied due to privacy constraints and data heterogeneity across clients. Existing FL-specific solutions inadequately address the tension between gradient magnitude equalization and noise mitigation for rare classes.
AI.method: Two components: (1) FedCGNM — a client-side optimizer that partitions classes into groups by minimizing within-group variance, maintains a momentum buffer per group, normalizes each group's momentum to unit length, and sums the normalized momentums as the update direction. (2) FedHOO — an X-armed-bandit algorithm exploiting federated parallelism to efficiently search over resampling-rate combinations at linear cost for small-client federations. A theoretical convergence analysis is provided accounting for time-varying resampling rates.
AI.result: FedCGNM consistently outperforms baseline methods on four public long-tailed benchmarks and one proprietary chip-defect dataset. FedHOO yields additional performance gains in small-scale federated settings.
AI.conclusion: Class-grouped normalized momentum effectively balances gradient magnitudes across majority/minority classes while suppressing rare-class gradient noise, and the XAB-based resampling-rate optimizer further improves results in small-client regimes.

title: An Exploratory Study on LLM-Generated Code and Comments in Code Repositories
comment: Accepted to The Journal of Systems & Software (JSS) on 1 July 2026
summary: The use of LLMs in software development has become increasingly widespread on tasks such as code generation and summarization. Reports from large technology companies showed that around 20% to 30% of their code are generated by LLMs. However, there remains skepticism about the practical usage of LLM-generated code and comments, such as concerns on more time for debugging the generated code and the unnaturalness of the generated comments. In this paper, we study the code and comments detected as likely to be generated by LLMs and their characteristics, the differences between company- and community-maintained repositories, and how likely bugs are associated with LLM-generated code. We conduct extensive experiments on active company- and community-maintained repositories from 2021 to 2025 using various tools and techniques that detect code and comments generated by LLMs. Based on our detector-based proxy analysis, the results suggest that code detected as likely to be generated by LLMs decreased over time and appeared frequently in test cases, while that of comments remains relatively stable. Proxy results further suggest that code detected as likely to be generated by LLMs shows substantial intra-repository code clones, whereas comments exhibit a relatively low proportion of grammatically correct sentences. In addition, the company-maintained repositories show a higher percentage of code and comments detected as likely to be generated by LLMs, and only a small percentage of the human-labelled bugs are detected as being likely associated with LLM-generated code.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically analyzes LLM-generated code and comments in company- and community-maintained repositories (2021–2025) using detector-based proxies. It finds that LLM-generated code declined over time, concentrates in test cases, exhibits high intra-repo cloning, and rarely associates with human-labelled bugs; LLM-generated comments remain stable but show low grammatical correctness; and company repos contain higher proportions of LLM-generated content.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread LLM adoption for code generation (20–30% at large tech companies), skepticism persists regarding debugging overhead and comment quality. The authors aim to empirically characterize LLM-generated code and comments, compare company vs. community repositories, and assess whether LLM-generated code correlates with bugs.
AI.method: The authors conduct a large-scale empirical study on active repositories from 2021–2025. They employ LLM-content detection tools and techniques as proxies to identify code and comments likely generated by LLMs, then analyze temporal trends, distribution across file types, intra-repository cloning rates, grammatical correctness, organizational differences, and associations with human-labelled bug reports.
AI.result: (1) LLM-generated code detection rates decreased over time and frequently appeared in test files. (2) LLM-generated comment detection remained relatively stable. (3) LLM-detected code shows substantial intra-repository cloning; LLM-detected comments have low grammatical correctness. (4) Company-maintained repositories contain higher percentages of LLM-detected code and comments. (5) Only a small fraction of human-labelled bugs are associated with LLM-detected code.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLM usage patterns in code are shifting (declining overall, concentrated in tests), comments remain linguistically flawed, company repos adopt LLMs more heavily, and LLM-generated code does not substantially contribute to bug reports—partially alleviating debugging concerns.

title: Profit-Based Counterfactual Explanations for Product Improvement: A Case Study of Manga Sales in Japan
summary: Counterfactual explanation (CE) is widely used to enhance the interpretability of machine learning models and support data-driven decision-making based on model predictions. However, existing CE methods typically require two exogenously specified inputs: a desired output value (target) and a distance function that quantifies changes in explanatory variables. In regression settings, neither the validity of target specification nor the practical interpretation of the distance metric has been sufficiently addressed. Furthermore, most existing CE methods focus on altering predictions rather than optimizing a decision objective, even though real-world decision-making often requires explicit objective maximization. To address these limitations, we formulate CE as a profit maximization problem in management and marketing contexts and propose a framework termed profit-based counterfactual explanation (PBCE). PBCE eliminates the need for exogenous target specification by directly maximizing profit as the primary optimization objective. Concurrently, the distance term is reinterpreted as the cost of modifying product attributes, providing a clear and economically grounded interpretation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Profit-Based Counterfactual Explanation (PBCE), which reformulates counterfactual explanations as a profit maximization problem, eliminating the need for exogenous target specification and reinterpreting distance as the economic cost of modifying product attributes.
AI.motivation: Existing CE methods in regression settings suffer from two key weaknesses: (1) they require an externally specified target output value whose validity is questionable, and (2) the distance function lacks practical, interpretable meaning. Moreover, current approaches focus on altering predictions rather than optimizing decision objectives, which misaligns with real-world decision-making that requires explicit objective maximization.
AI.method: The authors formulate counterfactual explanation as a profit maximization problem tailored to management and marketing domains. In PBCE, profit serves directly as the optimization objective, replacing the need for a pre-specified target. The distance metric is reinterpreted as the cost incurred when modifying product attributes, giving it a clear, economically grounded interpretation within the optimization framework.
AI.result: Not specified in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the contribution is the PBCE framework itself, which addresses fundamental limitations of conventional CE by aligning the explanation mechanism with profit-driven decision-making.

title: Can Language Models Actually Retrieve In-Context? Drowning in Documents at Million Token Scale
summary: Language models (LMs) raise an intriguing alternative to vector-based retrieval: conditioning on an in-context corpus and directly generating a relevant answer. However, prior work has largely focused on proprietary systems or the smaller-scale reranking task, leaving corpus-scale in-context retrieval largely unexplored. In this work, we present the first systematic study of in-context retrieval on two scales practical retrievers demand: million-token corpora and length-generalization far beyond training-time sizes. We first introduce BlockSearch, a 0.6B LM retriever whose architectural and training modifications improve over prior LM baselines and length-generalize up to 10 times beyond its training regime. Nevertheless, retrieval still collapses under more extreme extrapolation. We trace this failure to an attention dilution effect: as the corpus grows, irrelevant documents dominate the softmax denominator, reducing the normalized mass on the gold document even when its pre-softmax score stays high. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce length-aware adjustments to the attention softmax and document-level sparse attention. With these modifications, at the million-token scale, our model matches dense retrieval on widely studied benchmarks (e.g, MS MARCO and NQ), while outperforming the concurrent model MSA despite being 7 times smaller. Furthermore, it significantly outperforms dense retrieval on tasks requiring entirely different notions of similarity, such as LIMIT, achieving a 3 times higher score. Together, our results position in-context retrieval a promising alternative to classical retrieval while emphasizing attention control under extreme context growth as a new challenge.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies in-context retrieval at million-token scale, identifies an "attention dilution" failure mode where irrelevant documents overwhelm softmax normalization, and proposes length-aware attention adjustments plus document-level sparse attention to solve it. Their 0.6B model matches dense retrievers on standard benchmarks, outperforms a 7× larger concurrent model, and triples performance on tasks requiring non-standard similarity.
AI.motivation: Prior work on language model–based retrieval has been limited to proprietary systems or small-scale reranking. Corpus-scale in-context retrieval — where an LM reads a large corpus in its context and directly generates answers — remains unexplored, particularly regarding how these models behave as corpora grow to millions of tokens and beyond their training length.
AI.method: The authors first build BlockSearch, a 0.6B LM retriever with architectural and training modifications that enable length generalization up to 10× training size. Analyzing its failure at extreme scales, they diagnose "attention dilution": as corpus size grows, irrelevant documents dominate the softmax denominator, suppressing the gold document's normalized attention mass even when its raw score remains high. To fix this, they introduce (1) length-aware adjustments to the attention softmax and (2) document-level sparse attention. These modifications restore retrieval quality at million-token scale.
AI.result: At million-token scale, the enhanced model matches dense retrieval on MS MARCO and NQ benchmarks, outperforms the concurrent MSA model despite being 7× smaller, and achieves 3× higher scores than dense retrieval on the LIMIT benchmark, which requires entirely different similarity notions.
AI.conclusion: In-context retrieval is a viable alternative to classical vector-based retrieval, but controlling attention under extreme context growth is a critical new challenge. Their length-aware modifications address the core attention dilution problem and enable competitive performance at scale.

title: How to Allocate Your Tokens? Scaling Laws with Training Steps and Batch Size
summary: We propose a scaling law that takes into account model size and training data while explicitly splitting the latter into training steps and batch size (called three-term law). Fitting the proposed law on a large set of training runs, we find that it correctly recovers the scaling of the optimal batch size. Moreover, because it makes use of training runs with suboptimal batch size, our proposed law can be robustly fit with a significantly smaller amount of training runs. We further show that the three-term law can be used to derive scaling laws for suboptimal batch sizes, and that it matches previous empirical findings related to the critical batch size.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a three-term scaling law that decomposes training data into training steps and batch size, alongside model size. This formulation accurately recovers optimal batch size scaling, enables robust fitting with fewer training runs by leveraging suboptimal batch size data, and generalizes to derive scaling laws for suboptimal batch sizes while matching prior findings on critical batch size.
AI.motivation: Existing scaling laws typically treat training data as a single monolithic variable (number of tokens), ignoring the distinct roles of training steps and batch size. This limits their ability to predict optimal batch size scaling behavior and requires many expensive training runs for robust fitting. The authors aim to disentangle these factors to improve both the accuracy and data efficiency of scaling law estimation.
AI.method: The authors propose a three-term scaling law that jointly parameterizes model size, training steps, and batch size as separate variables. They fit this law on a large set of training runs, including those with suboptimal batch sizes, to estimate the scaling coefficients. The formulation allows deriving the optimal batch size as a function of compute and model size, as well as predicting loss under suboptimal batch size configurations.
AI.result: The three-term law correctly recovers the known scaling behavior of optimal batch size. Because it incorporates runs with suboptimal batch sizes into the fit, it achieves robust parameter estimation using significantly fewer total training runs. The law also successfully derives scaling relations for suboptimal batch sizes and aligns with prior empirical observations regarding the critical batch size.
AI.conclusion: The three-term scaling law offers a more granular and data-efficient framework for predicting neural network scaling behavior by explicitly modeling the interaction between model size, training steps, and batch size, with practical implications for optimizing training configurations at scale.

title: Unveiling the Non-Monotonic Effect of Privacy on Generalization under Byzantine Robustness
summary: Recent work has established a fundamental trilemma between Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy (LDP), and optimization error in distributed learning. We show that this trilemma does not universally extend to generalization error, but instead depends critically on the privacy regime. Specifically, in the high-noise regime (strong privacy), we prove that increasing privacy reduces the generalization error, i.e., there is no tension between robustness and privacy. In the low-noise regime (weaker privacy), however, the tension between robustness and privacy reappears and increasing privacy indeed degrades generalization. Our theory explains this surprising non-monotonic behavior of the generalization error via matching lower and upper bounds on the algorithmic stability of Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints. We corroborate and further analyze these theoretical findings with empirical evaluations.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the established robustness-privacy-optimization trilemma by showing that the tension between Byzantine robustness and LDP does not universally hold for generalization error. Instead, the relationship is non-monotonic: in high-noise (strong privacy) regimes, increasing privacy improves generalization; in low-noise (weak privacy) regimes, the traditional tension re-emerges. The authors prove this via matching stability bounds and validate empirically.
AI.motivation: Prior work posited a fundamental trilemma among Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy (LDP), and optimization error in distributed learning. This paper investigates whether this trilemma extends to generalization error, challenging the assumption that robustness and privacy are universally in tension.
AI.method: The authors derive matching lower and upper bounds on the algorithmic stability of Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints. They analyze generalization error through the lens of differential privacy noise regimes, distinguishing between high-noise (strong privacy) and low-noise (weak privacy) settings, and corroborate findings with empirical evaluations.
AI.result: In the high-noise regime, increasing privacy reduces generalization error (no tension). In the low-noise regime, increasing privacy degrades generalization (tension reappears). This non-monotonic behavior is captured by stability bounds and confirmed empirically.
AI.conclusion: The robustness-privacy trilemma is not universal for generalization error; it is regime-dependent. Strong privacy can actually be beneficial for generalization in Byzantine-robust distributed learning, while weaker privacy reintroduces the trade-off.

title: Understanding Build Reproducibility in the F-Droid Ecosystem
comment: 2026 ACM Conference on Reproducibility and Replicability, Jul 2026, Delft, Netherlands
summary: The security of open source applications benefits considerably from the possibility of rebuilding their source and verifying the output. F-Droid, a prominent distribution for open source Android applications, systematically rebuilds them from source and tests their bitwise reproducibility at app publishing time. However, F-Droid offers no guarantee that app reproducibility will continue to hold in the future. As software ecosystems evolve, reproducibility may degrade, with potential negative consequences for software preservation and security. We present the first empirical study of build reproducibility in the F-Droid app ecosystem. Analyzing historical reproducibility logs, we find that the overall bitwise reproducibility rate has been steadily increasing over time (as new versions of apps are published). We then evaluate how reproducibility holds in time for fixed app versions, by attempting to rebuild 18 904 app versions that F-Droid had previously confirmed bitwise reproducible, published between September 2018 and February 2026, achieving an 83% rebuild success rate, and identify missing dependencies as the dominant cause of failure, accounting for 76% of non-rebuildable cases. Among successfully rebuilt apps, 94% are also bitwise reproducible-i.e., they still yield bitwise identical artifacts upon rebuild. Together, these results show that while bitwise reproducibility largely holds for apps that can be rebuilt, rebuildability itself is highly sensitive to temporal decay.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first empirical study of build reproducibility over time in the F-Droid Android app ecosystem. Analyzing historical data and attempting to rebuild ~19,000 previously reproducible app versions, the authors find that while 94% of successfully rebuilt apps remain bitwise reproducible, rebuildability itself degrades significantly over time—with missing dependencies causing 76% of failures.
AI.motivation: F-Droid systematically rebuilds open-source Android apps from source and verifies bitwise reproducibility at publishing time, but offers no guarantee that reproducibility persists into the future. As software ecosystems evolve, reproducibility may degrade — a phenomenon the authors term "temporal decay" — with negative consequences for software preservation and security. No prior empirical study had quantified this risk.
AI.method: The authors conducted a two-part empirical study: (1) analysis of historical reproducibility logs from the F-Droid ecosystem to observe trends in reproducibility rates over time as new app versions are published; (2) a large-scale rebuild experiment attempting to rebuild 18,904 app versions (published between September 2018 and February 2026) that F-Droid had previously confirmed as bitwise reproducible, then classifying failure causes and checking whether successfully rebuilt apps remained bitwise identical.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Overall bitwise reproducibility rates have been steadily increasing over time for newly published app versions. (2) In the rebuild experiment, 83% of previously reproducible app versions could be successfully rebuilt. (3) Missing dependencies dominated rebuild failures, accounting for 76% of non-rebuildable cases. (4) Among successfully rebuilt apps, 94% remained bitwise reproducible — i.e., yielded bitwise-identical artifacts upon rebuild.
AI.conclusion: Bitwise reproducibility largely holds for apps that can still be rebuilt, but rebuildability itself is highly sensitive to temporal decay, primarily driven by dependency unavailability. This reveals a critical gap in F-Droid's reproducibility guarantees and highlights the need for ecosystem-level preservation strategies (e.g., dependency archiving) to ensure long-term rebuildability and security verification.

title: Scaling with Confidence: Calibrating Confidence of LLMs for Adaptive Test Time Scaling
summary: Training large language models (LLMs) with reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly advanced their performance on reasoning and question-answering tasks. However, prevailing RL reward designs typically prioritize response correctness, neglecting to incentivize models to express their confidence accurately. This leads to a critical problem: performance gains are often accompanied by poor calibration between confidence and accuracy, misleading models to overconfidently hallucinate when uncertain. To address this limitation, we propose $\textbf{C}$orrectness and $\textbf{C}$onfidence $\textbf{C}$alibration $\textbf{R}$einforcement $\textbf{L}$earning ($\textbf{C3RL}$), a novel RL algorithm integrating correctness, calibration and dataset-informed reference accuracy rewards together. Comprehensive evaluation across 8 text and multimodal datasets demonstrates that C3RL enhances calibration without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming the current state-of-the-art method in both performance and calibration metrics. Utilizing the well-calibrated verbalized confidence from C3RL, we further introduce $\textbf{C}$onfidence-based $\textbf{A}$daptive Test Time $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{CAS}$), an adjustable inference-time strategy that allocates computational resources based on response confidence. Experiments show that CAS surpasses majority voting on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets while reducing the inference budget by up to 12.33 times. We believe the synergy of C3RL and CAS paves the way for deploying more reliable and resource-efficient LLMs. The code, data and models will be released.

AI.tldr: C3RL is a reinforcement learning algorithm that jointly optimizes LLMs for response correctness and confidence calibration, then uses the calibrated confidence for adaptive test-time compute scaling (CAS), achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than majority voting with up to 12.33× inference budget reduction.
AI.motivation: Current RL training for LLMs prioritizes answer correctness but neglects confidence calibration, causing models to become overconfident and hallucinate when uncertain. There is a need to decouple accuracy gains from poor calibration.
AI.method: C3RL introduces a multi-objective RL reward combining three components: (1) correctness reward, (2) calibration reward (aligning verbalized confidence with actual accuracy), and (3) dataset-informed reference accuracy reward. The resulting well-calibrated confidence enables Confidence-based Adaptive Test Time Scaling (CAS), an inference-time strategy that dynamically allocates compute based on response confidence levels.
AI.result: Across 8 text and multimodal datasets, C3RL improved calibration without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming the state-of-the-art in both performance and calibration metrics. CAS surpassed majority voting on in-domain and out-of-domain datasets while reducing inference budget by up to 12.33×.
AI.conclusion: The synergy of C3RL and CAS enables more reliable and resource-efficient LLM deployment, with code, data, and models to be released.

title: DiPS: Dialogue Policy Selection for High-Stakes Persuasion Agents
comment: Proceedings of the 27th Annual Meeting of the Special Interest Group on Discourse and Dialogue (SIGDIAL 2026)
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with persuasion in high-stakes scenarios. People's individual personalities and concerns require tailored strategies rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. To address this challenge, we focus on a fire-rescue scenario in which an operator must persuade a resident to evacuate as a high-stakes persuasion domain and propose Dialogue Policy Selection (DiPS), a Q-learning framework to dynamically select persuasion strategies adapted to the evolving conversational context. Specifically, we train a critic, trained to maximize the chance of evacuation success, to select a persuasion policy at each turn based on the resident's recent utterances.We then evaluate DiPS against multiple baselines in both simulated and real human interactions. We find that DiPS achieves higher evacuation success than a zero-shot LLM and generic RAG-augmented approach.

AI.tldr: DiPS is a Q-learning framework that dynamically selects persuasion strategies in a fire-rescue evacuation scenario, outperforming zero-shot LLM and RAG-augmented baselines in both simulated and real human interactions.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with high-stakes persuasion because individuals have distinct personalities and concerns, making generic one-size-fits-all approaches ineffective. A dynamic, context-adaptive strategy selection mechanism is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose DiPS (Dialogue Policy Selection), a Q-learning framework applied to a fire-rescue operator scenario. A critic model is trained to maximize evacuation success probability and selects a persuasion policy at each dialogue turn based on the resident's recent utterances, enabling dynamic adaptation to the evolving conversational context.
AI.result: DiPS achieves higher evacuation success rates compared to a zero-shot LLM baseline and a generic RAG-augmented approach, validated through both simulated interactions and real human participant studies.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, reinforcement-learning-based policy selection for persuasion strategies is more effective than static or retrieval-based methods in high-stakes, personality-dependent scenarios like fire-rescue evacuation.

title: Don't Let Gains FADE: Breaking Down Policy Gradient Weights in RL
summary: Reinforcement learning post-training dramatically improves LLM reasoning, but suffers from training instability and diversity collapse. Advantage functions offer an appealing fix: they reshape the training objective, reweight which rollouts drive learning, and are trivial to implement. Yet a proliferation of methods makes it unclear which advantage to use and when. We cut through the confusion with a unifying framework that decomposes any advantage into its positive and negative gradient mass along two orthogonal axes. On the sign axis, imbalanced updates collapse either entropy or weight geometry. On the difficulty axis, hard-problem focus sharpens signal but costs sample size. Both trade-offs shift during training: exploration favors balance and hard focus; exploitation favors suppression and medium focus. This motivates FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy), a self-adapting advantage that reads training dynamics to schedule the gradient weight automatically. FADE reaches peak pass@1 20k steps earlier than the best static baseline at the 7B scale and 2k steps earlier at the 32B , while achieving the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME.

AI.tldr: FADE introduces a unifying framework for advantage functions in RL post-training of LLMs, decomposing them along sign and difficulty axes. The method automatically schedules gradient weights based on training dynamics, achieving faster convergence and better accuracy-diversity trade-offs than static baselines.
AI.motivation: RL post-training for LLM reasoning suffers from training instability and diversity collapse. While advantage functions can mitigate these issues by reshaping training objectives and reweighting rollouts, the proliferation of methods creates confusion about which advantage to use and when. The paper aims to unify these approaches and provide an adaptive solution.
AI.method: The authors propose a unifying framework that decomposes any advantage function into positive/negative gradient mass along two orthogonal axes: (1) the sign axis, where imbalanced updates collapse entropy or weight geometry; (2) the difficulty axis, where hard-problem focus sharpens signal but reduces effective sample size. They observe that these trade-offs shift during training — exploration favors balance and hard focus, while exploitation favors suppression and medium focus. This motivates FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy), which reads training dynamics to automatically schedule gradient weights.
AI.result: FADE reaches peak pass@1 20,000 steps earlier than the best static baseline at the 7B scale and 2,000 steps earlier at 32B, while achieving the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME.
AI.conclusion: The two-axis decomposition provides a principled lens for understanding advantage functions, and dynamic scheduling via FADE outperforms static approaches in both convergence speed and accuracy-diversity trade-offs across multiple benchmarks and model scales.

title: AI Writes Faster Than Humans Can Review: A Longitudinal Study of an Enterprise 2x Mandate
summary: Enterprises increasingly mandate AI coding tools and report large productivity gains, yet longitudinal evidence on how such a mandate unfolds is scarce. In this paper, we present a quantitative case study of a documented enterprise "2x" mandate at a mid-sized, AI-forward company that has been committed to doubling merged pull requests per engineer since mid-2025. In a panel of 802 developers and 196,212 pull requests (January 2024-April 2026), per-capita throughput eventually doubled, reaching 2.09x the pre-mandate baseline in April 2026, among the largest gains reported from a field deployment of AI coding tools to our knowledge. A staggered difference-in-differences design links the within-developer share of this gain to AI adoption and to a further gain that grows with accumulated use, with the mandate acting as a catalyst rather than a direct driver. Because adoption and usage intensity were not randomly assigned, we read this evidence as strongly implicating an adoption-and-use channel rather than as exact causal attribution. The gain is broadly shared across seniority yet concentrated in newer code and not separable across model generations. Adoption also restructured code review around automation: per-reviewer load roughly doubled and automated review overtook human review, while merge and revert rates held steady.

AI.tldr: A longitudinal study of an enterprise "2x" AI coding mandate finds per-capita pull request throughput doubled (2.09x baseline) by April 2026 among 802 developers. Gains are linked to AI adoption and accumulated use via staggered difference-in-differences, with adoption restructuring code review toward automation while merge/revert rates remained stable.
AI.motivation: Enterprises are increasingly mandating AI coding tools and claiming large productivity gains, but there is scarce longitudinal evidence on how such mandates actually unfold in real-world settings. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a quantitative case study of a documented enterprise mandate.
AI.method: A quantitative case study using a panel of 802 developers and 196,212 pull requests spanning January 2024 to April 2026. The authors employ a staggered difference-in-differences design to estimate the within-developer effect of AI adoption on throughput, distinguishing between adoption effects and gains from accumulated use. The mandate is treated as a catalyst, not a direct causal driver.
AI.result: Per-capita merged pull requests reached 2.09x the pre-mandate baseline by April 2026. AI adoption and accumulated usage intensity are strongly associated with throughput gains, though adoption was not randomly assigned. Gains are broadly distributed across seniority levels but concentrated in newer code and not separable by model generation. Code review was restructured: per-reviewer load roughly doubled, automated review overtook human review, while merge and revert rates held steady.
AI.conclusion: The enterprise "2x" mandate succeeded in doubling throughput, with evidence strongly implicating an adoption-and-use channel facilitated by the mandate as a catalyst. The productivity gains did not compromise code quality metrics (merge/revert rates), but the restructuring of code review toward automation raises important questions about long-term engineering practices.

title: Spatial Support Matters: Geometry-Aware Graph Fusion for Rainfall Field Reconstruction
summary: Fine-scale rainfall reconstruction is critical for urban flood modeling, but real rainfall sensing systems observe the field through incompatible spatial supports: gauges measure points, microwave links measure paths, and radar/satellite products measure gridded areas. These differences in measurement support impose geometrically distinct constraints on the rainfall field, yet existing heterogeneous graph approaches reconcile such sources in feature space, giving each its own embedding while discarding the geometry of its support. We propose a geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network that represents each observation according to its support type (0D point, 1D line, or 2D grid) as a distinct node layer, and fuses them through cross-support message passing into a point-support prediction layer from which the field is reconstructed. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, allowing the same trained model to reconstruct the field at user-defined target locations or display grids. On Singapore data, the proposed method reduces RMSE by 23.2\% over the classical interpolation baseline, inverse-distance weighting, and consistently outperforms other neural architectures such as convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. A generalization study using data from Sydney, Australia lets us characterize when multi-support fusion helps: the available skill appears to depend on gauge spacing relative to the spatial correlation length of the field, so fusion delivers the largest gains where the field is under-sampled relative to its correlation length and little when it is already resolved. Code and models will be open-sourced upon paper acceptance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a geometry-aware heterogeneous graph neural network that fuses rainfall observations from incompatible spatial supports (point gauges, line-of-sight microwave links, gridded radar/satellite) via cross-support message passing, achieving 23.2% RMSE reduction over IDW baseline on Singapore data, with generalization insights from Sydney showing fusion benefits depend on gauge spacing versus spatial correlation length.
AI.motivation: Urban flood modeling requires fine-scale rainfall reconstruction, but real sensing systems observe rainfall through geometrically incompatible supports: 0D points (gauges), 1D paths (microwave links), and 2D grids (radar/satellite). Existing heterogeneous graph methods reconcile these only in feature space, discarding the geometric constraints of each support type, which limits their ability to properly fuse multi-support observations.
AI.method: A geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network is proposed, where each observation support type (0D, 1D, 2D) forms a distinct node layer in the graph. Cross-support message passing fuses information across these layers into a point-support prediction layer for field reconstruction. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, enabling arbitrary user-defined target locations without retraining.
AI.result: On Singapore data, the method reduces RMSE by 23.2% over inverse-distance weighting (classical baseline) and consistently outperforms convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. A generalization study on Sydney data reveals that multi-support fusion helps most when gauge spacing is large relative to the field's spatial correlation length (under-sampled regime), and offers little gain when the field is already well-resolved.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware multi-support fusion via heterogeneous graph neural networks effectively reconciles disparate rainfall observations. The benefit is conditional: fusion is most impactful when the field is under-sampled relative to its correlation length. Code and models will be open-sourced.

title: Beyond Skepticism: Evaluating LLMs Pedagogical Intent Reasoning with the Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance Framework
summary: The capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) to reason about pedagogical intent within instructional communication remains underexplored, particularly in educational domains such as translation pedagogy. To address this, we propose the \textbf{Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV)} framework, a novel computational formalism that reframes communicative vigilance as an adaptive mechanism for optimizing learning through intent inference. APV formalizes the problem via a Bayesian Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine (PIIE), which models how instructors select content to maximize pedagogical utility and how vigilant learners should inversely reason about latent instructional configurations -- encompassing genre, stance, and incentives. We evaluate APV through a three-tier hierarchy: distinguishing instructional genre, reasoning about structured pedagogical setups, and generalizing to authentic educational discourse. Experiments on leading LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) show that APV substantially improves model vigilance. It achieves the strongest discrimination between pedagogical and exposure-based content, correlates highly with human judgments ($r=0.958$), and maintains robust performance on naturalistic data where baseline methods degrade. This work establishes a unified framework for assessing and enhancing LLMs' understanding of pedagogical motives, advancing the development of more reliable AI-assisted learning systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Adaptive Pedagogical Vigilance (APV) framework, which uses a Bayesian inference engine (PIIE) to model how LLMs can infer latent instructional intent (genre, stance, incentives) from pedagogical communication. Evaluated across three tiers, APV significantly improves LLMs' ability to discriminate pedagogical from non-pedagogical content, correlates strongly with human judgment (r=0.958), and generalizes robustly to naturalistic data.
AI.motivation: LLMs' capacity to reason about pedagogical intent — understanding why an instructor selects particular content — is underexplored, especially in domains like translation pedagogy. Existing approaches lack a formal computational framework for modeling how learners should vigilantly infer latent instructional configurations from communicative acts.
AI.method: The APV framework formalizes communicative vigilance as an adaptive optimization problem. Its core is the Bayesian Pedagogical Intent Inference Engine (PIIE), which models: (1) how instructors select content to maximize pedagogical utility given latent variables (genre, stance, incentives), and (2) how vigilant learners inversely infer these latent configurations. Evaluation follows a three-tier hierarchy: distinguishing instructional genre, reasoning about structured pedagogical setups, and generalizing to authentic educational discourse.
AI.result: APV achieves the strongest discrimination between pedagogical and exposure-based content across leading LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5). It yields a high correlation with human judgments (r=0.958) and maintains robust performance on naturalistic data where baseline methods degrade.
AI.conclusion: The APV framework provides a unified, principled approach for assessing and enhancing LLMs' understanding of pedagogical motives. By formalizing communicative vigilance as Bayesian intent inference, it advances the development of more reliable AI-assisted learning systems capable of reasoning about why content is taught, not just what is taught.

title: Beyond Textual Repository Exploration: Dual-Modal Structural Reasoning for Agentic Issue Resolution
summary: Recent advances in agentic program repair have significantly improved issue resolution by enabling iterative repository exploration. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on sequential, text-based code navigation, which fundamentally limits their ability to reason over large-scale long-horizon repositories with complex and long-range dependencies. As issue-resolution agents traverse repositories through fragmented textual observations, structural information such as module organization, call relationships, and dependency chains must be repeatedly reconstructed across interaction steps, often leading to exploration drift and incomplete localization. We present DUALVIEW, a dual-modal structural scaffolding framework that brings visual reasoning into repository exploration for issue-resolution agents. DUALVIEW represents repository structure through four complementary graph views: Module Coupling Graph (MCG), Function Call Graph (FCG), Class Hierarchy Graph (CHG), and Program Dependence Graph (PDG), and exposes them through a queryable interface with visual and textual responses. Rather than reconstructing repository structure from a sequence of textual observations, agents can directly reason over persistent visual representations of code dependencies, enabling more effective exploration and understanding of long-horizon codebases. We evaluate DUALVIEW on SWE-bench Pro and Verified. Results show that DUALVIEW consistently improves issue-resolution performance across different agent architectures and model families. Further ablation studies demonstrate that the gains arise not only from textual structural information but also from visual externalization of repository dependencies, which better supports long-horizon repository exploration.

AI.tldr: DUALVIEW introduces visual repository structure graphs (MCG, FCG, CHG, PDG) as a scaffolding framework for issue-resolution agents, replacing sequential text-based navigation with persistent visual/structural reasoning. It consistently improves SWE-bench performance across architectures.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic program repair methods use sequential, text-based code navigation, forcing agents to repeatedly reconstruct structural information (module organization, call relationships, dependency chains) from fragmented textual observations across interaction steps. This causes exploration drift and incomplete localization, especially in large-scale repositories with long-range dependencies.
AI.method: DUALVIEW is a dual-modal structural scaffolding framework that exposes four complementary graph views of repository structure: Module Coupling Graph (MCG), Function Call Graph (FCG), Class Hierarchy Graph (CHG), and Program Dependence Graph (PDG). These are made accessible through a queryable interface supporting both visual and textual responses, allowing agents to directly reason over persistent representations rather than reconstructing structure incrementally.
AI.result: Evaluated on SWE-bench Pro and Verified, DUALVIEW consistently improves issue-resolution performance across different agent architectures and model families. Ablation studies show gains stem from both textual structural information and visual externalization of dependencies, with the latter particularly benefiting long-horizon repository exploration.
AI.conclusion: Visual structural scaffolding via persistent dependency graphs significantly enhances repository exploration for issue-resolution agents, overcoming the limitations of sequential text-based navigation. The dual-modal approach (visual + textual structural views) is broadly beneficial across agent designs and model families.

title: Autonomous discovery of traffic laws with AI traffic scientists
summary: Universal traffic laws describe recurrent patterns in congestion, mobility and driving behavior across cities, providing a scientific basis for transportation planning, management and control. Their discovery, however, remains expert-driven, requiring candidate regularities to be identified from heterogeneous observational evidence or validated through intervention experiments. Although autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems have advanced scientific discovery in controlled laboratory settings, extending them to complex transportation domains remains a challenge. Here we present TrafficSci, an agentic AI system that formulates traffic-law discovery as an iterative, auditable workflow integrating evidence scoping, critic-judge hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation. Across four case studies spanning population, network, control and trajectory scales, TrafficSci autonomously rediscovers three established traffic laws and identifies an unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior, statistically consistent across eight cities and two trajectory datasets. TrafficSci provides a route for extending AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled domains to complex urban systems.

AI.tldr: TrafficSci is an agentic AI system that autonomously discovers traffic laws through an iterative workflow combining evidence scoping, hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation. It rediscovers three established laws and identifies a new intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior across multiple cities.
AI.motivation: Traffic law discovery has traditionally been expert-driven, requiring manual identification of candidate regularities from heterogeneous data or controlled intervention experiments. While AI has advanced scientific discovery in controlled lab settings, extending autonomous discovery to complex transportation systems remains an open challenge.
AI.method: TrafficSci frames traffic-law discovery as an iterative, auditable workflow with three core components: (1) evidence scoping to gather heterogeneous observational data, (2) critic-judge hypothesis induction to propose candidate laws with internal critique, and (3) observational-interventional validation that tests hypotheses against both passive data and targeted intervention experiments across multiple scales.
AI.result: Across four case studies at population, network, control, and trajectory scales, TrafficSci autonomously rediscovered three established traffic laws and identified a previously unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior. This new finding was statistically consistent across eight cities and two trajectory datasets.
AI.conclusion: TrafficSci demonstrates a viable pathway for extending AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled laboratory domains to complex urban systems, enabling autonomous identification of both known and novel empirical regularities in transportation.

title: ProWAFT: A ROMA-LPD Instance for Workload-Aware and Dynamic Fault Tolerance in FPGA-Based CNN Accelerators
summary: SRAM-based FPGAs provide an attractive platform for energy- and latency-constrained CNN inference at the network edge, yet transient faults can lead to silent errors that compromise reliability. Always-on redundancy (e.g., full TMR) improves correctness but incurs substantial performance and energy overhead, while reactive recovery may introduce unacceptable latency on the critical path. We propose \textbf{ProWAFT}, a proactive workload-aware fault-tolerance framework for FPGA-based CNN accelerators that uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR across reconfigurable partitions. ProWAFT quantifies workload criticality, models fault propagation and reconfiguration overhead, and selects configurations that minimize a composite objective over latency, energy, and reliability risk. Implemented on a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU104 platform with six reconfigurable regions and evaluated on a 500-task trace derived from ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNet-Lite under time-varying SEU injection, ProWAFT achieves lower composite cost than static TMR and reactive reconfiguration while maintaining high task success rate and near-baseline throughput with low online decision overhead.

AI.tldr: ProWAFT is a proactive fault-tolerance framework for FPGA-based CNN accelerators that uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR based on workload criticality, achieving better composite cost (latency, energy, reliability) than static TMR or reactive approaches.
AI.motivation: SRAM-based FPGAs are attractive for edge CNN inference but suffer from transient-fault-induced silent errors. Existing solutions are inadequate: always-on redundancy (e.g., full TMR) incurs high performance/energy overhead, while reactive recovery introduces unacceptable critical-path latency. A balanced, workload-aware approach is needed.
AI.method: ProWAFT quantifies workload criticality, models fault propagation and reconfiguration overhead, and formulates a composite objective (latency, energy, reliability risk). It uses partial reconfiguration to selectively apply TMR across reconfigurable partitions, selecting configurations that minimize the composite cost. Evaluated on Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU104 with six reconfigurable regions.
AI.result: Under a 500-task trace (ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-Lite) with time-varying SEU injection, ProWAFT achieves lower composite cost than both static TMR and reactive reconfiguration, maintains high task success rate and near-baseline throughput, with low online decision overhead.
AI.conclusion: Proactive, workload-aware selective TMR via partial reconfiguration effectively balances reliability, performance, and energy for FPGA-based CNN inference, outperforming both static full redundancy and reactive recovery strategies under realistic fault conditions.

title: Towards Learning Representations of Policies in Two-Player Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games
summary:
We investigate the problem of learning useful policy representations (embeddings) in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games. We make three contributions: First, we introduce methods of creating datasets of policies for a given game. Second, we propose methods to learn policy representations. Third, we introduce downstream tasks to evaluate the effectiveness of such representations.
  We evaluate each dataset method, embedding method, and downstream task on Kuhn and Leduc Poker. Although our methods are very basic, we demonstrate that useful behavioral representations are present in the learned embeddings. To our knowledge, this work is among the first to systematically compare self-supervised learning techniques for learning policy representations in games. Our code is available at https://github.com/VitamintK/ssl-project for others to extend.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates self-supervised learning of policy embeddings for two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games, proposing dataset creation methods, embedding techniques, and downstream evaluation tasks, with experiments on Kuhn and Leduc Poker.
AI.motivation: To explore whether useful behavioral representations (embeddings) of policies can be learned in imperfect-information games, enabling downstream tasks like policy comparison, clustering, or transfer learning — an area that had not been systematically studied before.
AI.method: The authors propose three methodological pillars: (1) methods to generate datasets of policies for a given game, (2) self-supervised learning techniques to produce policy embeddings from those datasets, and (3) downstream evaluation tasks to assess the quality and utility of the learned representations. Experiments are conducted on Kuhn Poker and Leduc Poker as testbeds.
AI.result: Even with basic methods, the learned embeddings contain useful behavioral representations, as demonstrated by the downstream tasks. The work provides an initial systematic comparison of self-supervised techniques for policy representation learning in games.
AI.conclusion: This is among the first systematic studies of self-supervised policy representation learning in games. Despite the simplicity of the methods, meaningful policy embeddings emerge, and the authors release their codebase to facilitate further research in this direction.

title: ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems
