summary: Agentic systems enhance their capabilities by invoking external tools and maintaining persistent memory. However, these external dependencies introduce novel attack surfaces. Recent tool and memory poisoning attacks show that maliciously crafted tool descriptors and poisoned memory can covertly bias agent behavior. These threats reflect a deeper issue: the lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state for planning and execution. We present ElephantAgent, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend against contextual state poisoning. Inspired by prior state-continuity mechanisms (e.g., Nimble), ElephantAgent extends this protection to the evolving contextual state of agentic systems. We define the contextual state as the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's entire context (e.g., tool state and memory). Before processing each query, ElephantAgent recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest. Using replicated trusted hardware, ElephantAgent maintains a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions and detects out-of-band state tampering. To handle in-band semantic abuse, ElephantAgent additionally provides Historical Traceability, enabling conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.

AI.tldr: ElephantAgent is a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend against tool and memory poisoning in agentic AI systems. It uses replicated trusted hardware to maintain a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions, recomputes digests before each query, and provides Historical Traceability for post-hoc audit and recovery.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems face novel attack surfaces from external dependencies (tools and persistent memory). Existing attacks like tool descriptor poisoning and memory poisoning can covertly bias agent behavior. The fundamental problem is the lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state across planning and execution cycles.
AI.method: ElephantAgent defines a bounded, security-critical "contextual state" (tool state and memory). Before each query, it recomputes a digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest. It uses replicated trusted hardware to maintain a linearizable ledger of authorized state transitions, detecting out-of-band tampering. For in-band semantic abuse, it provides Historical Traceability — enabling conditional post-hoc audit and rollback to a known-good prior state.
AI.result: The protocol detects out-of-band contextual state tampering through digest mismatch against the authorized ledger. It further enables post-hoc forensic audit and recovery for in-band semantic attacks via its Historical Traceability mechanism, allowing rollback to a previously authorized good state.
AI.conclusion: Contextual State Continuity, enforced through trusted hardware-backed digests and a linearizable ledger, provides a principled defense against both out-of-band poisoning and in-band semantic manipulation in agentic systems, with the added benefit of auditable recovery.

title: Underspecification does not imply Incoherence: The Risks of Semantic Collapse in Coding Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly effective at generating code when task descriptions are clear and precise. Yet, in practice, user-provided task descriptions are often ambiguous, incomplete, or contradictory, leaving critical aspects of the intended program behavior underspecified. In such cases, multiple behaviorally distinct interpretations may satisfy the description equally well, yet semantically differ in ways that matter/affect the user intent. A natural expectation, often assumed by researchers, is that prompt underspecification manifests as incoherence: When asked multiple times, an LLM produces multiple semantically distinct implementations reflecting the ambiguity of the task description. In this paper, we challenge this assumption. We find that LLMs frequently collapse onto a single incorrect interpretation of the task description, consistently generating coherent but behaviorally misaligned code. We term this failure mode detrimental semantic collapse and find that it affects over 10% of tasks in MBPP, 3% in HumanEval, and 32% of LiveCodeBench, all benchmarks assumed to be well-specified. By deliberately injecting underspecification issues in the benchmark prompts, the rate rises to over 5 times, exposing a fundamental blind spot in disambiguation and correctness estimation techniques that rely on incoherence as a proxy for prompt underspecification.

AI.tldr: LLMs often fail not by producing diverse incorrect outputs (incoherence), but by consistently converging on a single behaviorally misaligned interpretation of underspecified prompts—a phenomenon the authors term "detrimental semantic collapse." This affects 10%+ of standard benchmark tasks and increases 5× when underspecification is deliberately injected, undermining methods that use incoherence as a proxy for detecting ambiguity.
AI.motivation: The prevailing assumption in LLM research is that prompt underspecification leads to incoherence—i.e., multiple semantically distinct outputs when queried repeatedly. This assumption underpins disambiguation and correctness estimation techniques. The authors challenge this assumption, hypothesizing that LLMs may instead collapse onto a single but wrong interpretation, creating a blind spot in existing evaluation and mitigation strategies.
AI.method: The authors analyze three code-generation benchmarks (MBPP, HumanEval, LiveCodeBench) by: (1) measuring semantic diversity across multiple samples per task to detect collapse vs. incoherence; (2) manually inspecting cases where outputs are coherent but misaligned with intended behavior; (3) deliberately injecting underspecification into benchmark prompts to quantify how collapse rates change under controlled ambiguity.
AI.result: Detrimental semantic collapse occurs in over 10% of MBPP tasks, 3% of HumanEval tasks, and 32% of LiveCodeBench tasks—all benchmarks presumed to be well-specified. When underspecification is deliberately introduced, the collapse rate increases by over a factor of five. This reveals that incoherence-based proxies for detecting underspecification are fundamentally unreliable.
AI.conclusion: Detrimental semantic collapse is a significant and previously unrecognized failure mode in LLM code generation. Reliance on output incoherence as a signal of prompt ambiguity is insufficient and can mask systematic misalignment. The paper calls for new disambiguation and correctness estimation methods that do not depend on this flawed proxy.

title: Diverse Evidence, Better Forecasts: Multi-Agent Deliberation Under Information Asymmetry
summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used for forecasting future events, as deliberation among multiple LLMs is believed to improve reasoning and calibration. Yet existing approaches overlook a critical design choice: what information each agent receives. When all agents are given identical evidence, deliberation collapses into herding rather than genuine belief revision, leaving multi-agent systems little better than a single agent. We identify this as a fundamental gap and propose designed information asymmetry to close it: by partitioning evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets, each agent holds exclusive knowledge that can only reach others through deliberation. We theoretically show that this decomposition reduces inter-agent error correlation, and instantiate it in InfoDelphi, a framework combining relevance-aware evidence routing, rationale-based iterative deliberation, and confidence-weighted aggregation. On PolyGym, a benchmark of 375 binary forecasting questions derived from real-world prediction markets, InfoDelphi outperforms the strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12--18% in Brier score and 4--8 percentage points in accuracy. More detailed experiments confirm that removing information asymmetry eliminates most deliberation gains, establishing diversity of input as the key enabler of effective multi-agent reasoning.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM forecasting systems fail when agents share identical evidence due to herding. The authors propose designed information asymmetry — partitioning evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets — to foster genuine deliberation. Their framework, InfoDelphi, reduces inter-agent error correlation and outperforms both single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12–18% in Brier score on a 375-question forecasting benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent forecasting systems give all agents identical evidence, causing deliberation to collapse into herding (agents irrationally converging rather than engaging in genuine belief revision). This makes multi-agent systems little better than single-agent ones. The authors identify this as a fundamental gap: the lack of input diversity undermines the theoretical benefits of multi-agent deliberation.
AI.method: The paper proposes InfoDelphi, a framework with three core components: (1) relevance-aware evidence routing that partitions information into shared public evidence and disjoint private evidence per agent; (2) rationale-based iterative deliberation where agents exchange arguments derived from their private knowledge; and (3) confidence-weighted aggregation of final forecasts. The authors provide theoretical analysis showing that information asymmetry reduces inter-agent error correlation, and validate the approach on PolyGym, a benchmark of 375 binary forecasting questions from real-world prediction markets.
AI.result: InfoDelphi outperforms the strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12–18% in Brier score and 4–8 percentage points in accuracy on PolyGym. Ablation studies confirm that removing information asymmetry eliminates most deliberation gains, establishing diversity of input as the key enabler of effective multi-agent reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Designed information asymmetry is critical for effective multi-agent deliberation in forecasting. Input diversity, rather than mere agent multiplicity, drives the gains. InfoDelphi demonstrates that partitioning evidence into shared and private subsets enables agents to contribute unique knowledge during deliberation, substantially improving forecast accuracy and calibration.

title: When Does Generating More Help? Disentangling Fixed-Source Synthesis from Source Expansion in Synthetic Data Scaling
summary: Synthetic data can be scaled along two routes: Source Expansion (SE), which enlarges the source by adding seed materials or generators, and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), which holds the source fixed and scales the generation budget. Existing scaling studies typically expand the source as the data grows, conflating SE with FSS and leaving FSS underexplored. We isolate FSS by holding the seed-question pool and teacher model fixed, varying only the per-question response budget under Rejection Sampling (RS). We adapt the rectified scaling law to FSS, deriving it from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source. Empirically, the derived form, fit on low budgets, predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher--student pair. At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets; at large budgets, adding seed questions outperforms spending the same budget on more responses. Within FSS, however, neither synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol outperforms plain RS at matched budgets. FSS is thus a bounded scaling axis and a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. We will release our code and data to facilitate further research.

AI.tldr: The paper isolates Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS) from Source Expansion (SE), showing that scaling response budget under a fixed source follows a rectified scaling law; at large budgets, expanding the source outperforms spending on more responses, and no synthesis protocol variant beats plain Rejection Sampling within FSS.
AI.motivation: Prior scaling studies conflate two axes of synthetic data scaling — enlarging the source (SE) vs. increasing generation budget on a fixed source (FSS). FSS remains underexplored because typical setups expand the source as data grows. The authors aim to isolate FSS to understand its scaling behavior independently and to establish it as a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols.
AI.method: The authors fix the seed-question pool and teacher model, varying only the per-question response budget under Rejection Sampling (RS). They adapt the rectified scaling law to FSS, deriving it analytically from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source. They fit this law on low budgets and extrapolate to held-out high budgets, then compare SE vs. FSS at matched total-sample budgets, and also test variants within FSS (synthesizing new questions from seeds, altering synthesis protocols).
AI.result: The derived rectified scaling law, fit on low budgets, accurately predicts performance at held-out highest budgets for all teacher–student pairs. At small matched budgets, SE and FSS perform comparably; at large budgets, adding seed questions (SE) outperforms increasing responses (FSS). Within FSS, neither synthesizing additional questions from existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol outperforms plain RS at matched budgets.
AI.conclusion: FSS is a bounded scaling axis, fundamentally limited by source coverage, and serves as a well-controlled experimental setting for comparing synthesis protocols fairly. For maximizing performance at scale, source expansion is the more effective route.

title: The risk of KV cache compression
summary: Transformer inference on long sequences is expensive because softmax attention repeatedly reads from a large KV cache. The prevalent approach to this bottleneck is KV cache compression, which replaces the full cache with a compact summary. Despite its practical importance, the design of such summaries is largely driven by empirical experimentation. On the theoretical side, existing results show that KV cache compression can be impossible in the worst case, but offer little systematic guidance for designing algorithms in regimes where accurate compression is possible. We bridge this gap by characterizing the minimax risk of KV cache compression in terms of the intrinsic compressibility of a cache, revealing when and how accurate compression is possible. These results yield novel design principles for KV cache compression under causal masking that map efficiently to prefill and autoregressive decoding while achieving minimax-optimal risk. We instantiate these principles in a practical algorithm and report promising performance on LongBench in targeted experiments. Overall, our results provide a principled avenue for practical KV cache compression with theoretical guarantees.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a theoretical framework for KV cache compression in transformer inference, characterizing minimax risk in terms of intrinsic cache compressibility. It derives design principles for causal-masked settings, maps them to efficient prefill/decoding stages, and instantiates them in a practical algorithm with strong LongBench results.
AI.motivation: KV cache compression is critical for efficient long-sequence transformer inference, but existing designs are driven by heuristics rather than theory. Prior theoretical work only provides worst-case impossibility results, offering no guidance on when and how accurate compression is achievable.
AI.method: The authors characterize the minimax risk of KV cache compression as a function of intrinsic compressibility, revealing conditions under which accurate compression is possible. From these bounds, they derive design principles tailored to causal masking that map efficiently onto the prefill and autoregressive decoding phases, achieving minimax-optimal risk.
AI.result: The derived principles are instantiated in a practical algorithm. Targeted experiments on LongBench demonstrate promising performance, validating that the theoretically-grounded approach is competitive in practice.
AI.conclusion: The work bridges theory and practice for KV cache compression, providing a principled approach with theoretical guarantees. It shows that minimax-optimal compression is achievable by exploiting intrinsic cache compressibility under causal masking constraints.

title: kNNGuard: Turning LLM Hidden Activations into a Training-Free Configurable Guardrail
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in domains requiring guardrails to detect unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts. Existing guardrails predominately rely on fine-tuning to build classifiers, which often suffer from low generalization and high inference latency. We present kNNGuard, a training-free guardrail that utilizes the activation space of an off-the-shelf LLM. Given a small bank of 50 safe and unsafe prompts, kNNGuard extracts hidden activations and performs multi-layer kNN fusing activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification. Across six domains spanning topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails while running 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail, and 10x faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier without gradient updates or fine-tuning. Domain adaptation requires only updating the labeled bank, which can be constructed in under 10 seconds and several orders of magnitude faster than established guardrails. We also analyze the impact of system prompts, layer selection, and integration into production LLM pipelines as a configurable, low-latency guardrail.

AI.tldr: kNNGuard is a training-free, activation-based guardrail for LLMs that uses k-nearest neighbors over hidden states from a small bank of 50 labeled prompts, achieving competitive F1 scores with 2.7–10× faster inference than fine-tuned classifiers while enabling rapid domain adaptation in under 10 seconds.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM guardrails rely on fine-tuned classifiers that suffer from poor generalization across domains and high inference latency. There is a need for a lightweight, fast, and easily adaptable guardrail that does not require gradient updates or retraining.
AI.method: kNNGuard extracts hidden activations from multiple layers of an off-the-shelf LLM using a small reference bank of 50 safe and 50 unsafe prompts. It performs multi-layer k-nearest neighbor classification by fusing activation-space and embedding-space similarity scores, without any fine-tuning. Domain adaptation is achieved simply by updating the labeled prompt bank.
AI.result: Across six domains covering topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 scores compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails. It runs 2.7× faster than the best comparable guardrail and 10× faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier. The labeled bank can be constructed in under 10 seconds — several orders of magnitude faster than existing guardrails.
AI.conclusion: kNNGuard offers a configurable, low-latency, training-free alternative to fine-tuned guardrails that is well-suited for production LLM pipelines, with strong performance, fast inference, and near-instant domain adaptation via bank updates.

title: Epic-Organized vs. Requirement-Aligned Gherkin: An Empirical Evaluation of LLM-Based Acceptance Criteria Generation
comment: Accepted for publication at the International Conference on Software Engineering of Emerging Technologies (SEET 2026)
summary: Automated authoring of Gherkin Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) acceptance criteria remains a manual bottleneck in requirements engineering. This study investigates whether epic-organized LLM-generated Gherkin produces higher quality and coverage than requirement-aligned generation. We compare our Timeless (an epic-organized LLM pipeline) approach against a naive large language model (LLM) baseline on four requirements documents (107 requirements) from the PURE dataset. Evaluation covers structural metrics, automated requirement coverage via TF-IDF and dense embeddings, and blind expert assessment by four researchers. In our evaluation, the JSON-constrained pipeline produced structurally valid scenarios across all generated outputs, while the zero-shot baseline achieved 99% structural validity. Semantic coverage was comparable to the baseline, with Timeless achieving 94.3% semantic Requirement Coverage Rate compared with 92.9% for the baseline. TF-IDF produced lower coverage scores for the epic-organized output, suggesting that lexical metrics may miss coverage when scenarios paraphrase requirements at a higher level of abstraction. Expert raters prefer the epic-organized strategy on Correctness (4.61 vs 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs 3.50). Overall, the results suggest that epic-organized generation can improve perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage, although broader replication is needed before generalizing this finding.

AI.tldr: This paper compares epic-organized vs. requirement-aligned LLM-based Gherkin scenario generation, finding that epic-organized generation (Timeless) yields comparable semantic coverage but superior expert-rated correctness, executability, and completeness.
AI.motivation: Automated authoring of Gherkin BDD acceptance criteria remains a manual bottleneck in requirements engineering. The authors investigate whether structuring generation around epics (higher-level user stories) rather than aligning directly to individual requirements improves quality and coverage.
AI.method: The authors propose Timeless, a JSON-constrained LLM pipeline that organizes Gherkin generation around epics. They compare it against a zero-shot LLM baseline on four requirements documents (107 requirements) from the PURE dataset. Evaluation uses: (1) structural validity metrics, (2) automated requirement coverage via TF-IDF and dense embeddings (semantic Requirement Coverage Rate), and (3) blind expert assessment by four researchers rating Correctness, Executability, and Completeness.
AI.result: Timeless achieved 100% structural validity vs. 99% for the baseline. Semantic coverage was comparable (94.3% vs. 92.9% Requirement Coverage Rate). TF-IDF scored epic-organized output lower, suggesting lexical metrics miss coverage when scenarios paraphrase at higher abstraction. Expert raters significantly preferred epic-organized generation: Correctness (4.61 vs. 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs. 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs. 3.50).
AI.conclusion: Epic-organized LLM generation improves perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage. However, broader replication is needed before generalizing this finding.

title: Separating Expert Retention from Autonomous Source Inference in Raw-ECG-Replay-Free Continual ECG Deployment
summary:
In multi-source ECG deployment, models may need to incorporate new data sources when earlier raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed. Freezing a pretrained backbone and assigning each source an isolated classifier prevents parameter interference, but deployment still requires selecting an expert when source metadata are unavailable. We study this distinction through \ours{}, an incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each arriving domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert, while a lightweight router is fitted only on retained training features and domain labels from sources observed so far. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the two most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
  On CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, source-aware expert selection reaches $0.7915\pm0.0036$ Macro-F1 and a matched offline independent-head reference reaches $0.7885\pm0.0009$, supporting strong source-aware expert retention. Without source IDs, an MLP router reaches $0.7756\pm0.0027$ and top-2 margin fusion reaches $0.7782\pm0.0022$. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small ($+0.0026$), with a 95\% confidence interval from paired bootstrap that includes zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap remains $0.0111$--$0.0133$, identifying autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed, but frozen training features are retained for router updates; the method is therefore not memory-free.

AI.tldr: An incremental expert bank for multi-source ECG classification uses frozen ECGFounder features and a lightweight router to handle new data sources without raw ECG replay. A top-2 margin fusion rule slightly outperforms hard routing, but the primary bottleneck remains autonomous source inference when source metadata are unavailable.
AI.motivation: In real-world multi-source ECG deployment, new data sources must be incorporated without retaining or replaying earlier raw ECGs. While freezing a pretrained backbone and using isolated per-source classifiers prevents parameter interference, the challenge is expert selection when source metadata are unavailable at inference time. The gap between source-aware (oracle) selection and autonomous routing needs systematic quantification.
AI.method: The method builds an incremental expert bank atop frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each new domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert. A lightweight MLP router is fitted exclusively on retained training features and domain labels from previously seen sources. At inference, rather than committing to a single routed expert, a validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the predictions of the two most likely experts (top-2 fusion). Training features are retained but raw ECGs are not replayed.
AI.result: On CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing datasets: source-aware expert selection achieves 0.7915±0.0036 Macro-F1, matching an offline independent-head reference (0.7885±0.0009). Without source IDs, MLP routing reaches 0.7756±0.0027 and top-2 margin fusion reaches 0.7782±0.0022. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small (+0.0026), with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval that includes zero. The top-2-to-oracle gap remains 0.0111–0.0133 across three domain orders.
AI.conclusion: Source-aware expert selection nearly matches offline multi-head baselines, validating the frozen-backbone expert-bank design. However, when source IDs are absent, both hard routing and top-2 fusion leave a nontrivial gap to the oracle, identifying autonomous source inference as the primary remaining bottleneck. The method is not memory-free, as frozen training features must be retained for router updates.

title: Rethinking Speech-LLM Integration for ASR: Effective Joint Speech-Text Training by Interleaving
summary: Speech-LLM integration has shown promising results by leveraging extensive textual pretraining, yet its specific benefits for automatic speech recognition (ASR) remain unclear. We observe that as supervised ASR training data increases, the contribution of LLM priors becomes less evident, and simple speech-text joint training under-utilizes textual knowledge. We therefore propose Joint Speech-Text Interleaved Pretraining (JSTIP), an ASR-oriented pretraining strategy that constructs word-level and segment-level interleaved speech-text sequences within aligned pairs for speech-LLM architectures that accept continuous inputs. Experiments on 38k hours of ASR data show consistent entity accuracy improvement compared to ASR-only and joint speech-text training baselines. JSTIP achieves on-par entity recognition performance using domain transcription text compared to synthetic speech-text pairs, simplifying domain adaptation. Benefiting from textual pretraining and domain text data, JSTIP is competitive with open-source ASR and Speech-LLM systems in medical entity recognition. The zero-shot speech question answering behaviors further suggest that interleaving reduces the speech-text modality gap and preserves the LLM generative prior, which is likely the reason for the entity improvements on the ASR task.

AI.tldr: JSTIP proposes interleaved speech-text pretraining for ASR-oriented speech-LLM architectures, improving entity recognition by reducing the speech-text modality gap while preserving LLM generative priors, especially beneficial in domain adaptation with text-only data.
AI.motivation: As supervised ASR data scales up, the benefit of LLM priors diminishes, and naive joint speech-text training under-utilizes textual knowledge. The authors aim to better leverage LLM pretraining for ASR, particularly for entity recognition and domain adaptation.
AI.method: JSTIP constructs word-level and segment-level interleaved speech-text sequences from aligned pairs, designed for speech-LLM architectures accepting continuous inputs. It interleaves text tokens within speech representations during pretraining on 38k hours of ASR data.
AI.result: Consistent entity accuracy gains over ASR-only and joint speech-text baselines. Domain adaptation with transcription text alone achieves on-par performance with synthetic speech-text pairs. Competitive medical entity recognition against open-source ASR and Speech-LLM systems. Zero-shot speech QA shows reduced modality gap and preserved generative prior.
AI.conclusion: Interleaved speech-text pretraining effectively bridges the speech-text modality gap while retaining LLM generative capabilities, explaining entity recognition improvements. JSTIP enables effective domain adaptation using only text data, reducing reliance on synthetic speech generation.

title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
summary: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors--memory capture and memory retention--and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

AI.tldr: Recurrent memory agents degrade on long contexts because memory retention—not memory capture—is the primary bottleneck. The paper proposes Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a training-free architecture that partitions memory into independent heads with a select-then-update strategy, preventing overwriting. MHM-LRU, a lightweight instantiation, dramatically improves retention and end-to-end accuracy from 100K to 1M tokens.
AI.motivation: Recurrent memory agents suffer from systematic performance degradation as context length grows. The authors aim to diagnose the root cause of this failure and provide a practical, training-free architectural solution that decouples memory retention from model behavior, enabling reliable long-context processing without retraining.
AI.method: The paper first decomposes performance into memory capture (encoding new info into memory) and memory retention (preserving previously stored info), quantitatively identifying retention as the dominant bottleneck. To address this, they propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM): memory is partitioned into multiple independent heads. At each step, a stage-wise select-then-update strategy picks exactly one head to update while shielding the rest from overwriting. A specific instantiation, MHM-LRU, uses a Least-Recently-Updated policy to guarantee uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead.
AI.result: On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improved the memory retention rate from under 30% to 73.96%. The method consistently improved both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K–1M token range, generalizing across different model families, scales, and task types.
AI.conclusion: Architectural optimization via multi-head memory partitioning with structured overwrite protection is a practical, cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory. MHM offers a general, training-free framework that shifts the retention burden from model behavior to architectural design.

title: HaloGuard 1.0: An Open Weights Constitutional Classifier for Multilingual AI Safety
summary: We present HaloGuard 1.0, an open-weights implementation of the constitutional-classifier paradigm for input safety. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on English and multilingual prompt-safety benchmarks at roughly one-tenth the model size of current leading open guard models. The safety constitution is the organising structure of the corpus: a natural-language constitution of 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories drives synthetic data generation, with exhaustive one-to-one paired counterfactuals that hold topic and vocabulary fixed while flipping intent, a two-tier harmless design that separately targets boundary and baseline false positives (FPs), and balanced multilingual materialisation across 46 languages that treats language as a surface form appearing on both sides of the boundary rather than as an adversarial signal. Across seven prompt-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B attains the best average F1 (90.9) of any open guard we evaluate, outperforming baselines up to 27B parameters (over 30 times larger) while holding false-positive rate (FPR) to 4.3 and false-negative rate (FNR) to 9.5. The HaloGuard 1.0-4B variant reaches average F1 of 92.1 and FPR of 3.5, spending its extra capacity on precision rather than recall. A structured adjudication of the remaining failures indicates that most apparent missed-harm cases are benchmark mislabels rather than genuine model misses. An always-on adversarial red-teaming protocol continuously hardens the guard against both content-level and agentic attacks. We release the models as open weights.

AI.tldr: HaloGuard 1.0 is an open-weights input safety guard model using a constitutional-classifier paradigm. It achieves state-of-the-art safety performance at a fraction of competing models' size, driven by a detailed safety constitution with 46 policies, 2,940 subcategories, counterfactual data generation, and multilingual coverage across 46 languages.
AI.motivation: Current open guard models for prompt safety are large and resource-intensive. There is a need for smaller, more efficient guard models that maintain or exceed state-of-the-art safety performance while reducing false positives (over-refusal) and handling multilingual inputs effectively without treating language as an adversarial signal.
AI.method: The constitutional-classifier approach organizes a safety constitution of 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories to drive synthetic data generation. Key innovations include: (1) one-to-one paired counterfactuals that hold topic and vocabulary fixed while flipping harmful intent; (2) a two-tier harmless design separately targeting boundary and baseline false positives; (3) balanced multilingual materialisation across 46 languages, treating language as a surface form rather than an adversarial cue; and (4) an always-on adversarial red-teaming protocol for continuous hardening against content-level and agentic attacks.
AI.result: HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B achieves the best average F1 of 90.9 across seven prompt-safety benchmarks among open guards, outperforming models up to 27B parameters (~30× larger), with FPR of 4.3 and FNR of 9.5. The 4B variant reaches F1 of 92.1 and FPR of 3.5, using extra capacity for precision. Structured adjudication reveals most apparent failures are benchmark mislabels rather than genuine model misses.
AI.conclusion: The constitutional-classifier paradigm enables compact, efficient guard models that surpass much larger alternatives in prompt safety. Open-weights release promotes transparency and community adoption, while continuous adversarial red-teaming ensures robustness against evolving attacks.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Software Testing with Scalable Quantum Programs
summary: Quantum software testing (QST) checks whether quantum programs behave according to their intended specifications. A key requirement for QST research is a benchmark that supports rigorous empirical evaluation on programs that are testable and better reflect current software development practices. However, existing studies heavily rely on small hard-coded or circuit-level benchmarks, while available quantum programs are scattered across repositories without clear selection criteria, which limits fair comparison and systematic reproducibility. To this end, we present Qolumbina, a benchmark infrastructure for controlled QST experiments on scalable quantum programs. Qolumbina curates 40 programs from open-source repositories, turns them into test-ready subjects through systematic selection, refactoring, specifications, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces. We also propose QST-oriented criteria to characterize quantum programs along functionality, output behavior, development complexity, and quantum-specific execution complexity. Using these criteria, our empirical study shows that Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties and supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks. Through controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches, we demonstrate the feasibility of using Qolumbina for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, and highlight backend-dependent effects that can influence QST result interpretation.

AI.tldr: Qolumbina is a benchmark infrastructure for quantum software testing (QST) that curates 40 test-ready quantum programs from open-source repositories, introduces QST-oriented characterization criteria, and enables controlled, reproducible, and scalable empirical evaluation of QST approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing QST research relies on small, hard-coded, or circuit-level benchmarks, while available quantum programs are scattered across repositories without clear selection criteria. This limits fair comparison, systematic reproducibility, and scalability analysis in QST studies.
AI.method: The authors built Qolumbina by systematically curating 40 quantum programs from open-source repositories, applying selection criteria, refactoring them, adding specifications, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces. They also defined QST-oriented criteria to characterize programs along four dimensions: functionality, output behavior, development complexity, and quantum-specific execution complexity, and conducted controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches.
AI.result: Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties and supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks. Controlled experiments demonstrated its feasibility for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, and revealed backend-dependent effects that can influence QST result interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Qolumbina fills a critical gap in QST infrastructure, enabling rigorous, reproducible, and scalable empirical evaluations. It highlights the importance of backend-aware analysis in QST and provides a foundation for future benchmarking and comparison of quantum software testing techniques.

title: Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code at https://github.com/JoshuaSP/epistemic-goggles and generated documents, questions, and teacher rollouts at https://huggingface.co/datasets/joshuapenman/epistemic-goggles-artifacts
summary: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

AI.tldr: Language models finetuned on explicitly fictional documents still internalize their claims (Negation Neglect). Goggles introduces a gradient-level intervention during LoRA finetuning that imparts a chosen epistemic frame, enabling models to learn from content while recognizing it as fictional ~91% of the time, compared to ~9% without intervention. The frame persists under continued finetuning and generalizes to unseen documents.
AI.motivation: Standard finetuning on documents annotated as fictional fails to prevent models from absorbing the documents' claims—a phenomenon termed "Negation Neglect." Models correctly identify claims as fictional only ~9% of the time when trained with annotations. This motivates a need for a robust mechanism that allows models to learn from data while maintaining the correct epistemic stance toward it, particularly for training on known-misaligned or untrusted data without adopting its behaviors.
AI.method: Goggles is a learned module that intervenes on the gradient during LoRA-based supervised finetuning, rather than modifying the input data directly. It edits the gradients flowing to the LoRA parameters, encoding a specific epistemic frame (e.g., "this document is fictional" or "this is part of an AI safety evaluation"). A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to any new documents. The method operates entirely at the gradient level, leaving the training data unannotated.
AI.result: Models trained with Goggles on unannotated fictional documents correctly flag content as fictional ~91% of the time, compared to ~9% for models trained with explicit fictional annotations. Capability benchmarks (GPQA, TruthfulQA) match or exceed baselines. The imparted epistemic frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes toward the document claims, whereas prior annotation-based interventions revert. Goggles also supports alternative frames beyond fiction (e.g., treating documents as part of an AI safety evaluation).
AI.conclusion: Goggles demonstrates that gradient-level epistemic frame interventions can effectively decouple learning from belief, enabling language models to train on known-misaligned data without internalizing undesirable behaviors. This suggests a viable path toward safely leveraging untrusted or problematic training data.

title: PARTREP: Learning What to Repeat for Decoder-only LLMs
summary: While decoder-only LLMs excel at a vast array of natural language tasks, it suffers from an asymmetric information flow induced by causal attention: later tokens are richer in contextual grounding than earlier ones. A simple and effective remedy is prompt repetition -- just appending a second copy of prompt before generation can redistribute grounding across positions and improve reasoning performance. However, full repetition of the original prompt doubles the KV cache footprint and quadruples attention cost during prefill, making it impractical for long-context settings. We propose PartRep, a selective augmentation method that appends only the most informative tokens -- rather than the entire prompt. We use token-wise negative log-likelihood (NLL) as a selection signal, motivated by the hypothesis that less predictable tokens are less recoverable from surrounding context and therefore benefit more from late-position repetition. To avoid the heavy cost of a full forward pass for scoring, we train a lightweight gate that predicts high-NLL tokens from early-layer hidden states, enabling token selection during mid-prefill via early exit. Across eight benchmarks (including MMLU, GSM8K, and RULER) and three model families (Qwen2.5, Llama3.2, Gemma4), PartRep retains most of the gains of full repetition while using only 59.4\% of its KV cache and 79.0\% of its prefill FLOPs.

AI.tldr: PartRep selectively repeats only high-NLL (less predictable) tokens instead of the full prompt, using a lightweight early-exit gate to avoid full forward-pass scoring. It retains most reasoning gains of full repetition while reducing KV cache by ~40% and prefill FLOPs by ~21%.
AI.motivation: Decoder-only LLMs suffer from asymmetric information flow due to causal attention, where later tokens have richer context than earlier ones. Full prompt repetition mitigates this but doubles KV cache and quadruples prefill attention cost, making it impractical for long contexts. A more efficient selective approach is needed.
AI.method: PartRep uses token-wise negative log-likelihood (NLL) as a selection signal, based on the hypothesis that less predictable tokens benefit more from late-position repetition. To avoid the cost of a full forward pass for NLL scoring, a lightweight gate is trained to predict high-NLL tokens from early-layer hidden states, enabling token selection during mid-prefill via early exit. Only selected tokens are appended before generation.
AI.result: Across eight benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, RULER, etc.) and three model families (Qwen2.5, Llama3.2, Gemma4), PartRep retains most of the gains of full prompt repetition while using only 59.4% of the KV cache and 79.0% of the prefill FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: Selective token repetition guided by NLL-based importance, implemented efficiently via early-exit gating, is a practical and effective method for mitigating causal attention's asymmetric information flow in decoder-only LLMs without the prohibitive overhead of full prompt repetition.

title: Wind-Aware Reinforcement Learning Control of a Small Quadrotor Using Learned Onboard Wind Estimation in Simulated Atmospheric Turbulence
summary: Small multirotor aircraft are increasingly tasked with operations in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control. This work illustrates a two-stage learning pipeline that first estimates the local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and then exploits that estimate inside a reinforcement learning (RL) flight controller. The wind estimator, an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer, recovers the horizontal wind vector with a per-flight root-mean-square error of 0.40 m/s and a direction error of 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes, an accuracy near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent profiles with a skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. A proximal policy optimization controller receiving the frozen estimator's output reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind proportional-derivative baseline across mean winds of 4 m/s to 12 m/s, winning on 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation decomposes this improvement into a kinematic component, available without wind information, and a wind-perception component; the perception share rises with wind speed, from small in light winds toward roughly half the total benefit in strong winds, consistent with the quadratic scaling of aerodynamic drag. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds of 13 m/s to 15 m/s, where the baseline fails catastrophically.

AI.tldr: A two-stage learning pipeline combining a wind estimator (attention-augmented gated recurrent network) with an RL flight controller (PPO) reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% for small multirotors in turbulent boundary-layer winds, with the perception component contributing increasingly at higher wind speeds.
AI.motivation: Small multirotors operating in the atmospheric boundary layer face turbulent winds comparable to their airspeed, which degrade trajectory tracking and defeat conventional feedback control. Existing controllers lack explicit wind perception, limiting their robustness in these conditions.
AI.method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Kármán turbulence (with power-law shear and veer) estimates the horizontal wind vector from onboard kinematics and dynamics; (2) a frozen wind estimator feeds into a PPO-trained RL flight controller. A three-way ablation isolates kinematic vs. wind-perception contributions.
AI.result: The wind estimator achieves 0.40 m/s RMSE and 3.2° direction error on unseen wind regimes, with a skill score of 0.861 on vertical ascent profiles. The PPO controller reduces horizontal tracking error by 48% vs. a wind-blind PD baseline (4–12 m/s winds), winning 100% of episodes. The perception share of improvement grows with wind speed, reaching roughly half the total benefit in strong winds. The controller degrades gracefully at 13–15 m/s out-of-distribution winds where the baseline fails catastrophically.
AI.conclusion: Explicit wind perception via a learned estimator significantly enhances RL-based flight control for small multirotors in turbulent conditions. The wind-perception benefit scales with wind speed, consistent with quadratic drag scaling, and the combined system generalizes robustly beyond its training distribution.

title: Privacy-Preserving and Verifiable Approximate Distributed Coded Computing
summary: Distributed machine learning enables collaborative model training without centralizing data, but it also exposes learning processes to privacy leakage and malicious manipulation. Existing defenses typically address these threats in isolation and are often tailored to specific learning paradigms or model architectures, limiting their applicability in realistic deployments. In particular, federated learning and decentralized learning exhibit distinct adversarial surfaces that are rarely addressed within a unified framework. In this paper, we present a model-agnostic framework for adversary-resistant distributed learning that jointly addresses privacy preservation and malicious behavior across both federated and decentralized settings. Our approach combines paradigm-specific defense mechanisms with GPBACC, a privacy-enhancing coded computing technique applicable to arbitrary machine learning models. For federated learning, we integrate robust aggregation strategies to mitigate the impact of malicious participants, while for decentralized learning we employ approximate decode-and-compare and group testing techniques to enable lightweight verification and adversary isolation without relying on a trusted aggregator. Crucially, we evaluate the proposed framework through an explicit, attack-driven analysis. We implement representative privacy attacks and malicious behaviors, and empirically demonstrate that the combination of GPBACC with robust aggregation and verification mechanisms significantly reduces privacy leakage and improves resilience against active adversaries. These results suggest that privacy-enhancing coded computing, when combined with appropriate adversary-resistance strategies, provides a practical and deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a model-agnostic framework for adversary-resistant distributed learning that unifies privacy preservation and malicious behavior defense across both federated and decentralized settings. It combines GPBACC (a privacy-enhancing coded computing technique) with paradigm-specific defenses: robust aggregation for federated learning, and approximate decode-and-compare plus group testing for decentralized learning. Attack-driven empirical evaluation demonstrates significant reductions in privacy leakage and improved resilience against active adversaries.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses in distributed machine learning address privacy leakage and malicious manipulation in isolation, are tailored to specific paradigms or architectures, and fail to provide a unified framework covering both federated and decentralized learning. A comprehensive, model-agnostic solution that jointly handles both threats across settings is lacking.
AI.method: The authors propose a unified framework combining (1) GPBACC, a model-agnostic privacy-enhancing coded computing technique, with (2) paradigm-specific adversary-resistance mechanisms: robust aggregation strategies for federated learning, and approximate decode-and-compare with group testing for decentralized learning to enable lightweight verification and adversary isolation without a trusted aggregator. The framework is evaluated via an explicit attack-driven analysis implementing representative privacy attacks and malicious behaviors.
AI.result: Empirical results show that combining GPBACC with robust aggregation (federated) and verification mechanisms (decentralized) significantly reduces privacy leakage and improves resilience against active adversaries compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Privacy-enhancing coded computing (GPBACC), when paired with appropriate adversary-resistance strategies, provides a practical and deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning across both federated and decentralized paradigms.

title: Mitigating Package Hallucinations in Large Language Models via Model Editing
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in software engineering tasks, such as code generation, library recommendation, and dependency configuration. However, recent studies show that LLMs may suffer from package hallucination, where they generate non-existent or invalid package names. These hallucinations can be exploited in software supply chain attacks, as attackers may register malicious packages under hallucinated names. Therefore, mitigating package hallucination is important for improving the reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development. In this paper, we introduce BOUND, a lightweight localized model editing framework for mitigating package hallucinations in LLMs. BOUND formulates package hallucination mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem, where the boundary refers to the model's ability to distinguish valid packages from hallucinated package names under a given task context. It first locates modules related to package hallucination through a risk-aware localization strategy, and then edits these modules with lightweight LoRA adapters using a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated packages, and preserves locality behavior. Experimental results show that BOUND effectively reduces package hallucinations while preserving valid package recommendations. In the package recommendation task, BOUND reduces package-level hallucination rate (Package-HR) by 79.9% on edit prompts and by 65.4% on unseen prompts. The learned package-validity boundary further generalizes to other package-related tasks, reducing Package-HR by 12.8% in code generation and by 34.0% in pip install recommendation. These results show that BOUND refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs and improves the reliability of package-related outputs.

AI.tldr: BOUND is a lightweight model editing framework that mitigates LLM package hallucinations by locating risk-related modules and applying LoRA adapters with a boundary-aware objective, achieving up to 79.9% reduction in package hallucination rates while preserving valid recommendations.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit package hallucination—generating non-existent or invalid package names—which poses a security risk for software supply chain attacks (attackers can register malicious packages under hallucinated names). Existing solutions are insufficient, motivating a targeted, lightweight approach to improve reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development.
AI.method: BOUND formulates package hallucination mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem. It employs: (1) a risk-aware localization strategy to identify modules responsible for package hallucination, and (2) lightweight LoRA adapters trained with a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated packages, and preserves locality (i.e., does not degrade unrelated capabilities).
AI.result: BOUND reduces Package-HR by 79.9% on edit prompts and 65.4% on unseen prompts in package recommendation. It generalizes to other tasks: 12.8% reduction in code generation and 34.0% reduction in pip install recommendation. Valid package recommendations are preserved throughout.
AI.conclusion: BOUND effectively refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs, significantly reducing package hallucinations across multiple tasks while maintaining recommendation quality. The approach demonstrates that localized, boundary-aware model editing is a promising direction for improving LLM reliability in software engineering contexts.

title: COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows
summary: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

AI.tldr: COMFYCLAW is an agentic framework for ComfyUI workflow-based image generation that distills execution trajectories, errors, and VLM verifier feedback from previous runs into a progressively disclosed skill library, demonstrating that skill evolution improves agent reliability and performance on recurring visual workflow tasks.
AI.motivation: As agents are increasingly deployed for recurring, domain-specific workflows, they need mechanisms to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from prior runs. However, existing approaches lack structured memory for reusable skills in the context of workflow-based image generation.
AI.method: COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes stage-organized tools, auto-reverts invalid edits, and employs a region-level VLM verifier that translates visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework maintains a progressively disclosed skill library that distills trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from prior runs into reusable Agent Skills.
AI.result: Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotators also prefer COMFYCLAW over non-skill-evolution variants.
AI.conclusion: Skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction, suggesting that structured memory and feedback distillation are valuable for agentic systems in domain-specific, repeated tasks.

title: On the Limits of Steering Vectors for Preference-Aligned Generation
summary: Steering vectors have emerged as a promising approach to controlled text generation, offering interpretable, training-free mechanisms for shaping model outputs. However, their practical generality remains poorly understood. We study the limits of steering vector generalization along three dimensions: trait expressibility, task transfer, and multi-trait composition. Using the PLUME writing personalization benchmark, we extract steering vectors for a range of preferences and evaluate them on summarization and email-writing tasks across two open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct). We find that steering effectiveness varies substantially across traits. We further show that steering effectiveness can degrade when vectors extracted from positive and negative style examples are transferred to downstream writing personalization tasks. Finally, we compare common methods for composing multiple steering vectors and find that all methods suffer significant drops in trait expression as more vectors are added, with a tradeoff between coherence and expressibility that requires per-setting hyperparameter tuning. Taken together, our results suggest that steering vectors face meaningful limits as a general-purpose tool for preference alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates the generalization limits of steering vectors across three dimensions — trait expressibility, task transfer, and multi-trait composition — finding that steering effectiveness is trait-dependent, degrades under task transfer, and suffers significant expressibility loss when composing multiple vectors, suggesting steering vectors are not yet a general-purpose alignment solution.
AI.motivation: Steering vectors are increasingly popular for controlled text generation due to their interpretability and training-free nature, but their practical generality — whether they work reliably across different traits, tasks, and in combination — remains poorly understood and under-characterized.
AI.method: Using the PLUME writing personalization benchmark, the authors extract steering vectors for various style/trait preferences from positive and negative examples. They then evaluate these vectors on summarization and email-writing tasks using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, systematically testing trait expressibility (do different traits steer differently?), task transfer (do vectors from one task work on another?), and multi-trait composition (do combined vectors preserve expressibility?).
AI.result: Steering effectiveness varies substantially by trait (some traits steer well, others poorly). Task transfer degrades steering performance relative to in-domain use. When composing multiple steering vectors via common methods (e.g., addition, weighting), trait expression drops significantly as more vectors are added, revealing a coherence–expressibility tradeoff that requires per-setting hyperparameter tuning.
AI.conclusion: Steering vectors face meaningful practical limits as a general-purpose preference alignment tool; their reliability is constrained by trait specificity, poor cross-task generalization, and composability challenges that demand careful per-use-case calibration.

title: Certified World Models as Sensing Clocks: Drift-Aware Deadlines for Active Perception
summary: Certified world models estimate how long their predictions remain valid. We turn this validity horizon into an operational sensing clock: a rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. Starting from an audited equivariant world model, we derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals and show that deployable deadlines in learned world models must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes carry the deployed guarantee. On a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the resulting clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic bench where all schedulers share the exact model, isolating the scheduling rule), the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. We also report limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term. Thus the contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a certified sensing clock derived from world models with validity horizons, providing agents with formal deadlines for when to re-sense their environment. The key insight is that deployable deadlines require drift-awareness: naive on-manifold Lyapunov rates overestimate validity, while calibrated rollout-drift envelopes yield certificates that hold in deployment. The approach is validated on a frozen VN-JEPA model and a synthetic theorem-bed, showing reduced tail violations compared to expected-belief scheduling.
AI.motivation: Certified world models can estimate how long their predictions remain valid, but there is no operational mechanism to translate these validity horizons into actionable sensing schedules for embodied agents. The gap lies in deploying such certificates reliably: naive approaches overestimate how long an agent can safely "coast" without re-sensing, risking prediction failures in deployment.
AI.method: Starting from an audited equivariant world model, the authors derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals. They introduce drift-aware deployment: rather than relying solely on on-manifold Lyapunov rates (which overestimate coasting validity), they calibrate native rollout-drift envelopes that carry the deployed guarantee. The resulting sensing clock is evaluated on (1) a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model measuring interval-simultaneous certificate violation, and (2) a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (synthetic benchmark) that isolates scheduling rules by sharing the exact model across all schedulers.
AI.result: On the frozen VN-JEPA model, the sensing clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In the theorem-bed, the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. Limitations include: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term.
AI.conclusion: The primary contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and a drift-aware deployment method, not an empirical claim that spectral clocks dominate all non-spectral schedulers. The work establishes the theoretical and practical foundation for using certified world models to make formal guarantees about when agents must re-sense, with explicit acknowledgment of current empirical limitations.

title: Steerability via constraints: a substrate for scalable oversight of coding agents
comment: Accepted to the Deep Learning for Code Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Coding agents are capable; human oversight is the bottleneck. Unconstrained agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review increasingly costly. We argue that the same methods used for decades to manage large human engineering teams: access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling; transfer directly to coding agents, and are cheaper (in token) than recent agentic scaffolding. We sketch a start-to-end system on this principle, and report a controlled experiment in scalable oversight: a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase containing 11 inserted backdoors. Recall rises from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI), with substrate and tools contributing independently. We choose Python deliberately: substrate-level oversight gains are largest where the language gives the fewest guarantees by default; the principles extend to languages like Rust.

AI.tldr: Human oversight, not agent capability, is the bottleneck for coding agents. Applying traditional software engineering governance—access control, network policies, enforced conventions—to agent workflows is cheaper and more effective than complex agentic scaffolding. A controlled experiment shows that a constrained substrate plus a lightweight CLI tool improves backdoor detection recall from 54.5% to 90.9% in a Python codebase.
AI.motivation: Unconstrained coding agents introduce security vulnerabilities, degrade codebase scalability, and inflate human review costs. The authors argue that proven governance mechanisms from managing human engineering teams should be directly transferred to coding agents, providing scalable oversight more efficiently than recent agentic scaffolding approaches.
AI.method: The paper proposes a start-to-end system where coding agents operate under traditional software engineering constraints: access control, network policies, and strict coding conventions enforced by tooling. A controlled experiment tests scalable oversight: a small reviewer model (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase with 11 inserted backdoors, comparing unconstrained vs. constrained-substrate conditions with a lightweight ~200-line `docs` CLI tool.
AI.result: Backdoor detection recall improved from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus `docs` CLI). The substrate constraints and tooling contributed independently to the gain. Python was chosen deliberately because its minimal language-level guarantees maximize the benefit of substrate-level oversight.
AI.conclusion: Substrate-level constraints and lightweight tooling provide substantial, independent improvements in oversight effectiveness for coding agents. These gains are largest in permissive languages like Python but generalize to languages with stronger guarantees such as Rust. The approach is both cheaper (in token cost) and more effective than agentic scaffolding.

title: Prompt Coverage Adequacy
summary: In recent years, it has become increasingly evident that large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents raise the level of abstraction in software development by shifting the focus from writing precise procedures to expressing intents and goals. This paradigm shift introduces new challenges, particularly in how testing should be guided when prompts, rather than code, become primary development artifacts. To address this challenge, we propose Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel coverage criterion designed to support the testing of code generated from task descriptions. Prompt Coverage Adequacy serves as an analog to traditional code coverage, but operates at the level of prompts used in LLM and agent-based programming. Specifically, it measures how well a given test suite satisfies the requirements expressed in a prompt by leveraging the attention mechanisms of LLMs. We evaluate a simple instantiation of this criterion, based on attention boosting, across two datasets and multiple LLMs. Our results demonstrate that Prompt Coverage is associated with fault-detection effectiveness and can uncover over 30+% more faults than traditional code coverage when used to guide test generation. These findings suggest that Prompt Coverage Adequacy can serve as a foundation for developing testing metrics better suited to the emerging paradigm of LLM-driven software development, addressing the limitations of classical coverage criteria in this new context.

AI.tldr: Proposes Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel test coverage criterion for LLM-generated code that measures how well test suites satisfy prompt requirements using attention mechanisms. Experiments show it uncovers 30%+ more faults than traditional code coverage when guiding test generation.
AI.motivation: The shift from writing code to expressing intents via prompts in LLM-driven software development renders traditional code coverage criteria inadequate. When prompts become primary development artifacts, new testing approaches are needed to assess how well generated code satisfies the original task descriptions.
AI.method: Introduces Prompt Coverage Adequacy, analogous to traditional code coverage but operating at the prompt level. Leverages LLM attention mechanisms to measure how well a test suite satisfies prompt requirements. A simple instantiation using attention boosting is evaluated across two datasets and multiple LLMs.
AI.result: Prompt Coverage correlates with fault-detection effectiveness and uncovers over 30% more faults than traditional code coverage when used to guide test generation.
AI.conclusion: Prompt Coverage Adequacy provides a foundation for developing testing metrics suited to LLM-driven software development, addressing limitations of classical coverage criteria in this new paradigm.

title: Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models
summary: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Generic TB-Coverage, a coverage-aware expert pruning method for MoE language models that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2, C4) and preserves high-utility experts across multiple corpora via a fixed-budget coverage rule, outperforming existing methods especially under aggressive pruning budgets.
AI.motivation: MoE language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but existing pruning methods rely on a single aggregated importance score biased toward dominant calibration patterns, and they require downstream calibration data. The authors aim to develop a pruning method that works with only generic text corpora and avoids bias by preserving cross-corpus expert coverage.
AI.method: Generic TB-Coverage profiles per-expert utility separately on each generic corpus (WikiText2 and C4) rather than collapsing into a single score. It enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. The method is evaluated on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25%, 50%, and 75% retention budgets.
AI.result: The method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. Gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25% and 50% retain). Improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.
AI.conclusion: Preserving cross-corpus expert coverage serves as an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning, enabling strong pruning performance without requiring downstream calibration data.

title: PairCoder++: Pair Programming as a Universal Paradigm for Verified Code-Driven Multimodal and Structured-Artifact Generation
comment: Accepted by ACL 2026. Project Page: https://yisuanwang.github.io/PairCoder/
summary: Code is the medium through which large language models generate structured artifacts: charts, scientific figures, vector graphics, CAD models, 3D scenes, and hardware designs are all produced by writing programs. In this regime single pass inference is brittle, because the compiler, renderer, or simulator that decides whether the artifact exists is invisible to the model.
