We present PairCoder, which grounds review in the toolchain and realizes it as two agent pair programming: a Driver agent writes the program, a Navigator agent reviews it against verification evidence (diagnostics, execution results, and renderings of the current artifact beside the target), and the two switch roles when errors persist. Across 17 public benchmarks and seven models from three vendors, PairCoder improves essentially every benchmark whose artifact is verifiable, on full official metric suites rather than execution alone (for example, Blender scene executability 0.20 to 0.78; TikZ compile rate up 10 to 30 points on every model), at 2.9 to 9.2 times single model cost (about 7 times overall). The improvements concentrate where the toolchain provides an informative oracle and the baseline leaves headroom, and the method ties or mildly regresses where the oracle is weak; we frame pair programming as a reliable recipe for verified code driven generation.

AI.tldr: PairCoder introduces a two-agent pair programming framework (Driver writes code, Navigator reviews against toolchain verification evidence) that substantially improves LLM code generation for verifiable artifacts across 17 benchmarks, with gains concentrated where the toolchain provides informative feedback.
AI.motivation: Single-pass LLM inference for generating structured artifacts via code is brittle because the compiler, renderer, or simulator that validates the artifact is invisible to the model. The model cannot see diagnostics, execution results, or renderings to correct its errors.
AI.method: PairCoder employs two agents in a pair programming setup: a Driver agent writes the program, and a Navigator agent reviews it against verification evidence (diagnostics, execution results, renderings of current vs. target artifact). The two agents switch roles when errors persist, creating an iterative refinement loop grounded in toolchain feedback.
AI.result: Across 17 public benchmarks and 7 models from 3 vendors, PairCoder improves nearly every benchmark with verifiable artifacts. Key results: Blender scene executability from 0.20 to 0.78; TikZ compile rate improvements of 10–30 points on every model; overall cost is 2.9–9.2× single model cost (≈7× average). Improvements concentrate where the toolchain provides an informative oracle and baseline has headroom; the method ties or mildly regresses where the oracle is weak.
AI.conclusion: Pair programming with toolchain-grounded review is a reliable recipe for verified code-driven generation, with consistent gains across diverse domains whenever the verification oracle is sufficiently informative.

title: Evolutionary Feature Engineering for Structured Data
comment: 9 page main content, 41 pages in total
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization. We introduce Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE), a framework for using LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations for structured data. EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, allowing them to be inserted directly into existing machine learning pipelines. During evolution, candidate programs are refined using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback on validation set. We instantiate EFE in two settings. For time-series forecasting, EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations that improve off-the-shelf time-series foundation models. It reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) 3% or more when averaged across datasets and improvements are as much as 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset. Notably, these improvements occur with recent TSFMs such as Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add useful interpretable features and remove redundant ones, improving or matching existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods. We found EFE-Tab to be particularly effective on classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability. Overall, EFE demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data.

AI.tldr: EFE uses LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations (as Python programs) for structured data, improving both time-series forecasting accuracy (up to 19%) and tabular prediction interpretability.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as search operators in evolutionary optimization, but their potential for automatically discovering effective data preprocessing transformations (feature engineering) for structured data remains underexplored. The authors aim to leverage LLM-based evolution to generate interpretable, dataset-specific preprocessing pipelines that improve downstream ML performance.
AI.method: EFE represents preprocessing transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, directly insertable into ML pipelines. Evolution refines candidate programs using dataset context, summary statistics, and validation-set performance feedback. Two instantiations are introduced: EFE-Time (invertible, dataset-specific normalizations for time-series foundation models like Chronos-2) and EFE-Tab (compact feature programs for tabular prediction that add interpretable features and remove redundant ones).
AI.result: EFE-Time reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) by ≥3% on average across datasets, with up to 19% improvement on COVID-Deaths, even with modern TSFMs like Chronos-2. EFE-Tab improves or matches existing LLM-based feature engineering methods, and is particularly effective for classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based evolution can simultaneously improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically engineering features for structured data, demonstrating a promising direction for automated feature engineering.

title: HTTP REST API Structure Learning
summary: Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) are essential in software development, enabling web services, mobile apps, and microservices. However, their widespread use introduces significant security risks, highlighting the importance of API security. This paper presents HTTP REST API Learning (HRAL), a novel unsupervised anomaly detection approach that models the structure and behavior of API endpoints directly from network traffic, without relying on predefined rules or documentation. HRAL enables robust detection of malicious activity by understanding how APIs behave and flagging deviations as potential threats. We evaluate HRAL across varying levels of OpenAPI documentation detail and compare it with existing techniques. HRAL achieves strong performance, with an average recall of 82.07% and an F1-score of 87.24%, significantly outperforming alternatives when API documentation is limited. Moreover, our results approach the effectiveness of full API document definitions. When combined with signature-based rules such as the OWASP ModSecurity CRS, our system achieves 100% detection. These results highlight HRAL's effectiveness in real-world, partially documented API environments and its potential as a foundational layer for modern API security solutions.

AI.tldr: HRAL is an unsupervised anomaly detection system that learns API endpoint structure and behavior from network traffic, achieving 82.07% recall and 87.24% F1-score without needing API documentation, and reaching 100% detection when combined with OWASP ModSecurity CRS.
AI.motivation: APIs are critical yet vulnerable components in modern software. Existing security approaches often depend on predefined rules or complete API documentation (e.g., OpenAPI specs), which are frequently unavailable, outdated, or incomplete in real-world deployments. A documentation-independent anomaly detection method is needed.
AI.method: HRAL (HTTP REST API Learning) is an unsupervised anomaly detection approach that passively observes network traffic to automatically model the structure (endpoints, parameters, methods) and behavioral norms of REST APIs. It then flags deviations from learned models as potential threats, requiring no predefined rules or API documentation.
AI.result: HRAL achieved an average recall of 82.07% and F1-score of 87.24%, significantly outperforming alternatives when API documentation is limited. Its performance approaches that of systems using full API documentation. Combined with OWASP ModSecurity CRS signature-based rules, detection reached 100%.
AI.conclusion: HRAL demonstrates strong effectiveness in partially documented or undocumented API environments, making it a viable foundational layer for modern, real-world API security solutions, particularly when paired with complementary signature-based detection.

title: File-Level Copying Is an Implicit Dependency in Open Source
summary: File-level copying is a widespread but ungoverned form of software reuse. Copying files across repositories reduces supply-chain visibility: it removes the four observable signals a package manager provides for a declared dependency (provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance) with no mechanism to restore them. To characterize the scale and consequences of this unmanaged reuse, we present a mixed-method study of copying across the entire open-source ecosystem using World of Code (WoC). From a 0.1% commit sample, we extract 690,500 copy events and retain 3,912 rationale-bearing copy commits for intent labeling. We show that the 13 axial copy forms, spanning vendored dependencies, hardware/driver synchronization, scaffolding, UI assets, and direct source-code reuse, are unreliable proxies for developer intent: among rationale-bearing commits, hardware/driver copies are predominantly fork-maintenance work (78%), while dependency-vendoring copies more often signal upstream bypass (70%) than offline availability. These visibility gaps are form-specific: security and license risk concentrate in complementary copy forms. Copied sources are frequently stale (median 155 days; 38.5% over one year old) and seldom record a recoverable origin (4.3% documented), let alone a checkable version (2.0% versioned); even vendored copies record where they came from only 10% of the time. Security risk concentrates in vendored dependencies: 17,314 CVE-risk copy commits in the full-WoC graph, 88% in the dependency-vendoring form; 80% score CVSS >= 7.0 and upstream-fix adoption is only 47%-84%. License risk concentrates in direct source-code reuse: 41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% in the source-code form, with 39 verified high-star violations (kappa = 0.752). Both risks reach packaged software and are invisible to dependency scanners operating on declared metadata alone.

AI.tldr: A large-scale study of file-level copying across open-source repositories reveals widespread ungoverned reuse. Different copy forms (vendoring, source-code copying, hardware sync, etc.) carry distinct risks: vendored dependencies concentrate security vulnerabilities (CVE-risk), while direct source-code reuse concentrates license violations. Most copies are stale, lack recoverable provenance, and are invisible to package-manager-based dependency scanners.
AI.motivation: File-level copying across repositories is prevalent but unmanaged — it bypasses the provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance signals that declared package-manager dependencies provide. The scale, forms, and consequences of this practice are unknown, creating hidden supply-chain risks.
AI.method: A mixed-method study using the World of Code (WoC) infrastructure. From a 0.1% commit sample, 690,500 copy events were extracted. 3,912 rationale-bearing copy commits were manually labeled for developer intent. Copy forms were taxonomized into 13 axial categories. Full-WoC graph analysis assessed CVE-risk (CVSS scoring, upstream-fix adoption) and license-risk (pre-validation candidates, manual verification with inter-rater reliability kappa=0.752).
AI.result: The 13 axial copy forms are unreliable proxies for intent: hardware/driver copies are 78% fork-maintenance; dependency-vendoring copies signal upstream bypass (70%) over offline availability. Copied files are stale (median 155 days, 38.5% >1 year old); only 4.3% document origin, 2.0% record a checkable version; vendored copies record provenance only 10% of the time. Security risk: 17,314 CVE-risk copy commits, 88% in vendored dependencies, 80% score CVSS ≥7.0, upstream-fix adoption only 47–84%. License risk: 41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% in source-code form, 39 verified high-star violations. Both risks propagate to packaged software and evade metadata-based scanners.
AI.conclusion: File-level copying represents a significant, form-specific supply-chain visibility gap. Current dependency scanners operating solely on declared metadata miss both security vulnerabilities (concentrated in vendoring) and license violations (concentrated in direct source reuse). The authors call for tooling that can detect and attribute copied code across the ecosystem.

title: Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization
summary: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett–Luce objective for listwise preference optimization that handles ranking-label uncertainty. The robust loss decomposes into a nominal PL loss plus a worst-case correction computable in O(K log K), offering strong offline (convex, O(ε⁻²) sample complexity) and online (weakly convex, Õ(ε⁻²) stationarity) guarantees, with experiments showing preserved clean-label performance and improved robustness under noise.
AI.motivation: Existing robust preference optimization focuses on pairwise supervision with robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. However, in listwise settings, observed rankings over candidate lists can be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. This ranking-label uncertainty is not addressed by current methods, motivating a principled robust listwise preference optimization framework.
AI.method: The authors propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett–Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition: nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction. The worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from K! enumeration to O(K log K). For offline fixed-list settings, projected stochastic subgradient is applied to the convex objective. For online policy-induced settings, weak convexity is established and Moreau-envelope stationarity is analyzed.
AI.result: Theoretically: (1) offline setting achieves global ε-suboptimality with O(ε⁻²) sample complexity; (2) online setting achieves Õ(ε⁻²) Moreau-envelope stationarity. Empirically: the robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise in offline LLM alignment; in online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pointwise TV-robust Plackett–Luce objective provides a tractable and theoretically grounded framework for listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty, with strong empirical performance in both offline and online LLM alignment settings.

title: The Grammar Does the Work: Functional vs. Lexical Dependency Length Minimization Across Universal Dependencies
summary: Dependency length minimization (DLM) is a well-documented processing universal, but previous studies report a single mean dependency distance (MDD) per language, obscuring variation across syntactic relation types. We analyze 122 languages in UD and SUD (version 2.17), showing that DLM operates on two distinct levels. Grammar-driven optimization targets functional dependencies (det, case, aux), which are universally short (mean 1.71, $σ$ = 0.33) and invariant across typologically diverse languages. Processing-driven optimization operates on lexical dependencies (nsubj, obj, obl), which are longer (mean 2.87), highly variable ($σ$ = 0.63), and constrained by word-order typology. This asymmetry holds in SUD despite reversed head direction (r = 0.92). We conclude that ''the grammar does the work'' of minimization by scaffolding sentences with local functional attachments, leaving processing pressures to determine the ordering of lexical heads.

AI.tldr: Dependency length minimization operates on two distinct levels: grammar-driven optimization yields universally short functional dependencies, while processing-driven optimization shapes longer, more variable lexical dependencies constrained by word-order typology.
AI.motivation: Prior DLM research collapses all dependency types into a single mean dependency distance per language, obscuring systematic variation across syntactic relation types. The authors aim to disentangle these distinct patterns.
AI.method: Analysis of 122 languages from Universal Dependencies (UD) and Surface-Syntactic Universal Dependencies (SUD) v2.17, comparing mean dependency distances across functional (det, case, aux) vs. lexical (nsubj, obj, obl) relation types, and assessing cross-linguistic variability and correlations with word-order typology.
AI.result: Functional dependencies are universally short (mean 1.71, σ = 0.33) and invariant across languages. Lexical dependencies are longer (mean 2.87), highly variable (σ = 0.63), and constrained by word-order typology. This asymmetry replicates in SUD despite reversed head direction (r = 0.92).
AI.conclusion: Grammar handles minimization by scaffolding sentences with local functional attachments, while processing pressures govern the ordering of lexical heads — a "grammar does the work" principle.

title: X-LogSMask: Expand Transformer for Graph-Structured Data
summary: Transformers have become general-purpose architectures, but their all-to-all self-attention is poorly matched to graph data, whose interactions are sparse, structured and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch through structural encodings, hybrid message-passing modules or learned attention constraints, often introducing additional complexity and limited interpretability. Here we introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects symmetrically normalized graph topology directly into attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. By assigning different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different attention heads, X-LogSMask gives each head a defined structural radius and supports multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. We further show that a standard Transformer encoder can be interpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention. Across 20 node-, edge- and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers equipped with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration. These results show that simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without changing the Transformer architecture. The code is available at https://github.com/LiLeyan-0120/X-LogSMask.

AI.tldr: X-LogSMask introduces an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects graph topology directly into Transformer attention logits, enabling topology-aware, multi-scale graph learning without modifying the Transformer architecture, achieving SOTA on 13 of 20 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers rely on all-to-all self-attention, which is poorly suited to graph data characterized by sparse, structured, and multi-scale interactions. Existing Graph Transformers attempt to address this via structural encodings, hybrid message-passing, or learned attention constraints, but these add complexity and reduce interpretability. A simpler, more principled way to infuse graph topology into self-attention is needed.
AI.method: X-LogSMask applies a logarithmic transformation of symmetrically normalized graph topology (powers of the normalized adjacency matrix) as an additive mask to attention logits before softmax. Different attention heads receive different powers of the adjacency matrix, assigning each head a distinct structural radius for multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. The logarithmic transform acts as a topology-aware gating signal: it suppresses unsupported (non-adjacent) node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention among structurally connected nodes. The method is motivated by recasting a standard Transformer encoder as one-step message passing on a complete graph, with X-LogSMask serving as a topology-constrained alternative.
AI.result: Across 20 node-level, edge-level, and graph-level benchmarks, X-LogSMask-equipped Transformers achieved state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remained competitive even in a lightweight single-layer configuration.
AI.conclusion: Simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without altering the core Transformer architecture. X-LogSMask demonstrates that directly injecting symmetrically normalized graph topology into attention logits is both performant and interpretable.

title: Coding Agents Are Guessing: Measuring Action-Boundary Violations in Underspecified DevOps Instructions
summary:
LLM coding agents are increasingly deployed to act autonomously on real production infrastructure. They execute shell commands, modify repositories, and call operational APIs. However, completing a task is not sufficient for safety. A wrong action can cause severe consequences. Existing agent benchmarks largely emphasize task completion, leaving open how agents behave under benign but underspecified instructions.
  We present UnderSpecBench, a benchmark for measuring action-boundary violations in coding agents (i.e., Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode) on DevOps tasks. UnderSpecBench includes 69 task families grounded in documented incidents, CVEs, or tool behavior and organized across four DevOps capability domains and nine operational control surfaces. To isolate underspecification from task difficulty, each task keeps the same environment and ground-truth safe action while varying the instruction along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius. The resulting 2,208 prompt variants are evaluated with deterministic, side-effect-based oracles that separate Safe Success, Wrong Target, and OverScope outcomes; non-action runs are further classified as clarification, refusal, or deferment.
  Across five agent x model configurations using OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex, the evaluation results show that underspecification does not mainly make agents fail; it makes them guess. 55.8-67.8% of runs violate at least one boundary. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity. These findings show that completion-centric evaluation can overstate safe autonomy and motivate mitigations at the model, harness, and system layer.

AI.tldr: UnderSpecBench is a benchmark that evaluates how LLM coding agents behave under underspecified DevOps instructions. Rather than focusing on task completion, it measures action-boundary violations — revealing that agents "guess" dangerously: 55.8–67.8% of runs violate at least one safety boundary, with target ambiguity being the primary driver of unsafe actions.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents are increasingly deployed on real production infrastructure where wrong actions can cause severe consequences. Current benchmarks emphasize task completion but fail to assess safety under benign yet underspecified instructions. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically measuring action-boundary violations when instructions lack clarity on intent, target, or blast radius.
AI.method: The authors constructed UnderSpecBench with 69 task families grounded in real documented incidents, CVEs, and tool behaviors, spanning four DevOps capability domains and nine operational control surfaces. Each task holds the environment and ground-truth safe action constant while varying instruction specificity along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius — yielding 2,208 prompt variants. Evaluation uses deterministic, side-effect-based oracles that classify outcomes into Safe Success, Wrong Target, OverScope, and (for non-action runs) clarification, refusal, or deferment. Five agent × model configurations (OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex) were tested.
AI.result: Underspecification does not primarily cause agents to fail — it causes them to guess. Across configurations, 55.8–67.8% of runs violated at least one boundary. Target underspecification sharply degraded action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduced action propensity. The findings indicate that completion-centric evaluation significantly overstates safe autonomy.
AI.conclusion: Completion-focused benchmarks overstate the safe autonomy of LLM coding agents. The high rate of boundary violations under underspecification motivates layered mitigations at the model, harness, and system levels to prevent unsafe guessing behavior in production deployments.

title: DRL-CLBA: A Clean Label Backdoor Attack for Speech Classification via DDPG Reinforcement Learning
summary: Deep learning models for speech classification are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious triggers cause misclassification at inference time. While sample-specific attacks can bypass many defenses, they often rely on poisoned label attack, making them detectable via manual data defense. In this paper, we propose DRL-CLBA, a novel clean label backdoor attack for speech classification that leverages Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning. We also utilize deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchors. The proposed reinforcement learning framework effectively optimizes target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's deep latent space, enabling label-migration-free poisoning of target samples. Experimental results across three datasets and four different DNNs demonstrate that DRL-CLBA achieves a high attack success rate, effectively bypassing some backdoor defenses. The attack demonstrates strong resistance against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses, exposing critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems.

AI.tldr: DRL-CLBA is a clean-label backdoor attack for speech classification that uses DDPG reinforcement learning and deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers, achieving high attack success while bypassing multiple defenses.
AI.motivation: Existing backdoor attacks on speech classification either rely on poisoned labels (making them detectable via manual inspection) or lack stealth. The authors aim to develop a clean-label backdoor attack where target samples retain their original labels, eliminating the need for label tampering and evading manual data defenses, thus exposing a more severe vulnerability in speech-controlled systems.
AI.method: DRL-CLBA combines three components: (1) Deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchor points; (2) a DDPG-based reinforcement learning agent that optimizes target samples toward these trigger-bearing anchors in the model's deep latent space; (3) clean-label poisoning where target samples preserve their original labels, avoiding label migration. The RL agent learns to craft poisoned samples that cluster near anchor representations while remaining perceptually and semantically faithful to their original class.
AI.result: Experiments on three datasets and four DNN architectures show DRL-CLBA achieves high attack success rates. The attack effectively bypasses defenses including fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature detection, demonstrating strong resistance against multiple countermeasures.
AI.conclusion: Clean-label backdoor attacks via reinforcement learning and steganographic trigger embedding represent a critical and hard-to-detect threat to speech classification systems. The success against multiple defenses highlights significant vulnerabilities in speech-controlled applications.

title: TUDUM: A Turkish-Thinking Reasoning Pipeline for Qwen3.5-27B
summary: This paper presents TUDUM (Türkçe Düşünen Üretken Model), a project pipeline for adapting a Qwen-family 27B thinking model toward Turkish reasoning. The central problem is not only to answer Turkish prompts in Turkish, but to make the explicit reasoning trace itself Turkish. A thinking model may translate a Turkish prompt into an English-centered internal or visible scratchpad, solve the problem mostly in English, and only localize the final answer. TUDUM instead treats the generated <think>...</think> block as a trainable behavior. The pipeline starts from the project base checkpoint unsloth/Qwen3.5-27B, applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples using LoRA adapters, and then applies GRPO-family reinforcement learning on a proxy-filtered Turkish mathematics environment. The results are mixed. SFT made the model shorter and more consistently Turkish in its reasoning behavior, with large reductions in average response length and thinking exhaustion, but reduced benchmark accuracy. RL recovered some mathematical performance, especially AIME24 at the best early checkpoint, yet did not uniformly improve all benchmarks and did not exceed the base model on the reported Macro-6 average. The contribution is therefore best framed as a technically honest Turkish-thinking reasoning pipeline and evaluation, not as a claim of state-of-the-art Turkish reasoning. The released step-50 model is publicly available.

AI.tldr: TUDUM adapts a Qwen-family 27B model to perform explicit reasoning in Turkish (not just final answers) via SFT on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples followed by GRPO reinforcement learning. Results show consistent Turkish reasoning behavior but with reduced benchmark accuracy; RL partially recovers math performance but does not surpass the base model.
AI.motivation: Existing thinking models, even when prompted in Turkish, tend to translate internally to English for the reasoning trace and only localize the final answer. The authors aim to make the entire reasoning process — the explicit <think> block — genuinely Turkish, treating it as a trainable behavior rather than a post-hoc localization step.
AI.method: The pipeline uses unsloth/Qwen3.5-27B as the base checkpoint. First, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is applied on 15,991 Turkish reasoning examples using LoRA adapters. Then, GRPO-family reinforcement learning is conducted on a proxy-filtered Turkish mathematics environment to refine reasoning quality.
AI.result: SFT successfully produced shorter, more consistently Turkish reasoning traces with reduced response length and thinking exhaustion, but at the cost of benchmark accuracy. RL partially recovered mathematical performance (notably AIME24 at the best early checkpoint) but did not uniformly improve all benchmarks and did not exceed the base model's Macro-6 average.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is framed as a technically honest pipeline and evaluation for Turkish-native reasoning rather than a state-of-the-art claim. The step-50 checkpoint is publicly released.

title: Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the geometric properties of chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories in LLM hidden state space, introducing spectral and kinematic measures that predict task difficulty (0.93 AUC) and solution correctness from only the first 20% of generated tokens.
AI.motivation: While extensive research focuses on the content and length of CoT reasoning chains, their internal geometric structure in hidden state space remains unexplored. Understanding this geometry could reveal fundamental properties about reasoning complexity and enable early prediction of solution correctness.
AI.method: The authors formalize CoT reasoning chains as discrete curves in ℝ^d and characterize them using: (1) spectral analysis — introducing effective dimension d_ρ derived from the eigenvalue spectrum of the trajectory covariance matrix, where flatter spectra indicate harder tasks; (2) kinematic features — mean position, positional dispersion, initial/current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion. These are evaluated on MATH500 mathematical reasoning problems.
AI.result: The effective dimension d_ρ achieves 0.93 AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems. Kinematic features can predict solution correctness using only the first 20% of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, demonstrating that trajectory shape is a robust indicator of both task hardness and solution quality.
AI.conclusion: The geometry of internal CoT trajectories provides a principled window into reasoning processes. Flatter eigenvalue spectra (higher effective dimension) characterize harder tasks, and early-trajectory kinematic features enable correctness prediction, potentially informing future early-stopping strategies in LLM inference.

title: Guiding Human Validation of LLM-Generated Code via Verifiable Literate Programming
summary:
Vibe coding democratizes software development by allowing users to generate code via natural-language (NL) interaction with large language models (LLMs). However, the code is reliable only when it faithfully implements the user's intent, which is difficult and labor-intensive for users to validate. Existing validation methods either rely on LLM-assisted automated testing, which suffers from prompt ambiguity and model fallibility, or involve users only in partial software artifacts such as prompts and test cases, which may overlook corner cases and program details. Motivated by a bug study of LLM-generated code, we find that detailed human feedback is essential, as failures often stem from underspecified requirements or subtle semantic deviations.
  This paper presents verifiable literate programming (VLP), a human-in-the-loop framework designed to make the review/validation process of LLM-generated code accessible to users at all programming levels. At its core, VLP proposes unambiguous NL-based documentation as a readable intermediate layer between prompts and code. The documentation demonstrates concrete program semantics and enables users to provide feedback on potential intent-code mismatches. It supports human-involved, end-to-end repair and validation via three techniques: (i) an NL-style literate language with unambiguous syntax and mostly deterministic code-to-documentation translation, (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection that uses trace links between prompts and documentation to focus users' review effort on suspicious documentation lines, and (iii) a verification module that leverages user-validated documentation to derive API-usage checks and formal properties, which are then verified against the generated code using model checking. Our evaluation shows that VLP improves code pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5% with reasonable user effort.

AI.tldr: VLP introduces a human-in-the-loop framework that uses unambiguous natural-language documentation as an intermediate layer between prompts and code, enabling users at all skill levels to validate LLM-generated code through focused review, mismatch detection, and formal verification, boosting pass@1 from 28.7–73.2% to 65.4–93.5%.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated code from vibe coding often fails due to underspecified requirements and subtle semantic deviations. Existing validation methods (LLM-assisted testing or partial user involvement in prompts/test cases) are unreliable or miss corner cases. A bug study revealed that detailed human feedback is essential for catching intent-code mismatches, motivating a more accessible and thorough review framework.
AI.method: VLP comprises three techniques: (i) a literate language with unambiguous syntax and mostly deterministic code-to-documentation translation; (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection using trace links between prompts and documentation to highlight suspicious lines for user review; and (iii) a verification module that derives API-usage checks and formal properties from user-validated documentation, verified against code via model checking.
AI.result: VLP improved code pass@1 from a baseline range of 28.7%–73.2% to 65.4%–93.5% with reasonable user effort.
AI.conclusion: VLP demonstrates that interposing unambiguous, human-readable documentation between natural-language prompts and generated code—combined with focused mismatch detection and formal verification—enables effective, accessible human-in-the-loop validation of LLM-generated code.

title: Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem
summary: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

AI.tldr: A case study on reformalization — translating formal proofs between proof assistants — using the Jordan Curve Theorem as a test case across three pairs: Mizar→Lean, HOL Light→Lean, and HOL Light→Agda, analyzing pipeline design choices.
AI.motivation: To investigate the practical challenges and design decisions involved in reformalization (porting formal proofs between different proof assistants), extending the concept of autoformalization beyond natural language inputs.
AI.method: The authors conduct a case study by reformalizing the Jordan Curve Theorem across three distinct proof assistant pairs: (1) Mizar to Lean, (2) HOL Light to Lean, and (3) HOL Light to Agda. They analyze the resulting pipelines and compare outcomes.
AI.result: Three successful reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem were completed. The analysis identifies key pipeline design choices that significantly affect practical reformalization outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Reformalization between proof assistants is feasible, and pipeline design choices — such as how to handle differences in type theory, automation, and library mappings — are critical for practical success.

title: AIriskEval-edu: New Dataset for Risk Assessment in AI-mediated K-12 Educational Explanations
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the IEEE International Carnahan Conference on Security Technology (ICCST 2026), October 14, 2026
summary: This work introduces AIriskEval-edu-db2, a new dataset designed to train and evaluate auditors based on LLMs for an explainable pedagogical risk assessment in instructional content for grades K-12. The dataset comprises 1,639 explanations from 170 curated ScienceQA questions, covering science, language arts, and social sciences. For each question, the dataset includes an explanation written by a human teacher alongside 11 explanations generated by LLM-simulated teacher profiles associated with distinct pedagogical risks. We propose a comprehensive risk rubric aligned with established educational standards that covers five complementary dimensions: factual precision, depth and completeness, focus and relevance, student-level appropriateness, and ideological bias. A key contribution is the addition of 785 explanations with structured explainability annotations, including risk localization and risk description. The annotations are produced through a semi-automatic process with expert teacher validation. Finally, we present validation experiments comparing state-of-the-art proprietary models with a lightweight local Llama 3.1 8B model in both the pedagogical risk detection and the explainability assessment. These experiments evaluate whether supervised fine-tuning on AIriskEval-edu-db2 enables a locally deployable model to approach or outperform stronger frontier models while preserving privacy in educational auditing and assessment tasks.

AI.tldr: AIriskEval-edu-db2 is a dataset of 1,639 explanations for K-12 instructional content, featuring five-dimensional pedagogical risk assessment with structured explainability annotations. Fine-tuning a Llama 3.1 8B model on this dataset enables locally deployable, privacy-preserving auditing that rivals frontier proprietary models.
AI.motivation: The need for automated, explainable auditing of LLM-generated educational content to detect pedagogical risks — such as factual errors, age-inappropriateness, or ideological bias — while preserving student/teacher data privacy through locally deployable models rather than cloud-based proprietary systems.
AI.method: The authors curate 170 ScienceQA questions across three subjects, pairing each with one human-written explanation and 11 LLM-generated explanations simulating distinct teacher risk profiles. They define a five-dimension risk rubric (factual precision, depth/completeness, focus/relevance, student-level appropriateness, ideological bias). A semi-automatic pipeline with expert teacher validation produces 785 explanations annotated with risk localization and descriptions. Validation experiments compare proprietary frontier models against a supervised fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B on both risk detection and explainability tasks.
AI.result: Supervised fine-tuning on AIriskEval-edu-db2 enables the lightweight Llama 3.1 8B model to approach or outperform stronger proprietary models in pedagogical risk detection and explainability assessment, while maintaining the privacy benefits of local deployment.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and fine-tuning approach demonstrate that small, locally deployable models can serve as effective, privacy-preserving pedagogical risk auditors for K-12 educational content, offering a viable alternative to proprietary cloud-based LLMs in sensitive educational settings.

title: BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge? We introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. In controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), we measure coupling in text and image communication. Key findings: (1) text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls; (2) image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect; (3) group size moderates coupling direction -- K=5 produces homogenization while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, CI pending), suggesting a directional shift toward diversification; (4) cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) coupling is stateless -- driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence. These results establish LLM agent coupling as real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

AI.tldr: Inter-agent communication among LLMs causes representational homogenization, as measured by the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF). Text communication significantly homogenizes outputs (CAF=0.803), image communication shows similar effects, group size moderates direction (K=5 homogenizes, K=3 diversifies), and coupling is prompt-context-driven rather than cumulative.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed as communicating agents in multi-agent systems, it is critical to understand whether inter-agent communication causes their outputs to converge toward homogeneity, potentially reducing diversity, amplifying biases, or creating echo chambers. Prior work lacks systematic measurement of this coupling phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol that measures representational coupling using the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where JSD is Jensen-Shannon Divergence. CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. Controlled experiments use GPT-4o (N=30, ~9,900 API calls) across text and image modalities, with no-communication ablation, prompt-perturbation controls, varying group sizes (K=3 and K=5), cross-model replication (including DeepSeek), and analysis of stateful vs. stateless coupling dynamics.
AI.result: Five key findings: (1) Text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803, 95% CI [0.740, 0.873], Cohen's d=1.30, p<0.001). (2) Image communication homogenizes similarly (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]). (3) Group size moderates coupling direction: K=5 produces homogenization, while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, suggesting diversification). (4) Cross-model replication shows extreme CAF variation (0.034–0.803), with DeepSeek displaying dominant format artifacts. (5) Coupling is stateless — driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent coupling is real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level. These findings have direct implications for multi-agent system design, suggesting that communication protocols, group size, and prompt engineering can be tuned to either promote or mitigate representational convergence in deployed LLM agent systems.

title: Developers' Experience with Generative AI Beyond Productivity Assessment -- Insights from an Empirical Mixed-Methods Field Study
summary: With the growing adoption of AI-powered coding assistants, organizations and developers are increasingly seeking to optimize their interaction with these tools. Prior research has largely focused on output quality and productivity gains, with limited attention paid to developers' well-being and interaction experiences. This paper presents a developer-centered empirical mixed-methods study to investigate how professional developers engage with Generative AI (GenAI) in their natural work environment. Controlled data collection sessions are combined with natural work periods. Results show that developers are generally satisfied with GenAI, particularly for monotonous, repetitive, and structured tasks, and report perceived efficiency and productivity gains. Copilot interaction type preferences differ by task type and complexity: While both in-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve task efficiency and reduce perceived workload, combining these interaction types within a single task diminishes benefits. We propose a rule-of-thumb for selecting an interaction type based on task characteristics. During development-heavy tasks, results indicate that perceived cognitive load arises from AI interaction, while perceived productivity depends on AI output quality. Participation in this study positively influenced developers' awareness and intentional use of GenAI tools. These findings demonstrate the value of real-world, mixed-methods study designs to understand GenAI tools and developers' experiences with them.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods study of professional developers using GenAI coding assistants in natural work settings reveals that satisfaction is highest for repetitive/structured tasks. While both in-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve efficiency and reduce workload, combining them in a single task diminishes benefits. A rule-of-thumb for interaction type selection based on task characteristics is proposed.
AI.motivation: Prior research on AI-powered coding assistants has prioritized output quality and productivity metrics, neglecting developers' well-being and the qualitative nature of their interaction experiences. This study addresses that gap by centering on how professional developers actually experience and engage with GenAI tools in their natural work environments.
AI.method: A developer-centered empirical mixed-methods study combining controlled data collection sessions with natural work periods, examining professional developers' engagement with GenAI coding assistants across different task types, complexities, and interaction modalities (in-code suggestions vs. chat-based prompting vs. their combination).
AI.result: (1) Developers are generally satisfied with GenAI, especially for monotonous, repetitive, and structured tasks, reporting perceived efficiency and productivity gains. (2) Both in-code suggestions and chat-based prompting independently improve task efficiency and reduce perceived workload, but combining them within a single task diminishes benefits. (3) Perceived cognitive load during development-heavy tasks stems from AI interaction itself, while perceived productivity depends on AI output quality. (4) Study participation positively influenced developers' awareness and intentional use of GenAI tools.
AI.conclusion: Real-world, mixed-methods study designs are valuable for understanding GenAI tools and developer experiences. The findings yield a practical rule-of-thumb for matching interaction types to task characteristics, and highlight that interaction modality choices significantly impact cognitive load and productivity perceptions.

title: Meta-Benchmarks for Financial-Services LLM Evaluation
summary: Public LLM leaderboards optimise for global average performance and do not capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work: a model that leads on MMLU-Pro may underperform on document-grounded compliance reasoning, and a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly. We present a meta-benchmarking framework that organises 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates those into 38 BIAN banking business domains spanning sales, operations, risk, and support work. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination x coverage x recency), computed over a rolling model window, rewards benchmarks that still separate the best models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, suppressing saturated legacy tests automatically. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalisation; business-domain scores are weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos. We demonstrate the framework on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026, and describe the methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations with the aim of making the approach reproducible for institutions facing similar selection and governance challenges.

AI.tldr: A meta-benchmarking framework that maps 452 public benchmarks to 41 work activities and 38 banking business domains, using a multiplicative weighting scheme and pairwise Elo tournament to produce cross-benchmark-comparable scores for LLM selection in financial services, demonstrated on 288 models as of June 2026.
AI.motivation: Existing public LLM leaderboards optimize for global average performance and fail to capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work — a model excelling on general benchmarks like MMLU-Pro may underperform on domain-specific tasks such as document-grounded compliance reasoning, while coding leaders may fare poorly on multi-turn customer interactions. There is a need for a principled, reproducible framework to map benchmark results onto concrete banking work activities for model selection and governance.
AI.method: The authors construct a meta-benchmarking framework that (1) organizes 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities, then aggregates these into 38 BIAN banking business domains (sales, operations, risk, support); (2) applies a multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination × coverage × recency) computed over a rolling model window to reward benchmarks that still separate top models, are widely reported, and remain actively used while automatically suppressing saturated legacy tests; and (3) scales the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament with these weights, yielding cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalization. Business-domain scores are derived as weighted averages of constituent work-activity Elos.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models from 25 organizations as of June 2026. The multiplicative weighting scheme successfully suppresses saturated benchmarks and the Elo-based aggregation produces work-activity and business-domain scores that are comparable across benchmarks without requiring raw score normalization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed meta-benchmarking framework provides a reproducible, governance-ready methodology for financial institutions to evaluate LLMs against domain-specific work activities rather than relying on global leaderboard rankings. The approach is openly described — including taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations — to enable adoption by other institutions facing similar model selection and governance challenges.

title: NAVER LABS Europe Submission to the Instruction-following 2026 Short Track
summary: In this paper, we describe NAVER LABS Europe's submission to the instruction-following speech processing short track at IWSLT 2026. We participate again in the constrained setting, developing systems capable of jointly performing ASR, ST, and SQA from English speech into Chinese, Italian, and German. Building on our previous submission, ranked first in last year's short track, we update our multi-stage training pipeline by replacing the speech projector with SpeechMapper, a method for learning a speech-to-LLM embedding projector using only ASR data. In addition, we introduce a synthetic SQA dataset, fakACL, composed of artificially generated scientific presentations. This dataset is built by prompting the LLM backbone, segmenting the generated talks, and synthesizing speech with SeamlessM4T-large-v2. The combination of an improved speech projection mechanism and domain-specific synthetic data allows our model to outperform last year's best short-track system, while being considerably more compact and relying on a weaker LLM backbone. This year's results place our system tied for first place in the overall short track ranking.

AI.tldr: NAVER LABS Europe presents their IWSLT 2026 submission for instruction-following speech processing, featuring SpeechMapper (a speech-to-LLM projector trained solely on ASR data) and a synthetic SQA dataset called fakACL. Their compact system ties for first place in the short track, outperforming last year's winner.
AI.motivation: To improve upon their previous year's first-place system for joint ASR, ST, and SQA tasks under constrained settings, making the model more compact while boosting performance through better speech-LLM integration and domain-specific synthetic data.
AI.method: A multi-stage training pipeline with two key innovations: (1) SpeechMapper — a speech-to-LLM embedding projector learned using only ASR data, replacing the previous speech projector; (2) fakACL — a synthetic SQA dataset of artificial scientific presentations generated by prompting the LLM backbone, segmenting talks, and synthesizing speech via SeamlessM4T-large-v2.
AI.result: The combined approach outperforms last year's best short-track system while using a more compact architecture and a weaker LLM backbone. The system ties for first place in the overall IWSLT 2026 short track ranking.
AI.conclusion: SpeechMapper enables effective speech-to-LLM projection using only ASR supervision, and domain-specific synthetic data (fakACL) provides a significant performance boost, together yielding a state-of-the-art compact system for multilingual instruction-following speech tasks.

title: SINA: A Fully Automated Circuit Schematic Image to Netlist Generator Using Artificial Intelligence
summary: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have revolutionized Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) for circuit design tasks. However, their application to analog and mixed-signal domains remains limited by the lack of machine-readable representations of existing circuit design knowledge. Circuit schematic images found in research manuscripts, textbooks, and websites constitute a vast repository of validated designs; however, these visual representations cannot be directly processed by EDA tools. Converting them into machine-readable netlists is essential for enabling simulation, verification, and building comprehensive databases for AI-based models. Current conversion methods lack generalization across both Integrated Circuit (IC) and Printed Circuit Board (PCB) level schematics. Moreover, they struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish between connected junctions and crossing wires. In this paper, we propose SINA, an open-source circuit schematic image-to-netlist generator. SINA is a fully automated pipeline that integrates deep learning for robust component detection, connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for component reference designator extraction, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. SINA handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics and incorporates dedicated crossing-wires detection to differentiate wire intersections from connections. We validate the correctness of the generated netlists using graph isomorphism techniques. Our experiments demonstrate an overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: SINA is an open-source, fully automated pipeline that converts circuit schematic images into machine-readable netlists by integrating deep learning-based component detection, connected-component labeling for connectivity inference, OCR for reference designators, and a VLM for designator assignment, achieving 96.67% netlist accuracy (2.72× improvement over prior work) while handling both IC- and PCB-level schematics with explicit crossing-wire detection.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-driven EDA tools cannot process schematic images directly, and current image-to-netlist methods lack generalization across IC and PCB domains, struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish junctions from wire crossings. A vast corpus of validated analog/mixed-signal designs exists only as images in literature, motivating an automated, generalizable converter.
AI.method: SINA employs a four-stage pipeline: (1) deep learning for robust component detection, (2) connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, (3) OCR for extracting component reference designators, and (4) a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. A dedicated crossing-wire detection module differentiates wire intersections from actual connections. Correctness is validated via graph isomorphism.
AI.result: SINA achieves 96.67% overall netlist generation accuracy, representing a 2.72× improvement over state-of-the-art approaches. It successfully handles both IC-level and PCB-level schematics.
AI.conclusion: SINA provides a robust, generalizable solution for converting schematic images into netlists, unlocking the vast repository of analog/mixed-signal designs in the literature for downstream EDA and AI-based circuit design applications. Its open-source nature facilitates further research and adoption.

title: SkillFuzz: Fuzzing Skill Composition for Implicit Intents Discovery in Open Skill Marketplaces
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly automate software engineering tasks through reusable skills, natural-language instruction documents that guide planning and execution. Open skill marketplaces enable users to assemble agents by co-activating community-contributed skills, but marketplace operators typically audit skills in isolation. As a result, individually benign skills may interact to redirect an agent toward unintended objectives, which we term implicit intents. Detecting such intents is challenging because the effect emerges only through skill composition, execution environments are often unavailable at admission time, and the space of possible co-activations grows exponentially with marketplace size. In this paper, we formulate implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions, where skill compositions are the unit under test, planning artifacts expose agent intent before execution, and deviations from a skill-free baseline serve as a differential oracle. Based on this formulation, we propose skillfuzz, the first execution-free testing approach that extracts structured skill contracts and uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to prioritize potentially conflicting compositions. Across representative skill-marketplace workloads, skillfuzz discovers over 1,000 distinct implicit intents under a fixed query budget, confirms more than 80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions during execution-time validation, and identifies substantially more high-severity implicit intents than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space they require.

AI.tldr: SkillFuzz is an execution-free fuzzing framework that discovers "implicit intents" — unintended agent behaviors emerging from the composition of individually benign skills in LLM-based agent marketplaces. It uses contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search to efficiently explore the combinatorial skill interaction space, identifying over 1,000 distinct implicit intents with high validation rates.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agent marketplaces allow users to compose agents from community-contributed skill documents, but marketplace operators typically audit skills in isolation. Individually benign skills can interact synergistically to redirect agents toward unintended objectives ("implicit intents"). Detecting these is difficult because: (1) the effect emerges only through composition, (2) execution environments are often unavailable at admission time, and (3) the co-activation space grows exponentially with marketplace size.
AI.method: SkillFuzz formulates implicit-intent discovery as a fuzzing problem over skill compositions. It extracts structured "skill contracts" from natural-language skill documents, then employs contract-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to prioritize and explore potentially conflicting compositions. The approach is execution-free: it uses planning artifacts (the agent's generated plan before execution) as the observable signal, with deviations from a skill-free baseline serving as a differential oracle to detect implicit intents.
AI.result: Across representative skill-marketplace workloads, SkillFuzz discovers over 1,000 distinct implicit intents under a fixed query budget. During execution-time validation, it confirms more than 80% of the highest-risk flagged compositions. It identifies substantially more high-severity implicit intents than alternative search strategies while exploring only a fraction of the pairwise interaction space those alternatives require.
AI.conclusion: SkillFuzz demonstrates that execution-free, contract-guided fuzzing with MCTS is an effective and efficient approach for auditing compositional safety risks in LLM agent skill marketplaces, significantly outperforming alternative search strategies in both coverage and precision.

title: Path-level Hindsight Instructions for Semantic Exploration in Vision-Language Navigation
summary: On-policy exploration is a crucial component for training robust Vision-Language Navigation agents, as it exposes the policy to a broader state distribution. However, such exploration inevitably leads to trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, resulting in a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing Phi-Nav, a unified on-policy framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to align instructions with the agent's actual exploratory journey. Specifically, Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) the agent performs oracle-guided on-policy exploration, sampling a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and 3) the agent conducts a second imitation pass, treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration. Through this process, Phi-Nav bridges the critical semantic supervision gap inherent in on-policy methods, transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals. Evaluations on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks show that Phi-Nav yields competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines. These results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

AI.tldr: Phi-Nav is an on-policy VLN framework that uses a three-stage hindsight reasoning cycle — oracle-guided exploration, hindsight instruction synthesis, and a second imitation pass — to bridge the semantic supervision gap in on-policy training. It achieves competitive R2R-CE and RxR-CE results with fewer expert demonstrations.
AI.motivation: On-policy exploration in VLN exposes agents to broader state distributions but causes semantic mismatch between observed visual trajectories and original instructions. This creates a supervision gap where exploratory trajectories lack aligned language guidance, limiting the effectiveness of on-policy training.
AI.method: A three-stage dual-supervision cycle: (1) oracle-guided on-policy exploration with expert action feedback; (2) a hindsight speaker that synthesizes path-level instructions grounded in collected visual observations; (3) a second imitation pass using the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration.
AI.result: Competitive performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines.
AI.conclusion: Semantic exploration is essential in VLN, and Phi-Nav demonstrates that hindsight reasoning can effectively transform semantically unlabeled exploratory movement into dense training signals, making it a practical solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

title: Beyond Supervised Clarification: Input Rewriting with LLMs for Dialogue Discourse Parsing
summary: Rewriting inputs to improve frozen downstream models has become a common strategy in modern NLP pipelines. Prior work on incremental dialogue discourse parsing (DDP) shows that supervised clarification models can rewrite fragmentary or underspecified utterances, such as resolving ellipsis or references, to improve parsing accuracy. In this work, we revisit this idea under realistic deployment conditions, where no clarification supervision is available and the clarifier must rely on zero-shot prompting or feedback from a frozen parser. Across three Segmented Discourse Representation Theory (SDRT) datasets and multiple parsers, we find that last-utterance clarification is far less reliable than suggested by supervised settings. Parser-agnostic rewriting often introduces more regressions than repairs, as edits that enable fixes also disrupt discourse cues relied upon by the parser. A best-of-8 rewriting analysis further reveals a practical ceiling: a large fraction of errors are not repairable through input rewriting alone. A parser-aware clarifier trained with GRPO reduces regressions by up to 37% by learning conservative abstention, yet still fails to produce selectivity-aware clarifications that consistently improve parsing. Together, these findings recast clarification as a selective intervention problem. We identify rewritability prediction, deciding whether an utterance is repairable before intervention, as the key missing capability for input-side optimization of frozen discourse parsers, and a critical direction for improving agentic pipelines more broadly.

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines input rewriting for dialogue discourse parsing under realistic zero-shot conditions, finding that unsupervised clarification often introduces more regressions than repairs. Even with parser-aware training (GRPO), clarifiers fail to achieve selectivity-aware rewriting. The authors identify "rewritability prediction" — deciding whether an utterance is repairable before intervening — as the critical missing capability.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed supervised clarification models can improve dialogue discourse parsing by rewriting fragmentary utterances. However, real-world deployment lacks clarification supervision. This paper investigates whether zero-shot or parser-feedback-driven clarification can reliably improve frozen parsers in practice.
AI.method: The authors evaluate utterance-level clarification across three SDRT dialogue datasets and multiple frozen parsers. They compare: (1) zero-shot prompted clarifiers, (2) parser-agnostic rewriting, (3) best-of-8 rewriting analysis to assess error repairability, and (4) a parser-aware clarifier trained with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) that learns conservative abstention to reduce regressions.
AI.result: Zero-shot and parser-agnostic rewriting introduce more regressions than repairs; even best-of-8 rewriting shows a large fraction of errors are fundamentally unrepairable through input rewriting alone. The GRPO-trained parser-aware clarifier reduces regressions by up to 37% via conservative abstention but still cannot produce consistently beneficial, selectivity-aware clarifications.
AI.conclusion: Clarification should be reframed as a selective intervention problem. The key missing capability is rewritability prediction — determining whether an utterance can be repaired before attempting clarification. This capability is critical not only for discourse parsing but for improving agentic NLP pipelines more broadly.

title: MKGR: Multimodal Knowledge-Graph Representation Learning for Cold-Start Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction
summary: Accurate protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction is central to functional genomics, disease mechanism discovery, and drug development. A difficult setting arises when candidate interactions include proteins that have no observed PPI edges during training, where models relying on network topology alone often lose useful context. This paper presents \method, a multimodal representation framework for cold-start PPI prediction. \method\ combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs, including protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, and protein-lncRNA associations. The sequence branch extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions, while graph attention encoders learn modality-specific protein embeddings from sparse biomedical associations. A bridge reconstruction objective regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, and a pair-level gating module adaptively integrates sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair. Experiments on two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings show that \method\ consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.

AI.tldr: A multimodal framework combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four biomedical knowledge graphs (protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, protein-lncRNA) for cold-start PPI prediction, using a bridge reconstruction objective and pair-level gating to integrate sequence and graph evidence, outperforming baselines across multiple metrics.
AI.motivation: Cold-start PPI prediction—where candidate proteins lack observed interaction edges during training—poses a significant challenge because models relying solely on network topology lose critical contextual information, limiting their applicability in functional genomics and drug discovery.
AI.method: The proposed method employs a dual-branch architecture: (1) a sequence branch that extracts contextual representations from structurally informed protein sequence regions, and (2) a graph attention branch that learns modality-specific protein embeddings from four biomedical knowledge graphs (protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, protein-lncRNA). A bridge reconstruction objective regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, and a pair-level gating module adaptively fuses sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair.
AI.result: Experiments on two benchmark datasets under both novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings demonstrate that the method consistently outperforms competitive sequence-based, network-based, and knowledge-graph-based baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.
AI.conclusion: Integrating region-aware sequence encoding with heterogeneous biomedical knowledge graphs via adaptive gating and bridge reconstruction regularization yields a robust solution for cold-start PPI prediction, significantly advancing predictive performance in settings where traditional network-topology methods fail.

title: Understanding Agent-Based Patching of Compiler Missed Optimizations
summary: Compiler missed optimizations refer to cases in which compilers failed to optimize certain code. It takes many compiler developers' efforts to implement or patch such missed optimizations. In this paper, we present a systematic study of how well agents patch compiler missed optimizations. We identify a significant challenge that patching a missed optimization requires more than just fixing the reported case, and instead requires generalizing to similar cases. We construct a benchmark of real-world LLVM missed optimization issues and compare agent-generated patches with patches from developers in terms of optimization scope. Our results show that coding agents often optimize the given examples, but many generated patches either cover only part of the developer-intended scope or partially overlap with it; in some cases, they further generalize beyond the reference patch. We further introduce historical-knowledge augmentation techniques that leverage prior LLVM optimization pull requests through retrieval and distillation, showing that they improve developer-aligned generalization and yield practical benefits when applied to real-world IR.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether AI coding agents can effectively patch compiler missed optimizations in LLVM. The key finding is that agents often fix the specific reported case but struggle with generalizing to the broader scope that human developers intend. The authors introduce historical-knowledge augmentation via retrieval and distillation of prior optimization PRs, which improves generalization alignment with developers.
