AI.motivation: Patching compiler missed optimizations is labor-intensive for developers because simply fixing the reported case is insufficient — the patch must generalize to similar code patterns. The authors aim to systematically evaluate whether LLM-based coding agents can perform this generalization and, if not, how to bridge the gap.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark from real-world LLVM missed optimization issues. They compare agent-generated patches against human developer reference patches, evaluating optimization scope coverage. They propose two historical-knowledge augmentation techniques: (1) retrieval-augmented generation using prior LLVM optimization pull requests, and (2) knowledge distillation from historical patches, to improve generalization alignment.
AI.result: Coding agents typically optimize the given examples but frequently produce patches that cover only a subset of the developer-intended scope or partially overlap with it. Some agent patches over-generalize beyond the reference patch. Historical-knowledge augmentation via retrieval and distillation improves developer-aligned generalization and yields practical benefits on real-world IR.
AI.conclusion: Patching compiler missed optimizations requires generalization beyond the reported case, which current coding agents struggle with. Augmenting agents with historical knowledge from prior optimization PRs significantly improves their ability to produce patches that align with developer-intended scope, demonstrating a promising direction for automated compiler maintenance.

title: Mastermind: Strategy-grounded Learning for Repository-Scale Vulnerability Reproduction
summary: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a demanding software engineering (SE) task: an agent must inspect a codebase, infer the input grammar that reaches a vulnerable path, construct a proof-of-conceptv(PoC), and verify that the crash disappears on the patched build. Recent LLM agents can often execute these steps when the approach is correct, yet they still fail by choosing the wrong strategy. This paper argues that strategy, rather than the full action trajectory, is the right learning unit for such SE agents: it is compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse across attempts. We present Mastermind, a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience. A trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through SFT and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records that guide subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, allowing strategy learning to improve multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capability. We evaluate Mastermind on CyberGym using 260 training tasks and 200 held-out evaluation tasks. With GPT-5.5 as the frozen executor, Mastermind achieves an 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini and GLM~5.1 from 45.0% and 58.5% to 60.0% and 71.0%. These results demonstrate that learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents.

AI.tldr: Mastermind introduces a dual-loop framework for repository-level vulnerability reproduction that separates strategy learning from task execution. A trainable planner learns reusable strategies via SFT and milestone-based GRPO, guiding frozen LLM executors. The framework achieves 84.5% pass rate on CyberGym, significantly outperforming existing approaches, and demonstrates cross-model transferability.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents for vulnerability reproduction often fail not because they cannot execute individual steps correctly, but because they choose the wrong overall strategy. The authors argue that strategy—rather than full action trajectories—is the optimal learning unit: it is compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse across attempts. Prior approaches (open-book context, Best-of-N sampling, iterative improvement) do not effectively capture and transfer high-level strategic knowledge.
AI.method: Mastermind employs a dual-loop architecture: (1) A trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and milestone-based Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). This planner is trained independently of any specific executor. (2) An experience loop maintains task-local strategy records that guide subsequent attempts. The planner outputs high-level strategies that steer frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capabilities, enabling strategy transfer across different executor models.
AI.result: Evaluated on CyberGym with 260 training and 200 held-out tasks: With GPT-5.5 as executor, Mastermind achieves 84.5% pass rate, substantially outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner improves GPT-5.4 mini from 45.0% to 60.0% and GLM 5.1 from 58.5% to 71.0%, demonstrating cross-model strategy transferability.
AI.conclusion: Learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale software engineering agents. The separation of strategy learning from action execution allows a single trained planner to improve multiple frozen executors, offering a practical path toward more capable and generalizable SE agents.

title: Towards a Phonology-Informed Evaluation of Multilingual TTS
summary: Neural TTS systems can sound natural across languages, but naturalness does not guarantee the preservation of sound contrasts that distinguish words from their grammatical forms. Standard metrics like MOS do not test for this. We propose a classifier-based framework that audits TTS output against language-specific phonological patterns using human speech as a benchmark. Testing Assamese advanced tongue root (ATR) vowel harmony with Meta's MMS TTS, we show that a classifier trained on human speech transfers to synthesized speech with minimal loss. The faithfulness audit reveals that [+ATR] mid vowels are realized as [-ATR] in 1/3 tokens despite an underlying [+ATR] specification, a bias absent in human speech. At the word level, predicted ATR labels classify harmony more accurately than transcription labels, indicating a gap between intended and produced phonology. The framework offers task-specific diagnostics and generalizes to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic cues.

AI.tldr: A classifier-based audit reveals that Meta's MMS TTS fails to faithfully produce Assamese ATR vowel harmony in ~1/3 of tokens, despite high naturalness, exposing a gap between intended and produced phonology that standard MOS cannot detect.
AI.motivation: Naturalness ratings (MOS) do not assess whether TTS systems preserve linguistically meaningful sound contrasts. There is a need for diagnostic frameworks that audit phonological faithfulness — the correct realization of contrasts that distinguish words and grammatical forms — in neural TTS output.
AI.method: A classifier trained on human speech is used to predict phonological feature values (e.g., [±ATR]) in both human and synthesized speech. The framework compares classifier predictions against underlying phonological specifications and transcription-based labels to quantify deviations. Tested on Assamese ATR vowel harmony using Meta's MMS TTS.
AI.result: The human-speech-trained classifier transfers to TTS output with minimal performance loss. The audit reveals a systematic bias: [+ATR] mid vowels surface as [-ATR] in approximately one-third of tokens in synthesized speech, a pattern absent in human speech. Predicted ATR labels classify harmony more accurately than transcription labels, indicating a mismatch between the TTS system's intended phonology and its acoustic realization.
AI.conclusion: The classifier-based framework provides targeted, task-specific diagnostics for phonological faithfulness in TTS and generalizes to any contrast with measurable acoustic cues, offering a principled complement to holistic naturalness evaluations like MOS.

title: DeadPool: Resilient LLM Training with Hot-Swapping via Zero-Overhead Checkpoint
summary: State-of-the-art large language model (LLM) training takes tens of thousands of graphics processing units (GPUs) for months and encounters failures across the software and hardware stack. Existing fault-tolerance mechanisms either impose non-trivial overhead during failure-free execution or suffer from prolonged recovery latency, particularly under scenarios where a small subset of compute nodes experience permanent failures. %The tradeoff between failure-free overhead and recovery latency forms a space forms a Pareto frontier We present DeadPool to simultaneously address both optimization objectives. DeadPool incorporates a fault-tolerance mechanism that restores LLM training via hot-swapping, namely by replacing failed nodes with spare nodes without terminating the complete job. The hot-swapping of DeadPool is enabled by two ideas: First, it exploits an off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing mechanism for spatial redundancy. Second, it introduces a communicator reconstruction protocol that replaces failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime. DeadPool efficiently overlaps the in-memory checkpointing with computation, thus introducing zero overhead during error-free execution. Upon permanent node failures, DeadPool can rebuild memory states with minimal recomputation by leveraging in-memory checkpoints. We evaluate DeadPool across scales (up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs) and LLMs (up to 65B parameters), and observe zero checkpoint overhead with hot-swapping recovery completing in under 40 seconds. These results show that DeadPool simultaneously achieves both zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery cost.

AI.tldr: DeadPool is a fault-tolerance mechanism for large-scale LLM training that achieves zero-overhead error-free execution and sub-40-second recovery via hot-swapping failed nodes with spares, using off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing and runtime communicator reconstruction.
AI.motivation: LLM training on tens of thousands of GPUs over months inevitably encounters hardware/software failures. Existing fault-tolerance mechanisms impose a tradeoff: they either incur non-trivial overhead during failure-free operation or suffer prolonged recovery latency, especially under permanent node failures. DeadPool aims to simultaneously eliminate both overheads.
AI.method: DeadPool combines two key ideas: (1) off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing that overlaps checkpoint creation with computation for spatial redundancy, introducing zero overhead during error-free execution; and (2) a communicator reconstruction protocol that dynamically replaces failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime without terminating the entire job. Upon permanent failure, memory states are rebuilt with minimal recomputation using the in-memory checkpoints.
AI.result: Evaluated at scales up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and LLMs up to 65B parameters, DeadPool demonstrated zero checkpoint overhead during error-free execution and hot-swapping recovery completion in under 40 seconds.
AI.conclusion: DeadPool successfully breaks the existing tradeoff between failure-free overhead and recovery latency, simultaneously achieving zero-overhead execution and extremely low recovery cost for large-scale LLM training.

title: Reasoning effort, not tool access, buys first-try reliability in agentic code generation: an observational study
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Dataset and evaluation artifacts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21134406
summary: Agentic coding assistants are increasingly given extra capabilities, such as browser based testing tools and design oriented system prompts, on the assumption that more capability yields better software. This study tested that assumption directly. Ninety independent agent runs built the same application, a real time retrospective board, from one detailed specification, each scored on a fixed 14 criterion functional rubric (42 point maximum) and a visual quality review. The runs spanned several model generations, two agent harnesses, two reasoning effort levels, a testing tool, and two design oriented prompts. Capability tier dominated: frontier models clustered near the ceiling while a low cost local model fell to 24 to 37 points. A criterion level analysis revealed what run totals conceal. Container deployment was the dominant defect, failing first try in 44 percent of runs, with its failure rate shifting sharply across model generations while mean totals moved less than a point. The testing tool raised cost by 42 to 68 percent without improving functional score or reliability, even on interface visible criteria. Raising reasoning effort from High to xHigh lifted first try perfect runs from 28 percent to 89 percent and cut corrective prompts about five fold, for 9 to 29 percent more cost. A design oriented prompt raised visual quality, 4.5 versus 3.0 on a 5 point scale, without lifting function, and a one paragraph paraphrase of its directive reproduced the entire lift. The practical lesson is to match the fix to the failure: most first run failures came from weak reasoning, which a stronger model or more effort prevents, not from visible flaws a checking tool would catch.

AI.tldr: A large-scale experiment with 90 independent agent runs building the same application found that model capability tier dominates outcomes, reasoning effort dramatically improves first-try success, but adding a browser-based testing tool increased cost with no functional improvement. Design-oriented prompts lifted visual quality without affecting function.
AI.motivation: To empirically test the common assumption that giving agentic coding assistants extra capabilities (browser-based testing tools, design-oriented system prompts) yields better software, rather than relying on untested intuition about what improves agent performance.
AI.method: Ninety independent agent runs built the same real-time retrospective board application from a single detailed specification. Each run was scored on a 14-criterion functional rubric (42-point max) and a visual quality review. The experiment spanned multiple model generations, two agent harnesses, two reasoning effort levels (High vs. xHigh), presence/absence of a testing tool, and two design-oriented prompts.
AI.result: (1) Frontier models clustered near the ceiling while a low-cost local model scored 24–37 points. (2) Container deployment was the dominant defect, failing first-try in 44% of runs, with failure rates shifting sharply across model generations even as mean totals barely moved. (3) The testing tool raised cost 42–68% with no functional score or reliability improvement. (4) Raising reasoning effort from High to xHigh lifted first-try perfect runs from 28% to 89% and cut corrective prompts ~5×, for only 9–29% more cost. (5) A design-oriented prompt raised visual quality from 3.0 to 4.5 on a 5-point scale without affecting function; a one-paragraph paraphrase reproduced the entire lift.
AI.conclusion: Match the fix to the failure: most first-run failures stem from weak reasoning, which stronger models or higher reasoning effort prevent, not from visible flaws a checking tool would catch. Adding tools without diagnosing the actual failure mode wastes resources.

title: SimWorlds: A Multi-Agent System for Dynamic 3D Scene Creation
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to translate natural language into 3D scenes in a procedural way, but existing systems focus on static output. Dynamic 4D scenes from text alone, in which liquids flow, particles emit, rigid bodies cascade, and articulated mechanisms move, remain largely unexplored despite their value as editable content and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two challenges set the dynamic case apart from static text-to-scene work: an agent must jointly coordinate spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in a single coherent scene, and verifying motion correctness from rendered video is fundamentally harder than judging a single image. We present SimWorlds: a multi-agent framework that produces dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text, with Blender-specific procedural knowledge, a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages, a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, and a runtime-state inspection tool suite that catches mechanism failures the rendered image cannot reveal. We also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for assessing both visual fidelity and physical consistency of the procedural dynamic 3D scenes generated from text prompts. Experiments show that SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines.

AI.tldr: SimWorlds is a multi-agent framework that generates dynamic, editable 4D scenes (3D + time) from text prompts using Blender, employing a planner-coder-reviewer workflow with physics solvers, a deterministic verifier, and runtime-state inspection tools. It is evaluated on a new benchmark, 4DBuildBench, and outperforms existing baselines for dynamic scene generation.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based text-to-3D systems produce only static output. Dynamic 4D scenes — involving flowing liquids, emitting particles, cascading rigid bodies, and moving articulated mechanisms — remain unexplored despite their value for editable content creation and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. The dynamic case introduces two distinct challenges: (1) jointly coordinating spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in one coherent scene, and (2) verifying motion correctness from rendered video, which is significantly harder than assessing a single static image.
AI.method: SimWorlds is a multi-agent framework with: (a) Blender-specific procedural knowledge to guide generation; (b) a planner-coder-reviewer workflow that enforces a fixed, ordered sequence of construction stages; (c) a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier to ensure structural coherence; and (d) a runtime-state inspection tool suite that detects mechanism failures invisible in rendered images. The authors also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark measuring both visual fidelity and physical consistency of procedurally generated dynamic 3D scenes from text prompts.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that SimWorlds outperforms prior baselines for dynamic Blender scene generation on the 4DBuildBench benchmark, excelling in both visual fidelity and physical consistency metrics.
AI.conclusion: SimWorlds advances text-to-scene generation from static 3D to dynamic 4D by addressing the coordination of physics, time, and spatial layout through a structured multi-agent pipeline with verification and inspection tools. This unlocks new possibilities for editable dynamic content creation and physics-grounded synthetic data generation.

title: Object Aligner: A Configurable JSON Schema Similarity Score for Graphs, Applied to LLM Prompt Optimization
comment: 28 pages, This is a submitted version of a manuscript under review at IEEE Access; it has not been peer reviewed
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often asked to produce JSON conforming to a fixed schema, powering information extraction, tool calling, agentic planning, and knowledge-graph construction. Measuring how closely an output matches a gold reference is essential yet surprisingly hard: exact match is brittle, text similarity ignores structure, and an LLM judge is expensive, opaque, and non-deterministic. We address this with Object Aligner (OA), an open-source Python library that scores two JSON objects deterministically by recursively aligning their trees (the Hungarian algorithm for unordered collections, sequence alignment for ordered ones) and awarding partial credit at the granularity the schema declares. The Object Aligner is configured entirely through a set of JSON Schema extensions, so adapting it to a new task involves annotating a schema rather than writing code. Complex structured data, however, are rarely flat trees: records may form graphs or hypergraphs keyed by arbitrary identifiers, breaking the assumptions of prior similarity metrics. Our central contribution, referential alignment, closes this gap by inferring a bijection between gold and candidate identifiers and scoring every reference through it, so the score is invariant to relabeling. Since recovering this bijection exactly is graph isomorphism, the Object Aligner approximates it with Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement. An order-sensitive sequence regime targets ranking and planning. Since the same alignment localizes every mismatch, the Object Aligner emits ranked repair suggestions at no extra cost. Used as a reward inside the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner helps or stays neutral across all datasets.

AI.tldr: The Object Aligner (OA) is an open-source Python library for deterministically scoring JSON outputs against a gold reference by recursively aligning tree structures, supporting referential alignment across graph-structured data, and emitting ranked repair suggestions — all configured through JSON Schema extensions rather than code.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for evaluating JSON outputs against gold references are inadequate: exact match is brittle, text similarity metrics ignore structural constraints, and LLM-based judges are expensive, opaque, and non-deterministic. Furthermore, real-world structured data often forms graphs or hypergraphs keyed by arbitrary identifiers, which breaks the assumptions of prior tree-based similarity metrics.
AI.method: OA recursively aligns two JSON trees, using the Hungarian algorithm for unordered collections and sequence alignment for ordered ones, awarding partial credit at schema-declared granularity. Configuration is done via JSON Schema extensions. The key innovation — referential alignment — infers a bijection between gold and candidate identifiers using Weisfeiler-Leman color refinement (approximating graph isomorphism), making scores invariant to relabeling. The alignment also localizes every mismatch, enabling ranked repair suggestions.
AI.result: When used as a reward signal within the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner helps or stays neutral across all datasets evaluated.
AI.conclusion: The Object Aligner provides a deterministic, interpretable, and schema-configurable alternative to brittle exact-match or expensive LLM-judge approaches for evaluating structured JSON outputs, with the novel capability of handling referential (graph) structures via Weisfeiler-Leman alignment.

title: CALM: Interpretable Cross-Modal Alignment for Biomarker Discovery from Unpaired Data
summary: The interaction between brain structure and genetic influences is key to understanding neuropsychiatric disorders. However, most large-scale datasets are unimodal, providing either neuroimaging or genetics data. We propose CALM, a framework that learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from completely disjoint populations. CALM aligns the two modalities in a shared latent space via linear projections that simultaneously match the class-conditional latent distributions and ensure group separability. These projections provide interpretable pathway--ROI associations. When trained on unimodal imaging and genetics datasets, CALM generalizes to an unseen paired dataset, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. We also demonstrate stability of the learned associations against a paired baseline. Our experiments on autism spectrum disorder reveal immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions and are consistent with established literature. Thus, CALM opens the door to leveraging large unimodal repositories for studying cross-modal interactions in brain disorders across disparate datasets.

AI.tldr: CALM is a framework that learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from completely disjoint (unpaired) imaging and genetics datasets by aligning modalities in a shared latent space through linear projections. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods and reveals biologically meaningful pathway–ROI links in autism spectrum disorder.
AI.motivation: Most large-scale datasets in neuropsychiatric research are unimodal (neuroimaging or genetics only), hindering the study of brain–gene interactions. Existing multimodal fusion methods typically require paired data from the same subjects. CALM addresses the unmet need to discover cross-modal associations using entirely disjoint populations.
AI.method: CALM learns linear projections that map brain ROI features and genetic pathway features into a shared latent space. The optimization simultaneously enforces two objectives: (1) matching class-conditional latent distributions across modalities, and (2) ensuring class separability. The linear projections yield directly interpretable pathway–ROI association weights, bridging the two modalities without requiring any paired samples.
AI.result: Trained on unimodal imaging and genetics datasets, CALM generalizes to unseen paired data and outperforms several state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. The learned associations are stable against a paired baseline. In autism spectrum disorder, CALM identifies immune and metabolic genetic pathways linked to specific cortical regions, consistent with existing literature.
AI.conclusion: CALM enables leveraging large-scale unimodal repositories to study cross-modal brain–gene interactions in neuropsychiatric disorders, opening new avenues for integrative analysis without requiring costly paired multimodal data collection.

title: Repair the Amplifier, Not the Symptom: Stable World-Model Correction for Agent Rollouts
summary: As agent planning moves from short tool chains toward persistent workflows with thousands or tens of thousands of steps, failures will occur inside large planning graphs rather than in isolated predictions. Replanning the entire graph after every mistake is neither computationally realistic nor desirable: full-graph replay consumes large context budgets, exposes the LLM to many irrelevant symptoms, and can degrade long-context retrieval. This paper studies the missing component in such systems: a world-model corrector that repairs the failed planning graph in place. We compare two families of correctors. The first is the common engineering approach: scan nodes and edges, choose a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it. We implement strong engineering LLM correctors and find that they can help, especially when given very large contexts. The second family is our approach, WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair): instead of scanning for visible symptoms, it works backward from subgraph amplification, identifies the nodes and edges that keep re-amplifying error, and sends only that causal subgraph to the LLM. Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and gives the LLM a cleaner repair target.

AI.tldr: As agent workflows scale to thousands of steps, failures occur within large planning graphs. Full replanning is infeasible; this paper proposes WM-SAR, a world-model corrector that identifies and repairs only the causal error-amplifying subgraph, substantially outperforming engineering-based local repair correctors under realistic token budgets.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents transition from short tool-use chains to persistent, long-horizon workflows with thousands of steps, failures manifest within large planning graphs rather than as isolated prediction errors. Full-graph replanning is computationally prohibitive, wastes context budgets, and degrades long-context retrieval. There is a missing component: a mechanism to repair failed planning graphs in place without reprocessing the entire graph.
AI.method: The authors compare two families of world-model correctors: (1) engineering correctors that scan nodes/edges, select a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it; and (2) WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair), which works backward from subgraph amplification to identify nodes and edges that repeatedly amplify errors, then sends only that causal subgraph to the LLM for targeted repair.
AI.result: WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization using only a compact region, and provides the LLM with a cleaner, more focused repair target.
AI.conclusion: Causal subgraph identification via error amplification backtracking is a more effective repair strategy than symptom-based local scanning. WM-SAR enables scalable, token-efficient planning-graph repair for long-horizon agent workflows.

title: Using embeddings to predict spoken word duration and pitch in Mandarin monosyllabic words
summary: Time-normalized f0 contours of Mandarin words in conversational speech have been shown to be predictable in part from their contextualized embeddings (CEs). The present study investigates whether CEs also predict spoken word duration for 7470 tokens of Mandarin monosyllabic CV words extracted from a Mandarin corpus of spontaneous speech. We show that CEs indeed are predictive for duration, above chance level, not only at the type level, but also at the level of individual tokens, as indicated by the results obtained with the type-wise and token-wise permutation baselines. We also show that the predicted durations are sufficiently precise to back-transform predicted f0 contours in [0,1] normalized time to contours on the ms time scale. The resulting predicted contours approximate empirical contours and also outperform a permutation baseline.

AI.tldr: Contextualized embeddings (CEs) predict both f0 contours and spoken word duration in Mandarin spontaneous speech at both type and token levels. Predicted durations are precise enough to convert normalized f0 contours to millisecond-scale contours that approximate empirical data.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed CEs predict time-normalized f0 contours of Mandarin words in conversational speech. However, to map these normalized contours back to real-time (ms) contours, word duration information is essential. This study investigates whether CEs can also predict spoken word duration, enabling full reconstruction of f0 contours on an absolute time scale.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 7,470 tokens of Mandarin monosyllabic CV words from a spontaneous speech corpus. They tested whether CEs predict word duration using type-wise and token-wise permutation baselines to establish chance-level performance. Predicted durations were then used to back-transform f0 contours from [0,1] normalized time to the millisecond time scale, comparing the resulting contours against empirical contours and permutation baselines.
AI.result: CEs predicted word duration above chance level at both type and token levels. The predicted durations were sufficiently precise for back-transforming normalized f0 contours; the resulting ms-scale contours approximated empirical contours and outperformed the permutation baseline.
AI.conclusion: Contextualized embeddings carry substantial phonetic detail, capturing not only pitch-related information but also temporal properties of spoken words. This dual predictability enables the reconstruction of full f0 trajectories in absolute time from lexical and contextual information alone.

title: Message Passing Based Two-Timescale Bayesian Learning for Joint Channel and Memory Hardware Impairments Tracking
summary: Hardware impairments in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling, severely degrading channel estimation. This paper employs a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to model the intra-slot memory of the hardware impairments and proposes a message-passing-based two-timescale Bayesian deep learning (MP-TTBDL) framework for joint channel and impairment tracking. Owing to small-scale fading, the wireless channel varies rapidly across slots, whereas hardware impairments drift slowly due to hardware aging and environmental variations. To capture these distinct physical timescales, a fastvarying Markov prior and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior are assigned to the sparse channel and the network parameters, respectively. Based on a multi-slot factor graph formulation, a message-passing algorithm is developed. Specifically, the inter-slot messages admit closed-form updates, while the intra-slot factor graph, due to its complex recurrent structure, is partitioned into a channel tracking module and an impairments calibration module. The channel tracking module performs sparse channel estimation via turbo orthogonal approximate message passing (Turbo-OAMP), and the impairments calibration module updates the impairment parameters via a specially designed deep approximate message passing (DAMP) procedure, with the two modules iteratively exchanging extrinsic information through expectation propagation (EP) until convergence. Simulation results show that the proposed framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators followed by channel estimation across different online impairment scenarios and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an MP-TTBDL framework that uses an RGRU to model hardware impairment memory and a two-timescale message-passing algorithm (Turbo-OAMP for fast-varying channels, DAMP for slow-drifting impairments) with EP-based information exchange, achieving superior channel estimation under hardware impairments compared to conventional methods.
AI.motivation: Hardware impairments in massive MIMO receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling that severely degrade channel estimation. The wireless channel varies rapidly (small-scale fading) while hardware impairments drift slowly (aging, environmental changes), requiring a framework that captures these distinct physical timescales.
AI.method: An RGRU models intra-slot memory of hardware impairments. A two-timescale Bayesian deep learning framework assigns a fast-varying Markov prior to the sparse channel and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior to network parameters. A multi-slot factor graph is constructed, with inter-slot messages in closed form. The intra-slot graph is partitioned into: (1) a channel tracking module using Turbo-OAMP for sparse channel estimation, and (2) an impairments calibration module using a specially designed DAMP procedure, with both modules exchanging extrinsic information via EP iteratively until convergence.
AI.result: Simulation results demonstrate that the MP-TTBDL framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators followed by channel estimation across various online impairment scenarios and SNR conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MP-TTBDL framework effectively handles the two-timescale nature of wireless channels and hardware impairments, leveraging message-passing and deep learning to deliver robust, low-error channel estimation in impaired massive MIMO receivers.

title: TestEvo-Bench: An Executable and Live Benchmark for Test and Code Co-Evolution
comment: TestEvo-Bench leaderboard and data explorer are hosted at https://www.testevo-bench.com
summary:
Software tests and code evolve together: a code change should be followed by new or updated tests that record the new software behavior. Yet existing test generation and update benchmarks often isolate the test from the code change, and rely on static metadata that does not verify whether a test is executable or semantically tied to the code change. This makes it difficult to evaluate whether a test automation agent understands how a code change should propagate into the test suite.
  We introduce TestEvo-Bench, a benchmark of test and code co-evolution tasks mined from software repositories, with two tracks: in test generation, the agent shall write new tests to capture the new software behavior; in test update, the agent shall adapt failing existing tests to the changed software behavior. Each task is anchored to a real commit history and packaged with environment configuration to support execution-grounded metrics such as pass rate, coverage, and mutation score. TestEvo-Bench is also a live benchmark: each task records the timestamp of the test and code changes, and new tasks are periodically mined by our automated pipeline, so evaluation can be restricted to tasks postdating a model's training cutoff to reduce data leakage risk. The current snapshot contains 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks, curated from 59,950 candidate co-evolution records across 152 open-source Java projects. We experiment with four state-of-the-art agents that combine strong harnesses (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and SWE-Agent) with strong foundation models (Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro). Results show that they achieve up to 77.5% success rate on test generation and 74.6% on test update. However, success rate is materially lower on the most recent benchmark tasks and drops significantly under limited per-task cost.

AI.tldr: TestEvo-Bench is a live benchmark for evaluating test automation agents on real-world software test and code co-evolution tasks, featuring execution-grounded metrics. Current agents achieve up to 77.5% success on test generation and 74.6% on test update, but performance degrades on recent tasks and under cost constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks isolate tests from code changes and rely on static metadata, failing to verify executability or semantic alignment. This makes it difficult to evaluate whether an agent truly understands how code changes should propagate to tests.
AI.method: TestEvo-Bench mines real commit histories from 152 open-source Java projects, yielding 746 test generation and 509 test update tasks. Each task is packaged with environment configuration and supports execution-grounded metrics (pass rate, coverage, mutation score). It is a live benchmark with timestamped tasks and periodic automated mining to reduce data leakage risk.
AI.result: Four SOTA agents (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, SWE-Agent combined with Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieve up to 77.5% success on test generation and 74.6% on test update. However, success rates drop materially on the most recent tasks and degrade significantly under limited per-task cost.
AI.conclusion: TestEvo-Bench provides a more realistic and rigorous evaluation framework for test co-evolution, revealing that even strong agents struggle with recent code changes and cost-efficiency, highlighting key areas for improvement in test automation.

title: Verifiable Knowledge Expansion through Retrieval-Grounded Formal Concept Analysis
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, Accepted to the 8th epiDAMIK ACM SIGKDD International Workshop on Epidemiology meets Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery (epiDAMIK 2026)
summary: Ontology construction requires deciding which objects, attributes, and structural relations should be accepted as valid knowledge. Language models can propose such structures from text, but their outputs can still be unsupported or inconsistent. This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework that uses formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for knowledge expansion. Starting from seed attributes, FCA proposes implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle then validates each implication or returns a counterexample. The oracle also supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals, making accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections inspectable. In a rare ataxia setting constructed from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs obtain relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. The lower implication scores reflect a stricter evaluation of derived implications, where one missed or extra relation can affect several implication judgments. Ablations show that incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores. However, identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even when the candidate objects and attributes are fixed.

AI.tldr: A retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework paired with formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for ontology construction. The FCA proposes implications over a formal context, and the SLM oracle validates, corrects, and expands them. Tested on rare ataxia data from Orphadata, the approach yields modest F1 scores, with larger seed sets improving performance. Ablations highlight the difficulty of identifying positive object-attribute pairs even in fixed settings.
AI.motivation: Ontology construction from text using language models suffers from unsupported or inconsistent outputs. There is a need for a verifiable, inspectable knowledge expansion framework that combines the generative breadth of language models with the rigor of symbolic reasoning.
AI.method: The framework uses formal concept analysis (FCA) to propose attribute implications over a growing formal context, starting from seed attributes. A retrieval-grounded small language model (SLM) oracle validates each implication or returns a counterexample. The oracle also handles incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals. All decisions—accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections—remain inspectable.
AI.result: Evaluated on rare ataxia data from Orphadata with 10-seed runs: relation F1 = 0.29–0.52; closure-based implication F1 = 0.22–0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. Lower implication scores reflect stricter evaluation where one error can affect multiple judgments. Ablations show incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting improve closure-based implication scores, though identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains challenging.
AI.conclusion: Combining retrieval-augmented SLMs with FCA-based symbolic verification yields an inspectable ontology construction pipeline. While performance is modest, the approach demonstrates that symbolic verification loops can help ground language model outputs, though challenges remain in accurately identifying positive object-attribute relations.

title: EduArt: An educational-level benchmark for evaluating art history knowledge in large language models
summary: Large language models now score near ceiling on general benchmarks, but these aggregate measures reveal little about how models behave within single disciplines. Existing art-focused evaluations rely on synthetic questions and rarely report item-level properties. This paper introduces EduArt, an educational-level benchmark for art-historical knowledge and visual reasoning in multimodal LLMs. EduArt comprises 871 human-authored questions from Italian secondary-school exercises and US Advanced Placement Art History exams, spanning two languages and seven formats from multiple choice to in-text word placement and error identification. Twelve models from six provider families were evaluated under a default answer-only condition and a motivation condition requiring written justification, and characterized using Classical Test Theory and a logistic regression isolating the effects of format, language, image presence, and model. The benchmark showed strong psychometric properties (mean discrimination 0.514, 82.3 percent good discriminators), while multiple-choice accuracy saturated near ceiling for six models, showing recognition formats alone cannot distinguish frontier models. Format was a strong independent predictor of accuracy: models exceeding 94 percent on multiple choice fell to 23.9 percent on open completion (Claude Opus 4.6) and 6.2 percent on error identification (Claude Sonnet 4.6). The motivation condition changed accuracy in a predominantly negative, family-dependent direction. These dissociations indicate that art-historical knowledge and the ability to deploy it are distinct capabilities, and that single-format benchmarks overestimate what models can reliably do. Mapping this capability profile is a precondition for responsible use of multimodal LLMs in art-historical scholarship, where tasks demand producing and manipulating content rather than selecting from fixed options.

AI.tldr: EduArt is a 871-question multimodal benchmark for art-historical knowledge spanning 7 formats and 2 languages. While six models hit near-ceiling on multiple-choice, performance collapsed on open-ended formats (e.g., Claude Opus 4.6 dropped from >94% MC to 23.9% on open completion), demonstrating that recognition-based benchmarks severely overestimate model capabilities and that knowledge recall vs. deployment are dissociable skills.
AI.motivation: Current LLM benchmarks saturate at ceiling, masking within-discipline behavior. Existing art-focused evaluations rely on synthetic, non-transparent items. There is no rigorous, item-level psychometric benchmark for multimodal LLMs in art history that captures the format-dependent nature of model performance.
AI.method: EduArt comprises 871 human-authored questions from Italian secondary-school exercises and US AP Art History exams, covering 7 formats (multiple choice, open completion, error identification, in-text word placement, etc.), two languages, and image-conditional items. Twelve models from six families were tested under (a) answer-only and (b) motivation (written justification) conditions. Analysis used Classical Test Theory (discrimination indices) and logistic regression to isolate effects of format, language, image presence, and model.
AI.result: Strong psychometrics: mean discrimination = 0.514, 82.3% items classified as good discriminators. Multiple-choice accuracy saturated near ceiling for six models. Format was a strong independent predictor: models exceeding 94% MC dropped to 23.9% (open completion, Claude Opus 4.6) and 6.2% (error identification, Claude Sonnet 4.6). The motivation condition produced predominantly negative, model-family-dependent accuracy shifts.
AI.conclusion: Art-historical knowledge and the ability to deploy it are distinct, dissociable capabilities. Single-format (especially recognition-based) benchmarks systematically overestimate model competence. Responsible use of multimodal LLMs in art-historical scholarship requires mapping this full capability profile, particularly for generative/manipulative tasks rather than passive selection.

title: Revisiting Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Compressed Communication
summary: Decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) is a popular framework for distributed applications with streaming data. To tackle the communication bottleneck, previous studies have investigated D-OCO with compressed communication and proposed several algorithms that are variants of online gradient descent (OGD). However, for D-OCO with exact communication, the best existing algorithms are variants of follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL). In this paper, for the first time, we propose two FTRL-type algorithms for D-OCO with compressed communication. Compared with OGD-type algorithms, our algorithms are more elegant in both algorithmic design and theoretical analysis. The key insight is that the dual update mechanism of FTRL allows us to make a simple application of the technique for average consensus with communication compression. More specifically, our first algorithm considers the full-information setting, and can match the existing regret bounds. Our second algorithm is designed for the bandit setting, and can significantly improve both the regret bounds and communication costs of existing algorithms.

AI.tldr: Proposes two FTRL-type algorithms for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication, improving upon existing OGD-type methods in both full-information and bandit settings.
AI.motivation: Previous D-OCO with compressed communication only used OGD-type algorithms, while the best exact-communication D-OCO algorithms are FTRL-based. There is a gap in applying FTRL to compressed communication settings, which could offer more elegant design and better theoretical guarantees.
AI.method: Leverages the dual update mechanism of FTRL combined with average consensus techniques with communication compression. Two algorithms are presented: one for full-information feedback and one for the bandit setting.
AI.result: The full-information algorithm matches existing regret bounds. The bandit algorithm significantly improves both regret bounds and communication costs compared to prior work.
AI.conclusion: FTRL-type algorithms are superior to OGD-type counterparts for D-OCO with compressed communication, achieving better regret bounds and lower communication costs, especially in the bandit setting.

title: Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models
comment: Equal contribution: Thomas Fontanari and Simone Petruzzi
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Unlike standard diffusion-based approaches, DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising a natural question: do these models internally represent denoising progress, and how is such information used downstream? In this work, we show that DLMs do in fact encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep within their residual streams. We find that this signal can be reliably extracted using probes across layers, indicating that denoising progress is decodable from internal activations. We further demonstrate that steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep allows us to systematically modulate its notion of denoising progress, leading to predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. Finally, we analyse the geometry of the identified representation, showing that it exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space, and shedding light on how such a signal is processed by these models.

AI.tldr: Diffusion Language Models internally encode a latent representation of the diffusion timestep in their residual streams, which can be probed, steered, and exhibits structured geometric properties in activation space.
AI.motivation: DLMs lack explicit timestep conditioning, unlike standard diffusion models, raising the open question of whether and how they internally represent denoising progress.
AI.method: The authors use linear probes trained on residual stream activations across layers to decode timestep information; then apply steering vectors along low-dimensional subspaces associated with the inferred timestep to modulate model behavior; finally, analyze the geometric structure of the identified representation in activation space.
AI.result: Timestep information is reliably decodable from internal activations across layers; steering along the timestep subspace systematically modulates model confidence and entropy in predictable ways; the representation exhibits structured, interpretable geometric properties.
AI.conclusion: DLMs do internally represent denoising progress despite lacking explicit timestep conditioning, and this latent signal is functionally significant, geometrically structured, and causally manipulable.

title: OpenSafeIntent: Evaluating Intent-Calibrated Safe Completion Across Dual-Use Prompt Sets
summary: Safe completion requires models to provide useful assistance without enabling harm, but this behavior is difficult to evaluate with isolated prompts. We introduce OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark of controlled prompt-sets that vary intent while holding the underlying task fixed. Each datapoint contains benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of the same task. This design lets us evaluate whether models calibrate assistance across intent shifts, rather than merely appearing safe on average. Across a broad model suite, we find that prompt-level safety hides important failures: models often fail to remain safe across matched intent variants, dual-use behavior is brittle under paraphrase, high-level answers on risky topics are not reliably safe, and responses that reframe ambiguous requests into safer tasks are substantially less likely to cross the safety boundary. Our results suggest that safe completion should be evaluated as intent-calibrated behavior over controlled task variants, not as a single safety-helpfulness tradeoff over independent prompts.

AI.tldr: OpenSafeIntent introduces a benchmark with benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of the same task to evaluate whether models calibrate assistance across intent shifts. It finds that prompt-level safety metrics mask failures: models struggle with intent calibration, dual-use behavior is fragile under paraphrase, and reframing risky requests into safer tasks reduces safety violations.
AI.motivation: Current safety evaluation relies on isolated, independent prompts, which cannot capture whether a model appropriately calibrates its assistance when the same underlying task is framed with different intents (benign, dual-use, or malicious). This makes it hard to distinguish models that are genuinely safe from those that merely appear safe on average.
AI.method: The authors construct OpenSafeIntent, a benchmark where each datapoint is a controlled prompt-set containing benign, dual-use, and malicious variants of an identical underlying task. This paired design enables direct comparison of model behavior across intent shifts for the same task. They evaluate a broad suite of models on this benchmark, measuring intent-calibrated safety rather than aggregate prompt-level safety.
AI.result: Prompt-level safety metrics hide critical failures: models frequently fail to remain safe across matched intent variants; dual-use behavior is brittle under paraphrasing; high-level answers on risky topics are not reliably safe; and responses that reframe ambiguous requests into safer tasks significantly reduce the likelihood of crossing the safety boundary.
AI.conclusion: Safe completion should be evaluated as intent-calibrated behavior over controlled task variants, not as a single safety-helpfulness tradeoff over independent prompts. The OpenSafeIntent benchmark provides a more rigorous framework for auditing this capability.

title: UniWind: Toward Unified Day-Ahead Wind Power Forecasting via Physics-Informed State Routing
summary: Day-ahead wind power forecasting is essential for cost-effective power-system operation. It is primarily driven by future meteorological conditions while retaining temporal dependencies in power generation. In practice, observed wind-farm power often entangles physically available power with local environmental effects and latent operational states, such as shutdowns and curtailment. Existing physical models provide useful constraints but adapt poorly across wind farms, whereas data-driven models can capture rich correlations but often conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations. In this study, we propose UniWind, a wind power forecasting model based on physics-informed state routing. UniWind first employs a Physical Prior Estimator to construct a site-calibrated physical prior by combining site-conditioned monotonic warping with a shared physical power curve. It further applies a physical upper-bound constraint to shape this prior as a soft envelope of available wind power generation. UniWind then proposes a Latent State Encoder to model operating-state embeddings and transforms the physical prior into final power forecasts through a State-aware Power Corrector, which uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction. Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind.

AI.tldr: UniWind is a day-ahead wind power forecasting model that combines a physics-informed prior (site-calibrated warped power curve with upper-bound constraints) with a latent operating-state encoder and state-aware correction module, achieving strong accuracy and zero-shot transfer across 20+ real-world wind farms.
AI.motivation: Existing wind forecasting methods suffer from a gap: physical models adapt poorly across sites, while data-driven models conflate meteorological effects with latent operational states (shutdowns, curtailment). A unified approach is needed that leverages physical constraints while explicitly disentangling available wind power from state-induced deviations.
AI.method: UniWind consists of three components: (1) A Physical Prior Estimator that learns a site-calibrated physical prior via site-conditioned monotonic warping of a shared power curve, regularized by a physical upper-bound constraint serving as a soft envelope. (2) A Latent State Encoder that learns embeddings of operating states (e.g., curtailment, shutdown). (3) A State-aware Power Corrector that uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction to transform the physical prior into final forecasts.
AI.result: Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on over 20 real-world datasets demonstrate UniWind's accuracy and robustness in day-ahead wind power forecasting.
AI.conclusion: UniWind effectively bridges physics-based and data-driven paradigms by explicitly separating meteorological availability from operational-state effects, enabling both accurate site-specific forecasting and robust zero-shot transfer to unseen wind farms.

title: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
summary: LLM agents increasingly perform autonomous actions through external tools, leading to complex and evolving safety risks. However, existing safety testing targets expert-designed safety violations, and the corresponding outcomes are evaluated by hard-coded rules, making them costly to extend as agents evolve. To this end, we present Vera, an end-to-end automated safety testing framework that instantiates software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic agents through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline. First, a literature-driven exploration continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. Second, combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions produces executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. Third, adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interaction based on runtime observations, while evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report. We evaluate Vera on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9\% under multi-channel attacks; we also release Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings. These results indicate that modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunhao-Feng/Vera.

AI.tldr: Vera is an automated safety testing framework for LLM agents that uses a three-stage self-reinforcing pipeline to continuously discover risks, compositionally generate executable safety cases, and adaptively evaluate agent behavior in sandboxed environments. Evaluated on four production agent frameworks, Vera achieved up to 93.9% attack success rates, demonstrating pervasive safety weaknesses.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent safety testing relies on expert-designed violations and hard-coded evaluation rules, which are expensive to maintain and extend as agents rapidly evolve. There is a need for automated, scalable, and maintainable safety evaluation infrastructure that can keep pace with the expanding attack surface of autonomous tool-using agents.
AI.method: Vera employs a three-stage self-reinforcing pipeline: (1) **Literature-driven exploration** continuously mines research to structure risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. (2) **Combinatorial composition** cross-products taxonomy dimensions to produce executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. (3) **Adaptive execution** runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent orchestrates multi-turn interactions based on runtime observations, with evidence-grounded verifiers judging outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report.
AI.result: Evaluated on OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, and Claude Code, Vera revealed average attack success rates of 93.9% under multi-channel attacks. Vera-Bench, a benchmark of 1,600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings, was released.
AI.conclusion: Modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. Vera demonstrates that automated, evidence-grounded safety testing can systematically uncover pervasive vulnerabilities that static or self-reported evaluation would miss.

title: SPLIT: Cross-Lingual Empathy and Cultural Grounding in English and Ukrainian LLM Responses
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Benchmark paper introducing SPLIT for evaluating empathy, linguistic naturalness, and cultural grounding in English and Ukrainian LLM responses
summary: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in emotional-support contexts and crisis-related situations. Nevertheless, their cross-lingual abilities in these circumstances remain underexplored. Existing benchmarks emphasize multilingual performance but rarely examine crisis-related empathy and cultural grounding in low-to-mid-resource languages. We introduce SPLIT, a 500-prompt benchmark designed to evaluate LLM consistency in generating emotionally grounded responses across five categories: Stress, Panic, Loneliness, Internal Displacement, and Tension. We evaluate three technically diverse LLMs across three dimensions: Empathetic Accuracy, Linguistic Naturalness, and Contextual & Cultural Grounding. The framework aims to assess and compare the quality of LLM responses in both English and Ukrainian languages, as well as to explore the reliability of the LLM-as-a-jury paradigm. Our findings reveal that Gemini-2.5-Flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct degrade when transitioning to Ukrainian, while DeepSeek-V3 remains comparatively stable within our benchmark. We additionally find that human and AI evaluators agree weakly on empathy and naturalness but diverge on cultural grounding. We further argue that producing Ukrainian text is not equivalent to producing Ukrainian emotional support. Our findings may assist in the future development of more culturally tailored benchmark designs, as well as encourage a stronger emphasis on human-centered evaluation.

AI.tldr: SPLIT is a benchmark of 500 prompts evaluating LLMs' cross-lingual emotional support across English and Ukrainian. Testing Gemini-2.5-Flash, LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, and DeepSeek-V3 on empathetic accuracy, linguistic naturalness, and cultural grounding reveals that most models degrade in Ukrainian, human-AI evaluator agreement is weak on cultural grounding, and producing Ukrainian text ≠ providing Ukrainian emotional support.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in emotional-support and crisis contexts, yet their cross-lingual capabilities in low-to-mid-resource languages remain underexamined. Existing multilingual benchmarks overlook crisis-related empathy and cultural grounding, creating a gap in understanding whether LLMs can provide culturally appropriate emotional support beyond English.
AI.method: The authors introduce SPLIT, a 500-prompt benchmark spanning five emotional categories (Stress, Panic, Loneliness, Internal Displacement, Tension). Three LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Flash, LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V3) are evaluated across three dimensions: Empathetic Accuracy, Linguistic Naturalness, and Contextual & Cultural Grounding, in both English and Ukrainian. The study also tests the reliability of the LLM-as-a-jury evaluation paradigm by comparing human and AI evaluator judgments.
AI.result: Gemini-2.5-Flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct show performance degradation when transitioning from English to Ukrainian, while DeepSeek-V3 remains comparatively stable. Human and AI evaluators exhibit weak agreement on empathy and naturalness and diverge on cultural grounding assessments. The authors argue that generating grammatically correct Ukrainian text is not equivalent to delivering culturally appropriate Ukrainian emotional support.
AI.conclusion: Cross-lingual emotional support remains a significant challenge for LLMs. The divergence between human and automated evaluation, especially on cultural grounding, underscores the necessity of human-centered evaluation frameworks. The findings advocate for more culturally tailored benchmark designs and caution against conflating linguistic fluency with genuine cultural competence in emotional-support contexts.

title: SCAPE: Accurate and Efficient LLM Training with Extreme Sparse Communication
summary: Communication increasingly dominates the cost of Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, especially under data-parallel and sharded training schemes, where gradient synchronization and parameter reconstruction overhead increase with model size and system scale. Existing communication-reduction methods either sparsify raw gradients, which can be unstable for modern Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, or quantize communication, whose savings are fundamentally bounded by bit width and often incur additional runtime overhead. We present SCAPE, a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM training that exploits the stability of AdamS's first-moment to enable aggressive sparsification without loss of LLM quality. Instead of constructing masks from raw gradients, SCAPE derives them from first-moment-based statistics, partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, and delays mask usage by one step so that mask synchronization can overlap with computation. SCAPE also reconstructs the quantities required for second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer, avoiding an additional collective. We implement SCAPE in Megatron-LM and evaluate its convergence by pre-training GPT-345M on OpenWebText and Llama-500M on SlimPajama-6B using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on TACC Vista. In both models, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under 90\% and 99\% sparsity. For Llama-500M, SCAPE reduces end-to-end pre-training wall-clock time by up to 43.3\% while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, SCAPE achieves up to 3.26$\times$ speedup per step compared to dense AdamS.

AI.tldr: SCAPE is a communication-efficient distributed optimizer that leverages AdamS's stable first-moment statistics to enable aggressive gradient sparsification (90–99%) without compromising LLM training quality, achieving up to 43.3% wall-clock reduction and 3.26× per-step speedup.
AI.motivation: Communication dominates LLM pre-training cost in data-parallel/sharded regimes due to gradient synchronization and parameter reconstruction. Existing solutions are inadequate: raw-gradient sparsification is unstable with Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, and quantization savings are fundamentally capped by bit width with additional runtime overhead.
AI.method: SCAPE derives sparsification masks from first-moment statistics (instead of raw gradients), partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, and delays mask usage by one step to overlap mask synchronization with computation. It reconstructs second-moment update quantities from a single synchronized sparse buffer, eliminating an extra collective communication.
AI.result: Evaluated on GPT-345M (OpenWebText) and Llama-500M (SlimPajama-6B) using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under 90% and 99% sparsity. For Llama-500M, end-to-end wall-clock time drops up to 43.3% versus dense AdamW/AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, per-step speedup reaches 3.26× over dense AdamS.
AI.conclusion: SCAPE demonstrates that first-moment-driven sparsification is both stable and highly effective for communication reduction in large-scale LLM pre-training, outperforming prior sparsification and quantization approaches while fully preserving model quality.

title: MMIR-TCM: Memory-Integrated Multimodal Inference and Retrieval for TCM Clinical Decision Support
summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) diagnosis, particularly through tongue inspection, faces persistent challenges in subjectivity and reproducibility. The application of multimodal artificial intelligence to TCM clinical tasks, such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation, is significantly hampered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, as well as the lack of large-scale, standardized datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce MMIR-TCM, a novel framework that emulates the diagnostic process of TCM experts by integrating multimodal large language model(MLLM) with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Employing a three-stage architecture, MMIR-TCM integrates a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation, and a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The framework was developed and validated using MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset that we introduce specifically for advanced TCM research. To properly evaluate our framework's clinical accuracy, which existing metrics fail to capture, we also developed TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric incorporating semantic understanding and diagnostic importance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

AI.tldr: MMIR-TCM is a multimodal AI framework for TCM tongue diagnosis that combines memory-augmented segmentation, a fine-tuned MLLM (Qwen3-VL), and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to bridge the semantic gap between visual features and clinical reasoning. Validated on a newly introduced large-scale dataset (MedTCM) with a novel evaluation metric (TDEU), it outperforms GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.
AI.motivation: TCM tongue inspection suffers from subjectivity and poor reproducibility. Existing multimodal AI approaches are hindered by (1) the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual diagnostic reasoning, and (2) the absence of large-scale, standardized multimodal TCM datasets, limiting progress in syndrome differentiation and prescription generation.
AI.method: The MMIR-TCM framework uses a three-stage architecture: (1) Memory-SAM, a training-free memory-augmented segmentation module for robust tongue extraction; (2) a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL MLLM for generating structured tongue diagnoses; and (3) a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The authors also introduce MedTCM, a large-scale multimodal TCM dataset, and TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric with semantic understanding and diagnostic importance weighting.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments show that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash, particularly in clinical accuracy as measured by the TDEU metric, which existing evaluation metrics fail to capture.
AI.conclusion: MMIR-TCM effectively bridges the visual-textual semantic gap in TCM diagnosis through its integrated memory-SAM, fine-tuned MLLM, and RAG components. The introduction of MedTCM and TDEU addresses critical data and evaluation gaps, establishing a new benchmark for multimodal AI in traditional medicine.

title: WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios
comment: This work appears in the ICML 2026 Workshop on Weight-Space Symmetries (WSS): from Foundations to Practical Applications. Our source code is available at github.com/SprocketLab/WARP
summary: Foundation models are routinely released to the public, yet the data recipes used to train them -- such as domain mixture weights that determine how different sources are sampled -- are rarely disclosed. This creates an access asymmetry: researchers study the resulting models but lack visibility into the training distribution that produces them. Prior works for inferring training data, such as membership inference, detect at the level of individual samples and thus cannot characterize the global composition of the training corpus. We introduce WARP, a framework that recovers a fine-tuned model's training mixtures directly from its released weights. WARP interpolates between the base and fine-tuned models using model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory and expose a geometric footprint of the training data in the weight space. From these simulated footprints, WARP extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures. In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.

AI.tldr: WARP recovers the training domain mixture of a fine-tuned model directly from its weights by interpolating between base and fine-tuned models to expose geometric footprints of training data, outperforming membership inference methods.
AI.motivation: Foundation models are widely released but their training data recipes (e.g., domain mixture weights) are rarely disclosed, creating an asymmetry where researchers can study models but not the distributions that produced them. Prior methods like membership inference operate at the individual sample level and cannot capture global training corpus composition.
AI.method: WARP interpolates between the base and fine-tuned model weights via model merging to generate pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the training trajectory. These simulated checkpoints produce geometric footprints in weight space. Geometric features are then extracted and mapped to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures.
AI.result: On controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE of 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming both membership inference baselines and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Training data composition can be effectively inferred from model weights alone using weight-space interpolation, providing a practical tool for auditing and understanding fine-tuned models without requiring access to training data or trajectories.

title: Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code
summary: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

AI.tldr: HECATE introduces the first complexity assessment tool for LLM-integrated applications, measuring both prompt and code layers. Using a Hoare-logic-inspired "Prompt-as-Specification" framework, it generates 52 candidate metrics across 25 dimensions, validates them against 118 components from 18 repositories, and identifies 10 significant metrics. Seven are newly introduced, emphasizing "structural breadth" over volume. Prompt-layer metrics retain independent significance, establishing prompt complexity as a distinct dimension.
AI.motivation: Existing software complexity metrics operate exclusively at the code level, but LLM-integrated applications derive substantial runtime behavior from the prompt layer. No prior tool can assess complexity across both layers, leaving a critical gap in understanding and maintaining these hybrid systems.
AI.method: HECATE employs Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism treating each prompt as a behavioral specification. The tool identifies 25 complexity dimensions from published taxonomies and generates 52 candidate metrics.
