These are empirically evaluated against 118 components from 18 open-source repositories, using maintenance activity (derived from version history) as a proxy for complexity. Metrics losing significance after controlling for code size are discarded. A held-out validation set of 20 components from 6 repositories tests generalizability.
AI.result: Only 10 of 52 metrics survive the empirical filtering. Seven are newly introduced, capturing "structural breadth" (e.g., LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates) rather than sheer volume. Among conventional metrics, only RFC, Halstead N, and Halstead V survive — RFC shares the breadth-oriented character, while N and V persist only as residual size effects. The top-performing new metrics outperform all three conventional ones. Prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric serves as a covariate, confirming prompt complexity as an independent dimension. Held-out validation confirms generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Prompt complexity constitutes a distinct, measurable dimension in LLM-integrated applications that cannot be reduced to code-level metrics. Structural breadth — counting distinct structural elements rather than volume — proves more predictive of maintenance effort than traditional size-based metrics. HECATE provides the first validated tool for dual-layer complexity assessment in this emerging application class.

title: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Benchmark available in inspect_evals (UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

AI.tldr: Pre-Flight is an open-source benchmark of 300 aviation-specific multiple-choice questions evaluating LLMs on ground operations, ICAO/FAA regulations, and operational scenarios. Even the strongest 2026 model reaches only 82.7% accuracy against a ~95% expert baseline, revealing a persistent reliability gap that the authors argue must be addressed before deploying generative AI in aviation operations.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLM benchmarks fail to measure safe, correct reasoning about aviation-specific operational knowledge. Given aviation's high-stakes, regulated nature, this gap is consequential. The authors aim to provide a rigorous, domain-specific evaluation to determine whether LLMs can be responsibly deployed in non-safety-critical aviation operations.
AI.method: The authors constructed Pre-Flight, a benchmark of 300 multiple-choice questions covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and FAA regulations, and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with air traffic management, ground operations, and commercial flying expertise. Models were evaluated using the Inspect evaluation framework with standard accuracy scoring. An informal expert reference (~95%) was established via a quiz administered to aviation professionals at a conference. A rolling leaderboard is maintained as new models are released.
AI.result: The strongest evaluated model (released in 2026) achieved 82.7% accuracy, representing only gradual improvement from ~75% in early 2025. A substantial gap of over 12 percentage points remains below the ~95% expert-level reliability reference.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation like Pre-Flight is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non-safety-critical aviation operations. The persistent gap below expert reliability indicates that current LLMs are not yet suitable for operational aviation use without careful oversight.

title: Unlocking Speech-Text Compositional Powers: Instruction-Following Speech Language Models without Instruction Tuning
summary: Instruction tuning for speech language models (SLMs) is substantially more challenging than for text-based large language models (LLMs), as it requires learning a new modality and a wide range of speech-specific instructions in addition to those supported by text LLMs. Existing SLM training approaches largely replicate the text LLM training paradigm by synthesizing large-scale speech pre-training and instruction-tuning datasets. However, this strategy is difficult to scale, since speech sequences are significantly longer than text sequences. In this paper, we propose SpeechCombine, an instruction-following speech language model trained without any instruction tuning, using only a single round of speech pre-training on 30k hours of data. Starting from a text LLM base model, we perform continuous pre-training on speech utterances to obtain a speech-adapted model, and then directly combine its weights with the weight difference between the instruction-tuned and base versions of the text LLM. Our results show that this simple combination strategy not only preserves the knowledge and capabilities of the original text LLM, but also effectively transfers them to the speech domain. These findings suggest a new direction for SLM training that avoids reliance on massive speech data.

AI.tldr: SpeechCombine trains speech language models without instruction tuning by combining speech-adapted weights with the weight delta from text LLM instruction tuning, using only 30k hours of speech pre-training.
AI.motivation: Instruction tuning for SLMs is challenging due to longer speech sequences and the difficulty of scaling speech instruction datasets. Existing approaches that replicate text LLM training paradigms are hard to scale.
AI.method: Starting from a text LLM base model, the authors perform continuous pre-training on speech utterances (30k hours) to obtain a speech-adapted model. They then directly combine its weights with the weight difference (delta) between the instruction-tuned and base versions of the same text LLM, bypassing any speech-specific instruction tuning.
AI.result: The simple weight combination strategy preserves the original text LLM's knowledge and capabilities while effectively transferring them to the speech domain, all without requiring speech instruction tuning.
AI.conclusion: This opens a new direction for SLM training that avoids reliance on massive speech data and complex multi-stage instruction tuning pipelines.

title: Model Merging as Probabilistic Inference in Fine-Tuning Parameter Space
comment: Accepted for Publication at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2026
summary: Model merging aims to combine existing single-task solutions into a multi-task solution without additional data-driven fine-tuning.~Most existing approaches achieve this using geometric properties of local solution spaces. However, such geometric views provide limited guidance for scoring how statistically useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks during merging. To address this, we formulate model merging from a new perspective of probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over the merged parameters. We show that several existing model merging methods arise as special cases of our framework under energy designs that impose implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals between merged and task-specific models. Empirically, we find that these residuals are often heavy-tailed which exposes a mismatch with the imposed light-tailed Gaussian structures. We address this with a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts, which better captures the observed residual behavior while admitting a provably convergent inference procedure. Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-arts baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/MinhLong210/PoE-EBM-Merging.git.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a probabilistic framework for model merging based on Product-of-Experts (PoE) with energy-based models, showing that existing methods implicitly assume Gaussian residuals (light-tailed), while real residuals are heavy-tailed. The authors introduce Cauchy experts to better capture this behavior, achieving SOTA performance.
AI.motivation: Existing model merging methods rely on geometric properties of local solution spaces, offering limited statistical guidance on how useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks. The authors identify a mismatch: current methods implicitly assume Gaussian (light-tailed) distributions on directional residuals, but empirical observations reveal heavy-tailed behavior.
AI.method: The authors reformulate model merging as probabilistic inference under a Product-of-Experts (PoE) framework, where each single-task solution defines an energy-based model (EBM) over merged parameters. They show existing merging methods emerge as special cases with Gaussian energy designs. To address the heavy-tailed residual mismatch, they propose a Cauchy-based heavy-tailed PoE design with a provably convergent inference procedure.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, validating the heavy-tailed Cauchy expert design.
AI.conclusion: The PoE-EBM framework unifies existing merging methods and reveals their implicit Gaussian assumption. Switching to heavy-tailed Cauchy experts better models real residual distributions and yields superior merging performance across diverse settings.

title: Actual causality in fault trees
summary: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

AI.tldr: Fault trees are extended beyond traditional "what can go wrong?" analysis to answer "why has it gone wrong?" by applying Halpern & Pearl's actual causality theory. The paper classifies all notions of actual causality in terms of fault tree structure and shows how minimal cut sets correspond to actual causes.
AI.motivation: Fault trees are well-established for prospective risk assessment (minimal cut set analysis), but they lack a formal framework for retrospective failure diagnostics — explaining why a specific failure occurred. The authors aim to bridge this gap by connecting fault trees to a rigorous theory of actual causality.
AI.method: The authors apply Halpern & Pearl's formal theory of actual causality to fault tree models. They systematically map the different causality notions (including "cause," "sufficient cause," and "but-for cause") onto the graph-theoretic and logical (Boolean) structure of fault trees, using minimal cut sets as the linking device.
AI.result: A complete classification is given: each variant of actual causality in Halpern & Pearl's framework is characterized in terms of structural properties of the fault tree. Minimal cut sets are formally shown to yield actual causes under these definitions.
AI.conclusion: Fault trees can serve a dual purpose — both prospective risk analysis and retrospective failure diagnostics — when augmented with actual causality theory. The classification provides a principled bridge between minimal cut set analysis and causal explanation of system failures.

title: Challenges and Recommendations for LLMs-as-a-Judge in Multilingual Settings and Low-Resource Languages
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge has become the dominant evaluation paradigm for many natural language generation tasks, due to shortcomings of conventional metrics and high correlations with human judgment, albeit mostly in English. There are now attempts to extend LLM-as-a-Judge to multilingual settings including low-resource languages. However, LLMs have limited proficiency in low-resource languages, and there is often no adequate human validation in these settings. To highlight the scope of the problem and current practices, we explore the use of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators in ACL Anthology papers focusing on multilingual settings and low-resource languages across a diverse set of tasks. Out of 650 papers mentioning LLM-as-a-judge, only 33 of them focus on low-resource or multilingual settings. Our in-depth analysis of these papers indicates inconsistent evaluation outcomes, a tendency to overtrust LLM judgments in multilingual settings, and the widespread reliance on a single judge model per study. To help the NLP community further, we conclude with recommendations about how to use LLM-as-a-Judge in multilingual and low-resource settings.

AI.tldr: A meta-analysis of ACL Anthology papers reveals that LLM-as-a-Judge is rarely validated for low-resource/multilingual settings — only 33 out of 650 papers address this — and exhibits inconsistent outcomes, overtrust in LLM judgments, and reliance on single judge models. The authors provide recommendations for robust multilingual evaluation.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge has become a standard evaluation paradigm for NLG tasks, showing high correlation with human judgment primarily in English. However, extending this paradigm to multilingual and low-resource language settings is problematic because LLMs have limited proficiency in these languages and human validation is often absent. The authors aim to systematically assess the scope and reliability of this practice.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic survey of ACL Anthology papers that mention LLM-as-a-Judge, identifying 650 such papers. They then filtered for papers specifically focusing on multilingual settings or low-resource languages (33 papers). An in-depth analysis of these 33 papers was performed to assess evaluation practices, consistency of outcomes, degree of reliance on LLM judgments, and judge model diversity.
AI.result: Only 33 out of 650 papers (≈5%) mentioning LLM-as-a-Judge address low-resource or multilingual settings. The analysis revealed: (1) inconsistent evaluation outcomes across studies, (2) a systematic tendency to overtrust LLM judgments without adequate human validation in multilingual contexts, and (3) widespread reliance on a single judge model per study rather than ensemble or multi-model approaches.
AI.conclusion: LLM-as-a-Judge is currently under-validated and potentially unreliable in multilingual and low-resource settings. The authors provide actionable recommendations for the NLP community to improve robustness, including better validation practices and avoiding overreliance on single-model judgments.

title: A Mathematical Introduction to Diffusion Models
comment: Lecture notes for the John Tukey Summer Graduate School on Mathematics of Generative Models at SLMath (June 22nd, 2026 -- July 2nd, 2026)
summary: These notes give a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the viewpoint of sampling, tracing a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, their error analysis, and inference-time control. Throughout, the material is layered into core definitions and identities proved in full, representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems stated with a proof roadmap. The intended audience is beginning graduate students with a background in probability but no prior exposure to stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

AI.tldr: A proof-oriented pedagogical introduction to diffusion models from a sampling perspective, covering classical sampling dynamics, modern diffusion samplers, error analysis, and inference-time control, aimed at beginning graduate students with probability background.
AI.motivation: To provide a self-contained, layered educational resource that bridges classical sampling theory and modern diffusion models, making the subject accessible to graduate students with probability knowledge but no prior exposure to SDEs, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.
AI.method: The material is structured in three layers of increasing rigor: (1) core definitions and identities with full proofs, (2) representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and (3) research-level theorems stated with proof roadmaps. The exposition traces a single coherent arc from classical sampling dynamics through to modern diffusion samplers.
AI.result: A comprehensive set of lecture notes that systematically derives diffusion models, their error bounds, and inference-time control techniques, all from first principles in sampling theory.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models can be understood as a natural evolution of classical sampling ideas, and this perspective, combined with layered exposition, makes the field accessible to mathematically mature readers without specialized background in stochastic analysis.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to CRAE 2026; to appear in SPIE Proceedings. Best Poster Award
summary: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

AI.tldr: CLAP is a closed-loop agent post-training framework that transforms noisy business data into structured training and evaluation artifacts, incorporating validation, diagnostics, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide adapter release suitability. Experiments on manufacturing scenarios show modest gains from LoRA-SFT, but only 3/5 batches improve; GRPO reveals high KL risks, and RAG proves essential for factual extraction despite added latency.
AI.motivation: Domain agents in industrial settings suffer from noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, mismatch between offline evaluation and real application performance, and risks associated with releasing adapters. These challenges make it difficult to reliably determine whether a fine-tuned adapter is truly beneficial for deployment.
AI.method: CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training) converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. The pipeline integrates data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to assess adapter suitability. QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT is applied, with GRPO used for KL risk assessment and application-chain replay for evaluating RAG-oriented adapters under realistic conditions.
AI.result: Across five anonymized manufacturing batches, LoRA-SFT yields average gains of 0.0098 in overall score, 0.0240 in pass rate, and 0.0280 in evidence accuracy, with reductions in hallucination and wrong facts. However, only 3 of 5 batches improve, some regress, and GRPO exposes high KL divergence risks. Application-chain replay with 100 cases shows that an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value extraction, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over a base+RAG setup but increases latency.
AI.conclusion: Domain-agent post-training should be managed through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying solely on training completion or a single offline metric. The closed-loop approach provides a more reliable basis for adapter deployment decisions.

title: BamiBERT: A New BERT-based Language Model for Vietnamese
summary: In this paper, we introduce BamiBERT, a new BERT-based pre-trained language model for Vietnamese that addresses key limitations of PhoBERT -- the current de facto Vietnamese text encoder. Trained from scratch on a 129GB corpus of general-domain Vietnamese text for 20 epochs, BamiBERT supports an extended context length of up to 2048 tokens and operates directly on raw input, eliminating the need for external word segmentation. Across 8 Vietnamese benchmarks, it achieves the best score on 11 of 15 metrics and the second-best on 3 others, setting a new state of the art among "base"-sized Vietnamese encoders and demonstrating strong cross-domain generalization. We release BamiBERT at: https://huggingface.co/Qualcomm-AI-Research/BamiBERT

AI.tldr: BamiBERT is a new BERT-based pre-trained language model for Vietnamese, trained from scratch on a 129GB corpus. It extends context length to 2048 tokens, removes the need for external word segmentation, and achieves state-of-the-art results among base-sized Vietnamese encoders across 8 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: PhoBERT, the current de facto Vietnamese text encoder, has key limitations that BamiBERT aims to address: dependency on external word segmentation and restricted context length. The authors seek to build a stronger, more practical Vietnamese encoder that operates directly on raw text.
AI.method: BamiBERT is a BERT-based model trained from scratch on a 129GB general-domain Vietnamese text corpus for 20 epochs. It supports up to 2048-token context length and processes raw input without external word segmentation. Evaluation is performed across 8 Vietnamese NLP benchmarks covering 15 metrics.
AI.result: BamiBERT achieves the best score on 11 out of 15 metrics and the second-best on 3 others, setting a new state of the art among base-sized Vietnamese encoders with strong cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: BamiBERT establishes a new state of the art for base-sized Vietnamese text encoders, outperforming PhoBERT while offering practical advantages such as longer context and segmentation-free processing. The model is publicly released on Hugging Face.

title: Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine for Solving High-Frequency Partial Differential Equations
summary: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency solutions remains a central challenge in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias -- the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency components preferentially. This paper proposes a Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM) framework that addresses this limitation through an additive mechanism for weight initialization. Rather than multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, the method translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping the variance fixed at unity, thereby avoiding the variance amplification inherent in scaling-based methods. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons, while FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for improved robustness. Theoretical analysis shows that the frequency variance under the proposed framework remains bounded and approaches unity regardless of target frequency, in contrast to the quadratic growth of conventional approaches. The method preserves the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, requiring only a single linear solve. Experiments on seven benchmark problems spanning six equation types -- Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, and advection-diffusion -- on both regular and complex geometries show that the linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The code and data accompanying this manuscript will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xgxgnpu/Physics-informed-vibe-coding/tree/main/FS-PIELM.

AI.tldr: FS-PIELM tackles spectral bias in physics-informed neural networks for high-frequency PDE solutions by shifting (rather than scaling) the mean of Gaussian weight initialization distributions, achieving 1–5 orders of magnitude accuracy improvement over existing PIELM variants while maintaining single-linear-solve efficiency.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed machine learning suffers from spectral bias — neural networks preferentially learn low-frequency components, making high-frequency PDE solutions difficult. Existing scaling-based approaches amplify weight variance quadratically, causing instability. A principled initialization strategy is needed that enables high-frequency learning without variance explosion.
AI.method: The authors propose Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM), which translates the mean of a unit-variance Gaussian weight distribution by a target frequency rather than scaling weights. Two variants: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes per neuron; FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for robustness. The method uses an additive mechanism that keeps variance bounded near unity regardless of target frequency, with theoretical analysis proving the variance remains O(1) versus O(ω²) for scaling methods. Only a single linear solve is required, preserving ELM efficiency.
AI.result: Across seven benchmark problems covering six equation types (Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, advection-diffusion) on regular and complex geometries, FS-PIELM-L achieved best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants.
AI.conclusion: The additive frequency-shift initialization strategy effectively mitigates spectral bias without the variance instability of scaling-based methods. FS-PIELM offers a computationally efficient, robust solution for high-frequency PDEs using extreme learning machines. Code and data are publicly available.

title: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement
summary: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

AI.tldr: LLM safety training predominantly conducted in English creates an "epistemic gap" where models confidently produce harmful content for low-resource language inputs. The authors introduce STEER, a gradient-guided attack that iteratively translates refusal-triggering words into low-resource languages, achieving up to 96.7% attack success rate and transferring even to GPT-4o-mini.
AI.motivation: LLM safety alignment is overwhelmingly English-centric, leaving it unknown whether safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and code-switched inputs. The authors aim to demonstrate and systematically exploit this multilingual safety generalization gap.
AI.method: STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement): a gradient-guided attack that (1) identifies tokens/words contributing most to the model's refusal behavior via gradient analysis on the refusal logit, (2) iteratively translates those high-importance words into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Evaluated across six open-source 8B models on JailbreakBench and AdvBench, compared against random code-switching and GCG baselines, with transfer testing on GPT-4o-mini.
AI.result: STEER achieves up to 93.0% ASR on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, substantially outperforming random code-switching and GCG. The attack transfers to GPT-4o-mini with 35.5% ASR without white-box access, indicating the vulnerability is architecture-agnostic and stems from the English-centric alignment data distribution.
AI.conclusion: Safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. The authors argue that robust multilingual safety requires broader language coverage during alignment training and explicit out-of-distribution detection with abstention mechanisms.

title: CheckRLM: Effective Knowledge-Thought Coherence Checking in Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning
summary: Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) have significantly improved performance on complex tasks by extending the reasoning chain. However, these chains are prone to containing factual errors, particularly in knowledge-intensive tasks. To address this issue, we propose CheckRLM, a framework that improves the reliability of the reasoning process through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by timely checking and correcting factual errors. Specifically, CheckRLM extracts factual claims from the reasoning chain to identify and localize subtle knowledge inconsistencies during inference. Upon detection of errors, a refinement mechanism performs minimal-cost yet precise corrections by leveraging external knowledge, ensuring coherence between the reasoning chain and correct knowledge. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CheckRLM substantially outperforms existing baselines, exhibiting a strong capability to mitigate error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning with lower costs. The code and data are available at https://github.com/AI9Stars/CheckRLM.

AI.tldr: CheckRLM is a framework that improves reasoning reliability in Reasoning Language Models by using Retrieval-Augmented Generation to detect and correct factual errors in reasoning chains in real-time, outperforming baselines while reducing error accumulation at lower cost.
AI.motivation: While Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) improve complex task performance via extended reasoning chains, these chains frequently contain factual errors, especially in knowledge-intensive tasks. Existing approaches lack timely, cost-effective mechanisms for detecting and correcting such errors during inference.
AI.method: CheckRLM extracts factual claims from the reasoning chain during inference to identify and localize subtle knowledge inconsistencies. Upon error detection, a refinement mechanism performs minimal-cost, precise corrections by leveraging external knowledge via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), ensuring coherence between the reasoning chain and correct knowledge.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show CheckRLM substantially outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating strong capability in mitigating error accumulation in long-horizon reasoning with lower computational costs.
AI.conclusion: CheckRLM offers an effective, cost-efficient solution for improving factual reliability in RLM reasoning chains by combining claim extraction, timely error checking, and minimal-cost refinement via RAG.

title: Predicting Closed-Loop Performance of Latent World Models: Offline Checkpoint Selection for MPC and Model-Based RL Under Non-Markovian Rewards in LunarLander
comment: Preprint, 19 pages (16 main text + 3 pages appendix), 7 figures, 4 tables. Video: https://youtu.be/4PxHFW_TYUw , Code: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM
summary: We study how to predict the downstream closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model from validation-time diagnostics alone. Choosing the right checkpoint from a world-model training run is difficult: validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE keep improving long after closed-loop performance has collapsed. We present a suite of structural validation-time diagnostics drawn from optimal-control theory and apply them to Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, which features shaped rewards. We train an RSSM [5, 4] world model on it and treat per checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. By evaluating 40 metrics against this oracle, we find that the strongest single predictor is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which measures the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace. We combine ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number offline checkpoint selection score, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF). The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and the same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy. Code and data: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem of selecting the best checkpoint during world model training, since validation loss and multi-step prediction error continue improving even after closed-loop performance degrades. The authors propose structural diagnostics from optimal control theory, identifying the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) as the strongest single predictor of downstream performance. They combine ROF with three regularizers into a composite score (CROF) for offline checkpoint selection, demonstrating that a CROF-selected world model enables a model-based A2C policy to outperform model-free A2C by ~24.5 return points with ~65× fewer real-environment interactions on LunarLander v3.
AI.motivation: World model training presents a critical checkpoint selection problem: standard metrics like validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE correlate poorly with closed-loop performance — they can keep improving long after the model's usefulness for planning/control has collapsed. Without a reliable offline metric, practitioners must resort to expensive online evaluation (running the full closed-loop policy) to select checkpoints, defeating much of the purpose of world model training. The authors aim to find validation-time diagnostics that reliably predict closed-loop quality without requiring environment interaction.
AI.method: The authors train an RSSM (Recurrent State-Space Model) world model on Gymnasium's LunarLander v3. For each training checkpoint, they compute: (1) an oracle metric — the CEM-MPC (Cross-Entropy Method Model Predictive Control) closed-loop return; and (2) a suite of 40 validation-time diagnostics, many drawn from optimal control theory. These include the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which quantifies how much of the reward prediction depends on the observable (vs. unobservable) latent subspace, plus structural regularizers. They evaluate each metric's correlation with the oracle and construct the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF) by combining ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number score for offline checkpoint selection. The selected world model is then used for both model-based A2C training and zero-shot CEM-MPC.
AI.result: ROF emerges as the strongest single predictor of closed-loop performance among the 40 metrics tested. The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that achieves ~24.5 higher return than a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline while using approximately 65× fewer real-environment interactions. The same CROF-selected world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy, confirming the general utility of the checkpoint selection approach.
AI.conclusion: Structural diagnostics from optimal control theory — particularly the Reward Observability Fraction — provide reliable offline signals for world model checkpoint selection, outperforming naive metrics like validation loss. The CROF score offers a practical, single-number criterion that enables sample-efficient model-based RL by ensuring the selected world model is genuinely useful for downstream control tasks, not just prediction.

title: CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection
comment: Published in The Visual Computer. Author manuscript version
summary: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

AI.tldr: CamoNAS is a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search framework for Camouflaged Object Detection that automatically searches cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, using an RGB-frequency dual-stream design with learnable wavelet transforms, achieving SOTA on four COD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and heuristic multi-scale feature fusion, which lack systematic optimization. There is a need for automated architecture design tailored to the unique challenges of COD (weak edges, ill-defined boundaries).
AI.method: CamoNAS introduces a hierarchical NAS search space spanning both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths. It employs an RGB-frequency dual-stream architecture where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream, enhancing frequency-domain cues critical for detecting camouflaged objects.
AI.result: CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance across four major COD benchmarks: CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, and CHAMELEON.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the effectiveness of Neural Architecture Search for Camouflaged Object Detection, showing that automatically searched architectures can outperform manually designed models for this challenging task.

title: On the Role of Directionality in Structural Generalization
summary: Several SLOG test categories explicitly involve directional distinctions (modifier position shifts, argument extraction positions), yet AM-Parser, the previous SOTA, uses an AM algebra whose operations do not encode direction. We redesign the symbolic backend around CCG directed types (deterministic CKY + single linear decoder, 30K learnable parameters). Under the same BERT-base encoder, the system achieves 75.9$\pm$6.4% LF exact match, surpassing AM-Parser (70.8$\pm$4.3%). Per SLOG's own category groupings, gains are highly directional: the CCG system outperforms AM-Parser on all 5 position-shift categories (+29.9pp), while AM-Parser outperforms on all 6 recursive-depth categories. Replacing the encoder with DeBERTa-v3-large yields 90.7$\pm$4.9%, with the largest encoder gains in recursive-depth categories, complementary to directionality's gains. Directional representations shift the bottleneck from the symbolic layer (AM-Parser's 0% category ceiling) to the neural layer, which improves with encoder upgrades.

AI.tldr: A CCG-based directed symbolic backend replaces AM algebra, achieving substantial gains on position-shift SLOG categories (+29.9pp) with BERT-base. Directional representations shift the bottleneck from symbolic to neural layers, enabling further gains with stronger encoders like DeBERTa-v3-large (90.7% LFEM).
AI.motivation: AM-Parser, the previous SOTA on SLOG, employs an AM algebra with operations that lack directional encoding, despite many SLOG test categories explicitly testing directional distinctions (e.g., modifier position shifts, argument extraction positions). This suggests a fundamental representational mismatch between the task demands and the symbolic formalism.
AI.method: The authors redesign the symbolic backend around CCG (Combinatory Categorial Grammar) directed types, implementing a deterministic CKY parser with a single linear decoder comprising only 30K learnable parameters. This sits atop a BERT-base encoder. Ablation extends to DeBERTa-v3-large to probe encoder-symbolic interaction.
AI.result: Under BERT-base, the CCG system achieves 75.9±6.4% LF exact match (vs. AM-Parser's 70.8±4.3%). Gains are asymmetric: CCG outperforms AM-Parser on all 5 position-shift categories (+29.9pp average), while AM-Parser retains advantage on all 6 recursive-depth categories. DeBERTa-v3-large yields 90.7±4.9%, with largest gains in recursive-depth categories — complementary to the directionality gains from the CCG backend.
AI.conclusion: Directional symbolic representations shift the performance bottleneck from the symbolic layer (where AM-Parser hit 0% on certain categories) to the neural encoder. This architectural refactoring makes the system more responsive to encoder upgrades, demonstrating a principled division of labor between symbolic and neural components.

title: Finite-Lag Operator Geometry of Recurrent Representations
summary: Recurrent representations are trajectories, but representation geometry is often measured from static snapshots. We develop finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs $(X_t,X_{t+Δ})$. The primitive is the conditional transport law $Q_Δ(dy\mid x)$, estimated by a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this directed finite-lag law we derive a source-centered transport tensor $G_Δ$, which decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation $W_Δ^ρ$, which summarizes directed lagged flow. We prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence of scalar summaries, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result showing that source-centered transport detects deterministic recurrent motion not recorded by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities in terms of the update $A_Δ$, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces finite-lag operator geometry to analyze recurrent neural representations from observed state transitions, decomposing transport into conditional spread, coherent displacement, and coordinate circulation, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation on repeat-copy networks.
AI.motivation: Recurrent neural representations evolve as trajectories over time, yet standard representation geometry methods rely on static snapshots, failing to capture directed, lagged dynamics. There is a need for a principled geometric framework that operates directly on observed source-successor pairs to quantify how hidden states transport over finite time intervals.
AI.method: The authors develop a finite-lag operator geometry built on the conditional transport law Q_Δ(dy|x) estimated via dense Gaussian source-smoothing. From this, they derive: (1) a source-centered transport tensor G_Δ that decomposes into conditional spread and coherent displacement; (2) an antisymmetric coordinate circulation W_Δ^ρ capturing directed lagged flow. They prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation theorem distinguishing deterministic recurrent motion from infinitesimal carré-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates quantities in terms of the update matrix A_Δ, source covariance, and innovation covariance.
AI.result: Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance-matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture-dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while showing that coherent displacement fraction depends on metric and resolution choices.
AI.conclusion: Finite-lag operator geometry provides a rigorous, interpretable toolkit for analyzing directed dynamics in recurrent neural networks, capturing transport phenomena invisible to static or infinitesimal methods. The approach opens avenues for architecture diagnostics and deeper understanding of temporal representation structure.

title: SkillCoach: Self-Evolving Rubrics for Evaluating and Enhancing Agentic Skill-Use
summary: Skills are becoming a reusable operational layer for LLM agents, encoding SOPs, domain rules, tool workflows, scripts, and validation routines. In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills make reliable skill-use difficult. Final verifier success is too coarse for both evaluation and training, since an agent may pass through trial and error while selecting distractor skills, skipping required steps, composing workflows incorrectly or omitting final checks. We introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and enhancing agentic skill-use. SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. It keeps the external verifier as a separate outcome signal, allowing process quality to be distinguished from accidental task success. The evolved rubrics further serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories. Experiments show that evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

AI.tldr: SkillCoach is a self-evolving rubric framework that evaluates LLM agent skill-use along four process dimensions—selection, following, composition, and reflection—using rubrics derived from real rollouts. It separates process quality from outcome success, yielding better evaluation and training supervision than final-verifier-only approaches.
AI.motivation: In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills cause agents to select distractors, skip steps, compose workflows incorrectly, or omit final checks. Final verifier success is too coarse for evaluation and training, as agents can succeed accidentally despite flawed skill-use, masking underlying process failures.
AI.method: SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real agent rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. An external verifier is retained as a separate outcome signal, decoupling process quality from accidental task success. Evolved rubrics are iteratively refined and used as process supervision to select high-quality training trajectories.
AI.result: Evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.
AI.conclusion: Process-oriented rubrics that evolve from real data offer a more granular and reliable alternative to outcome-only evaluation, enabling both better diagnosis of skill-use failures and more effective training signal selection for LLM agents.

title: World Wide Models: Literary Tools for Cultural AI
summary: LLMs stage a new form of cultural encounter that is massive, automated, and monolingual. Literary disciplines have always negotiated cultural struggles with comparative reading of literature, narratological and poetic analysis, critical theory, world literature, and translation. These tools have now become indispensable for building culturally literate AI. The essay develops a layered framework toward more nuanced textual models and pluralistic interpretations of AI, emphasizing the natural intersections of literature and AI development, connecting current debates in critical theory with structural monolingualism, and suggesting a new application of world literature approaches to address global AI textuality through macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability.

AI.tldr: The essay proposes a world-literature-inspired framework for developing culturally literate AI, arguing that literary-critical tools—comparative reading, narratology, translation theory—are essential for countering the massive, monolingual, automated textuality of LLMs and for enabling pluralistic, globally-aware AI interpretation.
AI.motivation: LLMs create an unprecedented form of cultural encounter that is massive in scale, automated in operation, and structurally monolingual. This poses a fundamental challenge: how to build AI systems that are genuinely culturally literate rather than reductive. The author argues that literary disciplines—which have long grappled with cross-cultural textual struggle through comparative literature, critical theory, narratology, and translation studies—now offer indispensable conceptual tools for addressing this challenge.
AI.method: The essay develops a layered analytical framework that (1) connects current debates in critical theory with the problem of structural monolingualism in AI, (2) maps the natural intersections between literary studies and AI development, and (3) adapts world literature methodologies—specifically macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability—as a lens for analyzing global AI textuality.
AI.result: The paper argues that literary-critical tools are not merely ancillary but indispensable to AI development. It positions the concepts of macrostructure (large-scale textual patterns), circulation (how texts travel and transform across contexts), and untranslatability (resistance to seamless cross-linguistic transfer) as key analytical categories for building and evaluating culturally nuanced AI models.
AI.conclusion: A world-literature approach—attending to macrostructure, circulation, and untranslatability—offers a productive pathway toward more nuanced textual models and pluralistic AI interpretations. Literary disciplines must be integrated into AI development to counter structural monolingualism and to ensure that AI systems reflect the complexity of global cultural and textual diversity.

title: Efficient Temporal Point Processes via Monotone Alternating Splines
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) have widespread applications across various domains. Compared to modeling the conditional intensity of a TPP, modeling its cumulative conditional intensity function (CCIF) improves computational efficiency and eliminates numerical approximation errors. However, current CCIF parameterizations uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which we identify as suffering from three structural deadlocks--convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and violations of CCIF modeling requirements--that fundamentally restrict their representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics. To resolve these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel framework called Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS). By leveraging distinct interpolation and extrapolation components, MAS provides a flexible and efficient framework for modeling CCIFs. Theoretically, MAS's interpolation provides strong fitting accuracy, while its extrapolation supports robust generalization, reducing the irreducible approximation gaps of MNNs. Extensive experiments show that MAS achieves superior performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS), a new framework for modeling cumulative conditional intensity functions (CCIFs) of temporal point processes, overcoming three structural limitations of existing Monotone Neural Networks (convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and CCIF requirement violations). MAS uses distinct interpolation and extrapolation components to achieve strong fitting accuracy and robust generalization, outperforming MNNs on synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Current CCIF parameterizations uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which suffer from three structural deadlocks: (1) convexity restrictions, (2) saturation limits, and (3) violations of CCIF modeling requirements. These limitations fundamentally restrict representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics. The authors aim to resolve these bottlenecks with a more flexible and theoretically sound framework.
AI.method: The paper introduces Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS), a framework that decouples CCIF modeling into distinct interpolation and extrapolation components. The interpolation component provides strong fitting accuracy on observed data, while the extrapolation component supports robust generalization beyond training regions, thereby reducing the irreducible approximation gaps inherent to MNNs.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that MAS achieves superior performance compared to existing MNN-based approaches for CCIF modeling in temporal point processes.
AI.conclusion: MAS successfully overcomes the three structural deadlocks of MNNs—convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and CCIF requirement violations—providing a flexible, efficient, and theoretically grounded alternative for modeling CCIFs in temporal point processes, with demonstrated empirical superiority.

title: Spec-AUF: Accept-Until-Fail Training under Train-Inference Misalignment for Masked Block Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting a block of tokens that the target model verifies left-to-right, committing only the longest accepted prefix. Block (DLM-style) drafters predict the whole block in parallel, which is fast but trained with a full-block cross-entropy that supervises every position against the gold continuation -- even though inference discards every token after the first rejection. Recent acceptance-aware objectives patch this by reweighting the full-block loss; we instead use teacher-forced learning as a motivation for how supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix. A mask-only block drafter has no input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, so AUF approximates that prefix-sensitive supervision on the loss side by keeping the cross-entropy support only through the drafter's first predicted failure. AUF is a single, detached change to the CE support -- no auxiliary objective, no verifier rollouts, and no change to the inference pipeline or the exactness contract. Within fixed drafter backbones and serving settings on Qwen3-8B, AUF raises the DFlash drafter's average emitted length $τ$, averaged over six benchmarks, from 2.40 to 2.61, with a gain on every benchmark, and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56 to 2.68). Two findings sharpen the picture: the decay-only baseline reaches higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse, and on DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, the standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.

AI.tldr: AUF (Accepted Until Failure) modifies the cross-entropy loss for block drafters in speculative decoding by truncating supervision at the first predicted rejection point, raising average emitted length from 2.40→2.61 on DFlash and 2.56→2.68 on Domino without changing inference.
AI.motivation: Standard block drafters are trained with full-block cross-entropy supervising every token position, yet at inference, only the prefix up to the first rejection is kept. This mismatch wastes supervision on positions that are discarded. Moreover, mask-only block drafters lack an input-side channel for conditioning on the gold prefix, so the authors seek a loss-side correction that concentrates supervision on the accepted prefix.
AI.method: AUF truncates the cross-entropy support at the drafter's first predicted failure — the first position where the drafter's argmax disagrees with the gold token. This is a single, detached modification: no auxiliary objectives, no verifier rollouts, and no changes to inference or the exactness contract. Teacher-forced learning motivates the principle that supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B across six benchmarks, AUF lifts DFlash's average emitted length τ from 2.40 to 2.61 (gains on every benchmark) and Domino's from 2.56 to 2.68. Notably, a decay-only baseline achieves higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse. Once AUF truncates support, standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert on DFlash.
AI.conclusion: Concentrating supervision only on the accepted prefix via a simple CE support truncation is sufficient and superior to full-block or reweighted losses. The finding that higher token accuracy can coexist with worse decoding performance underscores the importance of acceptance-aware training, and AUF renders additional decay weighting redundant.

title: HULAT2 at MER-TRANS 2026: Governed Multi-Agent Simplification for Spanish Easy-to-Read Generation
summary: This paper describes the participation of HULAT2-UC3M in the Spanish track of MER-TRANS 2026, a shared task on multilingual Easy-to-Read translation. Three fully automatic Spanish runs were submitted. RUN1 and RUN2 used a LangGraph-based multi-agent workflow combining Gemini 2.5 Flash and RigoChat-7B-v2, parallel generation strategies, internal quality signals, Event-Condition-Action routing, controlled editing and traceable decisions. RUN1 used the base workflow, while RUN2 activated an additional lexical-support layer based on a glossary and lexical resources. RUN3 was a RigoChat-based generate-evaluate-regenerate baseline with prompt engineering and LoRA-based adaptation. The official leaderboard reports BLEU-Orig, BLEU-Gold, SARI and BERTScore. During development, additional internal signals were also inspected, including semantic fidelity, readability, lexical simplicity, syntactic clarity and factual consistency. According to official SARI, RUN1 was the best HULAT2 run, with 44.0543 points, followed by RUN2 with 43.1049 and RUN3 with 38.5136. These results indicate that, in this task setting, signal-guided multi-agent routing outperformed the linear regeneration baseline. They also show that adding lexical support did not automatically improve reference-based scores. Further segment-level and document-level analysis are required to assess readability, factual consistency and user-oriented adequacy.

AI.tldr: The paper presents HULAT2-UC3M's participation in the MER-TRANS 2026 shared task on multilingual Easy-to-Read translation for Spanish. Three automatic runs were submitted: two multi-agent LangGraph-based workflows (with and without lexical support) and one LoRA-adapted regeneration baseline. The signal-guided multi-agent approach (RUN1, SARI: 44.05) outperformed the baseline (RUN3, SARI: 38.51), while lexical support unexpectedly reduced performance.
AI.motivation: To develop fully automatic systems for Easy-to-Read (E2R) Spanish translation that balance simplification, readability, and semantic fidelity, and to evaluate whether multi-agent routing with internal quality signals outperforms linear regeneration approaches.
AI.method: Three automatic runs: RUN1 uses a LangGraph multi-agent workflow with Gemini 2.5 Flash and RigoChat-7B-v2, parallel generation, internal quality signals, Event-Condition-Action routing, controlled editing, and traceable decisions. RUN2 extends RUN1 with a glossary-based lexical-support layer. RUN3 is a RigoChat-based generate-evaluate-regenerate baseline with prompt engineering and LoRA adaptation. Evaluation uses BLEU-Orig, BLEU-Gold, SARI, BERTScore, plus internal signals (semantic fidelity, readability, lexical simplicity, syntactic clarity, factual consistency).
AI.result: RUN1 achieved the best SARI score (44.0543) among the team's submissions, followed by RUN2 (43.1049) and RUN3 (38.5136). Signal-guided multi-agent routing significantly outperformed the linear regeneration baseline. Adding lexical support (RUN2) did not improve reference-based scores and slightly degraded performance.
AI.conclusion: In this task setting, signal-guided multi-agent routing with internal quality signals is more effective than linear regeneration for E2R translation. Lexical support layers do not automatically yield improvements in reference-based metrics. Further segment-level and document-level analysis is needed to assess readability, factual consistency, and user-oriented adequacy.

title: Role-Aware Neural Convex Divergence Heads for Asymmetric Representation Learning
summary: Many representation learning problems involve directed relations, such as lexical entailment, sentence entailment, ontology hierarchy, and citation links. Standard Euclidean, cosine, and Mahalanobis heads are symmetric, while generic neural scorers can model directionality but provide limited geometric structure. This paper proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning. The head applies source- and target-role projections before evaluating an input-convex neural Bregman divergence, yielding a nonnegative structured score in the role-projected space. We characterize its projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature. Experiments on lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed graph benchmarks compare symmetric distances, unstructured asymmetric scorers, order/hyperbolic baselines, plain ICNN-Bregman heads, and the proposed role-aware variant. Across ten random seeds on the main semantic and ontology benchmarks, role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads while preserving zero observed negative divergence rate. The results also identify a boundary case: on large fixed-feature citation prediction, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines remain stronger in ranking accuracy. Overall, the proposed head is best understood as a structured and interpretable plug-in distance module for tasks where directional relations matter.

AI.tldr: Proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning that applies source/target projections before an input-convex neural Bregman divergence, improving directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads while maintaining zero negative divergence rate.
AI.motivation: Standard similarity heads (Euclidean, cosine, Mahalanobis) are symmetric and cannot capture directed relations like entailment or hierarchy. Generic neural scorers can model directionality but lack geometric interpretability. A structured, asymmetric distance module with clear geometric properties is needed.
AI.method: A role-aware neural convex divergence head built on input-convex neural networks (ICNN) that computes Bregman divergences. Source and target embeddings undergo role-specific linear projections before entering the convex function, producing a nonnegative asymmetric score. The paper formalizes projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature properties.
AI.result: On lexical, sentence, and ontology benchmarks across 10 random seeds, role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads with zero negative divergence rate. On large fixed-feature citation prediction, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines remain stronger in ranking accuracy — identified as a boundary case.
AI.conclusion: The role-aware neural convex divergence head serves as a structured, interpretable plug-in distance module well-suited for tasks where directional relations matter, though symmetric/hyperbolic alternatives may be preferable for large-scale fixed-feature ranking scenarios.

title: Know Your Source: A Public Knowledge Store for Media Background Checks
summary: LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly used for automated fact-checking (AFC) and related tasks. By grounding LLM outputs in retrieved evidence, RAG-based systems provide transparent justifications while allowing external information to be updated independently of the underlying model. However, existing approaches often assume retrieved evidence is reliable, although real-world information may be conflicting, outdated, and can originate from unreliable or biased sources. Recent work on *source-critical reasoning* addresses this challenge through media background checks (MBCs) (Schlichtkrull, 2024), which assess the credibility of evidence sources to support downstream fact verification. However, generating MBCs relies on costly proprietary search APIs, limiting reproducibility. To mitigate this issue, we introduce MEDIAREF, a publicly available knowledge store of web-sourced documents that enables reproducible, low-cost evaluation of MBC generation across 200 media sources. We describe a reproducible methodology for constructing and updating the collection, assess widely used LLMs on the MBC generation task, and demonstrate that MEDIAREF supports higher-quality MBC generation through both automatic and qualitative evaluation.

AI.tldr: MEDIAREF is a publicly available knowledge store of web-sourced documents for 200 media sources, designed to enable reproducible, low-cost evaluation of media background check (MBC) generation for source-critical reasoning in RAG-based fact-checking, demonstrating improved MBC quality over reliance on proprietary search APIs.
AI.motivation: RAG-based fact-checking systems assume retrieved evidence is reliable, but real-world information is often conflicting, outdated, or biased. Source-critical reasoning via media background checks (MBCs) addresses this, but existing MBC generation relies on costly proprietary search APIs, limiting reproducibility. A reproducible, publicly available knowledge store is needed to enable low-cost, reproducible MBC evaluation.
AI.method: The authors introduce MEDIAREF, a publicly available knowledge store covering 200 media sources. They describe a reproducible methodology for constructing and updating the collection from web-sourced documents, and evaluate widely used LLMs on the MBC generation task using both automatic and qualitative metrics.
AI.result: MEDIAREF supports higher-quality MBC generation compared to existing approaches, as demonstrated through both automatic evaluation and qualitative assessment across multiple widely used LLMs.
AI.conclusion: MEDIAREF provides a reproducible, low-cost alternative to proprietary search APIs for MBC generation, advancing source-critical reasoning in RAG-based automated fact-checking.

title: Denser $\neq$ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training
summary: Continual post-training enables foundation models to acquire new knowledge while preserving existing capabilities. Recent work suggests that on-policy learning can mitigate forgetting, with on-policy self-distillation emerging as a particularly attractive approach. In this work, we revisit this optimistic view through self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO). Our experiments show that SDPO can accelerate in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and well aligned, but it struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios. In continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can even collapse, whereas on-policy reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO adapt more conservatively and better preserve prior capabilities. Further analyses reveal that denser self-distillation induces larger drift in both parameter space and response space, and can amplify high-frequency formatting artifacts through a self-reinforcing teacher--student loop. These findings suggest that on-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can accelerate specialization when teacher targets are stable and token-level supervision is reliable, but it should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Moenupa/SDPO-CL.

AI.tldr: Self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO) accelerates in-domain specialization but causes stronger forgetting and potential collapse in continual post-training compared to conservative on-policy RL methods like GRPO. Dense self-distillation induces larger parameter/response drift and amplifies formatting artifacts via self-reinforcing loops. On-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning.
AI.motivation: Recent work has suggested that on-policy self-distillation is an attractive approach for mitigating forgetting during continual post-training of foundation models. This paper revisits this optimistic view to rigorously test whether self-distillation truly serves as a reliable stabilizer for continual learning.
AI.method: The authors introduce Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and conduct systematic experiments comparing it against on-policy reinforcement learning methods (specifically GRPO) across continual post-training settings. They analyze drift in parameter space and response space, and examine the self-reinforcing teacher-student loop effects, including high-frequency formatting artifacts.
AI.result: SDPO accelerates in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and well-aligned, but struggles with out-of-distribution generalization. In continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can collapse, while GRPO adapts more conservatively and better preserves prior capabilities. Denser self-distillation induces larger parameter-space and response-space drift and amplifies formatting artifacts through self-reinforcing loops.
AI.conclusion: On-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can accelerate specialization under stable teacher targets and reliable token-level supervision, but should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training.

title: ContextSniper: AntTrail's Token-Efficient Code Memory for Repository-Level Program Repair
summary: Large language model agents can repair real repository issues, but they often spend large context budgets on whole-file reads, broad searches, and long terminal outputs where useful evidence is mixed with irrelevant code and logs. This paper presents ContextSniper, AntTrail's token-efficient code memory layer for repository-level program repair. As the coding specialization of AntTrail's broader agent memory engine, ContextSniper implements the Sniper feature for precision evidence selection: it retrieves candidate code and runtime evidence, ranks it with hybrid retrieval signals, filters long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and returns compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt. We evaluate ContextSniper on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code, using 50 task runs per host-agent condition. ContextSniper reduces total token use by 51.5% and logged cost by 36.4% for OpenClaw, and reduces total token use by 38.9% and estimated cost by 27.3% for Claude Code. Submitted-resolution rates decrease slightly, from 26.0% to 24.0% for OpenClaw and from 32.0% to 30.0% for Claude Code. ContextSniper's pilot testing scripts are open-sourced at https://github.com/Calluking/ContextSniper

AI.tldr: ContextSniper is a token-efficient code memory layer that reduces LLM agent token consumption in repository-level program repair by up to 51.5% through precision evidence selection, with only a marginal drop in resolution rates.
AI.motivation: LLM-based repair agents waste large context budgets on verbose operations (whole-file reads, broad searches, long terminal outputs), where useful evidence is diluted by irrelevant code and logs. This inefficiency drives up cost and limits scalability.
AI.method: ContextSniper, part of AntTrail's agent memory engine, implements a "Sniper" feature: (1) retrieves candidate code and runtime evidence, (2) ranks candidates using hybrid retrieval signals, (3) filters long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and (4) returns compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt.
AI.result: Evaluated on SWE-bench Lite across 50 runs per host-agent: with OpenClaw, token use dropped 51.5% and logged cost 36.4%; with Claude Code, token use dropped 38.9% and estimated cost 27.3%. Submitted-resolution rates decreased slightly from 26.0%→24.0% (OpenClaw) and 32.0%→30.0% (Claude Code).
AI.conclusion: ContextSniper achieves substantial token and cost savings with only a minor trade-off in repair accuracy, demonstrating that intention-aware, compact evidence selection is a viable strategy for making LLM-based program repair agents more efficient.

title: The Future of NLP may not be at NLP Conferences: Scholarly Migration Patterns in Natural Language Processing
summary: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has traditionally been published in its core disciplinary venues like ACL. However, advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to a blurring of the disciplinary lines between NLP and general Machine Learning (ML), with authors regularly publishing in venues from both fields. Here, we ask whether the disciplinary center of gravity is shifting. Using NLP research published from 2010 to 2026 and studies of both established and new authors, we find that a migration is taking place. First, comparing the pre- and post-LLM eras, established authors lost 19.2pp of share at flagship *ACL main-conference tracks while gaining 14.8pp in the newer Findings tracks, and general ML venues rose 8.6pp, even when adjusting for parallel growth in the fields. Second, among newer authors who debut with at least three first-author NLP-topic papers, the share whose work appears mostly at *ACL venues fell from 84% (2019) to 74% (2024), while the share appearing mostly at general ML venues rose from 5% to 21%. Using causal inference techniques, we estimate that these general ML venues confer a significant citation premium, which influences venue selection. Together, these results point to a significant shift in where NLP research is published.

AI.tldr: NLP research is migrating away from traditional *ACL venues toward general ML venues, driven partly by citation premiums offered by the latter. Established authors lost significant share in ACL main tracks while gaining in Findings tracks, and new authors increasingly publish in general ML venues.
AI.motivation: The blurring of disciplinary boundaries between NLP and general ML, accelerated by the rise of LLMs, raises the question of whether the disciplinary center of gravity in NLP research is shifting away from traditional NLP-specific venues.
AI.method: The authors analyzed NLP research publications from 2010–2026, examining venue distribution shifts for established authors (pre- vs. post-LLM eras) and new authors (debuting with ≥3 first-author NLP papers). They also applied causal inference techniques to estimate the citation premium of general ML venues.
AI.result: Established authors lost 19.2 percentage points of share in flagship *ACL main-conference tracks post-LLM, while gaining 14.8pp in Findings tracks and 8.6pp in general ML venues. Among new authors, those publishing mostly at *ACL venues dropped from 84% (2019) to 74% (2024), while those at general ML venues rose from 5% to 21%. A significant causal citation premium was found for general ML venues.
AI.conclusion: There is a clear and significant shift in where NLP research is published, with both established and new authors increasingly favoring general ML venues, influenced in part by citation incentives.

title: Set Diffusion: Interpolating Token Orderings Between Autoregression and Diffusion for Fast and Flexible Decoding
comment: ICML 2026. We provide the code at https://github.com/kuleshov-group/setdlms
