summary: Discrete diffusion models have steadily improved in quality relative to autoregressive (AR) models. However, these models are normally constrained to fixed-length generation and do not support key-value (KV) caching. Block diffusion partially bridges diffusion and AR by generating token blocks left-to-right, but its fixed-size sequential blocks limit decoding flexibility and parallelism. Here, we present a new class of language models, set diffusion, comprised of (i) a likelihood parameterization that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets and (ii) a set-causal diffusion architecture that supports KV cache updates after every inference step. By factorizing over token sets instead of fixed-size blocks, tokens can be decoded in arbitrarily-ordered sets, including sliding-window sets, enabling faster inference and support for any-order decoding. Set diffusion achieves better speed-quality tradeoffs on mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation compared to prior diffusion language models while offering stronger infilling performance than block diffusion. We provide the code, along with the model weights and blog post on the project page: https://m-arriola.com/setdlms/

AI.tldr: Set diffusion introduces a new class of language models that factorize over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets with a set-causal diffusion architecture supporting KV caching, enabling arbitrarily-ordered decoding with faster inference and better speed-quality tradeoffs than prior diffusion language models.
AI.motivation: Discrete diffusion models are constrained to fixed-length generation and lack KV caching support. Block diffusion partially addresses this with left-to-right block generation, but its fixed-size sequential blocks limit decoding flexibility and parallelism. The authors aim to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: Set diffusion consists of (1) a likelihood parameterization that factorizes over flexible-position, flexible-length token sets instead of fixed-size blocks, and (2) a set-causal diffusion architecture that supports KV cache updates after every inference step. Tokens can be decoded in arbitrarily-ordered sets (e.g., sliding-window sets), enabling any-order decoding.
AI.result: Set diffusion achieves better speed-quality tradeoffs on mathematical reasoning, summarization, and unconditional generation compared to prior diffusion language models, while offering stronger infilling performance than block diffusion.
AI.conclusion: Set diffusion unifies the strengths of diffusion and autoregressive generation by enabling flexible, efficient, and high-quality token generation through set-based factorization and set-causal architecture with KV caching.

title: Language Models as Measurement Apparatus for Culture
comment: Accepted to the Big Picture workshop co-located with ACL 2026. This version expands the camera-ready (adding Fig. 3 and section 6.3, as well as correcting minor typos) in Proceedings of The Big Picture v2: Crafting a Research Narrative, pp. 131--143, San Diego, CA, USA. Association for Computational Linguistics
summary: Language models are increasingly used to quantify cultural phenomena, but what makes such measurement distinctively cultural? This paper argues that NLP work on culture is a material-discursive practice: the apparatus -- model, data, annotation, evaluation -- participates in constituting the cultural reality it measures, rather than passively recording it. Drawing on Karen Barad's concept of the agential cut -- the contingent boundary between phenomenon and instrument -- I show that the apparatus's substantive design choices draw such boundaries, and that the boundary is entangled from the start because language models have already internalized much of the cultural material they measure. I illustrate this through three case studies on television and film dialogue (measuring structure, interaction, and deviation) and three examinations of the apparatus itself (erasure of cultural markers, attunement to historical material, and agency in an agentic workflow). This big picture analysis proposes a research program that is theory-driven, empirically rigorous, and culturally contingent, treating each agential cut as a conscious commitment, at once methodological and ethical.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that NLP-based cultural measurement is not a neutral recording of reality but a "material-discursive practice" where the apparatus (model, data, annotation, evaluation) actively co-constitutes the cultural phenomena it studies. Using Barad's "agential cut" concept, the author demonstrates through three case studies on media dialogue and three examinations of the apparatus itself that design choices draw contingent boundaries between instrument and phenomenon, and that language models are always already entangled with the cultural material they measure.
AI.motivation: To challenge the assumption that NLP tools passively measure pre-existing cultural realities, and to develop a theoretically grounded framework that treats cultural measurement with language models as an active, boundary-drawing practice with both methodological and ethical stakes.
AI.method: A theoretical analysis drawing on Karen Barad's agential realism and the concept of the "agential cut." The argument is grounded through three illustrative case studies on measuring structure, interaction, and deviation in television/film dialogue, plus three reflexive examinations of the apparatus: erasure of cultural markers, attunement to historical material, and agency in agentic workflows.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that substantive design choices in the NLP apparatus draw contingent boundaries between phenomenon and instrument, and that these boundaries are always already entangled because language models have internalized the cultural material they purport to measure. Each "agential cut" represents a conscious commitment with methodological and ethical implications.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes a research program for culturally-aware NLP that is theory-driven, empirically rigorous, and culturally contingent, where each agential cut is treated as a deliberate, consequential decision rather than a neutral technical step.

title: EHHN: An Event-driven Heterogeneous Hypergraph Network for Object-Centric Next Activity Prediction
summary: Next activity prediction helps service-oriented processes anticipate upcoming steps before delays, exceptions, or service-level risks occur. Most existing methods assume classical single-case event logs, whereas real service processes often involve events shared by multiple typed business objects. Object-centric event logs (OCELs) capture such interactions, but current predictors remain limited. Flattening-based approaches lose cross-object context, and native OCEL graph-based approaches encode multi-object events through pairwise relations. Existing models also do not jointly capture event-driven object state changes, inter-event timing, and global execution patterns. We propose EHHN, an Event-driven Heterogeneous Hypergraph Network for object-centric next activity prediction. EHHN represents each prediction prefix as a heterogeneous hypergraph, where event--object hyperedges bind retained co-participating objects and a lifecycle hyperedge groups the primary object's observed lifecycle events. Based on this representation, EHHN uses a dual-stream architecture in which a micro-spatial stream models event-driven object-state evolution and a macro-evolution stream captures temporal dynamics using retrieved global prototypes. The two streams are fused to predict the next activity. Experiments on four public OCEL benchmarks against nine baselines show that EHHN achieves the best accuracy and macro F1-score on all datasets, with improvements of up to 8.1 and 12.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines. Compared with the strongest OCEL-native graph baseline, EHHN also reduces peak GPU memory by up to 24 times. Code is available at https://github.com/chenkaitao1112/EHHN.

AI.tldr: EHHN proposes an event-driven heterogeneous hypergraph network for next activity prediction in object-centric event logs (OCELs), using dual-stream micro-spatial and macro-evolution modeling to jointly capture object state changes, inter-event timing, and global patterns, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and memory efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing next activity prediction methods are designed for classical single-case event logs, but real service processes involve multi-object interactions captured by OCELs. Flattening-based approaches lose cross-object context, while native OCEL graph-based methods only encode pairwise relations and fail to jointly capture event-driven object state changes, inter-event timing, and global execution patterns.
AI.method: EHHN models each prediction prefix as a heterogeneous hypergraph with two hyperedge types: event–object hyperedges bind co-participating objects, and lifecycle hyperedges group the primary object's observed events. A dual-stream architecture is employed: a micro-spatial stream models event-driven object-state evolution, and a macro-evolution stream captures temporal dynamics via retrieved global prototypes. The two streams are fused for final prediction.
AI.result: On four public OCEL benchmarks against nine baselines, EHHN achieves the best accuracy and macro F1-score on all datasets, with improvements up to 8.1 and 12.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines. It also reduces peak GPU memory by up to 24× compared to the strongest OCEL-native graph baseline.
AI.conclusion: EHHN demonstrates that heterogeneous hypergraph representations with dual-stream event-driven and temporal modeling significantly outperform both flattening-based and pairwise graph-based approaches for object-centric next activity prediction, while also being substantially more memory-efficient.

title: A-TMA: Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: Long term memory lets LLM agents act as persistent assistants, but user facts change. A useful memory system must know what is true now, what used to be true, and what changed. We study \emph{ghost memory}, a state coordination failure in which old, current, and transition facts coexist in the memory bank, remain mixed during retrieval, and mislead the answer model. We argue that memory systems should be understood and optimized from three levels: bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer time resolution. We propose ATMA, a state aware overlay for existing memory systems. ATMA keeps superseded and transition records in the bank, builds evidence packets for the query's requested state view, and exposes current, historical, and transition labels to QA. We further call for decoupled evaluation of bank, retrieval, and answer level failures, since final QA accuracy can hide where ghost memory occurs. To make this failure measurable, we build LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict heavy benchmark for ghost memory, and evaluate on LoCoMo for long conversation generalization. On LTP, Graphiti+ATMA improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over Graphiti. On LoCoMo, Graphiti+ATMA raises temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705. The gains are host dependent, but they indicate that explicit state roles can reduce memory failures hidden by final QA accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "ghost memory" — a failure mode where outdated, current, and transitional facts coexist in LLM agent memory, causing retrieval confusion. The authors propose ATMA, a state-aware overlay that labels records by temporal status (current/historical/transition) and improves conflict resolution. A new benchmark, LTP, quantifies these failures across bank, retrieval, and answer levels.
AI.motivation: LLM agents with long-term memory must track evolving user facts, but existing memory systems fail to distinguish what is currently true, what was historically true, and what changed. This leads to "ghost memory," where stale and current facts mix during retrieval and mislead answers. Current evaluation metrics like final QA accuracy mask where these failures originate, motivating a decoupled, multi-level analysis framework.
AI.method: The authors propose ATMA (A Temporal Memory Architecture), a state-aware overlay compatible with existing memory systems. ATMA operates at three levels: (1) bank maintenance — retaining superseded and transition records alongside current ones; (2) retrieval — constructing evidence packets tagged with the query's requested temporal view; (3) answer time — exposing current, historical, and transition labels to the QA model. They also introduce LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict-heavy benchmark designed to surface ghost memory failures, and evaluate using LoCoMo for long-conversation generalization.
AI.result: On LTP, Graphiti+ATMA improved conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over baseline Graphiti. On LoCoMo, Graphiti+ATMA raised temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705. Gains were host-system-dependent but consistently demonstrated that explicit state-role labeling reduces memory failures otherwise hidden by final QA accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Memory systems for LLM agents should be understood and optimized across three decoupled levels: bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer-time resolution. Explicit temporal state labeling via ATMA reduces ghost memory failures. Decoupled evaluation using benchmarks like LTP reveals failure points that aggregate QA accuracy obscures, enabling targeted improvements.

title: Will Scaling Improve Social Simulation with LLMs?
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) social simulations are a promising research method, but they are not yet faithful enough to be adopted widely. In this work, we investigate whether the current scaling paradigm in language modeling is likely to close these gaps, or whether simulation fidelity is orthogonal to general capabilities and therefore deserving of more research attention. We use scaling laws to study the relationship between LLMs' compute scale, general capability benchmarks, and the fidelity of social simulation in three representative sub-domains: opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, and longitudinal forecasting. Surprisingly, we discover strong compute scaling in all three settings, using a suite of 85 transformer LLMs with the Qwen3 architecture pre-trained on the DCLM web text corpus under fixed-compute budgets from $10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$ FLOPs. Then we evaluate 35 larger and more capable open-weight models up to 70B parameters, allowing us to predict downstream accuracy from loss. This reveals that the majority of behavioral and opinion simulation tasks will rapidly improve with scale, particularly when they involve populations that are well-represented in English web corpora. Longitudinal forecasting and underrepresented opinions scale more slowly, especially when they are less correlated with general knowledge and reasoning benchmarks like MMLU. In behavior simulation, scaling fails to improve model calibration with human cognitive biases like risk aversion, as well as human heuristics like learning correlated rewards from related tasks. On these tasks, even fine-tuned models fail to noticeably scale up performance from 0.5B to 8B parameters. Taken together, we conclude that scale will improve social simulations in most settings, but outliers exist, and improvements will be less reliable in low-resource domains.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether scaling up LLMs improves social simulation fidelity across opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, and longitudinal forecasting. Using 85 Qwen3-architecture models (10¹⁸–10²⁰ FLOPs) and 35 open-weight models up to 70B parameters, the authors find strong compute scaling in most settings, but scaling fails for human cognitive biases (e.g., risk aversion) and correlated reward learning. Fidelity improvements correlate with representation in English web corpora and general capability benchmarks, leaving low-resource domains less reliable.
AI.motivation: LLM-based social simulations are not yet faithful enough for widespread adoption. The authors seek to determine whether simply scaling models (the dominant paradigm) will close these fidelity gaps, or whether simulation fidelity is orthogonal to general capabilities and thus requires dedicated research attention.
AI.method: The authors employ scaling laws analysis using 85 transformer LLMs (Qwen3 architecture, pre-trained on DCLM web text corpus) under fixed compute budgets from 10¹⁸ to 10²⁰ FLOPs. They also evaluate 35 larger open-weight models (up to 70B parameters) to predict downstream accuracy from loss, across three social simulation sub-domains: opinion modeling, behavioral simulation, and longitudinal forecasting.
AI.result: Strong compute scaling was found in all three sub-domains. Most behavioral and opinion simulation tasks improve rapidly with scale, especially for populations well-represented in English web corpora. However, longitudinal forecasting and underrepresented opinions scale more slowly (particularly when uncorrelated with MMLU-like benchmarks). Critically, scaling fails to improve model calibration with human cognitive biases (e.g., risk aversion) and heuristics like learning correlated rewards — even fine-tuned models show no meaningful improvement from 0.5B to 8B parameters on these tasks.
AI.conclusion: Scale will improve social simulation fidelity in most settings, but notable outliers exist. Improvements are less reliable in low-resource domains, and some aspects of human-like cognition (risk aversion, correlated reward learning) appear fundamentally resistant to scaling, warranting dedicated research beyond the scaling paradigm.

title: EPnG: Adaptive Expert Prune-and-Grow for Parameter-Efficient MoE Fine-tuning
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale efficiently but remain costly to adapt due to redundant experts and uniform parameter allocation. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA ignore MoE routing dynamics, leading to suboptimal resource use. We propose EPnG, an adaptive prune-and-grow framework that reallocates LoRA capacity based on expert importance derived from router gate probabilities. EPnG prunes under-utilized experts and expands high-importance experts via rank growth with orthogonal initialization, while maintaining a fixed parameter budget. Across OLMoE and Qwen1.5-MoE, EPnG consistently outperforms LoRA under the same budget and achieves performance comparable to full fine-tuning while updating only 0.55%-0.72% of parameters (up to 140x-180x fewer). These results demonstrate that aligning PEFT with MoE routing yields a more effective and scalable fine-tuning strategy.

AI.tldr: EPnG is an adaptive prune-and-grow LoRA framework for MoE models that reallocates parameter budget based on expert importance from router probabilities, achieving full fine-tuning performance with only 0.55–0.72% of parameters updated.
AI.motivation: MoE models suffer from redundant experts and uniform parameter allocation during fine-tuning. Existing PEFT methods like LoRA ignore the routing dynamics inherent to MoE architectures, resulting in suboptimal resource utilization. There is a need for a fine-tuning approach that explicitly accounts for which experts are actually important.
AI.method: EPnG uses router gate probabilities to compute expert importance scores. Based on these scores, it prunes LoRA adapters from under-utilized experts and grows (expands) the rank of LoRA adapters for high-importance experts, using orthogonal initialization for the expanded dimensions. The total parameter budget is kept fixed throughout this reallocation process.
AI.result: On OLMoE and Qwen1.5-MoE benchmarks, EPnG consistently outperforms standard LoRA under identical parameter budgets. It matches full fine-tuning performance while updating only 0.55%–0.72% of parameters (140x–180x fewer parameters).
AI.conclusion: Aligning PEFT strategies with MoE routing dynamics—by adaptively reallocating capacity toward important experts—yields a more effective and scalable fine-tuning strategy than uniform LoRA allocation.

title: Atomic Task Graph: A Unified Framework for Agentic Planning and Execution
summary: LLM-based agents have shown strong potential for solving complex multi-step tasks, yet existing performance improvements often rely on either scaling to larger backbone models or task-specific fine-tuning. The former incurs substantial computational costs, while the latter typically generalizes poorly across different tasks. Although prompt-based control is training-free and broadly applicable, existing methods still leave input-output dependencies between subtasks implicit in textual trajectories, making verified intermediate results difficult to reuse. To address these limitations, we propose Atomic Task Graph (ATG), a unified control framework for planning and execution. Specifically, ATG maintains an explicit graph to expose dependencies and support reuse. During planning, it recursively decomposes a high-level task into subtasks, forming a sequence of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) whose evolution can be traced. During execution, the dependencies exposed by ATG allow independent branches to be executed in parallel, thereby improving execution efficiency. When failures are detected, ATG leverages the graph evolution history to localize the error source and repair only the affected region, preserving validated regions unchanged. Experiments show that ATG consistently outperforms strong baselines in success rate and execution efficiency across three interactive benchmarks using only 7B-8B backbones.

AI.tldr: ATG introduces an explicit graph-based control framework that decomposes tasks into directed acyclic graphs, enabling parallel execution, result reuse, and localized failure repair — achieving strong performance with smaller 7B-8B models.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-agent improvements either scale up expensive backbone models or use task-specific fine-tuning that generalizes poorly. Prompt-based methods are training-free but leave inter-subtask dependencies implicit, preventing reuse of verified intermediate results and efficient error recovery.
AI.method: ATG maintains an explicit directed acyclic graph (DAG) that captures input-output dependencies among subtasks. During planning, it recursively decomposes high-level tasks into evolving DAG sequences. During execution, independent branches run in parallel. Upon failure, ATG traces graph evolution history to pinpoint the error source and repairs only the affected subgraph, leaving validated regions intact.
AI.result: ATG consistently outperforms strong baselines in both success rate and execution efficiency across three interactive benchmarks, using only 7B-8B parameter backbone models.
AI.conclusion: Explicit dependency modeling via ATG enables smaller LLMs to achieve competitive or superior performance on complex multi-step tasks through better reuse, parallelism, and targeted error repair — offering a cost-effective alternative to scaling or fine-tuning.

title: Audio-Based Understanding of Audiobook Narration Appeal
summary: Narration is central to the audiobook listening experience, shaping how listeners engage with and understand the content. This work explores how narration qualities shape an audiobook's appeal, noting that their effects can vary by genre, title, and audience. We extract vocal and acoustic features (e.g., tone, pace, loudness) from LibriVox using pre-trained audio models and analyse their relationship with consumption data (specifically, view-rate) and their interplay with genre and title. Despite limited consumption data, we find that acoustic information alone has a robust association with appeal, even after accounting for title effects. We further validate these findings using more nuanced proprietary engagement metrics. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic computational study linking narration qualities, genre, title, and audiobook consumption, highlighting the potential of data-driven insights to improve audiobook personalisation and narrator casting.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic computational study linking narration qualities (vocal/acoustic features) to audiobook consumption, finding that acoustic information robustly predicts appeal even after controlling for title effects, with implications for personalization and narrator casting.
AI.motivation: Narration is central to the audiobook experience, yet no prior work has systematically and computationally examined how narration qualities (tone, pace, loudness) influence audiobook appeal across different genres, titles, and audiences.
AI.method: The authors extract vocal and acoustic features (e.g., tone, pace, loudness) from LibriVox audiobooks using pre-trained audio models and analyze their relationship with consumption data (view-rate), examining interplay with genre and title. Findings are further validated using proprietary engagement metrics.
AI.result: Acoustic information alone has a robust association with audiobook appeal, even after controlling for title effects. The relationship holds when validated against more nuanced proprietary engagement metrics, despite limited consumption data.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven analysis of narration qualities can improve audiobook personalization and narrator casting decisions, demonstrating the value of computational approaches to understanding listener engagement.

title: Single-Channel EEG-Based Cognitive Load Assessment in Online Learning: A Hybrid Deep Learning Approach
summary: Monitoring cognitive load during online learning could help instructors identify content that learners find difficult, but remote settings remove the visual cues that support this judgement in a classroom. We study whether a single-channel, consumer-grade EEG device (the NeuroSky MindWave Mobile 2) can distinguish easy from difficult educational-video content, using the publicly available dataset of Wang et al. [24] (ten learners, one excluded for excessive noise, leaving nine). We implement a hybrid CNN+LSTM+Attention model that combines the raw waveform with band-power features. In a within-subject setting, the model reaches up to 78.5% accuracy, compared with 55% for conventional feature-based classifiers; regularization (dropout and L2) closes the large gap between training and validation accuracy that we observe without it, keeping validation accuracy stable at roughly 68-73%. We are deliberately cautious about these numbers: with only nine subjects, within-subject evaluation is optimistic, and we argue that subject-independent evaluation -- in which no learner appears in both training and test data -- should be the standard for this task. To that end we release a reproducible evaluation pipeline. We frame the work as a feasibility study rather than a deployable system, and pair it with an open, notebook-based tool that records EEG, runs inference, and visualizes estimated cognitive load as a heatmap over the video timeline to help educators locate potentially challenging segments.

AI.tldr: Using a consumer-grade EEG device and a hybrid CNN+LSTM+Attention model, this study achieves up to 78.5% within-subject accuracy in distinguishing difficult from easy educational video content, while arguing that subject-independent evaluation should become the standard for cognitive load monitoring tasks.
AI.motivation: Remote online learning eliminates the visual cues instructors rely on in classrooms to gauge learner difficulty. The authors explore whether a low-cost, single-channel consumer EEG device can serve as a practical proxy for monitoring cognitive load during video-based learning, enabling instructors to identify challenging content without physical presence.
AI.method: The study uses the public Wang et al. dataset (9 learners after excluding 1 for noise). A hybrid CNN+LSTM+Attention architecture is implemented, combining raw EEG waveforms with band-power features. Regularization via dropout and L2 is applied to mitigate overfitting. Both within-subject and subject-independent evaluation paradigms are examined, and an open-source reproducible pipeline plus a notebook-based tool for EEG recording, inference, and heatmap visualization are released.
AI.result: Within-subject classification reaches up to 78.5% accuracy, substantially outperforming conventional feature-based classifiers (55%). Regularization closes a large train-validation gap, stabilizing validation accuracy around 68–73%. The authors caution that within-subject results are optimistic given the small sample (N=9) and advocate for subject-independent evaluation as the more rigorous standard.
AI.conclusion: This is framed as a feasibility study, not a deployable system. The results suggest consumer-grade EEG can capture cognitive-load signals but highlight the need for subject-independent benchmarks, larger datasets, and reproducibility. The accompanying open-source tool aims to bridge research and practical educational use.

title: OntoLearner: A Modular Python Library for Ontology Learning with Large Language Models
comment: 30 pages. Under review at Nature Communications. This version is reformatted with a different section structure; content is unchanged
summary: Ontology learning (OL) aims to automatically construct structured knowledge models from text, yet progress remains fragmented across methods, domains, and evaluation practices. Despite decades of research, OL lacks a shared infrastructure for systematic evaluation and ontology access. This absence has hindered progress and fragmented research, leaving the central challenges of OL largely unaddressed. We introduce OntoLearner, a modular, cross-domain, and first-of-its-kind framework that unifies ontology access, large language model (LLM)-driven learning pipelines, and standardized benchmarking. OntoLearner releases 180 machine-readable ontologies spanning 22 domains and provides pipeline-ready datasets with train/dev/test splits for three core OL tasks: term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relation extraction. Using this infrastructure, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of OL, evaluating 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs across domains and tasks. The results converge on a finding that reframes the central challenge of OL: failure modes scale with ontological complexity rather than model size or architectural sophistication. The primary bottleneck is not model capability, but a structural mismatch between how models encode knowledge and how ontologies organize it. These findings establish that effective OL is reachable through the cross-domain, multi-task benchmarking enabled by OntoLearner. OntoLearner is open-source (MIT license) at https://github.com/sciknoworg/OntoLearner/.

AI.tldr: OntoLearner is a modular framework unifying ontology access, LLM-driven learning pipelines, and standardized benchmarking across 180 ontologies in 22 domains. Large-scale evaluation of 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs reveals that the primary bottleneck in ontology learning is not model capability but a structural mismatch between how models encode knowledge and how ontologies organize it.
AI.motivation: Ontology learning research remains fragmented across methods, domains, and evaluation practices, lacking shared infrastructure for systematic evaluation and ontology access. This absence has hindered progress and left central challenges unaddressed.
AI.method: The authors introduce OntoLearner, a modular, cross-domain framework that integrates: (1) release of 180 machine-readable ontologies across 22 domains, (2) pipeline-ready datasets with train/dev/test splits for term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relation extraction, and (3) a standardized benchmarking infrastructure. Using this, they evaluate 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs across domains and tasks.
AI.result: Failure modes in OL scale with ontological complexity rather than model size or architectural sophistication. The primary bottleneck is a structural mismatch between how models encode knowledge and how ontologies organize it — not model capability per se.
AI.conclusion: Effective ontology learning is achievable through cross-domain, multi-task benchmarking as enabled by OntoLearner. The findings reframe the central challenge of OL away from model scaling toward addressing the structural misalignment between model knowledge representations and ontological organization.

title: Visually Grounded Self-Reflection for Vision-Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large vision-language models can reason over multimodal inputs by generating textual chains of thought (CoT). A key capability exhibited in CoT reasoning is self-reflection: revisiting earlier decisions and correcting previous errors. However, existing LVLMs often fail to properly attend to visual inputs during reflection, limiting their ability to translate feedback into grounded corrections, especially for out-of-distribution images. To address this issue, we propose a novel reinforcement learning training framework VRRL, with two components explicitly designed to elicit visually grounded self-reflection. First, we randomly mask trajectory prefixes during training to emphasize recovery from incorrect intermediate predictions rather than making early mistakes. Second, we introduce buffered roll-ins from an experience replay buffer to expose the model to diverse failure states that it must learn to correct. We evaluate our approach on visual grounding tasks involving tables and charts, as well as spatial navigation benchmarks. While off-the-shelf and conventionally fine-tuned models degrade substantially under distribution shift, our method substantially improves average out-of-distribution accuracy over standard RL and reflection-oriented fine-tuning baselines by using self-reflection effectively.

AI.tldr: VRRL is a reinforcement learning framework that trains LVLMs to perform visually grounded self-reflection by masking trajectory prefixes and using buffered roll-ins from experience replay, substantially improving out-of-distribution accuracy on visual grounding and spatial navigation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing LVLMs fail to properly attend to visual inputs during chain-of-thought self-reflection, particularly under distribution shift, limiting their ability to translate textual feedback into grounded corrections of earlier errors.
AI.method: VRRL (Visually-grounded Reflection RL) introduces two components: (1) random masking of trajectory prefixes during training to force recovery from incorrect intermediate predictions, and (2) buffered roll-ins from an experience replay buffer that expose the model to diverse failure states requiring correction.
AI.result: Off-the-shelf and conventionally fine-tuned models degrade substantially under distribution shift, while VRRL substantially improves average out-of-distribution accuracy compared to standard RL and reflection-oriented fine-tuning baselines on table/chart visual grounding and spatial navigation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly training for visually grounded self-reflection via prefix masking and diverse failure-state exposure enables LVLMs to robustly correct errors under distribution shift, significantly outperforming standard RL and fine-tuning approaches.

title: Expander Sparse Autoencoders: Parameter-Efficient Dictionaries for Mechanistic Interpretability
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose internal activations of neural networks into sparse linear combinations of learned features by fitting an overcomplete dictionary $\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ with $m<n$, and inferring a sparse code $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ from $\mathbf{h}\approx\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$. This inference problem closely resembles the canonical setup of compressed sensing, but dense decoders requires $O(mn)$ learned values, which becomes costly at large feature counts. We introduce Expander SAEs: TopK SAEs whose decoder and tied encoder are supported on a left-$d$-regular expander mask with $d\ll m$, learning only $dn$ decoder values while keeping the sparse-coding problem $(m,n,k)$ fixed. The same structure reduces storage and turns the matching-pursuit correlation step $\mathbf{W}^\top \mathbf{r}$ in OMP into an $O(dn)$ gather-and-reduce operation. Our experiments show that across Pythia-70M/160M, Qwen2.5-3B, and Llama-3.2-1B residual-stream activations, varying $d$ traces a consistent storage--fidelity frontier, and that at the most compressed modern-LM setting, Qwen2.5-3B with $d=7$ uses $293\times$ fewer learned decoder values than the full dense decoder while retaining $84$% of dense CE-loss recovered. Control experiments show that the improved storage--fidelity tradeoff is driven by sparse, diverse decoder support structure rather than by fewer learned decoder values, and that when sparse and dense decoders are compared at matched parameter count, part of the remaining gap comes from encoder amortisation. On the theoretical side, we show that expansion and column flatness are sufficient for identifiability of noiseless $k$-sparse codes, and we derive complementary sufficient conditions under which OMP recovers the support exactly.

AI.tldr: Introduces Expander SAEs, which use expander-graph-structured sparse decoders to drastically reduce learned parameters while maintaining sparse coding fidelity, demonstrated across multiple LLMs with theoretical guarantees for support recovery.
AI.motivation: Dense decoders in standard SAEs require O(mn) learned values, becoming prohibitively costly at large feature counts. This motivates a structured sparse decoder design that preserves the compressed sensing setup while dramatically reducing parameters and compute.
AI.method: Proposes Expander SAEs where the decoder (and tied encoder) are supported on a left-d-regular expander mask with d << m. This reduces learned parameters to O(dn), turns correlation computation into an O(dn) gather-and-reduce, and retains the (m,n,k) sparse-coding problem. Theoretical analysis establishes identifiability conditions via expansion and column flatness, plus sufficient conditions for exact support recovery under OMP.
AI.result: Across Pythia-70M/160M, Qwen2.5-3B, and Llama-3.2-1B, varying d traces a consistent storage–fidelity frontier. At d=7 on Qwen2.5-3B, achieves 293× fewer decoder parameters while retaining 84% of dense CE-loss recovery. Control experiments attribute gains to sparse, diverse support structure rather than mere parameter reduction, with residual gap partly due to encoder amortisation.
AI.conclusion: Expander SAEs offer a principled and practical approach to scaling sparse autoencoders by replacing dense decoders with expander-structured sparse ones, achieving favorable storage–fidelity tradeoffs supported by both empirical results and theoretical recovery guarantees.

title: Multimodal Knowledge Edit-Scoped Generalization for Online Recursive MLLM Editing
summary: Online multimodal knowledge editing requires injecting a continual stream of visual-textual corrections into multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with bounded overhead and minimal disruption to unrelated behaviors. Existing editors mainly emphasize edit reliability and long-horizon stability, but rarely control the semantic boundary of each edit. Our pilot analyses of post-edit behaviors and internal neuronal activities reveal a scope gap behind reliable edits: instance-level success neither guarantees transfer to valid cross-modal variants nor prevents leakage to unrelated inputs, while edit-related cross-modal responses concentrate in deeper semantic layers. Therefore, we formulate Edit-Scoped Generalization, reframing online MLLM editing from merely correcting an instance to controlling the propagation boundary of each edit. To this end, we propose ScopeEdit, a scope-aware online editor that decomposes each update into a modality-local absorption branch and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch. The local branch supports stable edit absorption, whereas the shared branch enables cross-modal propagation only when visual and textual evidence are sufficiently aligned. Both branches perform scope-separated write geometries in orthogonal low-rank spaces and maintain branch-wise preconditioners via Sherman--Morrison recursions, yielding constant per-edit overhead. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks, long-horizon edit streams, MLLM backbones, real-world VLKEB scenarios, and complex vision-language architectures show that ScopeEdit consistently improves the trade-off between in-scope cross-modal transfer and out-of-scope locality, while preserving edit reliability, stability and online efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/lab-klc/ScopeEdit.

AI.tldr: ScopeEdit introduces Edit-Scoped Generalization for online multimodal knowledge editing, decomposing each update into a local absorption branch and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch with orthogonal low-rank spaces, achieving better in-scope transfer and out-of-scope locality with constant per-edit overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM editors focus on edit reliability and stability but fail to control the semantic boundary of edits—instance-level success doesn't guarantee cross-modal transfer and causes leakage to unrelated inputs. A "scope gap" exists where edit-related cross-modal responses concentrate in deeper semantic layers without proper boundary control.
AI.method: ScopeEdit decomposes each update into two branches: (1) a modality-local absorption branch for stable edit absorption, and (2) an evidence-gated shared generalization branch for cross-modal propagation when visual-textual evidence aligns. Both use scope-separated write geometries in orthogonal low-rank spaces and maintain branch-wise preconditioners via Sherman-Morrison recursions for constant per-edit overhead.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks, long-horizon edit streams, MLLM backbones, real-world VLKEB scenarios, and complex vision-language architectures demonstrate that ScopeEdit consistently improves the trade-off between in-scope cross-modal transfer and out-of-scope locality while preserving edit reliability, stability, and online efficiency.
AI.conclusion: ScopeEdit successfully addresses the scope gap in online multimodal knowledge editing by providing controlled edit propagation, enabling reliable cross-modal generalization without sacrificing locality or efficiency.

title: Reasoning LLM Improves Speaker Recognition in Long-form TV Dramas
summary: Long-form TV dramas present a formidable challenge for comprehensive video understanding, where deciphering complex storyline often relies on \textbf{speaker recognition}, the task of accurately attributing each spoken utterance to its respective character. In this paper, we advance this field through two primary contributions. (1) We introduce \textbf{DramaSR-532K}, a large-scale benchmark comprising 532K annotated dialogue lines across more than 900 unique characters, necessitating the integration of auditory, linguistic, and visual cues for speaker recognition. (2) We propose \textbf{DramaSR-LRM}, a robust approach built upon a large reasoning model (LRM). DramaSR-LRM is designed to autonomously aggregate contextual evidence via multimodal tool-use, synthesizing diverse inputs to achieve high-fidelity attribution. Experimental results demonstrate that DramaSR-LRM significantly outperforms existing baselines, particularly on short utterances where acoustic biometrics are inherently unreliable. \textit{All the data and code will be made publicly available at the project page: https://www.github.com/198808xc/DramaSR-LRM.}

AI.tldr: DramaSR-532K is a large-scale benchmark for speaker recognition in TV dramas (532K dialogue lines, 900+ characters), and DramaSR-LRM is a multimodal large reasoning model that aggregates auditory, linguistic, and visual cues via tool-use to attribute utterances to characters, outperforming baselines especially on short utterances.
AI.motivation: Long-form TV dramas pose a significant challenge for video understanding, as comprehending complex storylines critically depends on speaker recognition — accurately linking each spoken line to the correct character. Existing methods struggle, particularly with short utterances where acoustic biometrics alone are unreliable, motivating a multimodal, reasoning-based approach.
AI.method: The authors introduce DramaSR-532K, a benchmark with 532K annotated dialogue lines across 900+ characters, requiring integration of auditory, linguistic, and visual cues. They then propose DramaSR-LRM, a large reasoning model (LRM) that autonomously aggregates contextual evidence through multimodal tool-use, synthesizing diverse inputs (audio, text, video) to perform high-fidelity speaker attribution.
AI.result: DramaSR-LRM significantly outperforms existing baselines, with particularly notable gains on short utterances where acoustic biometrics are inherently unreliable.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal large reasoning models that integrate auditory, linguistic, and visual evidence via tool-use offer a promising direction for robust speaker recognition in complex, long-form video content. The public release of the DramaSR-532K benchmark and DramaSR-LRM code aims to facilitate further research in this area.

title: Do LLMs Truly Generalize in the Molecular Domain? A Perturbation-Based Analysis
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promise in molecular discovery, yet a gap remains between their probabilistic nature over discrete sequential tokens and the rigid topological constraints of chemical space. This raises the question of whether molecular LLMs can generalize beyond the local neighborhoods induced by their sequence-based representations. To systematically investigate this question, we introduce a Molecular Perturbation framework that generates syntax-valid structural variants of training molecules under controlled Graph Edit Distance (GED) to probe the manifold regularity of molecular LLMs. Our analysis shows that even a single edit can cause substantial performance drops on common molecular tasks, revealing a narrow local trust region and fragile sensitivity to structural changes. Since similar molecules tend to exhibit similar properties, In-Context Tuning (ICT), which anchors predictions on structurally similar molecules, offers a natural way to mitigate such fragility. Our experiments also examine whether ICT confers robustness under controlled structural perturbations, and the results suggest that it can partially expand the local trust region and offer a promising direction for stabilizing molecular LLMs against structural variation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether molecular LLMs can generalize beyond their training distribution under controlled structural perturbations, finding that even single-atom edits cause significant performance drops. In-Context Tuning (ICT) on structurally similar molecules partially mitigates this fragility.
AI.motivation: There is a fundamental tension between the probabilistic, sequence-based nature of LLMs and the rigid topological constraints of chemical space. The authors aim to systematically probe whether molecular LLMs truly learn meaningful chemical representations or merely memorize local sequence patterns, questioning their generalization capacity beyond local neighborhoods.
AI.method: The authors introduce a Molecular Perturbation framework that generates syntax-valid structural variants of training molecules under controlled Graph Edit Distance (GED). This allows systematic probing of model performance as a function of structural dissimilarity. They also evaluate In-Context Tuning (ICT), which anchors predictions on structurally similar reference molecules, as a strategy to improve robustness against these perturbations.
AI.result: Even a single graph edit can cause substantial performance drops on common molecular tasks, revealing a narrow local trust region and fragile sensitivity to structural changes. ICT partially expands this local trust region, offering a promising direction for stabilizing molecular LLMs against structural variation.
AI.conclusion: Molecular LLMs exhibit fragile generalization characterized by a narrow local trust region. ICT provides a partial remedy by leveraging structural similarity to anchor predictions, but more robust approaches are needed for reliable molecular LLM deployment in chemical discovery.

title: Episodic-to-Semantic Consolidation Without Identity Drift
summary: Long-running adaptive intelligent agents face a structural tension between knowledge consolidation and information integrity. Memory consolidation is conventionally treated as an agent-changing operation: a model is fine-tuned, a prompt rewritten, a policy distilled, or a reflection appended to the context that governs future behaviour. In regulated autonomic deployment this is a liability because the agent operates under commitments and audit contracts that bind to a specific, cryptographically certified identity. We propose to treat consolidation not as a mutation of the planner or the identity manifest, but as a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem over episodic memory whose output is a separately addressable semantic knowledge layer; the identity hash does not read M^sem, so consolidation updates knowledge without changing the agent's certified identity. We give a formal account of the agent representation, prove identity invariance through a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set, specify a deterministic aggregation algorithm whose outputs are auditable database rows with explicit confidence and supporting-event provenance, and validate the construction with synthetic experiments demonstrating per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline. The construction is a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents in which lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, with an embodied service agent as the running case study.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel memory consolidation method for autonomous agents where semantic knowledge is derived from episodic memory via a deterministic function, stored in a separate layer that does not alter the agent's cryptographically certified identity hash. This enables knowledge accumulation while maintaining identity invariance, validated through synthetic experiments showing byte-equal identity and a ~80% reduction in unproductive planner attempts.
AI.motivation: Long-running adaptive agents face a structural tension: memory consolidation (fine-tuning, prompt rewriting, policy distillation) traditionally mutates the agent's identity, which is problematic in regulated autonomic deployments where agents operate under audit contracts tied to a cryptographically certified identity. Changing the agent breaks the certification, creating a liability.
AI.method: The authors propose treating consolidation as a deterministic function f: M^ep → M^sem mapping episodic memory to a separately addressable semantic knowledge layer. The agent's identity hash is computed only over the identity manifest (excluding M^sem), so consolidation updates knowledge without altering certified identity. They provide a formal account with a structural lemma proving identity invariance, specify a deterministic aggregation algorithm producing auditable database rows with explicit confidence scores and supporting-event provenance, and validate via synthetic experiments across 10 seeds.
AI.result: Synthetic experiments demonstrated per-field correctness of consolidated knowledge, byte-equal identity hash across all consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%]) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline.
AI.conclusion: The construction provides a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents where lessons accumulate as queryable semantic facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal throughout its operational lifetime. This is demonstrated through an embodied service agent case study.

title: LACUNA: A Testbed for Evaluating Localization Precision for LLM Unlearning
summary: LLMs memorize sensitive training data, including personally identifiable information (PII), creating a pressing need for reliable post hoc removal methods. Unlearning has emerged as a promising solution, with state-of-the-art(SOTA) methods often following a localize-first, unlearn-second paradigm that targets specific model parameters. However, existing benchmarks evaluate unlearning solely at the output level, leaving open the question of whether unlearning truly erases knowledge from a model's parameters or merely obfuscates it, a concern reinforced by the success of resurfacing attacks. To bridge this gap, we introduce LACUNA: the first unlearning testbed with ground-truth parameter-level localization. LACUNA injects PII of synthetic individuals into predefined parameters of 1B and 7B OLMo-based models via masked continual pretraining, enabling direct evaluation of whether unlearning targets the weights responsible for knowledge storage. We use LACUNA to benchmark current SOTA unlearning methods and find that, despite strong output-level performance, existing methods are highly imprecise and susceptible to resurfacing attacks. We further show that when localization is successful, even a simple gradient-based unlearning method achieves strong erasure and robustness to resurfacing attacks, highlighting the importance of precise unlearning. We release LACUNA to complement behavioral evaluations and drive further advances in robust, localization-based unlearning.

AI.tldr: LACUNA introduces the first unlearning benchmark with ground-truth parameter-level localization by injecting synthetic PII into predefined weights of OLMo models. The benchmark reveals that SOTA unlearning methods, while effective at output level, are imprecise and vulnerable to resurfacing attacks; precise localization dramatically improves erasure robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing unlearning benchmarks only evaluate at the output/behavioral level, leaving it unclear whether unlearning genuinely erases knowledge from model parameters or merely obfuscates it. The success of resurfacing attacks heightens this concern. A testbed with ground-truth knowledge of which weights store the target information is needed to rigorously assess localization quality.
AI.method: The authors create LACUNA by injecting PII of synthetic individuals into predefined, known parameters of 1B and 7B OLMo models via masked continual pretraining. This provides ground-truth labels for which weights encode the target knowledge. They then benchmark current SOTA unlearning methods against this testbed, measuring both output-level performance and parameter-level precision, and test robustness via resurfacing attacks.
AI.result: SOTA unlearning methods achieve strong output-level performance but are highly imprecise in targeting the actual parameters storing the knowledge, leaving them susceptible to resurfacing attacks. When localization is accurate, even simple gradient-based unlearning proves robust and effective at erasure.
AI.conclusion: Precise parameter-level localization is critical for robust unlearning. LACUNA is released as a complementary evaluation tool to drive progress in localization-based unlearning methods beyond behavioral metrics alone.

title: Gaming Consensus: Coordinated Manipulation in Crowdsourced Fact-Checking
summary: Crowdsourced fact-checking systems have been adopted by major social media companies such as X, Meta, TikTok and Google with the aim of combating misleading information at scale without relying on centralized editorial control. These systems have been developed around a common underlying concept: a bridging mechanism that identifies notes flagging misleading information when they receive support from people with different perspectives rather than simple majority support. To our knowledge the only publicly disclosed bridging algorithms deployed for fact-checking are based on matrix factorization, as deployed by both X and Meta, augmented with additional components addressing abuse, targeted manipulation, and contributor brigades. This work examines the core matrix factorization portion of these systems, presenting theoretical and empirical evaluations of the degree to which coordinated users could vote strategically by leveraging the latent representations to fabricate the appearance of synthetic consensus within the bridging mechanism. Using historic production data, we find that up to 10.7% of lower quality notes could be manipulated above consensus thresholds using less than 10 ratings. We complement these findings with a theoretical analysis, revealing counterintuitively that rating a note as "Not Helpful" can increase its helpfulness score, as well as a cost model quantifying manipulation effort. We have developed and deployed mitigations within X's Community Notes algorithm to address synthetic consensus.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the matrix factorization-based bridging algorithms used in crowdsourced fact-checking systems (deployed by X and Meta), revealing vulnerabilities where coordinated users can manipulate consensus thresholds with few ratings, and presents mitigations deployed in X's Community Notes.
AI.motivation: Major social media platforms (X, Meta, TikTok, Google) have adopted crowdsourced fact-checking with bridging mechanisms that prioritize cross-perspective agreement over majority vote. However, the only publicly disclosed bridging algorithms rely on matrix factorization, and their vulnerability to strategic manipulation by coordinated actors remains largely unexamined.
AI.method: The authors conduct both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation of the matrix factorization core in deployed bridging algorithms. Using historic production data, they assess how coordinated users can exploit latent representations to fabricate synthetic consensus. They also develop a cost model quantifying manipulation effort and counterintuitively show that "Not Helpful" ratings can increase helpfulness scores.
AI.result: Up to 10.7% of lower-quality notes can be manipulated above consensus thresholds using fewer than 10 ratings. The theoretical analysis reveals that rating a note as "Not Helpful" can paradoxically increase its helpfulness score due to how latent representations interact within the bridging mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The matrix factorization-based bridging algorithms contain exploitable vulnerabilities to synthetic consensus attacks. The authors developed and deployed mitigations within X's Community Notes algorithm to address these identified weaknesses.

title: Traceable Fault Diagnosis for Battery Energy Storage Systems via Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent O&M Assistant
summary: Large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESSs) require O&M decisions that combine alarms, cell-level measurements, device topology, diagnostic tables, historical cases, and maintenance documents. Monitoring platforms can flag threshold violations, but they often cannot explain whether voltage inconsistency, resistance drift, short-circuit risk, capacity divergence, or thermal abnormality needs intervention. This digest presents a traceable BESS fault-diagnosis assistant that uses retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning to connect operational data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and report generation. Reliability is improved through BESS-specific task routing, schema-constrained natural-language database access, hybrid text-image retrieval, and evidence-based answer synthesis. Preliminary internal evaluation is reported for routing, database access, and diagnostic reasoning.

AI.tldr: A retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning system is proposed for traceable BESS fault diagnosis, integrating operational data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and report generation with schema-constrained database access and hybrid text-image retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing BESS monitoring platforms can flag threshold violations but lack explanatory capability to determine whether alarms related to voltage inconsistency, resistance drift, short-circuit risk, capacity divergence, or thermal abnormality require actual intervention. O&M decisions demand synthesis of heterogeneous data sources (alarms, cell measurements, topology, diagnostic tables, historical cases, maintenance documents) that current systems cannot adequately integrate.
AI.method: A traceable fault-diagnosis assistant employing retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning with four key components: (1) BESS-specific task routing to direct queries to appropriate reasoning paths, (2) schema-constrained natural-language database access for structured operational data querying, (3) hybrid text-image retrieval to incorporate visual evidence alongside textual domain knowledge, and (4) evidence-based answer synthesis for generating diagnostic reports with traceable provenance.
AI.result: Preliminary internal evaluation results are reported for three system components: task routing accuracy, natural-language database access performance, and diagnostic reasoning quality. Specific quantitative metrics are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-agent architecture enhances reliability of automated BESS fault diagnosis by providing explainable, evidence-grounded assessments that connect disparate operational and documentary data sources, though the work remains at an early evaluation stage.

title: Many Voices, One Reward: Multi-Role Rubric Generation for LLM Judging and Reward Modeling
summary: Reliable reward and preference signals are critical for evaluating and optimizing large language models on open-ended tasks. Rubric-based judges offer a transparent way to decompose such judgments into explicit evaluation criteria, but existing annotation-free rubric generators typically rely on a single generic evaluator. As a result, they may overlook important dimensions of human preference, a failure mode we term dimensional blind spots. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-Role Rubric Generation (MRRG), a training-free and reference-free framework that elicits evaluation criteria from multiple complementary roles and consolidates them into an auditable rubric-based scorer. This scorer can be used both to validate pairwise preferences and to provide rewards for GRPO-style Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). Experiments on preference validation benchmarks show that MRRG consistently outperforms single-role rubric generation baselines across multiple backbone models. Further RLVR experiments demonstrate that MRRG yields a stronger reward signal for improving open-ended generation.

AI.tldr: MRRG proposes a multi-role rubric generation framework that elicits evaluation criteria from complementary perspectives to overcome "dimensional blind spots" in single-role approaches, producing auditable rubric-based scorers for preference validation and RLVR reward signals.
AI.motivation: Existing annotation-free rubric generators rely on a single generic evaluator, leading to "dimensional blind spots" — overlooked dimensions of human preference that are missed because a single perspective cannot capture the full spectrum of evaluation criteria.
AI.method: MRRG is a training-free, reference-free framework that: (1) elicits evaluation criteria from multiple complementary roles (rather than a single generic evaluator), (2) consolidates these multi-role criteria into a unified rubric-based scorer, which can then be used for validating pairwise preferences and providing reward signals for GRPO-style RLVR.
AI.result: MRRG consistently outperforms single-role rubric generation baselines across multiple backbone models on preference validation benchmarks. RLVR experiments further show that MRRG yields stronger reward signals for improving open-ended generation.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging multiple complementary roles to generate evaluation rubrics effectively addresses dimensional blind spots inherent in single-evaluator approaches, leading to more reliable preference validation and stronger RLVR training signals.

title: InduceKV: Fixed-Footprint Continual Adaptation of Multimodal LLMs via Inducing KV Memories
summary: Multimodal large language models must adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet continual improvement under bounded deployment footprint remains difficult because repeated parameter updates or growing replay stores can accumulate adaptation state over time. We study fixed-footprint continual adaptation: the deployed adaptation state is kept under a fixed memory budget, while the backbone model is left unchanged and task-specific updates are externalized. We propose InduceKV, a retrieval-based method that stores each selected training prefix as an attention-ready memory entry, consisting of a frozen retrieval key and compact layerwise key--value (KV) payloads that can be appended to the model's self-attention cache. Under a strict memory budget, InduceKV constructs a compact inducing set through bilevel selection: a lightweight calibration is fit for retrieval, while the selected memory balances current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention, and coverage in the frozen retrieval space. Across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning, InduceKV consistently improves over PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets. We further report backbone-matched, stage-1 CoIN, compute-matched, and scalability diagnostics, showing that the gains are not due to a stronger backbone, replay alone, or an unbounded candidate pool.

AI.tldr: InduceKV is a retrieval-based fixed-footprint continual adaptation method for multimodal LLMs that stores compact KV payloads with frozen retrieval keys under a strict memory budget, using bilevel selection to balance likelihood, retention, and coverage, outperforming PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines across multiple continual learning settings.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs need to adapt to evolving tasks/domains, but continual improvement under a bounded deployment footprint is challenging because repeated parameter updates or growing replay buffers accumulate adaptation state over time. The authors aim to enable fixed-footprint continual adaptation where the backbone is frozen and task-specific updates are externalized under a strict memory budget.
AI.method: InduceKV stores selected training prefixes as attention-ready memory entries, each with a frozen retrieval key and compact layerwise KV payloads that append to the self-attention cache. Under a memory budget, it constructs a compact inducing set via bilevel selection: a lightweight calibration is fit for retrieval, while selection optimizes for current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention of past knowledge, and coverage in the frozen retrieval space.
AI.result: InduceKV consistently improves over PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning. Backbone-matched, stage-1 CoIN, compute-matched, and scalability diagnostics confirm gains are not due to a stronger backbone, replay alone, or an unbounded candidate pool.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-footprint continual adaptation with retrieval-augmented KV memory is an effective paradigm for multimodal LLMs, with InduceKV's bilevel selection strategy providing robust performance under strict memory constraints without requiring backbone updates or growing state.

title: Adaptive Group-Based Counterfactual Explanations for Time-Series Rehabilitation Data
comment: To be published at IEEE CBMS 2026
summary: Counterfactual explanations (CEs) for multivariate time-series classifiers are often difficult to interpret in domains where experts reason in terms of semantic feature groups rather than individual channels. In rehabilitation movement analysis with multi-sensor inertial measurement units (IMUs), clinicians interpret motion through muscle-group and joint-segment abstractions; yet, most existing counterfactual methods operate at the channel level, producing scattered and biomechanically incoherent explanations. We propose a two-stage framework for group-based counterfactual generation in high-dimensional IMU data. We first show that Shapley-Adaptive (SA) group ranking preserves counterfactual validity but fails to enforce group-level sparsity, motivating the need for explicit group selection. We then introduce Learnable Gate (LG) methods, which incorporate trainable per-group relevance gates jointly optimized with perturbation masks. Experiments on the KneE-PAD rehabilitation dataset demonstrate that LG substantially improves modality-group sparsity compared to the channel-level M-CELS baseline while maintaining or improving validity, temporal smoothness, and generation efficiency. Exercise-specific analyses further show that group-structured counterfactuals yield concise, muscle-level corrective guidance aligned with clinical reasoning. Overall, the proposed framework enhances interpretability without sacrificing counterfactual quality, enabling more actionable explanations for rehabilitation movement analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage framework for generating group-based counterfactual explanations for multivariate time-series classifiers in rehabilitation. It introduces Learnable Gate (LG) methods that jointly optimize per-group relevance gates with perturbation masks, improving modality-group sparsity over channel-level baselines while maintaining validity and generating clinically interpretable, muscle-level corrective guidance from IMU data.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual explanation methods for multivariate time-series classifiers operate at the individual channel level, producing scattered, biomechanically incoherent explanations. In rehabilitation domains, clinicians reason in terms of semantic feature groups (muscle groups, joint segments) rather than raw sensor channels, creating a mismatch between explanation granularity and clinical interpretability.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) Shapley-Adaptive (SA) group ranking is shown to preserve counterfactual validity but lacks group-level sparsity. (2) Learnable Gate (LG) methods are introduced, incorporating trainable per-group relevance gates jointly optimized with perturbation masks to enforce explicit group selection. Evaluated on the KneE-PAD rehabilitation dataset against the M-CELS channel-level baseline.
AI.result: LG methods substantially improve modality-group sparsity compared to the M-CELS baseline while maintaining or improving validity, temporal smoothness, and generation efficiency. Exercise-specific analyses demonstrate that group-structured counterfactuals produce concise, muscle-level corrective guidance aligned with clinical reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed group-based framework enhances interpretability of counterfactual explanations without sacrificing quality, enabling more actionable explanations for rehabilitation movement analysis by aligning explanation granularity with how clinicians actually reason about motion.

title: Hidden Forgetting in Continual Multimodal Learning: When Accuracy Survives but Grounding Fails
summary: Multimodal large language models must continually adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet standard continual learning metrics mainly measure whether old answers remain correct, leaving the stability of multimodal grounding largely unexamined. We study this overlooked failure mode and ask whether a continually adapted MLLM can preserve not only what it answers, but also how it uses visual, textual, OCR, chart, and document evidence. We identify \emph{hidden evidence-use forgetting}, where answer accuracy is retained while the model silently shifts toward different or less grounded evidence channels, and propose \textsc{RCL}, a replay-free reliance-constrained continual learning framework. \textsc{RCL} freezes the previous checkpoint as a behavioral reference, estimates teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles through counterfactual channel interventions, and jointly optimizes task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation without adding inference-time cost. Across CoIN, COAST, MCITlib, and an evidence-sensitive multimodal stream, \textsc{RCL} consistently improves final performance and reduces forgetting over replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines, while substantially lowering modality reliance drift, dominant evidence flips, and hidden forgetting rates. These results suggest that robust continual multimodal learning requires preserving the evidence path behind correct answers, not merely the answers themselves.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "hidden evidence-use forgetting" in continually adapted multimodal LLMs—where answer accuracy persists but the model silently shifts to different or less grounded evidence channels. The authors propose RCL, a replay-free framework that freezes a previous checkpoint as a behavioral reference, estimates evidence-reliance profiles via counterfactual channel interventions, and jointly optimizes task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation, demonstrating improved grounding stability across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard continual learning metrics for multimodal LLMs only assess whether old answers remain correct, ignoring whether the model continues to use the same visual, textual, OCR, chart, or document evidence. The authors identify an overlooked failure mode: hidden evidence-use forgetting, where correctness is preserved but evidence grounding silently degrades or shifts to less appropriate modalities, undermining reliability and interpretability.
AI.method: RCL (Reliance-Constrained Continual Learning) is a replay-free framework with three components: (1) freezing the previous model checkpoint as a behavioral teacher; (2) estimating teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles through counterfactual interventions that ablate individual modality channels (visual, textual, OCR, chart, document) and measure output divergence; (3) jointly optimizing a three-term loss combining task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation—all without additional inference-time cost.
AI.result: Across CoIN, COAST, MCITlib, and a custom evidence-sensitive multimodal stream, RCL consistently improved final performance and reduced forgetting compared to replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines. It substantially lowered modality reliance drift, dominant evidence flips, and hidden forgetting rates, demonstrating that preserving evidence pathways is critical for robust continual multimodal learning.
AI.conclusion: Robust continual multimodal learning requires preserving not just answer correctness but also the evidence path behind those answers. RCL provides an effective, inference-cost-free mechanism to enforce evidence-use stability, suggesting that future continual learning evaluation should incorporate grounding fidelity metrics alongside accuracy.

title: Decomposer: Learning to Decompile Symbolic Music to Programs
summary: Musical performance involves executing a set of high-level musical instructions, yet recovering those instructions from the performance is a challenging inverse problem. We present Decomposer, a post-training framework for symbolic music decompilation: the task of recovering executable, editable music programs from symbolic music. We instantiate the task as MIDI-to-Strudel decompilation, where the model takes symbolic MIDI as input and produces a program in Strudel, a music programming language, that reconstructs the input when executed. The task poses two challenges: Strudel is a low-resource language with little naturally paired MIDI-code data, and optimizing faithful reconstruction of MIDI alone can collapse to unreadable note-by-note transliteration. We address these challenges in two stages. First, we construct Strudel-Synth, a synthetic corpus of paired Strudel programs and rendered MIDI, and use it for supervised fine-tuning. Second, we refine the model with reinforcement learning on unpaired MIDI, optimizing rewards for both MIDI reconstruction faithfulness and code readability. Our evaluation across synthetic and real-world MIDI benchmarks shows that Decomposer achieves substantially higher MIDI reconstruction faithfulness than closed-source LLMs while producing more readable and diverse code than the heuristic converter.

AI.tldr: Decomposer is a two-stage framework for decompiling symbolic MIDI into executable Strudel code, combining supervised fine-tuning on synthetic paired data with RL-based refinement on unpaired MIDI to optimize both reconstruction fidelity and code readability.
AI.motivation: Recovering high-level musical instructions from a performance (decompilation) is a challenging inverse problem. The Strudel language lacks paired MIDI-code data, and naive optimization for MIDI reconstruction leads to unreadable note-by-note transliteration rather than meaningful structured programs.
AI.method: Stage 1: Construct Strudel-Synth, a synthetic corpus of paired Strudel programs and rendered MIDI, used for supervised fine-tuning. Stage 2: RL-based refinement on unpaired MIDI using rewards that jointly optimize MIDI reconstruction faithfulness and code readability.
AI.result: Decomposer substantially outperforms closed-source LLMs in MIDI reconstruction faithfulness and produces more readable, diverse code compared to heuristic converters on both synthetic and real-world MIDI benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A post-training approach combining synthetic paired data and RL with dual reward signals can effectively tackle low-resource symbolic music decompilation, producing faithful yet human-readable music programs.

title: PACE: A Proxy for Agentic Capability Evaluation
summary: Evaluating LLM agents on benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA can be expensive, time-consuming, and requires complex infrastructure. A single evaluation can cost thousands of dollars and take days to complete. In contrast, non-agentic LLM benchmarks that test individual capabilities (e.g., reasoning, code generation) are fast and cheap to run. In this paper, we investigate whether performance on expensive agentic benchmarks can be accurately predicted by the performance on a small, carefully selected subset of atomic evaluation instances. We introduce PACE, a framework that constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting instances from existing non-agentic evaluations whose aggregate scores most reliably predict model performances on agentic benchmarks. Given a pool of candidate instances spanning atomic capabilities, PACE fits a regression that maps a model's scores on a compact subset of source instances to its score on the target agentic benchmark. The subset itself is curated by combining two complementary instance-selection strategies, target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection.
