We apply PACE to the 4 target agentic benchmarks in this paper, which yields PACE-Bench, the concrete proxy benchmark that we evaluate in the paper. Experiments across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks show that PACE-Bench predicts agentic scores with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) mean absolute error (MAE) under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, all at much less than 1% of the full agentic evaluation cost. We further analyze the selected proxy instances, revealing which skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands. PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing, without the overhead of full agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: PACE builds cheap proxy benchmarks from non-agentic tasks that accurately predict expensive agentic LLM benchmark scores, achieving under 4% MAE and over 0.80 Spearman correlation at less than 1% of the cost.
AI.motivation: Full agentic LLM evaluations (e.g., SWE-Bench, GAIA) are prohibitively expensive (thousands of dollars, days to run) and require complex infrastructure, whereas non-agentic atomic capability benchmarks are fast and cheap. The authors ask whether agentic performance can be reliably predicted from a small, curated subset of atomic evaluations.
AI.method: PACE (Proxy Agentic Capability Evaluation) selects a compact subset of non-agentic benchmark instances via two complementary strategies: (1) target-relevance local selection that picks instances most correlated with the target agentic score, and (2) globally informative global selection that ensures diversity and coverage. A regression model then maps model scores on this curated proxy subset to predicted agentic benchmark scores. Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) is used to evaluate prediction quality.
AI.result: Across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks, PACE-Bench achieves LOOCV MAE under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, while costing under 1% of full agentic evaluation. Instance analysis reveals which atomic skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands.
AI.conclusion: PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable agentic performance estimates during model development, selection, and routing without the overhead of full agent evaluations, demonstrating that expensive agentic benchmarks can be effectively approximated by cheap, carefully curated atomic evaluations.

title: Learning the Supports for Categorical Critic in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Value functions are an essential component in actor-critic based deep reinforcement learning (RL). Conventionally, these functions are trained as a regression task by minimising the mean squared error (MSE) relative to bootstrapped target values. Meanwhile, in distributional RL, a distribution of returns is modelled based on the distributional Bellman operator. This work investigates the Gaussian Histogram Loss (HL-Gauss), a recent approach that reframes value estimation as classification by encoding each scalar Bellman target as a Gaussian-smoothed categorical target. Despite its potential, applying histogram-based losses to RL presents inherent challenges, most notably the requirement to pre-define a fixed support interval, which is often complicated by the non-stationary and stochastic nature of target values typically found in RL tasks. In this work, we propose an approach that dynamically learns the lower and upper bounds of the support instead of assigning them beforehand. We derive an objective that jointly learns these bounds whilst learning the categorical representation of the scalar values, and we show that this objective forms an upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error. Our theoretical analysis further shows that this bound is tighter than that of non-learned supports of HL-Gauss. Empirically, the proposed objective enables stable adaptation of the support interval and matches HL-Gauss-based actor-critic algorithms on most continuous-control tasks whilst improving on a subset, without requiring a pre-specified support interval.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dynamic support interval learning method for histogram-based distributional RL (HL-Gauss) that jointly learns the lower/upper bounds and categorical value representation, eliminating the need for pre-specified support intervals while forming a tighter upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error.
AI.motivation: HL-Gauss reframes value estimation as classification using Gaussian-smoothed categorical targets, but it requires pre-defining a fixed support interval. This is problematic in RL due to non-stationary and stochastic target values, making it difficult to choose appropriate bounds a priori.
AI.method: The authors derive an objective that jointly learns the support interval bounds alongside the categorical representation of scalar values. They prove this objective forms an upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error and demonstrate theoretically that this bound is tighter than that of HL-Gauss with non-learned supports.
AI.result: The proposed method enables stable adaptation of the support interval and matches HL-Gauss-based actor-critic algorithms on most continuous-control tasks while outperforming on a subset, all without requiring a pre-specified support interval.
AI.conclusion: Dynamically learning the support bounds for histogram-based distributional RL is both theoretically sound (tighter bound on Bellman error) and empirically effective, removing a key practical limitation of HL-Gauss while maintaining or improving performance.

title: Algebraic Model Counting for Global Analysis of Optimal Decision Trees
comment: Proc. Joint European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML-PKDD 2026), LNCS, Naples, Italy, 7-11 September 2026
summary: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI requires a global assessment of the hypothesis space. We propose a formal framework for the exhaustive analysis of optimal and near-optimal decision trees, called Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC). Inspired by Algebraic Model Counting (AMC) in knowledge representation, ADTC reformulates diverse analytical tasks, such as optimization, counting, and sampling, into a unified sum-of-products computation over a semiring $R$. While the hypothesis space of decision trees is doubly exponential with respect to the maximum depth $Δ$, our dynamic programming algorithm achieves $O^*(n^{O(Δ)})$ time complexity in the number of features $n$, where $O^*$ suppresses polynomial factors. To handle complex constraints consisting of multiple tree metrics, we introduce model behavior tensors that aggregate semiring values via convolution products over a tensor semiring. This algebraic approach efficiently constructs a model profile that captures the global landscape and trade-offs between criteria such as accuracy, size, and fairness. We demonstrate the utility of our software, emtrees, on real-world datasets, illustrating how ADTC facilitates evidence-based model selection in sensitive domains.

AI.tldr: ADTC reformulates optimal and near-optimal decision tree analysis into a unified sum-of-products computation over semirings, enabling exhaustive exploration of the hypothesis space via dynamic programming with $O^*(n^{O(Δ)})$ complexity. Model behavior tensors capture multi-criteria trade-offs, implemented in the emtrees toolkit.
AI.motivation: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI demands a global, exhaustive assessment of the decision tree hypothesis space rather than relying on heuristic or local optima. Existing methods lack a unified formal framework for simultaneously handling optimization, counting, and sampling across multiple criteria like accuracy, size, and fairness.
AI.method: The authors propose Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC), inspired by Algebraic Model Counting (AMC) in knowledge representation. ADTC recasts analytical tasks (optimization, counting, sampling) as sum-of-products computations over a semiring R. A dynamic programming algorithm achieves $O^*(n^{O(Δ)})$ time complexity. For multi-criteria constraints, model behavior tensors are introduced, aggregating semiring values via convolution products over a tensor semiring to build a model profile capturing global trade-offs.
AI.result: The framework is implemented in the software emtrees and demonstrated on real-world datasets, showing how ADTC enables evidence-based model selection by exhaustively profiling the landscape of optimal and near-optimal trees across accuracy, size, and fairness dimensions.
AI.conclusion: ADTC provides a principled, algebraic foundation for exhaustive decision tree analysis, enabling practitioners to make informed, multi-criteria model selections in sensitive domains where reliability and explainability are paramount.

title: Regularized Variational and Spectral Log-Density-Ratio Estimation in the Gaussian Location Model
summary: We study ridge-regularized log-density-ratio estimation in the Gaussian location model with a common covariance matrix. By affine invariance, the model is written as q $\sim$ N(0, I), p $\sim$ N($Δ$, I), with linear features, where $Δ$ is a mean vector. The variational estimator is the empirical Kullback-Leibler (KL) log-normalized fit with a squared L2-penalty on its nonconstant coefficient, and the spectral estimator recently introduced in [1] replaces a single variational problem by a continuum of ridge-regularized least-squares problems. We derive high-dimensional deterministic asymptotic equivalents when the numbers of observations and dimension tend to infinity with fixed ratios. The regularized variational limit is characterized by a scalar entropy minimization problem derived from the convex-Gaussian-min-max theorem (CGMT), while the regularized spectral limit follows from deterministic equivalents for resolvents of weighted sums of two independent Gaussian sample covariance matrices. We use these formulas to compare population risks, with experiments focused on fixed-signal aspect-ratio sweeps and optimized regularization. Our conclusion is that with many observations, under the criteria and asymptotic regimes analyzed here, the well-specified variational estimator has the smaller risk, while with fewer observations, the spectral estimator is favored because its covariance-based construction has lower variance. We also study how a nuclear penalty can be used and partially analyzed to perform feature learning.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes ridge-regularized log-density-ratio estimation in a Gaussian location model, comparing variational (KL-based) and spectral estimators via high-dimensional asymptotics. The variational estimator excels with more observations, while the spectral estimator is favored in low-data regimes due to lower variance. A nuclear penalty extension for feature learning is also explored.
AI.motivation: To rigorously compare the population risks of two competing log-density-ratio estimators — the variational (empirical KL fit with L2 penalty) and the spectral (continuum of ridge-regularized least-squares problems) — under high-dimensional asymptotic regimes, and to determine which estimator is preferable under varying observation-to-dimension ratios.
AI.method: The authors employ high-dimensional deterministic asymptotic equivalents, where both observation count and dimension grow with fixed ratios. The variational estimator's limit is characterized via a scalar entropy minimization derived from the Convex Gaussian Min-max Theorem (CGMT). The spectral estimator's limit follows from deterministic equivalents for resolvents of weighted sums of two independent Gaussian sample covariance matrices. Population risks are then compared analytically and through numerical experiments with fixed-signal aspect-ratio sweeps and optimized regularization. A nuclear norm penalty is also introduced and partially analyzed for feature learning.
AI.result: In data-rich regimes (many observations), the well-specified variational estimator achieves lower population risk. In data-scarce regimes (fewer observations), the spectral estimator is favored because its covariance-based construction yields lower variance. The nuclear penalty approach is shown to have potential for feature learning but is only partially analyzed.
AI.conclusion: There is no uniformly superior estimator; the choice between variational and spectral estimators depends on the sample size relative to dimensionality. The spectral estimator's variance advantage makes it preferable in low-data settings, while the variational estimator's specification advantage dominates with more data. The nuclear penalty offers a promising direction for feature learning that warrants further analysis.

title: Evidence-State Rewards for Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Long-context reasoning requires models to locate, revise, and synthesize evidence distributed across lengthy inputs. Existing long-context RL methods usually reward final answers or static evidence extraction, offering little feedback on how intermediate actions change the model's evidence state. We propose Maven, a reinforcement learning framework with an editable evidence memory. Maven defines an answer-conditioned evidence-state value and rewards action-level state transitions: add actions are credited by marginal gain and hindsight contribution, link actions by evidence synergy, and drop actions by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence. These rewards are assigned to the corresponding action spans in GRPO. Across Llama and Qwen models on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, producing more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention. Our results show that long-context RL benefits from optimizing stateful evidence navigation rather than one-shot evidence extraction.

AI.tldr: Maven introduces a reinforcement learning framework for long-context reasoning that rewards intermediate evidence-state transitions (add, link, drop) using an answer-conditioned value function, outperforming outcome-only RL baselines on long-context benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing long-context RL methods only reward final answers or static evidence extraction, providing no feedback on how intermediate actions modify the model's evidence state during reasoning. This limits models' ability to effectively locate, revise, and synthesize evidence distributed across long inputs.
AI.method: Maven uses GRPO with an editable evidence memory and defines an answer-conditioned evidence-state value function. It assigns action-level rewards to three evidence operations: (1) Add actions credited by marginal gain and hindsight contribution; (2) Link actions rewarded by evidence synergy; (3) Drop actions rewarded by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence. Rewards are assigned to corresponding action spans during GRPO training.
AI.result: Across Llama and Qwen models evaluated on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, producing more sufficient evidence sets with lower distractor retention.
AI.conclusion: Long-context RL benefits more from optimizing stateful evidence navigation (sequential add/link/drop operations) than from one-shot evidence extraction, demonstrating that fine-grained action-level credit assignment is crucial for effective long-context reasoning.

title: Rank-Then-Act: Reward-Free Control from Frame-Order Progress
summary: We introduce Rank-Then-Act (RTA), a framework for learning control policies from expert video demonstrations without environment rewards. RTA trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) offline as a progress-based ordinal scorer, using a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective over shuffled frame sequences, which forces the model to recover temporal ordering from visual semantics rather than trivial time cues. Importantly, instead of using the scorer directly as a scalar reward model, we propose a correlation-based reward function for reinforcement learning: at each interaction window, we compute the Spearman rank correlation between predicted progress rankings and true temporal indices, yielding a bounded, scale-invariant learning signal. This design decouples reward learning from absolute calibration and enables stable transfer across tasks and environments. We evaluate RTA on discrete control benchmarks (PyBoy: Catrap, Kirby) and continuous control tasks (PointMaze, MetaWorld). RTA consistently matches or outperforms prior video-based reward learning methods and rank-based baselines, while demonstrating strong cross-task reuse of a single pretrained progress scorer. Our results suggest that correlation-structured supervision over video-derived ordinal signals is sufficient for policy learning, offering a scalable alternative to explicit reward design.

AI.tldr: RTA learns control policies from expert video demonstrations by training a VLM as a progress-based ordinal scorer via GRPO on shuffled frames, then uses Spearman rank correlation between predicted rankings and true temporal indices as a reward signal for RL — achieving strong results on both discrete and continuous control benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Learning control policies typically requires environment rewards or explicit reward engineering, both of which are expensive and non-scalable. Prior video-based reward learning methods struggle with calibration brittleness and fail to transfer across tasks. RTA addresses this by learning from the ordinal structure inherent in expert demonstrations, decoupling reward learning from absolute scale.
AI.method: RTA has two phases: (1) offline scorer training — a VLM is trained via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on shuffled frame sequences from expert videos to predict progress rankings, forcing reliance on visual semantics rather than temporal cues; (2) online RL — the trained scorer is used to compute Spearman rank correlation between predicted ordinal rankings and ground-truth temporal indices within an interaction window, producing a bounded, scale-invariant reward for policy optimization.
AI.result: RTA matches or surpasses prior video-based reward learning methods and rank-based baselines on discrete control (PyBoy: Catrap, Kirby) and continuous control (PointMaze, MetaWorld) benchmarks. A single pretrained progress scorer demonstrates strong cross-task reuse, validating the transferability of correlation-structured supervision.
AI.conclusion: Correlation-structured supervision over video-derived ordinal signals is sufficient for policy learning. RTA provides a scalable alternative to explicit reward design by leveraging the inherent temporal ordering in demonstrations, with the rank-correlation reward offering stable, transferable learning signals free from absolute calibration issues.

title: SUNTA: Hierarchical Video Prediction with Surprise-based Chunking
summary: Hierarchical state-space models (HSSMs) offer a promising approach to long-horizon prediction by segmenting sequences into temporal chunks. However, their performance hinges on how chunk boundaries are determined. While prior HSSMs typically rely on fixed-length chunking or similarity-based boundary detection, these methods often misalign with the intrinsic temporal structure of the data. We argue that chunking should instead be driven by prediction errors, which more directly indicate when longer-range context becomes necessary. Nevertheless, integrating surprise-based chunking into HSSMs introduces critical challenges, including hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and the absence of surprise signals during open-loop prediction. To address these issues, we propose Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction (SUNTA), a method that employs a decoupled training strategy to preserve surprise signals and uses internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries within imagined rollouts. Experiments on video prediction tasks in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate that SUNTA outperforms baselines, uniquely maintaining accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, whereas all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.

AI.tldr: SUNTA introduces surprise-based chunking for hierarchical state-space models, using prediction errors to determine chunk boundaries instead of fixed-length or similarity-based methods. A decoupled training strategy prevents hierarchical collapse, and internal inconsistency serves as a top-down surprise metric during open-loop prediction, enabling accurate video predictions over 250+ timesteps.
AI.motivation: Existing HSSMs rely on fixed-length chunking or similarity-based boundary detection, which often misalign with the data's intrinsic temporal structure. Prediction errors more directly signal when longer-range context is needed, but integrating surprise-based chunking into HSSMs causes hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and lacks surprise signals during open-loop generation.
AI.method: SUNTA employs two key innovations: (1) a decoupled training strategy that trains the chunking policy separately from the dynamics model to preserve meaningful surprise signals and prevent hierarchical collapse; (2) a top-down surprise metric called "internal inconsistency" that measures the mismatch between predicted and actual representations at higher abstraction levels, enabling boundary detection even during imagined (open-loop) rollouts where ground-truth is unavailable.
AI.result: On video prediction tasks in both 2D and 3D environments, SUNTA significantly outperforms baselines. All baseline methods degrade within the first 10 timesteps, while SUNTA uniquely maintains accurate predictions over 250 timesteps.
AI.conclusion: Prediction-error-driven chunking is superior to fixed-length or similarity-based approaches for HSSMs, and the decoupled training with internal inconsistency metric effectively resolves the challenges of surprise-based boundary detection in learned hierarchical dynamics models.

title: SABER: A Semantic-Aligned Brain Network Analysis Framework via Multi-scale Hypergraphs
comment: Accepted to IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo (ICME) 2026;
summary: Effective brain disease diagnosis requires the synergy of brain connectivity patterns and high-level semantic knowledge. Existing methods, however, largely treat semantics from large language models (LLMs) as auxiliary features or supervision, limiting their direct role in decision-making and constraining classification stability and robustness. To overcome this, we propose a semantic-aligned brain network framework that actively integrates LLM-derived semantics into the prediction process. Specifically, ROI-level semantics are first incorporated via global self-attention to enrich node representations and provide whole-brain context. Multi-scale hypergraphs are then constructed to explicitly model functional subnetworks and multi-ROI interactions, addressing the locality limitations of traditional GNNs and capturing high-order dependencies. Finally, a decision-level semantic alignment mechanism selectively injects patient-specific textual embeddings into graph representations, enabling semantics to directly guide predictions without perturbing the underlying network structure. Experiments on public brain network datasets ABIDE and ADHD-200 demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, enhanced stability, and improved interpretability, particularly in small-sample settings.

AI.tldr: Proposes a semantic-aligned brain network framework that directly integrates LLM-derived semantic knowledge into brain connectivity analysis via ROI-level semantic enrichment, multi-scale hypergraph modeling, and decision-level semantic alignment, achieving SOTA on ABIDE and ADHD-200 datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing methods treat LLM semantics merely as auxiliary features or weak supervision, limiting their direct role in decision-making and constraining classification stability and robustness in brain disease diagnosis.
AI.method: (1) ROI-level semantics are incorporated via global self-attention to enrich node representations with whole-brain context. (2) Multi-scale hypergraphs explicitly model functional subnetworks and multi-ROI interactions, capturing high-order dependencies beyond traditional GNN locality. (3) A decision-level semantic alignment mechanism selectively injects patient-specific textual embeddings into graph representations, enabling semantics to directly guide predictions without perturbing network structure.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance, enhanced stability, and improved interpretability on ABIDE and ADHD-200 public brain network datasets, with particularly strong gains in small-sample settings.
AI.conclusion: Directly integrating LLM-derived semantics into the decision-making process — rather than as auxiliary features — significantly improves brain disease classification accuracy, robustness, and interpretability, especially under data scarcity.

title: ContextNest: Verifiable Context Governance for Autonomous AI Agent
summary:
Autonomous AI agents increasingly depend on external knowledge stores, yet most retrieval pipelines provide relevance without durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, or point-in-time reconstruction. We formalize this as context governance and present ContextNext, an open specification and reference implementation for governed AI-consumable knowledge vaults. ContextNext does not replace Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG); it supplies the governance layer beneath retrieval, determining which artifacts are approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified before retrieval systems operate over them.
  The specification combines typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, source nodes for live data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and audit traces of agent context consumption. These mechanisms let organizations reconstruct which knowledge versions informed an agent output and whether those versions were AI-eligible when consumed.
  We report first empirical results from two controlled experiments. In a stale-version attack isolating the governance-versus-retrieval failure mode, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25 sparse retrieval, with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% versus 93-90%) at about one-third the input-token cost. In a retrieval-determinism experiment over a 1,060-document corpus, deterministic selectors and BM25 return stable document sets across repeated identical queries (Jaccard 1.0), while a dense+HNSW baseline is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210). These results suggest that context governance addresses failure modes retrieval quality alone is not designed to resolve. We release a core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.

AI.tldr: ContextNext is an open specification and reference implementation that adds a governance layer beneath RAG systems, providing provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, and point-in-time reconstruction for AI-consumable knowledge. Experiments show governed selection outperforms BM25 on answer quality (97% vs 90-93%) at lower token cost, and deterministic selectors guarantee stable retrieval (Jaccard 1.0) versus non-deterministic dense+HNSW (mean Jaccard 0.611).
AI.motivation: Current retrieval pipelines for autonomous AI agents provide relevance but lack durable guarantees around provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, and point-in-time reconstruction — collectively termed "context governance." Without such guarantees, organizations cannot reliably determine which knowledge versions informed an agent's output or whether those versions were approved and AI-eligible at the time of consumption.
AI.method: ContextNext introduces an open specification combining: (1) typed Markdown documents with metadata; (2) deterministic set-algebraic selectors; (3) contextnest:// URI references; (4) SHA-256 hash-chained version histories; (5) graph-level checkpoints; (6) source nodes for live data via Model Context Protocol (MCP); and (7) audit traces of agent context consumption. Two controlled experiments were conducted: a stale-version attack experiment comparing governed selection against BM25 sparse retrieval, and a retrieval-determinism experiment over 1,060 documents comparing deterministic selectors and BM25 against a dense+HNSW baseline.
AI.result: In the stale-version attack experiment, governed selection achieved a 97% answer-quality pass rate versus 93-90% for BM25, at roughly one-third the input-token cost. In the retrieval-determinism experiment, deterministic selectors and BM25 returned stable document sets (Jaccard 1.0) across repeated identical queries, while the dense+HNSW baseline proved non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210).
AI.conclusion: Context governance addresses failure modes that retrieval quality alone cannot resolve. By providing a governance layer beneath retrieval, ContextNext enables organizations to reconstruct agent knowledge provenance, enforce AI-eligibility of artifacts, and achieve deterministic, cost-efficient context selection. The core engine, CLI, and MCP server are released under open licenses.

title: Population-Based Multi-Objective Training of Discriminators for Semi-Supervised GANs
comment: The 2nd International Conference on Federated Learning and Intelligent Computing Systems (FLICS2026)
summary: Semi-supervised generative adversarial networks (SSL-GANs) can exploit large unlabeled datasets while retaining a classifier in the discriminator, but their training is often unstable. This paper proposes a population-based evolutionary training strategy in which discriminator learning is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem. Instead of aggregating the supervised and unsupervised components of the SSL objective into a single scalar loss, the method maintains a population of discriminators ranked by Pareto dominance, enabling the exploration of different trade-offs between classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination. This formulation aims to improve both roles of SSL-GANs: learning accurate classifiers and training generators capable of producing realistic samples. We analyze several variants, including an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation, to assess the role of multi-objective selection. Experiments on MNIST with limited labels show improved training robustness compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN state-of-the-art baselines, while the elitist variant consistently achieves the highest classification accuracy.

AI.tldr: Proposes a multi-objective evolutionary training strategy for semi-supervised GANs, where a population of discriminators is ranked via Pareto dominance to balance classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination, improving training stability and accuracy on limited-label MNIST.
AI.motivation: Standard SSL-GAN training is often unstable because the supervised and unsupervised loss components are aggregated into a single scalar, forcing a fixed trade-off. The authors aim to instead treat these as separate objectives to better explore trade-offs between classifier accuracy and discriminator quality, ultimately improving both classification performance and sample generation.
AI.method: Discriminator learning is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem with two objectives: (1) classification accuracy on labeled data, and (2) real/fake discrimination on unlabeled/generated data. A population of discriminators is maintained and ranked by Pareto dominance. Variants include an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation. The generator is trained against discriminators selected from the Pareto front.
AI.result: The proposed approach shows improved training robustness compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN baselines on MNIST with limited labels. The elitist variant consistently achieves the highest classification accuracy among all tested variants.
AI.conclusion: Multi-objective evolutionary optimization with Pareto-based selection provides a principled way to balance the dual objectives of SSL-GAN discriminators, leading to more stable training and better classifiers without sacrificing generative quality.

title: Enhancing Fitness Intelligence through Domain-Specific LLM Post-Training
comment: 8 pages, 6 tables, 2 figures. Accepted by the 12th International Conference on Big Data Computing and Communications (BigCom 2026)
summary: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) is typically delivered by human professionals, making it costly and inaccessible to many. While recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) show considerable promise for more inclusive fitness coaching, directly deploying prevailing general-purpose LLMs in SFC reveals critical limitations. These models often lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge integration, leading to weak performance on complex SFC scenarios. In this paper, we introduce FitOne, a series of fitness LLMs (with 8B and 32B parameters) designed to improve reliability and domain specialization for SFC applications. Built upon the Qwen3 foundation models, FitOne is developed through a three-stage post-training pipeline consisting of continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, using large-scale, high-quality datasets derived from rigorous knowledge engineering. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of FitOne on professional fitness certification exams, including ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS, as well as general capabilities such as knowledge reasoning and instruction following. Experimental results show that, while retaining strong general capabilities, FitOne-8B/32B achieves average improvements of up to 10.09%/9.29% and 12.73%/7.01% on the ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS exams, respectively, compared with the Qwen3 base models. Furthermore, in-depth ablation studies confirm the necessity of each training stage, highlighting the pipeline's effectiveness in balancing domain expertise enhancement with general ability retention. We believe this research advances LLM systems toward more reliable fitness intelligence and will inspire future research on developing domain-specific LLMs.

AI.tldr: FitOne introduces a series of domain-specific LLMs (8B/32B) for scientific fitness coaching, built on Qwen3 via a three-stage post-training pipeline (continual pre-training, SFT, RL). It significantly outperforms base models on professional fitness exams while retaining general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) is costly and inaccessible due to reliance on human professionals. General-purpose LLMs lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge for complex SFC scenarios, motivating the need for specialized, reliable fitness intelligence models.
AI.method: FitOne is built on Qwen3 foundation models using a three-stage post-training pipeline: (1) continual pre-training, (2) supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and (3) reinforcement learning (RL), all leveraging large-scale, high-quality datasets constructed through rigorous knowledge engineering. Two model sizes are developed: 8B and 32B parameters.
AI.result: FitOne-8B achieves average improvements of 10.09% on ACSM-EP and 12.73% on NSCA-CSCS exams over Qwen3 base; FitOne-32B achieves 9.29% and 7.01% respectively. Ablation studies confirm each training stage is necessary, and general capabilities are preserved.
AI.conclusion: The three-stage post-training pipeline effectively balances domain expertise enhancement with general ability retention, advancing LLMs toward more reliable fitness intelligence and offering a blueprint for domain-specific LLM development.

title: Zeus: Towards Tuning-Free Foundation Model for Time Series Analysis
summary: We present Zeus, a unified tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) that delivers superior performance across diverse analysis tasks without any task-specific fine-tuning. Unlike prior studies that primarily focus on zero-shot forecasting but require task-specific tuning for other tasks, Zeus bridges this gap by addressing two fundamental challenges in multi-task generalization. First, to reconcile point-level granularity with long-sequence scalability, Zeus incorporates a multi-scale Transformer featuring point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchy, effectively balancing fine-grained fidelity with computational efficiency. Second, to accommodate varying inductive biases across different tasks, Zeus introduces Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM), a unified strategy that supports heterogeneous tasks (e.g., extrapolation, interpolation, and global abstraction) within a single framework. Extensive experiments across five representative tasks demonstrate that Zeus consistently achieves competitive results in tuning-free settings, underscoring its potential as a general-purpose TSFM.

AI.tldr: Zeus is a tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model that uses a multi-scale Transformer with U-shaped hierarchy and Multi-Objective Temporal Masking to achieve strong zero-shot performance across heterogeneous tasks (forecasting, imputation, classification, etc.) without any task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing TS foundation models focus narrowly on zero-shot forecasting but require task-specific tuning for other tasks. The key gap is achieving multi-task generalization in a single tuning-free framework, which requires reconciling point-level granularity with long-sequence scalability and accommodating diverse inductive biases across heterogeneous tasks.
AI.method: Zeus employs two core innovations: (1) a multi-scale Transformer architecture with point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchy to balance fine-grained fidelity with computational efficiency; (2) Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM), a unified pretraining strategy that handles heterogeneous tasks — extrapolation, interpolation, and global abstraction — within a single framework.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across five representative time series tasks demonstrate that Zeus consistently achieves competitive results in tuning-free (zero-shot) settings, matching or approaching the performance of task-specific models.
AI.conclusion: Zeus demonstrates strong potential as a general-purpose, tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model, unifying multiple analytical tasks under a single framework and eliminating the need for per-task fine-tuning.

title: Coding-agents can replicate scientific machine learning papers
summary: Scientific machine learning papers typically make computational claims, e.g., that the relative mean square error is less than 5% or that the 95% predictive credible interval covers the test data. A coding agent can be prompted to replicate those claims from paper materials alone, but the prompt does not by itself reliably preserve progress or check whether generated evidence supports the paper's claims. We introduce Paper-replication, a workflow that makes each selected paper claim a target with recorded evidence, and implement it as a coding-agent skill. The workflow makes the agent record those targets, reconstruct the paper's method, run computational experiments, link generated outputs to provenance and comparisons with the paper's claims, record where matched evidence appears in the replication report, and pass validation checks before completion. We evaluate Paper-replication on twelve independent runs across four scientific machine learning papers. All twelve workspaces pass the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets are matched with report coverage. Even in this completed workspace state, repeated runs differ in how papers are divided into targets, in numerical fidelity to the source papers, in elapsed replication time, in the number of intermediate executions replaced before final evidence is accepted, and in the rules used to accept evidence. Paper-replication makes completion depend on workspace evidence and validation checks rather than on the agent's final message.

AI.tldr: Paper-replication is a coding-agent workflow that systematically reproduces computational claims from scientific ML papers by treating each claim as a verifiable target, recording evidence, and enforcing validation checks — ensuring completion depends on workspace evidence rather than the agent's final output.
AI.motivation: Current coding agents can be prompted to replicate paper claims, but they lack mechanisms to reliably track progress, verify that generated evidence actually supports claims, or ensure accountability in the replication process. There is a need for structured workflows that tie completion to verifiable evidence.
AI.method: Paper-replication structures the replication process around discrete claim targets. The agent: (1) records paper claims as targets, (2) reconstructs the paper's method, (3) runs computational experiments, (4) links outputs to provenance and compares with paper claims, (5) records where matched evidence appears in the report, and (6) passes validation checks before completion. The workflow is implemented as a coding-agent skill.
AI.result: Evaluated on twelve independent runs across four scientific ML papers, all twelve workspaces passed the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets were matched with report coverage. However, repeated runs exhibited variance in claim decomposition, numerical fidelity, elapsed time, intermediate execution replacement count, and evidence-acceptance rules.
AI.conclusion: Paper-replication successfully shifts completion criteria from the agent's final message to workspace evidence and validation checks, enabling more reliable and auditable automated paper replication. The observed variance across runs highlights inherent variability in LLM-driven replication that warrants further investigation.

title: Conditional Co-Ablation: Recovering Self-Repair Backups in Transformer Circuits
summary: Mechanistic interpretability often relies on component-level interventions to discover how a model produces a behavior. This guides attribution, capability knockout, and model pruning downstream to operate by scoring each unit by the effect of ablation in isolation. Such first-order scoring is natural when component importance is additive, but becomes misleading when a transformer self-repairs: after a primary component is removed, a dormant backup can take over, muting the primary's measured effect while the backup itself appears irrelevant on the intact model. We recast this failure as a recovery task, conditional circuit completion, and introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score that asks how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows once a primary set has been removed. This conditional growth exposes the second-order interaction that single-unit scores discard. On the GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines, including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82); counterfactual patching verifies that the recovered heads causally carry the repair. The same label-free procedure transfers to induction across eight models. Beyond discovery, the recovered backups correct self-repair-masked attribution, identify the components required for capability knockout, and yield repair-aware structured pruning scaling from 124M to 7B. Component importance is therefore not merely an isolated-unit property: in robust circuits, the components that matter can become visible only under the interventions that make them necessary.

AI.tldr: Traditional component-level ablation in mechanistic interpretability fails when transformer models exhibit self-repair—where backup components compensate for removed primary ones, masking their importance. The authors introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a second-order scoring method that measures how much a component's ablation effect grows after a primary set is removed, exposing hidden backup mechanisms. CoAx achieves 0.91 ROC-AUC in recovering backup heads on GPT-2-small's IOI circuit, outperforming all baselines, and generalizes across eight models for induction tasks. The method also improves attribution, capability knockout, and structured pruning.
AI.motivation: Standard first-order ablation scoring assumes component importance is additive and fails when transformers self-repair: after removing a primary component, dormant backups activate, muting the primary's measured effect while the backup appears irrelevant in the intact model. This makes critical components invisible under isolated interventions.
AI.method: The authors frame the problem as conditional circuit completion and propose Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score. After ablating a primary set of components, CoAx measures how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows relative to baseline. This conditional growth quantifies second-order interactions (backup behavior) that single-unit scores miss. The method requires no labels, relying solely on output distribution shifts.
AI.result: On GPT-2-small's IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82). Counterfactual patching verifies recovered heads causally carry the repair. The method transfers successfully to induction across eight models. It also corrects self-repair-masked attribution, identifies components necessary for capability knockout, and enables repair-aware structured pruning scaling from 124M to 7B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Component importance is not merely an isolated-unit property; in robust circuits, the components that matter can become visible only under interventions that make them necessary. CoAx provides a principled method for discovering these hidden backup mechanisms, with broad implications for mechanistic interpretability, model editing, and pruning.

title: A$^{2}$utoLPBench: An Auto-Generated, Agent-Friendly LP Benchmark via Inverse-KKT Construction
summary: Most LP-from-text benchmarks are static datasets of word problems written and labeled by hand. Once such a dataset is released, its size is fixed, its difficulty is fixed, and every problem can leak into the training data of future LLMs. We present \textbf{A$^{2}$utoLPBench}, a benchmark for testing LLM-driven agents on linear programming problems written in plain text. We first pick a feasible point and dual, then write down a problem for which that point is optimal and the objective value is known. The answer is known by construction, with no solver call and no human annotator. The evaluation environment bundles a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image whose usage instructions are written for an LLM-driven agent to read. With these in place, any agent can run the benchmark and get a calibrated score with one command. Because the benchmark is a generator rather than a fixed dataset, it has properties no fixed dataset can match: an unlimited supply of fresh problems, a difficulty knob set by $(n,m)$, ground-truth answers correct by construction, low LLM-side cost per problem relative to human authoring, repeatable scores across independent batches, and resistance to training-data leakage when fresh post-cutoff seed ranges are used.

AI.tldr: A²utoLPBench is a generative benchmark for LLM-driven agents solving linear programming problems in natural language. Instead of a static dataset, it synthesizes problems from a known optimal solution (feasible point + dual), ensuring ground-truth answers by construction, unlimited fresh problems, adjustable difficulty via (n,m), and resistance to training-data leakage.
AI.motivation: Static LP-from-text benchmarks suffer from fixed size, fixed difficulty, and risk of leakage into LLM training data. Human authoring is costly and does not scale. A generative benchmark that produces fresh, calibrated problems with known answers by construction solves these issues.
AI.method: The benchmark generates LP problems in reverse: first select a feasible primal-dual pair with a known optimal objective value, then synthesize the textual problem statement for which that point is optimal. No solver calls or human annotators are needed. The environment includes a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image with usage instructions designed for LLM-driven agents to interpret. Agents run the benchmark and receive a calibrated score via a single command.
AI.result: The benchmark offers unlimited fresh problems, tunable difficulty via (n,m) parameters, ground-truth answers correct by construction, low per-problem LLM cost relative to human authoring, repeatable scores across independent batches, and resistance to data leakage when using post-cutoff seed ranges.
AI.conclusion: A²utoLPBench demonstrates that generative benchmarking — constructing problems backward from known solutions — can overcome fundamental limitations of static datasets for evaluating LLM agents on structured reasoning tasks like linear programming.

title: Hybrid quantum-classical neural network for sentiment analysis
summary: Quantum machine learning has recently emerged as a promising paradigm that leverages the expressive power of quantum circuits to address complex learning tasks. In this work, we investigate the applicability of hybrid quantum-classical neural networks to sentiment analysis, a central problem in natural language processing. We focus on a dataset of tweets related to COVID-19, where the textual content is vectorized using TF-IDF and fed into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits. Our results show that hybrid models can achieve accuracy comparable to the classical baseline, while exhibiting distinct learning dynamics, especially in terms of validation loss and accuracy, that suggest a richer representational capacity. Moreover, when applying transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task, the hybrid models consistently outperform the classical counterpart, achieving an accuracy increase of 15 percentage points (from 66% to 81%) on the spam class, demonstrating enhanced generalization. These findings highlight the feasibility of employing QML for natural language processing and point toward the potential advantages of hybrid models as quantum hardware continues to advance.

AI.tldr: Hybrid quantum-classical neural networks applied to sentiment analysis achieve comparable accuracy to classical models while showing richer representational capacity. In transfer learning for SMS spam detection, hybrid models outperform classical counterparts by 15 percentage points (66% → 81%), suggesting enhanced generalization.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether hybrid quantum-classical neural networks can be effectively applied to NLP tasks — specifically sentiment analysis — and whether they offer representational or generalization advantages over purely classical feedforward networks.
AI.method: TF-IDF vectorized COVID-19 tweets are fed into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures with parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs). Performance is evaluated on in-domain sentiment analysis and out-of-domain transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task.
AI.result: Hybrid models match classical baseline accuracy on sentiment analysis with distinct learning dynamics (validation loss/accuracy curves). On transfer learning, hybrid models substantially outperform classical models, improving spam class accuracy from 66% to 81%.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid QML models are feasible for NLP tasks and exhibit superior generalization in transfer learning scenarios, suggesting potential advantages as quantum hardware matures.

title: A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks
summary: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated, and recent rubric-based evaluations such as HealthBench have shown that open-ended clinical performance is far from solved - its "Hard" subset top score remains 32%. We present a small, deliberately difficult evaluation dataset of five clinician-authored clinical scenarios spanning four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics), each accompanied by an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25-62 criteria per task; 184 criteria total) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. We evaluate three frontier models: GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.39 (GPT), and 0.37 (Gemini). The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical (weight-5) criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Three LLM autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria. We position this as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution: the five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline ready to develop into a large-scale benchmark.

AI.tldr: A small, clinician-authored evaluation dataset of five open-ended clinical scenarios (184 weighted rubric criteria) reveals that frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude, Gemini) achieve only 37-47% mean rubric pass rates, with a dangerous inversion: critical (weight-5) criteria pass at 32-42% while low-stakes criteria pass at 80-90%. Over half of critical criteria were unmet by any model. LLM autoraters achieve 93-95% agreement with expert labels.
AI.motivation: Medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated (e.g., multiple-choice exams), yet open-ended clinical reasoning remains far from solved — HealthBench's Hard subset tops at only 32%. The authors aim to address the gap in rigorous, granular evaluation of clinical decision-making by constructing a deliberately difficult, rubric-based assessment that can detect dangerous failure modes invisible to aggregate scoring.
AI.method: Five clinician-authored clinical scenarios were created across four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, obstetrics). Each scenario includes an atomic, weighted, MECE (Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive) rubric with 25-62 criteria (184 total), derived from clinician-drafted golden answers. Criteria are weighted on a 1-5 scale. Three frontier models (GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro) were evaluated. Three LLM autoraters were validated against expert met/not-met labels across 552 graded criteria.
AI.result: Mean rubric pass rates: Claude 0.47, GPT 0.39, Gemini 0.37. Critical finding: weight-5 (highest-priority) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, versus 80-90% for weight-1 criteria. Of 108 weight-5 criteria, 56 (52%) were satisfied by no model whatsoever. LLM autoraters reproduced expert labels with 92.8-94.7% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: This is positioned as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution demonstrating a scalable, defensible pipeline for rubric-based clinical evaluation. The critical-priority inversion — where models perform worst on the most clinically important criteria — underscores the inadequacy of current frontier models for high-stakes clinical applications and validates the need for atomic, weighted rubric evaluation over aggregate scoring.

title: A More Accurate Algorithm Comparison through A/B Testing using Offline Evaluation Methods
summary: A/B testing is the gold standard for selecting the better algorithm in online services. While offline evaluation has attracted attention as a safer alternative due to the high experimental costs and the potential risk of degrading user experience and revenue in A/B testing, it is widely recognized that the estimation accuracy of offline evaluation is substantially lower. As a result, final selection decisions are typically made through A/B testing. Contrary to this conventional view, we reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon in which A/B testing can produce a higher algorithm selection error rate than offline evaluation. This occurs because the sample mean estimator used in A/B testing does not induce positive correlation, which is crucial for reducing critical selection errors, namely underestimating the truly superior algorithm and overestimating the truly inferior one. In contrast, offline evaluation methods unintentionally generate this beneficial correlation by relying on shared offline data when estimating and comparing the performance of multiple algorithms. Building on this insight, we propose an estimator that intentionally induces positive correlation to improve algorithm selection in A/B testing. The key idea is to introduce a hypothetical middle algorithm and to estimate the performance difference between algorithms A, M, and B in a stepwise manner using shared data at each step. This approach enables the application of offline evaluation techniques in each step, thereby inducing positive correlation and reducing critical selection errors. Furthermore, we derive the optimal middle algorithm regarding the resulting variance and analyze its advantages over existing methods through bias-variance analysis. Experiments on real-world data demonstrate that our estimator achieves the same selection error rate as existing approaches while using only one half of the A/B testing data.

AI.tldr: Contrary to conventional wisdom, A/B testing can yield higher algorithm selection error rates than offline evaluation because its sample mean estimator lacks positive correlation. The authors propose a stepwise estimator using a hypothetical "middle algorithm" that intentionally induces positive correlation, halving the data needed to match existing A/B testing error rates.
AI.motivation: A/B testing, while the gold standard for online algorithm selection, has high experimental costs and risks degrading user experience. Offline evaluation is safer but widely considered less accurate. The authors challenge this view by identifying that A/B testing's independent sample mean estimator fails to induce positive correlation—a property critical for reducing the most damaging selection errors (underestimating superior algorithms and overestimating inferior ones). This insight motivates a new estimator design.
AI.method: The authors introduce a stepwise estimation procedure for A/B testing that introduces a hypothetical "middle algorithm" M. Instead of directly comparing algorithms A and B, the method estimates performance differences between A-M and M-B sequentially, sharing data across steps. This enables offline evaluation techniques (notably shared-data reliance) to be applied within each step, intentionally inducing positive correlation between estimates. The optimal middle algorithm is derived analytically based on variance minimization, and a bias-variance analysis is conducted to characterize advantages over standard estimators.
AI.result: The proposed estimator achieves the same algorithm selection error rate as standard A/B testing approaches while requiring only half the data, as demonstrated on real-world datasets. The induced positive correlation is shown to reduce both Type I (overestimating inferior algorithms) and Type II (underestimating superior algorithms) selection errors.
AI.conclusion: A/B testing's superiority for algorithm selection is not inherent but depends on the estimator used. By intentionally inducing positive correlation via a stepwise middle-algorithm framework, the proposed method significantly improves data efficiency without sacrificing selection accuracy, offering a practical path to safer and cheaper online experimentation.

title: UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development
summary: Software development is a complex task that demands cooperation among agents with diverse roles. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous multi-agent software development frameworks that leverage role-based collaboration to automate requirements analysis, coding, testing, and refinement. However, existing approaches typically assume that intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, leaving them vulnerable to hallucination propagation, where incorrect decisions generated in early development phases are transferred to downstream agents and negatively impact final software quality. To address this challenge, we propose UA-ChatDev, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that integrates uncertainty quantification into agent interactions. It introduces a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism based on token-level log probabilities to assess the confidence of agent responses and employs phase-aware threshold calibration to selectively trigger retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels. Extensive experiments on the SRDD benchmark demonstrate that UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent software development frameworks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Further ablation studies and communication analyses verify that uncertainty-aware interactions enhance code execution reliability.

AI.tldr: UA-ChatDev introduces uncertainty quantification into multi-agent software development to combat hallucination propagation. It uses token-level log probabilities for confidence estimation and phase-aware thresholds to trigger retrieval-based verification, outperforming existing frameworks on the SRDD benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM-based software development frameworks treat all intermediate agent outputs as equally reliable, making them susceptible to hallucination propagation—where incorrect early-phase decisions cascade downstream and degrade final software quality.
AI.method: UA-ChatDev integrates uncertainty quantification via a lightweight token-level log-probability mechanism to assess agent response confidence. It employs phase-aware threshold calibration that selectively triggers retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels, preventing unreliable outputs from propagating through the development pipeline.
AI.result: UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms both single-agent and multi-agent baselines on the SRDD benchmark across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Ablation and communication analyses confirm that uncertainty-aware interactions improve code execution reliability.
AI.conclusion: Integrating uncertainty awareness into multi-agent software development frameworks effectively mitigates hallucination propagation and improves software quality, demonstrating that confidence-calibrated, phase-aware verification is a promising direction for autonomous software engineering.

title: Probabilistic Low-Voltage Peak Load Forecasting with Time Series Foundation Models Evaluated on Application-Oriented Metrics
comment: A poster abstract of this publication will be available at the 15th DACH+ Conference on Energy Informatics (2026 in Linz, Austria)
summary: Low-voltage load forecasting is an important component in current and future energy systems with a high degree of electrification and decentralized generation. However, current forecasting methods require significant manual effort, often lack uncertainty estimation and proper peak prediction, and they are often not adequately evaluated in terms of grid requirements. In the present study, we provide an extensive evaluation of short-term net load forecasts of 200 real-world low-voltage feeders with a focus on the rapidly evolving time series foundation models. Our study compares Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2 and TabPFN-TS to six baseline models and demonstrates superior performance, in particular for Chronos-2. An ablation study, in which weather covariates are omitted, shows that time series foundation models adapt to increased uncertainty, despite the importance of weather information. A novel application-oriented metric links the model's forecasting capabilities in peak prediction to the trade-off in grid asset planning and operation between cost reduction and minimizing the risk of failure.

AI.tldr: Evaluation of time series foundation models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS) for short-term net load forecasting on 200 real-world low-voltage feeders, demonstrating Chronos-2's superior performance, robustness to omitted weather covariates, and a novel application-oriented metric linking peak prediction to grid planning trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Current low-voltage load forecasting methods require excessive manual effort, lack uncertainty estimation and proper peak prediction, and are inadequately evaluated against real grid requirements — a gap exacerbated by increasing electrification and decentralized generation.
AI.method: Extensive empirical evaluation comparing three time series foundation models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS) against six baseline models on short-term net load forecasts from 200 real-world low-voltage feeders. Includes an ablation study removing weather covariates to test robustness, and introduces a novel application-oriented metric that quantifies the trade-off between cost reduction and failure risk in grid asset planning.
AI.result: Time series foundation models — particularly Chronos-2 — demonstrate superior forecasting performance over baselines. The ablation study reveals that these models adapt to increased uncertainty when weather covariates are omitted, despite weather information being important. The proposed metric effectively captures the cost-risk trade-off in grid planning.
AI.conclusion: Foundation models, especially Chronos-2, offer a compelling off-the-shelf solution for low-voltage net load forecasting with reduced manual effort, robust uncertainty handling, and practical relevance for grid asset planning and operation.

title: Criticality-Based Guard Rail Validation for AI Agent Decisions in Autonomous Telecom Networks
summary: The evolution toward fully autonomous telecommunications networks (Autonomous Network Levels 4-5) requires AI/ML agents to make real-time network decisions without human intervention. However, no standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes, creating risks of erroneous autonomous decisions. This paper proposes the Guard Rail Validation (GRV) framework, a standardizable runtime architecture for intercepting and validating AI-driven decisions before execution. The framework evaluates decisions across multiple weighted dimensions -- including action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, and temporal behavioural patterns -- to determine a criticality level. Based on this level, graduated validation mechanisms are applied: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. The framework additionally provides cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14). We present the architecture, algorithmic procedures, O-RAN deployment model, and evaluate threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.

AI.tldr: Proposes GRV (Guard Rail Validation), a runtime framework for intercepting AI/ML inference outputs in autonomous telecom networks (Levels 4-5) before they trigger live changes, using multi-dimensional criticality scoring and graduated validation mechanisms, plus cross-agent conflict resolution and compliance logging.
AI.motivation: Autonomous networks at Levels 4-5 require AI/ML agents to make real-time decisions without human oversight, but no standardized runtime mechanism exists to validate individual inference outputs before they affect live network state. This creates significant risk of erroneous autonomous decisions propagating directly into production infrastructure.
AI.method: The GRV framework intercepts AI inference outputs and evaluates them across six weighted dimensions (action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, temporal behavioural patterns) to compute a criticality level. Based on this level, it applies graduated validation: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. It also includes cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging (EU AI Act Article 14 compliance). An O-RAN deployment model is provided.
AI.result: The paper evaluates threat coverage against known AI/ML attack vectors in telecommunications and presents the O-RAN deployment architecture, demonstrating that GRV can systematically address risks from adversarial attacks, model drift, and erroneous inference in fully autonomous network operations.
AI.conclusion: GRV offers a practical, standardizable runtime safeguard for fully autonomous telecom networks, bridging the gap between AI-driven automation and operational safety by ensuring no inference output directly alters live network state without proportional validation — aligning with emerging regulatory requirements such as the EU AI Act.

title: Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency
summary: Newer lightweight convolutional neural networks are often presented as improving predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but such claims require controlled evaluation. This study compares nine lightweight CNN model packages across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a shared downstream protocol. We report top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on an NVIDIA L4 and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers. EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest observed top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 97.57% and 86.98%, while RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet at 79.87%. EfficientNet-B0 remains within 0.22, 0.85, and 1.79 percentage points of the best result on the three datasets while using approximately 79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S. It also appears on every evaluated accuracy and resource Pareto frontier, making it the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMAC count, is the fastest model under both CPU thread settings, and records higher observed accuracy than MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all three datasets. Under random initialization, it leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S by 2.55, 1.76, and 0.99 points, with paired test-set intervals excluding zero for the fixed trained models. EfficientNet-B0 remains 3.29, 10.10, and 17.54 points below its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training, despite requiring about five times the recorded training time. SqueezeNet1.1 has the fewest parameters and lowest peak CUDA allocation, but substantially weaker accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between the L4 and CPU environments, showing that GMACs alone do not predict measured inference performance. Overall, newer designs provide selective rather than universal gains

AI.tldr: A controlled empirical comparison of nine lightweight CNN architectures across three image classification benchmarks reveals that newer models offer selective rather than universal improvements. EfficientNetV2-S leads accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, while EfficientNet-B0 provides the best accuracy-efficiency trade-off, appearing on every Pareto frontier. MobileNetV3-Small surpasses MobileNetV4-Conv-S in both accuracy and speed, and latency rankings diverge sharply between GPU and CPU, demonstrating that GMACs alone are poor predictors of real-world inference performance.
AI.motivation: New lightweight CNN architectures are frequently introduced with claims of superior predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but these claims often lack rigorous, controlled, head-to-head evaluation under a shared protocol. The authors aim to provide a standardized, multi-metric benchmark to determine whether newer designs genuinely deliver universal gains or only selective improvements over established baselines.
AI.method: Nine lightweight CNN model packages (including EfficientNet variants, MobileNet variants, RepViT, SqueezeNet, etc.) are compared across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet using a shared downstream training and evaluation protocol. Metrics include top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on NVIDIA L4 GPU and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU (single/multi-threaded), peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers. Both pretrained and random-initialization (scratch) training regimes are evaluated.
AI.result: EfficientNetV2-S achieves highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 (97.57%) and CIFAR-100 (86.98%); RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet (79.87%). EfficientNet-B0 trails the best by only 0.22–1.79 points while using ~79% fewer parameters and ~86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S, appearing on every Pareto frontier. MobileNetV3-Small outperforms MobileNetV4-Conv-S across all datasets (by 2.55, 1.76, 0.99 points under random init) and is faster under CPU. EfficientNet-B0 shows large accuracy drops without pretraining (3.29–17.54 points). Latency rankings differ sharply between L4 GPU and CPU environments.
AI.conclusion: Newer lightweight CNN designs provide selective rather than universal performance gains. EfficientNet-B0 emerges as the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget model. GMACs are an unreliable proxy for measured latency across heterogeneous hardware. Pretraining remains critical for performance, and MobileNetV3-Small challenges the assumed superiority of its successor, highlighting the value of controlled, multi-faceted benchmarking.

title: Purified OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation Without Losing How to Think
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving LLM reasoning, where a privileged teacher with access to reference solutions provides token-level supervision on the student's own generated trajectories. However, we find that OPSD consistently fails on long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning models, yielding at best marginal gains while destabilizing the reflective reasoning capability these models depend on. Through a novel decomposition of the teacher's supervision signal, we identify the root cause: the teacher's supervision is dominated by a reference-induced component that drives rote memorization of reference-specific shortcuts, while the question-conditioned, inference-transferable component is ignored or actively opposed. Based on this diagnosis, we propose a two-step solution. First, we construct a reference-only teacher (the same model conditioned on the reference without the question) to isolate the non-transferable component of the supervision signal; the residual after subtracting this component captures the question-conditioned, inference-transferable correction. Second, we use pointwise mutual information (PMI) as the mechanism to transform this residual into a well-formed PMI target distribution that the student can directly distill from, filtering out the reference-induced shortcut. Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.

AI.tldr: Standard on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) fails on long chain-of-thought models because the teacher's supervision is dominated by reference-specific shortcuts that promote rote memorization rather than transferable reasoning. The authors propose isolating this non-transferable component via a reference-only teacher and using pointwise mutual information (PMI) to construct a distilled target that preserves genuine reasoning capabilities.
AI.motivation: OPSD, while effective for standard LLM reasoning, consistently fails when applied to long chain-of-thought reasoning models — yielding marginal gains at best and actively destabilizing the reflective reasoning these models rely on. The authors aim to diagnose why this failure occurs and develop a remedy that retains OPSD's benefits without corrupting long-CoT reasoning behavior.
AI.method: The authors first decompose the teacher's supervision signal, revealing it is dominated by a reference-induced component (driving rote memorization) while the question-conditioned, inference-transferable component is suppressed. Their two-step solution: (1) construct a reference-only teacher (same model conditioned solely on the reference, without the question) to isolate the non-transferable component, and subtract it to obtain the question-conditioned residual; (2) apply pointwise mutual information (PMI) to transform this residual into a well-formed target distribution suitable for distillation, effectively filtering out reference-induced shortcuts.
AI.result: Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets show consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.
AI.conclusion: OPSD's failure on long-CoT models stems from dominance of non-transferable, reference-specific shortcuts in the teacher signal. The proposed PMI-based residual distillation effectively isolates and transfers only the question-conditioned reasoning component, yielding robust improvements without disrupting reflective reasoning capabilities.

title: Liquid Latent State Dynamics for Interpretable Turbofan Degradation Modeling
summary: Multivariate time-series models for prognostics are often evaluated by point prediction accuracy, yet their internal states rarely expose a coherent degradation process. We study liquid neural networks as latent dynamics models for aircraft engine health monitoring on the C-MAPSS benchmark. The proposed model encodes a history window into a latent state, evolves that state with a liquid transition model, and decodes future sensor observations. To separate health evolution from operating-condition variation, the latent state is factorized into degradation and condition components. Remaining useful life, monotonic risk, and latent-consistency losses supervise the degradation component, while condition prediction and decorrelation losses discourage operating-condition leakage. Across FD001--FD004, the full disentangled model improves overall sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 for a GRU baseline to 0.2266, with the largest gains on the multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. The learned degradation state also forms a clearer temporal degradation axis, reaching an average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960. Direct remaining-useful-life regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline, indicating that the proposed representation is currently more effective as an interpretable world model for degradation dynamics than as a calibrated lifetime regressor.
