These results suggest that liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and inspectable health-state modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a liquid neural network with a disentangled latent state (degradation vs. operating condition) for aircraft engine prognostics. It improves sensor forecasting RMSE over a GRU baseline and yields a more interpretable degradation trajectory, though direct RUL regression remains better with the GRU.
AI.motivation: Existing multivariate time-series models for prognostics are evaluated primarily on point prediction accuracy, but their internal latent states rarely represent a coherent, interpretable degradation process. There is a need for models that simultaneously forecast sensor observations and learn a disentangled, inspectable health-state representation.
AI.method: The authors use a liquid neural network as a latent dynamics model. A history window of sensor data is encoded into a latent state, which is factorized into degradation and condition components. The degradation component is supervised by remaining useful life (RUL), monotonic risk, and latent-consistency losses. The condition component is regularized by condition prediction and decorrelation losses to prevent operating-condition leakage. The liquid transition model evolves the latent state over time, and a decoder reconstructs future sensor observations. Evaluation is performed on the C-MAPSS benchmark (FD001–FD004).
AI.result: The fully disentangled liquid model reduces overall sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 (GRU baseline) to 0.2266, with the largest improvements on multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. The learned degradation state achieves an average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960, indicating a clearer temporal degradation axis. However, direct RUL regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline, suggesting the model excels as an interpretable world model for degradation dynamics rather than as a calibrated lifetime regressor.
AI.conclusion: Liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and inspectable health-state modeling. The disentangled representation yields better sensor predictions and a more coherent degradation trajectory, though further work is needed to match dedicated RUL regression performance.

title: Fast and Accurate Anomaly Detection in Time Series
summary: Anomaly detection is a critical and evolving field in Machine Learning, with applications targeting different domains such as cybersecurity, finance, healthcare, manufacturing and IoT (Internet of Things) systems. Traditionally, anomaly detection algorithms have been designed using both supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms. The fundamental challenge in real-world anomaly detection scenarios is related to the inherent class imbalance (anomalies are typically rare) and, for supervised methods, to the scarcity of labelled anomalous data. Indeed, labelling is both expensive and time-consuming. Conversely unsupervised methods do not require labelling, but may suffer from high false positive rates when deployed in safety-critical applications. In this work we introduce a novel unsupervised algorithm for anomaly detection in time series based on the Haar discrete wavelet and a suitably designed $t$-test. We establish the theoretical foundation of the proposed $t$-test and, through extensive experimentation across 343 datasets, demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A novel unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm for time series is proposed, combining Haar discrete wavelet transform with a specially designed t-test. Tested on 343 datasets, it outperforms existing unsupervised and self-supervised methods.
AI.motivation: Real-world anomaly detection suffers from severe class imbalance and a scarcity of labeled anomalous data. Supervised methods require expensive, time-consuming labeling, while unsupervised methods often yield high false positive rates — unacceptable in safety-critical applications. The authors aim to bridge this gap with a theoretically grounded unsupervised approach.
AI.method: The algorithm leverages the Haar discrete wavelet transform for time series decomposition, combined with a custom-designed t-test as the anomaly scoring mechanism. The theoretical foundations of this t-test are formally established, and the method is evaluated through extensive experiments on 343 datasets against state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.
AI.result: The proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks across extensive experimentation on 343 datasets.
AI.conclusion: The Haar wavelet-based t-test approach provides an effective, theoretically sound solution for unsupervised time series anomaly detection, overcoming limitations of both supervised methods (label dependency) and traditional unsupervised methods (high false positive rates).

title: AgenticSTS: A Bounded-Memory Testbed for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Memory for a long-horizon LLM agent is a contract about what each future decision is allowed to see. The simplest contract appends past observations, tool calls, and reflections to every prompt, which makes prior context easy to access but also turns it into a jumbled mixture in which the effect of any single memory component is hard to isolate. We introduce and instrument an alternative bounded contract: every decision is made from a fresh user message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. The prompt thus stays bounded across runs of any length, and any single layer can be ablated in isolation. We instantiate the contract in Slay the Spire 2, a closed-rule stochastic deck-building game whose runs require hundreds of tactical and strategic decisions. A public online benchmark of frontier LLMs on the same game reports zero wins at the lowest difficulty across five configurations, and the developer-reported human win rate at the same difficulty is 16%; the task is hard but not saturated. Within our harness, a fixed-A0 ablation shows the largest observed difference when triggered strategic skills are enabled: the no-store baseline wins 3/10 games and adding the skill layer 6/10. At this sample size the comparison is directional rather than statistically decisive (Fisher exact p\approx0.37); a cross-backbone probe and public accumulating-context baselines are reported as operational comparisons rather than controlled tests of the contract variable itself. We release a reproducible testbed: 298 completed trajectories with condition tags, frozen memory/skill snapshots, prompt records, and analysis scripts -- an agent design and a validated, reusable methodology for studying how explicit memory layers shape long-horizon LLM-agent decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a bounded memory contract for long-horizon LLM agents based on typed retrieval rather than raw transcript appending. Tested on Slay the Spire 2, a triggered strategic skills layer improves win rates from 3/10 to 6/10 over a no-store baseline. The authors release a reproducible testbed with 298 completed trajectories for studying explicit memory layers.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM agent architectures append all past observations, tool calls, and reflections into a growing prompt, creating an unstructured "jumbled mixture" where individual memory components cannot be isolated or ablated. The authors seek a bounded, modular alternative that keeps prompt size constant across arbitrarily long runs and allows isolated ablation of any single memory layer.
AI.method: The authors introduce a "bounded contract" where each decision prompt is assembled fresh via typed retrieval — pulling relevant memories, skills, and context from structured stores — rather than appending the raw cross-decision transcript. They instantiate this in Slay the Spire 2, a stochastic deck-building game requiring hundreds of decisions per run. Key ablation: a "no-store" baseline vs. enabling a triggered strategic skills layer. Evaluation uses Fisher's exact test and cross-backbone probes against public accumulating-context baselines.
AI.result: The no-store baseline wins 3/10 games; adding the triggered strategic skills layer achieves 6/10 wins. The difference is directional but not statistically significant (Fisher exact p≈0.37). Frontier LLMs on a public benchmark achieved zero wins at the lowest difficulty, and human win rate is 16%, confirming the task is hard but not saturated.
AI.conclusion: The bounded, typed-retrieval memory contract enables modular ablation studies of memory layers in long-horizon agents. The released testbed (298 trajectories with condition tags, frozen snapshots, prompts, and analysis scripts) provides a validated, reproducible methodology for studying how explicit memory layers influence agent decisions over extended horizons.

title: A Memory Efficient Unified Algorithm for Online Learning of Linear Dynamical Systems
summary: Motivated by the challenge of stabilizing a general unknown linear dynamical system (LDS) from observations, we study the natural prerequisite of online prediction. Our goal is to achieve sublinear regret with a memory footprint that adapts to the intrinsic complexity of the dynamics rather than the full hidden -- state dimension. We focus on the practically central regime of systems with low instability complexity -- eigenvalues outside the real stable interval that do not decay rapidly, together with non-semisimple modes-potentially embedded in an otherwise stable real spectrum of much higher dimension; we write $k$ for this count. This regime is the primary setting in which stabilization is plausible: we show that many systems with high instability complexity cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls. Thus, prediction is meaningful for stabilization precisely when the instability complexity is small. Within this regime, we introduce a unified online algorithm that handles every LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex or exploding modes) with a learnable parameter count of $\widetilde{O}(k)$. Finally, we prove a lower bound showing that $k$ is a valid complexity measure: any filter-based predictor needs at least $k$ filters. Experiments corroborate our theory: on a high-dimensional system, our predictor sharply outperforms prior methods at an equal parameter budget.

AI.tldr: This paper studies online prediction for unknown linear dynamical systems (LDS), aiming for sublinear regret with memory footprint scaling with the system's instability complexity (k) rather than full state dimension. The authors present a unified algorithm handling all LDS types with Õ(k) learnable parameters and prove a matching lower bound, validated by experiments.
AI.motivation: Stabilizing unknown LDS from observations is a fundamental challenge, but prior methods require memory scaling with the full hidden-state dimension, which is prohibitive for high-dimensional systems. The authors identify that prediction—a prerequisite for stabilization—is only meaningful when the system has low instability complexity (few eigenvalues outside the stable interval plus non-semisimple modes). They further motivate this by proving that high instability complexity systems cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls.
AI.method: The paper introduces a unified online prediction algorithm based on filtering that works for all LDS classes (including non-diagonalizable systems, complex eigenvalues, and exploding modes). The parameter count adapts to k—the number of unstable/non-semisimple modes—achieving Õ(k) learnable parameters. The algorithm is analyzed in the online regret framework, and a matching lower bound is proved showing any filter-based predictor requires at least k filters.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves sublinear regret with Õ(k) parameters independent of the full state dimension. The lower bound establishes k as a tight complexity measure. Experiments on a high-dimensional system show the predictor sharply outperforms prior methods at equal parameter budgets.
AI.conclusion: Prediction for LDS is feasible with memory scaling in the instability complexity k rather than state dimension. Since systems with large k cannot be stabilized anyway (exponential control cost), k is both necessary and sufficient for meaningful prediction toward stabilization. The unified algorithm and lower bound together establish a tight characterization of this problem.

title: A Hippocampus for Linear Attention: An Exact Memory for What the Recurrent State Forgets
summary: Linear-attention and state-space language models compress the prefix into a fixed-size recurrent state, yielding O(1) memory at the cost of a lossy exact memory: when many key--value associations compete, earlier facts are overwritten and needle recall degrades. Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems, we give linear attention a hippocampal complement. HOLA (Hippocampal Linear Attention) keeps the usual delta-rule state as a compressive memory and adds a bounded exact KV cache, forming a semiparametric test-time memory: the state models linearly compressible structure, while the cache stores associations that should not be forced through that state. The cache writes without a learned eviction module, keeping tokens with large beta * ||e||, the prediction residual actually committed to the state; a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma cache read then turns these exact KV pairs into sharp retrieval rather than soft averaging. At 340M parameters trained on 15B SlimPajama tokens, HOLA lowers Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), below a full-attention Transformer++ (26.88), and improves LAMBADA perplexity from 30.95 to 30.26. It also achieves the best linear in-context retrieval and remains much more robust than GDN or a matched HOLA+recency cache on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall out to 32k tokens (16x its training length).

AI.tldr: HOLA augments linear attention with a small exact KV cache that stores high-residual tokens, combining compressive memory with exact retrieval to dramatically improve perplexity and needle recall without learned eviction.
AI.motivation: Linear-attention and state-space models compress all prefix information into a fixed-size recurrent state (e.g., delta-rule), yielding O(1) memory but suffering from "lossy exact memory": when many key-value associations compete, earlier facts get overwritten, degrading recall on tasks like needle-in-a-haystack.
AI.method: HOLA keeps the standard delta-rule recurrent state as compressive memory and adds a bounded exact KV cache. The cache admits tokens based on beta * ||e|| — the magnitude of the prediction residual that would actually be committed to the state — without any learned eviction module. During reading, a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma mechanism transforms these exact KV pairs into sharp retrieval signals rather than soft averaging over the compressed state.
AI.result: At 340M parameters trained on 15B SlimPajama tokens, HOLA reduces Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), outperforming a full-attention Transformer++ (26.88). LAMBADA perplexity improves from 30.95 to 30.26. It achieves the best linear in-context retrieval and remains significantly more robust than GDN or a recency-cache baseline on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall up to 32k tokens (16× training length).
AI.conclusion: A small, principled exact KV cache — gated by residual magnitude and read via decoupled normalization — can effectively complement compressive linear attention, restoring exact recall capabilities without sacrificing O(1) memory efficiency in the common case.

title: Bayesian Sparse Low-Rank Adaptation for Large Language Model Uncertainty Estimation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning capabilities, but their task-specific fine-tuning is notoriously plagued by overconfidence, severely hindering trustworthy deployment. We propose Data-Adaptive Lower-Rank Adaptation (DALorRA), a simple and effective variational Bayesian sparse framework that shifts the paradigm of uncertainty quantification from the dense parameter space to the lightweight rank level of low-rank adaptation (LoRA). With the insight that LoRA essentially aggregates multiple rank-one components that may provide superfluous model capacity, DALorRA imposes stochastic masking on rank dimensions, enabling Bayesian regularization of model capacity during training and ensemble-like calibration during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate DALorRA's excellent calibration of LLMs without compromising reasoning accuracy.

AI.tldr: DALorRA introduces variational Bayesian sparse masking at the LoRA rank level for uncertainty quantification, achieving excellent calibration of LLMs without sacrificing reasoning accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLMs fine-tuned for specific tasks suffer from overconfidence, which undermines trustworthy deployment. Existing uncertainty quantification methods operate in dense parameter space, motivating a shift to the lightweight LoRA rank level.
AI.method: DALorRA imposes stochastic masking on the rank dimensions of LoRA, treating each rank-one component as potentially superfluous. This enables Bayesian regularization of model capacity during training and ensemble-like calibration during inference, all within a variational Bayesian sparse framework.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show DALorRA achieves excellent calibration of LLMs while maintaining reasoning accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Shifting uncertainty quantification from dense parameters to LoRA's rank level via stochastic masking is an effective, lightweight strategy for calibrating fine-tuned LLMs.

title: Beyond the Performance Illusion: Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization for Spatially Correlated Domains
summary: Performance evaluation in AI systems commonly assumes that random dataset splits produce independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) subsets. We show that this assumption often breaks down in spatiotemporally correlated domains such as aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, and medical imaging, leading to two systematic failures: data leakage, where correlated samples span training and validation splits and inflate performance estimates, and hidden stratification, where errors on minority subpopulations are obscured by aggregate metrics. To address these issues, we propose a unified evaluation and training framework for spatially correlated data. We introduce Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP), which constructs validation splits that reduce spatiotemporal leakage while preserving meaningful class balance, and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO), a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust training that stabilizes optimization under these stricter splits. Across multiple benchmarks, this combination yields consistently improved generalization, more reliable confidence calibration, and exposes failure modes that remain hidden under conventional random-split evaluation.

AI.tldr: Random-split evaluation in AI breaks down for spatiotemporally correlated data, causing data leakage and hidden stratification. The authors propose SASP for leakage-free validation splits and CDRO for stabilized robust training, together yielding better generalization, calibration, and failure-mode exposure.
AI.motivation: Standard ML evaluation assumes i.i.d. random splits, but in spatiotemporally correlated domains (aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, medical imaging), this assumption fails. Two critical failures arise: (1) data leakage inflates performance estimates when correlated samples appear in both training and validation; (2) hidden stratification obscures poor performance on minority subpopulations behind aggregate metrics. The paper is motivated by the absence of a unified framework that addresses both evaluation and training under spatial correlation.
AI.method: The authors propose two complementary components: (1) **SASP (Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning)** — a validation split strategy that explicitly accounts for spatial and temporal correlation structures to minimize leakage between splits while maintaining class balance for meaningful stratified evaluation; (2) **CDRO (Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization)** — a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust optimization that gradually increases robustness penalties during training, stabilizing optimization under the stricter, more challenging SASP splits compared to standard DRO.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmarks in spatiotemporally correlated domains, the SASP+CDRO combination demonstrates: (1) consistently improved generalization performance; (2) more reliable confidence calibration; and (3) exposure of failure modes that conventional random-split evaluation conceals, particularly on minority subpopulations previously hidden by aggregate metrics.
AI.conclusion: Standard i.i.d. evaluation is fundamentally inadequate for spatiotemporally correlated data. The proposed SASP+CDRO framework provides a principled, unified solution that yields more honest performance estimates, better-calibrated models, and reveals critical failure modes, representing an important step toward trustworthy evaluation in spatially structured domains.

title: Grounded autonomous research: a fault-tolerant LLM pipeline from corpus to manuscript in frontier computational physics
comment: 39 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop (https://openreview.net/forum?id=R5YXaPgUAx). Includes the pipeline-generated companion physics manuscript as an appendix. Data and scaffolding archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21126996
summary: Autonomous-research agents have demonstrated end-to-end LLM automation in machine-learning sandboxes where execution provides calibration. Frontier physical science differs categorically: physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are often underdocumented, and calibration must come from external literature anchors - which unscaffolded agents cite but do not confront, hallucinating plausible, unverifiable results from internal priors. We present a pipeline that runs end-to-end from a corpus of 11,083 recent condensed-matter physics arXiv papers to a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings (here on altermagnetic piezomagnetism): the agent autonomously conceives a research direction by mapping the corpus, calibrates methodology by reproducing published references, conducts novel first-principles computations, and writes the manuscript - grounded in literature throughout, across 47 fresh-context sessions in six phases sharing only on-disk state, with 2,162 literature-consultation events. Fault tolerance emerges from redundancy: fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review catch what any single session misses; pre- and post-pilot stages are fully autonomous, and pilot requires bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures - operational knowledge curation, not scientific direction. Two paired failure modes - a pre-architecture baseline and a no-pilot ablation - isolate structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the operative grounding mechanism. The primitives, characterized failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern lay a foundation for autonomous research in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics.

AI.tldr: A pipeline enabling an autonomous AI research agent to produce publication-grade condensed-matter physics findings (altermagnetic piezomagnetism) by grounding every decision in external literature through structured calibration checkpoints, with bounded human intervention only for reproduction failures.
AI.motivation: Frontier physical science differs from ML sandboxes because physical reasoning must underpin methodology choices, toolchains are underdocumented, and calibration must derive from external literature rather than execution feedback. Existing autonomous agents hallucinate plausible but unverifiable results because they cite literature without confronting it numerically.
AI.method: A multi-phase pipeline processing 11,083 condensed-matter arXiv papers: (1) agent maps corpus to conceive research direction, (2) calibrates methodology by reproducing published references, (3) conducts novel first-principles computations, (4) writes manuscript. Operates across 47 fresh-context sessions sharing only on-disk state, with 2,162 literature-consultation events. Employs redundancy for fault tolerance (fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, adversarial review). Two ablations (pre-architecture baseline and no-pilot ablation) isolate structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the key grounding mechanism. Human intervention is bounded and only required for operational knowledge curation during reproduction failures — not scientific direction.
AI.result: The pipeline produced a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings on altermagnetic piezomagnetism. The paired failure modes from ablations confirmed that structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints is the operative grounding mechanism preventing hallucination.
AI.conclusion: The primitives, characterized failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern establish a foundation for autonomous research agents in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics, where grounding against external literature is essential.

title: SA-HGNN: Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network for EEG-Based Depression Recognition
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely used to capture spatial functional connectivity patterns to improve electroencephalography (EEG)-based depression recognition performance. However, the functional connectivity of brain networks in patients with depression exhibits an inherent hierarchical structure, making it difficult to capture accurate connection patterns. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel model named Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network (SA-HGNN), which aims to accurately extract the authentic hierarchical structure of depression-affected brain networks. Specifically, the proposed model comprises three core modules. First, a Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction module dynamically constructs personalized brain network topologies to capture more complex spatial relationships within the brain network. Second, hyperbolic graph convolution is employed to overcome the representation bottlenecks of Euclidean space, leveraging hyperbolic geometry to precisely capture latent hierarchical relationships within the brain network. Finally, an Attention Pooling module adaptively filters out highly redundant noise channels in EEG signals, effectively mitigating the interference of inherent noise on the authentic hierarchical topology. Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method across resting-state and task-related paradigms, validating its robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in brain networks of patients with depression.

AI.tldr: SA-HGNN introduces a sample-adaptive hyperbolic approach for EEG-based depression recognition, combining personalized graph construction, hyperbolic geometry for hierarchical brain network modeling, and attention-based noise filtering to outperform existing methods across multiple paradigms.
AI.motivation: Existing GNN-based depression recognition methods fail to adequately capture the inherent hierarchical structure of functional connectivity in depression-affected brain networks, and Euclidean space representations create bottlenecks in modeling these latent hierarchical relationships.
AI.method: SA-HGNN consists of three modules: (1) Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction that dynamically builds personalized brain network topologies; (2) Hyperbolic Graph Convolution that leverages hyperbolic geometry to capture latent hierarchical relationships; (3) Attention Pooling that adaptively filters redundant noisy EEG channels to preserve authentic hierarchical topology.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate superior performance across both resting-state and task-related paradigms, with validated robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in depressed patients.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SA-HGNN effectively addresses the hierarchical modeling challenge in depression-affected brain networks by combining hyperbolic geometry with sample-adaptive graph learning and attention-based denoising, achieving state-of-the-art depression recognition performance.

title: DRIFTLENS: Measuring Memory-Induced Reasoning Drift in Personalized Language Models
summary: Personalization changes what a model says to a user; we show that it can also change the reasoning trajectory used to justify the response. Modern LLMs personalize interactions by storing user attributes, preferences, and prior context, then injecting this information into future prompts. We study whether such memory reshapes reasoning on open-ended questions where no single ground-truth answer exists. To quantify this effect, we introduce DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free framework that maps each expressed reasoning step to a value category and measures divergence between a question's no-memory trajectory and its trajectory under injected user-attribute memory. We first validate that DRIFTLENS distinguishes content-free pragmatic noise from substantive reasoning changes. Across four LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories, including age, occupation, and disability, user-attribute memory induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor, even when final answers remain fluent, on-topic, and plausible. We then evaluate GRPO- and DPO-based post-training methods for reducing drift. Both reduce drift, but neither uniformly dominates; effects on downstream capability, helpfulness, and instruction following are model-and reward-dependent. These results suggest that memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partly mitigated failure mode of personalized language models.

AI.tldr: User-attribute memory injected into LLM prompts causes measurable shifts in reasoning trajectories, even when final answers appear plausible. The proposed DRIFTLENS framework quantifies this "reasoning drift" without ground-truth answers, revealing that post-training methods only partially mitigate the effect.
AI.motivation: Personalization in LLMs relies on injecting user attributes and history into prompts. While prior work examines how personalization alters *what* models say, this paper investigates whether it also reshapes *how* models reason — i.e., the underlying justification trajectory — on open-ended questions lacking ground truth. The goal is to identify and measure a potential failure mode where personalization subtly distorts reasoning.
AI.method: The authors propose DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free evaluation framework. It maps each reasoning step in a model's chain-of-thought to a value category and computes divergence between trajectories with vs. without injected user-attribute memory. Pragmatic-noise baselines are established to isolate substantive drift from content-free variation. The framework is tested across four LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories (e.g., age, occupation, disability). Additionally, GRPO- and DPO-based post-training interventions are evaluated for drift reduction.
AI.result: User-attribute memory consistently induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor, even when final answers remain fluent, on-topic, and plausible. Both GRPO and DPO post-training methods reduce drift, but neither uniformly dominates; their effects on downstream capability, helpfulness, and instruction following are model- and reward-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partly mitigated failure mode of personalized LLMs, suggesting that current alignment and personalization techniques are insufficient to preserve reasoning integrity under user-context injection.

title: HERMES: A Multi-Granularity Labeling Substrate for Pre-training Data Mixtures
summary: Most data-mixing methods assume the corpus has already been partitioned into groups, and the choice of those groups determines what a mixer can express. Existing labels, including provenance, topic or format taxonomies, and flat embedding clusters, commit to one semantic axis at one granularity; changing the resolution rebuilds the labels. We argue the bottleneck is the label system, not the mixer, and provide a hierarchical one. HERMES is a data-derived labeling substrate: a Learned Semantic Transform followed by 3-stage residual vector quantization annotates each document once into a coarse-to-fine code whose prefix length controls granularity up to approximately 130k cells. At coarse granularity HERMES sits at a plateau with KMeans-family methods on standard clustering metrics, so the contribution is the substrate, not the clusterer. On 1B-parameter, 25B-token pre-training, the hierarchy exposes an interaction fixed-granularity pipelines cannot test: at one prefix length, a combined Stage-2 rule contrast, equal-subbucket coverage versus size-proportional within-bucket quality top-30%, lifts a 16-task capability macro-average by +0.0253; at the next finer level, the same rule loses its measurable edge as candidate pools contract approximately 5x. HERMES reframes data mixture design from choosing among fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-derived granularity hierarchy.

AI.tldr: HERMES introduces a hierarchical, data-derived labeling substrate using Learned Semantic Transform and residual vector quantization, replacing fixed-granularity label systems. It shows that data mixture effectiveness depends on navigating granularity levels, with certain mixing rules performing well at one resolution but losing advantage at finer resolutions where candidate pools shrink.
AI.motivation: Existing data-mixing methods rely on pre-partitioned corpora using fixed label systems (provenance, topic taxonomies, flat embedding clusters), which lock in one semantic axis at one granularity. Changing resolution requires rebuilding labels. The authors argue the bottleneck is the label system itself, not the mixing algorithm.
AI.method: HERMES employs a Learned Semantic Transform followed by 3-stage residual vector quantization to annotate each document with a coarse-to-fine code. Prefix length controls granularity, yielding up to ~130k cells. This creates a reusable, hierarchical labeling substrate from data itself, decoupled from any single semantic axis or resolution.
AI.result: At coarse granularity, HERMES matches KMeans-family methods on standard clustering metrics. In 1B-parameter, 25B-token pre-training: at one prefix length, a Stage-2 rule (contrast equal-subbucket coverage vs. size-proportional within-bucket quality, top-30%) boosts 16-task macro-average by +0.0253. At the next finer level, the same rule loses its edge as candidate pools contract ~5x.
AI.conclusion: HERMES reframes data mixture design from choosing among fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-derived granularity hierarchy. The interaction between mixing rules and granularity level is critical and cannot be tested in fixed-granularity pipelines.

title: Fourier Neural Operators for Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
summary: We propose an improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for modeling two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection by predicting time increments instead of full solutions, achieving higher accuracy than a standard FNO baseline. The resulting model is compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms inference), while maintaining similar accuracy as demonstrated in previous benchmarks. We show that although FNOs generalize to finer meshes, accuracy remains limited by the resolution of the training data.

AI.tldr: An improved Fourier Neural Operator predicts time increments for 2D Rayleigh-Bénard convection, achieving a compact (314k params, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms) model with accuracy exceeding standard FNO baselines, though performance remains bounded by training data resolution.
AI.motivation: To develop a more accurate, compact, and fast surrogate model for two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection by improving upon standard Fourier Neural Operators. The goal is to achieve high predictive accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for practical deployment.
AI.method: The authors modify the standard Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) architecture to predict time increments (i.e., the change from the current state) rather than directly outputting the full solution at the next timestep. The model is trained on simulation data and evaluated on its ability to generalize to finer discretization meshes. Model compactness metrics (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and inference speed (7 ms) are reported.
AI.result: The time-increment FNO achieves higher accuracy than a standard FNO baseline on the Rayleigh-Bénard convection task. The resulting model is compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms per inference). However, while FNOs can generalize to finer meshes, accuracy is fundamentally limited by the resolution of the training data — finer training data yields better predictions.
AI.conclusion: Predicting time increments rather than full states is an effective architectural modification to the FNO that boosts accuracy with negligible computational overhead. The mesh-invariance property of FNOs holds, but practitioners should recognize that training data resolution imposes a hard ceiling on achievable accuracy, regardless of the evaluation mesh.

title: Automated grading of Linux/bash examinations using large language models: a four-level cognitive taxonomy approach
summary: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations remains a challenge in computing education, where rising enrolments make manual marking difficult and rule-based autograders cannot handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. This paper evaluates whether four frontier Large Language Models (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM) can approximate expert judgment when grading short Linux/bash command responses. The study adopts a four-level cognitive taxonomy that combines cognitive complexity and operational impact, ranging from information retrieval (L1) and basic file manipulation (L2) to structural operations (L3) and advanced system management (L4). The models were tested with two prompt variants, a minimal baseline and a rubric-enhanced version, on 1200 real responses from second-year Computer Engineering students independently graded by three expert instructors. Gemini~3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1) = 0.888, MAE = 0.10, Bland-Altman bias = -0.014). Agreement declined consistently as taxonomy level increased, with the largest discrepancies at higher levels. Across all models, rubric quality had a larger effect than provider choice, with structured prompts consistently improving agreement. These results show that question complexity is a reliable predictor of the difficulty LLMs face in grading accurately, and they establish a principled, taxonomy-based framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading and which require human review, while also providing a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.

AI.tldr: Frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) were evaluated on grading Linux command-line exam responses across a four-level cognitive taxonomy. Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-enhanced prompting achieved the best human-AI agreement (ICC=0.888). Rubric quality mattered more than model choice, and agreement declined as taxonomic complexity increased, providing a principled framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading.
AI.motivation: Rising enrollments in computing education make manual grading of command-line examinations increasingly infeasible. Existing rule-based autograders are brittle — they cannot handle partial credit, semantically equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. This paper investigates whether frontier LLMs can serve as a scalable, reliable alternative that approximates expert human judgment.
AI.method: Four frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM) were tested on 1,200 real student responses to short Linux/bash command questions from second-year Computer Engineering students. Responses were independently graded by three expert instructors to establish ground truth. Two prompt variants were compared: a minimal baseline prompt and a rubric-enhanced prompt. Grading was structured around a novel four-level cognitive taxonomy: L1 (information retrieval), L2 (basic file manipulation), L3 (structural operations), and L4 (advanced system management). Agreement was measured using ICC(3,1), MAE, and Bland-Altman analysis.
AI.result: Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1) = 0.888, MAE = 0.10, Bland-Altman bias = −0.014). Across all models, rubric quality exerted a larger effect on agreement than provider/model choice. Agreement declined consistently as taxonomy level increased, with the largest discrepancies at L3 and L4. Structured, rubric-enhanced prompts consistently outperformed minimal prompts.
AI.conclusion: Question complexity, operationalized through the proposed taxonomy, is a reliable predictor of LLM grading difficulty. The taxonomy-based framework offers a principled method for determining which questions can be safely delegated to AI-assisted grading and which require human review. The study also contributes transferable evaluation protocols and prompt templates for adoption in other computing education contexts.

title: Ask the Right Comparison:Bias-Aware Bayesian Active Top-$k$ Ranking with LLM Judges
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as cheap, scalable judges that compare candidate outputs pairwise -- to rank responses, select models, or triage papers. Yet LLM judges are both noisy and systematically biased: they favor verbose or well-formatted answers and exhibit position effects, so simply aggregating their votes recovers a ranking of presentation, not of true quality. We study the practical goal of identifying the \topk{} items under a fixed comparison budget, and make two contributions. First, we cast judging as Bayesian inference over latent quality with explicit, judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by a shrinkage prior so that the data decide which biases a given judge actually exhibits. Second, we introduce a \topk-aware active acquisition rule that chooses the next comparison to maximally reduce uncertainty about \topk{} \emph{membership}, rather than about the full ranking. On a controlled benchmark with known ground-truth quality, judged by sixteen real LLMs spanning open and proprietary families (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o-mini/5.1/5.5, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Claude Haiku/Sonnet/Opus), naive aggregation plateaus at a wrong \topk{} on biased judges regardless of budget, while our bias-aware model recovers it; \topk-aware acquisition reaches this ceiling with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or a global-uncertainty (D-optimal) rule. Bias is real but heterogeneous and capability-dependent: cheap and mid-tier judges carry a strong verbosity bias that our model corrects (lifting recall from $\sim$$0.5$--$0.6$ to $0.84$--$1.0$), whereas the frontier judges we tested show little bias and already rank accurately, so bias-aware modeling changes little there.

AI.tldr: LLM judges exhibit systematic biases (verbosity, position) that corrupt pairwise rankings. The authors propose a Bayesian model with judge-specific bias covariates and a top-k-aware active acquisition strategy, demonstrating that bias correction recovers true top-k items while requiring fewer comparisons than naive aggregation or round-robin baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as cheap pairwise judges for ranking, model selection, and paper triage, but their judgments are noisy and systematically biased toward verbose/formatted outputs and subject to position effects. Simply aggregating votes recovers a ranking of presentation style rather than true quality, necessitating explicit bias modeling.
AI.method: Two contributions: (1) A Bayesian inference framework that models latent quality with explicit, judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by a shrinkage prior so the data determines which biases each judge exhibits. (2) A top-k-aware active acquisition rule that selects the next comparison to maximally reduce uncertainty about top-k membership, rather than the full ranking.
AI.result: On a controlled benchmark with ground-truth quality and 16 real LLM judges (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o/mini, Gemini, DeepSeek, Claude variants), naive aggregation plateaus at incorrect top-k regardless of budget. The bias-aware model recovers true top-k, with recall improving from ~0.5–0.6 to 0.84–1.0 for cheap/mid-tier judges. Top-k-aware acquisition reaches this ceiling with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or D-optimal rules. Frontier judges show minimal bias, so correction has limited impact there.
AI.conclusion: Bias in LLM judges is real, heterogeneous, and capability-dependent: cheaper models carry strong verbosity bias that the proposed model corrects effectively, while frontier models already rank accurately. Active top-k-aware acquisition substantially improves sample efficiency, making bias-corrected LLM judging both accurate and practical under fixed comparison budgets.

title: Fast Multi-dimensional Refusal Subspaces via RFM-AGOP
comment: Accepted to the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Steering and monitoring activations in Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for both safety and interpretability. Early work assumed behaviours are encoded along single linear directions, but recent findings suggest complex behaviours, such as the refusal to answer harmful queries, live in multi-dimensional subspaces. However, existing methods for extracting these subspaces are computationally expensive, which becomes prohibitive on reasoning models who produce long reasoning traces. By adapting the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm -- which can be computed efficiently -- with a probe-informed initialization, we are able to identify the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds, on reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models. While RFM allows for faster subspace identification, it also showed better performances on the ablation task than its alternatives. More work is planned to better understand the relations between subspaces found by different methods. If confirmed, RFM could be a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) with probe-informed initialization to efficiently identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces in LLMs (both reasoning and non-reasoning models) in seconds, outperforming existing computationally expensive methods on ablation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for extracting multi-dimensional behavioral subspaces (e.g., refusal to answer harmful queries) in LLMs are computationally prohibitive, especially for reasoning models with long reasoning traces. A faster, scalable alternative is needed for both safety and interpretability applications.
AI.method: The authors adapt the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm — known for computational efficiency — and augment it with a probe-informed initialization. This approach is applied to identify refusal subspaces in both reasoning models (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning models (Qwen 2.5).
AI.result: RFM with probe-informed initialization identifies the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds, dramatically faster than alternatives. It also achieves superior performance on the ablation task compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: RFM represents a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs. Further work is planned to investigate the relationships between subspaces identified by different methods.

title: EvoPolicyGym: Evaluating Autonomous Policy Evolution in Interactive Environments
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly expected to improve executable policies through feedback, yet existing evaluations often collapse this process into a final score or confound it with open-ended software-engineering progress. We introduce Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled evaluation setting in which a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. We instantiate this setting in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments that evaluates how agents iteratively improve explored policies. On the EvoPolicyGym suite, GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments. Beyond leaderboard results, EvoPolicyGym also provides trajectory-level diagnostics that distinguish how agents allocate budget, convert feedback into parametric tuning. These analyses show that strong autonomous policy evolution depends not only on isolated task wins, but on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Autonomous Policy Evolution (APE), a controlled evaluation framework where agents iteratively improve executable policies under a fixed interaction budget. EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark of 16 compact RL environments, is used to evaluate agents like GPT-5.5, which achieved top performance. Trajectory-level diagnostics reveal that success depends on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback, not just isolated task wins.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of autonomous agents' ability to improve policies through feedback either reduce performance to a single final score or conflate it with open-ended software engineering progress. This lacks controlled, diagnostic insight into how agents allocate budget and convert feedback into policy improvements.
AI.method: The authors propose Autonomous Policy Evolution (APE), a controlled setting where a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. They instantiate this in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark of 16 compact interactive RL environments, and evaluate agents using both aggregate rank scores and trajectory-level diagnostics that trace budget allocation and parametric tuning.
AI.result: GPT-5.5 achieved the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance across all 16 EvoPolicyGym environments. Trajectory-level diagnostics showed that strong autonomous policy evolution relies on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback, rather than merely winning isolated tasks.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous policy evolution is a distinct capability that benefits from structured, diagnostic evaluation. EvoPolicyGym provides such a framework, revealing that effective agents must learn task-specific mechanisms and optimize under feedback constraints, not just maximize final scores.

title: Predictive Conformal Slip Monitoring: An Empirical Evaluation of Rolling Split Conformal Prediction for Pre-Incident Traction Loss Detection
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables. codes and data available at:https://github.com/nearpot/predictive-conformal-slip-monitoring
summary: Conventional traction control architectures intervene only after the adhesion limit of a tire has already been breached. This paper investigates whether Rolling Split Conformal Prediction , monitoring the volatility of non-conformity residuals from a per-driver Random Forest model of expected slip behavior , can serve as a statistically grounded pre-incident warning signal, ahead of gross traction loss. Unlike an earlier internal draft of this work, the evaluation reported here corrects a confound in the slip proxy (vehicle speed is included as an explicit model feature, not left implicit in the target's denominator), uses every racing lap for each driver rather than only the fastest lap, and is scored against real, timestamped incident labels extracted from FIA Race Control Messages and track-limits lap deletions rather than narrated post-hoc. The result is negative: across 19 drivers and 55,563 test-phase telemetry samples, the rolling-volatility detector achieves a mean precision of essentially 0.0 and mean recall of 0.0 against 14 ground-truth incidents, while flagging on average 15.3% of all samples as anomalous , too high a false-alarm rate for any early-warning use. A static 95th-percentile threshold baseline performs no better in any way that would justify the added complexity of the conformal-volatility formulation. Residual autocorrelation diagnostics show the split-conformal exchangeability assumption is violated for every driver (Ljung-Box p < 0.001, n = 19/19), which is one plausible driver of the high false-alarm rate. We report this as a methodologically rigorous negative finding, diagnose its likely causes, and outline what a genuinely predictive version of this approach would require.

AI.tldr: A statistically grounded pre-incident warning system using Rolling Split Conformal Prediction on Random Forest slip models fails entirely (0.0 precision/recall) with an unacceptably high false-alarm rate (15.3%), due to violation of the exchangeability assumption across all drivers.
AI.motivation: Conventional traction control systems are reactive, intervening only after adhesion loss. The authors sought a proactive, statistically principled early-warning signal—based on conformal prediction and driver-specific behavioral modeling—that could anticipate traction loss before it occurs.
AI.method: Rolling Split Conformal Prediction monitors volatility of non-conformity residuals from per-driver Random Forest models of expected slip. Key methodological corrections from prior work: (1) vehicle speed included as explicit feature (eliminating denominator confound), (2) all racing laps used per driver, (3) ground-truth incident labels from FIA Race Control Messages and track-limits deletions. Evaluation across 19 drivers, 55,563 test telemetry samples, against 14 real incidents. Baseline: static 95th-percentile threshold. Exchangeability assumption tested via Ljung-Box on residuals.
AI.result: Strictly negative. Mean precision ≈ 0.0, mean recall = 0.0 against 14 ground-truth incidents. Detector flags 15.3% of all samples as anomalous (false-alarm rate too high for practical deployment). Static 95th-percentile baseline performs no better, offering no justification for conformal-volatility complexity. Ljung-Box test: p < 0.001 for all 19 drivers — exchangeability assumption universally violated.
AI.conclusion: This is a methodologically rigorous negative result. The split-conformal exchangeability assumption is systematically violated, likely driving the high false-alarm rate. The authors diagnose root causes and outline requirements for a genuinely predictive future approach.

title: Text-Driven 3D Indoor Scene Synthesis in Non-Manhattan Environments
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in 3D indoor synthesis for Manhattan environments. However, existing methods often fail to capture plausible object layout patterns in non-Manhattan settings, primarily because they struggle to model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, leading to high geometric violations and low physical fidelity. To address this challenge, we propose SPG-Layout, a novel text-driven framework designed to generate physically plausible indoor scenes within complex non-Manhattan environments. Specifically, we first utilize statistical priors of object distributions to guide the training process, enhancing environmental understanding and fidelity. Furthermore, mirroring human design workflows, we adopt a hierarchical layout strategy that prioritizes the placement of large objects, thereby substantially minimizing layout violations. By synergizing these components, SPG-Layout achieves a balanced optimization of semantic realism and physical plausibility. To evaluate performance in these complex settings, we constructed a new benchmark comprising 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods across both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments. The code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: SPG-Layout is a text-driven framework for generating physically plausible 3D indoor scenes in non-Manhattan environments, using statistical priors and a hierarchical layout strategy to reduce geometric violations and improve object placement fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based 3D indoor synthesis methods perform poorly in non-Manhattan settings because they cannot adequately model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, resulting in high geometric violations and low physical fidelity in generated layouts.
AI.method: SPG-Layout employs two key strategies: (1) leveraging statistical priors of object distributions to guide training for better environmental understanding, and (2) adopting a hierarchical layout strategy that mirrors human design workflows by prioritizing large object placement first to minimize layout violations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on a newly constructed benchmark of 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments show SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods across both Manhattan and non-Manhattan settings.
AI.conclusion: By synergizing statistical priors with hierarchical layout planning, SPG-Layout achieves a balanced optimization of semantic realism and physical plausibility, setting a new state-of-the-art for indoor scene synthesis in complex non-Manhattan environments.

title: ART for Diffusion Sampling: Continuous-Time Control and Actor-Critic Learning
summary: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where a learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard choices, but they rely on fixed prescriptions and can therefore be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control, so that a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate, ART provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. To solve this deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem. We prove that the randomized ART-RL formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimizer level, in the sense that its optimal Gaussian policy recovers the optimal ART time-warping rate through its mean. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor--critic updates for learning the schedule. Across experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation, ART-RL can be plugged into existing diffusion samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improving sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline unchanged. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalization, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

AI.tldr: ART-RL frames timestep allocation in diffusion sampling as a continuous-time control problem, learns adaptive schedules via reinforcement learning with Gaussian policies, and proves equivalence to the deterministic optimal control formulation, yielding plug-and-play schedule improvements that generalize across budgets, solvers, and datasets.
AI.motivation: Standard diffusion sampling uses uniform or hand-crafted timestep grids that are fixed and suboptimal. There is a need for a principled, data-driven method to adaptively allocate timesteps along the sampling trajectory to improve sample quality at matched computational budgets.
AI.method: The authors propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a deterministic continuous-time control formulation where the clock speed is the control variable, with a leading-order Euler error surrogate as the objective. They then introduce ART-RL, a randomized formulation using Gaussian policies that converts schedule learning into a continuous-time RL problem. They prove optimizer-level equivalence between ART and ART-RL, establish policy evaluation/improvement characterizations, and derive trajectory-based moment identities for actor-critic updates.
AI.result: ART-RL consistently improves sample quality across controlled low-dimensional settings and image generation when plugged into existing diffusion samplers, requiring only a change to the timestep grid. Learned schedules generalize without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.
AI.conclusion: ART-RL provides a principled, plug-and-play approach to adaptive timestep allocation in diffusion sampling that outperforms fixed schedules, with learned schedules exhibiting strong zero-shot generalization and seamless integration into existing pipelines.

title: Probing Chemical Language Models: Effects of Pre-training and Fine-tuning
summary: Chemical language models (CLMs) are trained with linearized representations such as SMILES, yet it remains unclear which chemically meaningful substructures they encode. To foster a better understanding of CLMs, we conduct a systematic study and probe for 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized models. We furthermore study how fine-tuning on chemical downstream tasks affects the learned representations of molecular substructures. Our results show that pre-training generally improves molecular structure awareness of CLMs, particularly in the upper layers. Moreover, randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer. Our analysis on two chemical downstream tasks further reveals that, interestingly, fine-tuning affects task-relevant molecular substructures more than others, indicating that the changes in the representations follow chemical theory.

AI.tldr: A systematic probing study reveals that pre-trained chemical language models (CLMs) encode chemically meaningful substructures, with pre-training improving structural awareness especially in upper layers, while even random models capture rings in early layers. Fine-tuning selectively affects task-relevant substructures in alignment with chemical theory.
AI.motivation: Despite the widespread use of chemical language models trained on linearized molecular representations like SMILES, there is limited understanding of which chemically meaningful substructures these models actually encode. The authors aim to uncover what structural knowledge CLMs internalize, how pre-training contributes to this awareness, and how fine-tuning for downstream tasks alters these representations.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic probing study targeting 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained CLMs and six randomly initialized (untrained) models. They employ probing classifiers to detect whether specific substructures are encoded in the hidden representations at different layers. Additionally, they analyze two chemical downstream tasks to assess how fine-tuning modulates substructure representations.
AI.result: Pre-training consistently improves molecular structure awareness, with the strongest gains observed in the upper layers of CLMs. Randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer, suggesting an architectural inductive bias. Fine-tuning on downstream tasks disproportionately affects task-relevant molecular substructures, indicating that representational changes induced by fine-tuning are consistent with chemical principles.
AI.conclusion: CLMs encode chemically meaningful substructures in their representations, with pre-training and fine-tuning each contributing distinctively: pre-training broadly enhances structure awareness, while fine-tuning selectively refines task-relevant features in a chemically coherent manner. This provides interpretability insights and supports the design of more transparent molecular deep learning models.

title: Online Safety Monitoring for LLMs
summary: Despite alignment training, LLMs remain prone to generating unsafe outputs at deployment time. Monitoring outputs online and raising an alarm when safety can no longer be assumed is therefore critical. We study a simple real-time monitor that turns a verifier signal from an external model into an alarm decision by thresholding, with the threshold calibrated via risk control. In experiments on mathematical reasoning and red teaming datasets, we show that this simple design is competitive with more advanced monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing.

AI.tldr: A simple real-time safety monitor that thresholds a verifier's signal and calibrates via risk control is shown to be competitive with more complex sequential hypothesis testing monitors for detecting unsafe LLM outputs.
AI.motivation: Despite alignment training, LLMs still produce unsafe outputs at deployment. Real-time online monitoring with alarm-raising capability is critical for safety assurance when safety guarantees can no longer be assumed.
AI.method: A real-time monitor that converts an external verifier model's signal into a binary alarm decision using thresholding, with the threshold calibrated through risk control. This simple approach is benchmarked against more sophisticated monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing.
AI.result: The simple threshold-based monitor with risk-controlled calibration performs competitively with advanced sequential hypothesis testing monitors on mathematical reasoning and red teaming datasets.
AI.conclusion: A straightforward thresholding design with proper risk control calibration suffices for effective real-time safety monitoring, questioning the necessity of more complex sequential hypothesis testing approaches in this setting.

title: Predicting Early Stages Of Alzheimer's Disease And Identifying Key Biomarkers Using Deep Artificial Neural Network And Ensemble Of Machine Learning Methodologies
summary: Alzheimers disease (AD) is a brain disorder that develops slowly and mainly affects memory, thinking, language, and daily activities. It is one of the most common causes of dementia and creates many difficulties for patients as well as their families. In the early stage, the symptoms are often mild and may look like normal ageing. For this reason, many people are diagnosed late, when the disease has already progressed. At present, there is no complete cure for AD. Still, early detection can help doctors manage the condition better and take suitable steps at the right time. In this study, a machine learning model is proposed to detect the early stages of Alzheimers disease using clinical details, neuropsychological test scores, and neuroimaging-related measures. The data used in this work is collected from the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). As the dataset has missing values, iterative imputation is applied to fill them. The dataset also has class imbalance, which is handled using Borderline SVM-SMOTE. After that, feature selection is carried out using wrapper-based and embedded methods so that only important features are used for training. The selected features are divided into training and testing sets, and feature scaling is applied. A stacking ensemble model is developed using Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM as base classifiers. Along with this, an artificial neural network is also trained on the same dataset. The performance of these models is compared using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. This study aims to find the best classifier and also identify important biomarkers that may help in the early diagnosis of Alzheimers disease.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a stacking ensemble machine learning model combined with an artificial neural network for early-stage Alzheimer's disease detection using clinical, neuropsychological, and neuroimaging data from ADNI, addressing missing data via iterative imputation and class imbalance with Borderline SVM-SMOTE.
AI.motivation: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with no cure, and late diagnosis is common because early symptoms resemble normal aging. Early detection can improve patient management, motivating the development of an accurate, data-driven diagnostic model.
AI.method: The study uses ADNI dataset with iterative imputation for missing values and Borderline SVM-SMOTE for class imbalance correction. Feature selection employs wrapper-based and embedded methods. A stacking ensemble is built with Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM as base classifiers, alongside an artificial neural network. Models are evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific numerical results; it states that model performance is compared across precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics to determine the best classifier and identify key biomarkers for early diagnosis.
AI.conclusion: The study aims to identify the best-performing classifier and pinpoint important biomarkers that can aid in the early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease, though explicit conclusions are not detailed in the abstract.

title: G-RRM: Guiding Symbolic Solvers with Recurrent Reasoning Models
summary:
In this work, we focus on SE-RRMs, a symbol-equivariant instantiation of RRMs that exhibits improved extrapolation to larger problem sizes. We propose a neuro-symbolic approach, ``Guiding with Recurrent Reasoning Models'' (G-RRM), which integrates SE-RRMs with symbolic solvers for constraint satisfaction problems. SE-RRMs act as neural solvers that generate full solution proposals and guide classical symbolic solvers, such as backtracking or SAT-based methods like Glucose 4.1 and CaDiCaL 3.0.0, that produce globally correct solutions. Centrally, we investigate when neural guidance with G-RRM improves the search efficiency of symbolic solvers. %
Our experiments show that the efficacy of G-RRM depends on two conditions: first, the problem instances must have an expansive combinatorial search space to expose potential gains, and second, the solver architecture must be capable of dynamically overwriting its branching choices to recover when neural hints are imperfect. When these conditions hold, guidance drives median conflict counts to zero and yields significant wall-clock speedups: on $9\times9$ Sudoku, where the SE-RRM correctly solves $91.1\%$ of instances, backtracking accelerates by $33.3\times$ and Glucose 4.1 by $1.70\times$ (median, $p<0.001$), with Glucose 4.1 retaining a $1.17\times$ speedup on perfect-hint $25\times25$ grids. In contrast, CaDiCaL 3.0.0, whose runtime is overhead-dominated and which always respects the injected branching hints rather than overwriting them, shows no significant speedup (median $1.02\times$, n.s.) and even a small significant mean slowdown ($0.90\times$) on $9\times9$. These results delineate the regimes in which neural guidance translates into practical speedups.

AI.tldr: G-RRM integrates neural SE-RRMs with symbolic solvers; neural guidance yields substantial speedups only when the search space is expansive and the solver can overwrite imperfect hints—backtracking and Glucose 4.1 benefit significantly on Sudoku, while CaDiCaL 3.0.0 does not due to overhead and rigid hint adherence.
AI.motivation: Investigate when and why neural guidance (via SE-RRMs) improves the search efficiency of classical symbolic solvers for constraint satisfaction problems, moving beyond accuracy metrics to practical runtime gains.
AI.method: A neuro-symbolic framework (G-RRM) where a symbol-equivariant recurrent reasoning model (SE-RRM) generates full solution proposals that guide symbolic solvers—backtracking, Glucose 4.1 (SAT-based), and CaDiCaL 3.0.0 (SAT-based). Evaluation on Sudoku problems of varying sizes ($9\times9$, $25\times25$) measures conflict counts and wall-clock speedups.
AI.result: On $9\times9$ Sudoku (SE-RRM solves 91.1%), backtracking accelerates 33.3× and Glucose 4.1 achieves 1.70× median speedup ($p<0.001$). On perfect-hint $25\times25$, Glucose 4.1 retains 1.17× speedup. CaDiCaL 3.0.0 shows no significant speedup (median 1.02×, n.s.) and a small significant mean slowdown (0.90×). Gains require expansive combinatorial search space and dynamic overwrite capability.
AI.conclusion: Neural guidance delivers practical speedups only under two conditions: large combinatorial search spaces and solver architectures that can dynamically override incorrect neural hints. This delineates the effective regime for neuro-symbolic integration in constraint solving.

title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions
summary: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based implementation, such as alerting on important log lines, repairing malformed JSON, or ranking search results by intent, and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs at the cost of locality, reproducibility, and price. We propose fuzzy-function programming: compiling such a function from a natural-language specification into a compact, locally-executable neural artifact. We instantiate this paradigm with Program-as-Weights (PAW), in which a 4B compiler trained on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset we release, emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory and running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes the foundation model from a per-input problem solver into a tool builder: invoked once per function definition, it produces a small reusable artifact whose subsequent calls per function application are cheap and offline.

AI.tldr: PAW (Program-as-Weights) compiles natural-language function specifications into compact neural adapters for a frozen interpreter. A 4B compiler trained on the 10M-example FuzzyBench dataset produces parameter-efficient adapters. A 0.6B interpreter executing these programs matches 32B-scale direct prompting performance at ~1/50th the memory, running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3.
AI.motivation: Many everyday programming tasks (log alerting, JSON repair, intent-based ranking) resist rule-based solutions and are increasingly delegated to LLM APIs, incurring costs in locality, reproducibility, and price. The authors aim to replace per-input LLM calls with a compile-once, run-locally paradigm.
AI.method: The authors introduce fuzzy-function programming and instantiate it as PAW (Program-as-Weights). A 4B-parameter compiler model is trained on FuzzyBench, a newly released 10M-example dataset. Given a natural-language function specification, the compiler emits parameter-efficient adapters (e.g., LoRA weights) for a frozen, lightweight 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter. The interpreter then executes the compiled program on arbitrary inputs locally.
AI.result: A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter running PAW programs matches the performance of directly prompting Qwen3-32B, while using ~1/50th of the inference memory and achieving 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3.
AI.conclusion: PAW reframes foundation models from per-input problem solvers into tool builders: a one-time compilation produces a compact, reusable neural artifact, enabling cheap, offline, reproducible execution for fuzzy programming tasks.

title: Dynamic Neural Graph Encoding of Inference Processes in Deep Weight Space
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. 28 pages, 5 figures
summary: The rapid advancements in using neural networks as implicit data representations have attracted significant interest in developing machine learning methods that analyze and process the weight spaces of other neural networks. However, efficiently handling these highdimensional weight spaces remains challenging. Existing methods often overlook the sequential nature of layer-by-layer processing in neural network inference. In this work, we propose a novel approach using dynamic graphs to represent neural network parameters, capturing the temporal dynamics of inference. Our Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) processes these graphs, preserving the sequential nature of neural processing. Additionally, we also leverage DNG-Encoder to develop INR2JLS (Implicit Neural Representation to Joint Latent Space) for facilitate downstream applications, such as classifying Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). Our approach demonstrates significant improvements across multiple tasks, surpassing the state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) that models neural network weight spaces as dynamic graphs to preserve the sequential nature of layer-by-layer inference, achieving ~10% improvement in INR classification on CIFAR-100-INR.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for analyzing neural network weight spaces treat them as static high-dimensional data, ignoring the sequential, layer-by-layer processing inherent to neural network inference. Efficiently handling these high-dimensional weight spaces while respecting their temporal dynamics remains an open challenge.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) representing neural network parameters as dynamic graphs that capture temporal dynamics of inference, (2) a Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) that processes these graphs while preserving sequential processing order, and (3) INR2JLS (Implicit Neural Representation to Joint Latent Space), built on DNG-Encoder, to map INRs into a shared latent space for downstream tasks such as classification.
AI.result: The approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving approximately 10% improvement in INR classification accuracy on the CIFAR-100-INR benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Modeling weight spaces as dynamic graphs with sequential processing preserved is highly effective for analyzing implicit neural representations, enabling significant performance gains on downstream tasks like INR classification.

title: ReContext: Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning
